docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Eight of the 111 families, drawn by fortvine in normal scores: Gaussian, Student t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Tawn's asymmetric logistic, an Archimax copula (gamma generator with an asymmetric logistic Pickands function) and a Khoudraji-Joe copula.

fortvine fits, evaluates and simulates bivariate (pair) copulas and regular-vine copulas. It is standard Fortran 2008 with OpenMP, needs nothing but the compiler, and can be called from Fortran, C, Python, R or any language that speaks the C ABI.

docs.title: fortvine
docs.text:
Vine copulas in modern Fortran: 111 pair-copula families with exact parameter scores, structure selection, densities, Rosenblatt transforms and simulation.

Get started Browse the families

docs.title: Thirty seconds of fortvine
docs.text:
FortranPythonR hello_fortvine.f90
program hello_fortvine
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 2000
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop
  real(dp) :: u1(n), w(n), u2(n)

  cop%family = FV_CLAYTON; cop%par(1) = 2.0_dp       ! Clayton copula, Kendall's tau = 0.5
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  call cop%hinv1(u1, w, u2)                          ! simulate (u1, u2) from it

  call cop%select(u1, u2)                            ! choose family, rotation and parameters by BIC
  print *, trim(fv_fam_name(cop%family)), cop%rotation, cop%par(1)
end program hello_fortvine

 clayton           0   2.1450855929878818

The sample is not seeded, so the last digits differ from run to run.

hello_fortvine.py
import fortvine as fv

cop = fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [2.0])              # Clayton copula, Kendall's tau = 0.5
u = cop.simulate(2000, seed=1)                   # simulate (u1, u2) from it

best = fv.Bicop().select(u)                      # choose family, rotation and parameters by BIC
print(best.family, best.rotation, best.parameters[0])

clayton 0 1.956774237371629
hello_fortvine.R
library(fortvine)
cop <- bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)               # Clayton copula, Kendall's tau = 0.5
set.seed(1)
u <- rbicop(2000, cop)                           # simulate (u1, u2) from it

best <- bicop(u)                                 # choose family, rotation and parameters by BIC
best

Bivariate copula ('bicop_dist'): family = clayton (3), rotation = 0, parameters = 1.879

The Python and R packages are bindings: every number above is computed by the same compiled Fortran library. The three samples come from different random number generators, so the estimates differ. bash build.sh builds build/libfortvine.a, the module files and a shared library; see Installation and the Quick start.

docs.title: What is in the box
docs.text: Area What fortvine provides Families elliptical (Gaussian, t); Archimedean (Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, AMH, BB1-BB3, BB6-BB10 and 6 new Laplace-transform compositions); extreme-value (Tawn, Galambos, Hüsler-Reiss, t-EV, BB5 and 9 new asymmetric and mixed Pickands families); Archimax (BB4 and 67 new); Khoudraji (3 new); Plackett, FGM; nonparametric TLL and Bernstein. All with 90/180/270 degree rotations where they apply. See Families. Pair copulas density, log-density, CDF, both h-functions and their inverses, maximum-likelihood fit with exact scores, family selection (log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, mBIC), Kendall's tau inversion, weights, discrete margins. See Pair copulas. Vines R-, C- and D-vine structures; Dissmann selection with Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, Hoeffding's D, Chatterjee's xi, mutual information and other tree criteria; truncation and thresholding by mBICv; fixed structures. See Vine copulas. Vine functions density on samples and on prediction grids, log-likelihood, Rosenblatt and inverse Rosenblatt, simulation, parameter counts, structure matrix, printing. Interfaces a typed Fortran API (fortvine_api), a C ABI (bind(C) kernels and fortvine_capi), and Python and R packages with every feature of the Fortran API. See C interface. Quality test suites over every family and rotation (density / h-function / CDF consistency, inverses, MLE recovery); the generic engine reproduces the hand-coded families to 1e-15-1e-9. See Validation.

docs.title: How it compares
docs.text:
fortvine follows the conventions of vinecopulib (rotations, structure arrays, selection algorithm), so the two can be compared one to one: on the benchmark data they reach the same maximum log-likelihoods, and fortvine gets there 7-12 times faster, from Fortran or from Python (2-3 times slower from R on Windows, still 7-9 times faster than rvinecopulib).

fortvine vinecopulib / pyvinecopulib torchvine language Fortran 2008 + OpenMP C++ (Python bindings) Python / PyTorch parametric families 108 11 10 asymmetric families 32 1 (Tawn) — nonparametric TLL, Bernstein TLL TLL exact parameter gradients yes (dual numbers) yes (analytic, 1.0) autograd GPU no no yes

All timings and the method are on the Benchmarks page.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
This page compares fortvine, used from Fortran, Python and R, with three other vine-copula packages on identical data:

  • fortvine three ways: the native Fortran library, the Python package and the R package. Both packages call the same compiled library, so their columns show what a user of each language actually gets;
  • pyvinecopulib 1.0.1 and rvinecopulib 0.7.2.1.0: the Python and R bindings of vinecopulib (C++), the reference implementation that fortvine's conventions follow;
  • torchvine 0.2.2: a pure-PyTorch reimplementation of the pyvinecopulib API (CPU build of PyTorch 2.15).

All numbers on this page come from bench/run_bench.py (with bench/bench_r.R for the R packages); the raw results are in bench/results/results.json. You can reproduce them on your own machine (see the end of the page).

docs.title: Set-up
docs.text:
machine Intel Core (Raptor Lake, 32 logical CPUs), Windows 11 fortvine (Fortran) gfortran 16.1 (WinLibs), -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fopenmp Python side Python 3.14.0, NumPy 2.5.5; fortvine built by pip install ./python (gfortran 16.1, -O3 -funroll-loops); pyvinecopulib 1.0.1 (PyPI wheel); torch 2.15.0+cpu, torchvine 0.2.2 R side R 4.3.2; fortvine built by R CMD INSTALL with Rtools43 (gfortran 12.3, R's default flags); rvinecopulib 0.7.2.1.0 (CRAN binary) family set the 12 families all libraries share: independence, Gaussian, Student t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, BB1, BB6, BB7, BB8, Tawn (torchvine has no Tawn) — with rotations criterion BIC everywhere threads "one thread" runs pin every library to one thread (FORTVINE_THREADS=1, num_threads=1, cores = 1, torch.set_num_threads(1))

Data. Pair-copula data are simulated with pyvinecopulib from each family at Kendall's \(\tau \approx 0.5\) (\(n = 5000\)). Vine data come from a heavy-tailed, skewed two-factor model turned into pseudo-observations (\(n = 2000\), \(d = 5, 10, 20\)), so that no library's own model class generated them. The R packages read the same files.

Timing. Wall-clock means after a warm-up call (a call longer than 2 s is timed once). The Python and R timings include the call overhead of the bindings. Every timed process is exempted from Windows 11's power throttling: Windows moves a process without a window to the efficiency cores after about two seconds of work, which slowed long calls by a factor of about 1.6 in a first run and would have favoured whichever library finishes quickly.

docs.title: What the numbers say
docs.text:
Same answers. Where the libraries fit the same model, fortvine (from any language), pyvinecopulib and rvinecopulib reach the same maximum: the log-likelihoods of every pair fit and every selected vine agree to the digits shown, and all five select the true family for every simulated pair. This is by design — fortvine reproduces vinecopulib's rotations, structure arrays, candidate pre-selection and Dissmann algorithm — and it makes the speed comparison a like-for-like one. torchvine estimates one-parameter families by inverting Kendall's \(\tau\), which is why its fits are the fastest in Table 4 and its maxima lower (by 0.01 to 24 log-likelihood units); its selection picks a different family for the Clayton, Joe and Tawn samples (it has no Tawn family) and its vines have lower likelihoods.

From Python, fortvine is as fast as from Fortran. The Python package passes NumPy arrays to the library without copies, and its timings agree with the native ones within the run-to-run noise in every table (geometric mean 1.0 in the figure above): the Python user gets the library's full speed.

From R, the toolchain costs a factor of about 2.7. The R package itself adds almost nothing: the native benchmark program compiled with R's compiler (Rtools43, gfortran 12.3) selects the \(d = 5\) vine in 1.31 s, the same as the R package, against 0.48 s with gfortran 16.1, and -O3 -march=native do not change it. The difference is the older compiler and its MinGW runtime on Windows; R on Linux and macOS uses other toolchains. Even so, fortvine from R selects vines 7–9× faster than rvinecopulib, selects pair copulas 8–23× faster and fits them 2–17× faster.

Pair-copula evaluation. The density is 1.3–4× faster than pyvinecopulib's for every family except Student t, where pyvinecopulib is faster (187 against 301 ns per point; fortvine evaluates the Student t density through the regularised incomplete beta function). The largest gaps are in the inverse h-function: fortvine inverts h with closed forms where they exist and with a safeguarded Newton step that uses the density as the exact derivative elsewhere, so the BB1, BB6, BB7, BB8 and Tawn inversions run in 0.6–1.0 µs per point against 5–11 µs, and the Frank inversion (closed form) in 22 ns against 2.9 µs; Joe's inversion is the exception (336 against 281 ns). torchvine, vectorised by PyTorch, is the fastest for a few simple families (Frank, Gaussian, Student t density).

Fitting. A maximum-likelihood fit of a known family is 2–7× faster than pyvinecopulib's (1–21 ms against 3–155 ms at \(n = 5000\)). Exact parameter scores from dual numbers let Newton/BFGS converge in a few steps, and large samples are fitted in two stages (a subsample first, then a short polish on all data).

Selection. Choosing among the 12 families and their rotations takes 50–100 ms in fortvine and 0.7–1.0 s in pyvinecopulib — 7–19× faster. Candidate pre-selection, racing (a cheap bound decides whether a candidate can still win before it is polished) and the shared closed-form kernels account for this.

Vines. Selecting a regular vine is 7–10× faster than pyvinecopulib on one thread and 6–12× faster on eight, with identical log-likelihoods. Density evaluation is 3–6× faster and simulation 8–18× faster. On eight threads a 20-dimensional vine is selected in 1.2 s.

Read these numbers with care

Benchmarks measure one machine, one operating system and one set of data. pyvinecopulib and rvinecopulib were run from their PyPI wheel and CRAN binary on Windows; native Linux builds may be faster, and so may the fortvine R package on Linux or macOS. torchvine is designed for GPUs and autograd, and its CPU timings do not show what it is built for. The scripts are in the repository so you can check the comparison on your own hardware.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to fortvine are recorded here. Versions follow semantic versioning.

First public release, under the GNU General Public License version 3 or later. Preferred citation: Shojaeezadeh, S. A. (2026), fortvine: a complete compendium to work on vine copula modeling, in preparation (also in CITATION.cff, R's citation("fortvine") and Python's fortvine.cite()). Python and R packages bind the same Fortran library.

docs.title: Pair copulas
docs.text:
• 111 families. 26 hand-coded families (codes 0-25): independence, Gaussian, Student t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, BB1-BB10, Tawn, Plackett, FGM, AMH, Galambos, Hüsler-Reiss, t-EV, and the nonparametric transformation local-likelihood (TLL) and Bernstein estimators; plus 85 generic families (codes 10000 and up) built by one engine, \(C = \Psi(\ell(\Phi(u), \Phi(v)))\): two-parameter Archimedean compositions, extreme-value copulas (Tawn mixed, asymmetric logistic and negative logistic models and their types, Khoudraji-Hüsler-Reiss, ...), Archimax copulas with one- and two-parameter outer generators, and Khoudraji asymmetrisations of Clayton, Joe and Frank. See the catalogue.
  • Rotations by 90, 180 and 270 degrees (vinecopulib convention); exact transposition of asymmetric families when a vine edge is flipped.
  • Log-density, density, distribution function, both h-functions and their inverses for every family, vectorised and parallel; log-space evaluation with cancellation-free and asymptotic forms throughout (Numerics).
  • Maximum likelihood with exact parameter scores from dual numbers (each family written once and compiled for real and dual types), projected Fisher-scoring (BHHH) steps with Levenberg-Marquardt damping, subsample-then-polish fitting, and analytic second derivatives for the one-parameter families (Exact parameter scores); estimation by inversion of Kendall's tau as an option.
  • Family selection by log-likelihood, AIC, BIC or mBIC, with vinecopulib-style preselection and racing of candidate fits.

docs.title: Vine copulas
docs.text:
• Regular vines with the natural-order structure array; fixed C- and D-vine constructors; R-vine matrix export in original labels.
  • Structure selection by Dissmann's algorithm with Prim's or Kruskal's maximum spanning tree and seven edge criteria (Kendall's tau, Spearman's rho, Joe's criterion, Hoeffding's D, Chatterjee's xi, KSG mutual information, Ferreira's criterion).
  • Truncation and thresholding, fixed or chosen by mBICv (vinecopulib's select_trunc_lvl and select_threshold).
  • Vine density and log-likelihood, a fast density on prediction grids (pdf_grid), Rosenblatt and inverse Rosenblatt transforms, reproducible simulation.
  • Observation weights for every fit and selection.
  • Discrete and mixed margins (vinecopulib convention, \(u = F(x)\), \(u^- = F(x^-)\)), including Brockwell's randomised Rosenblatt transform.
  • Non-simplified edges (relax): pair-copula parameters varying with the conditioning variables, with a constant-conditional-correlation test.
  • A pair-fit memo cache for repeated selections (tuning loops).

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Pure Fortran 2008 with OpenMP; no external dependencies. Likelihood sums are independent of the thread count.
  • Typed Fortran API (fortvine_api: fv_bicop, fv_vinecop, fv_controls) and a bind(C) interface exported from a shared library for C, C++, Python and other languages: the kernel routines fv_* and the extended interface fortvine_capi (fvc_*), which passes every feature of the typed API (weights, discrete margins, TLL/Bernstein, all controls, non-simplified vines, pdf_grid, fit cache, abort flag).
  • Python (pip install fortvine) and R (fortvine on CRAN) packages over the same library, with every feature of the Fortran API; their speed is in Benchmarks.
  • The Student t distribution function integrates the h-function in normal scores (accurate to about \(10^{-12}\) up to the corners), and BB8 fits run Newton from two starts (its likelihood has a ridge in \((\theta, \delta)\)).
  • Build with build.sh (static and shared library, tests, examples, benchmark driver) or fpm.
  • Two property test suites (test/test_fortvine.f90, test/test_genfam.f90) covering every family and rotation, vines, weights, discrete data, criteria and the generic engine (Validation).
  • Five documented example programs in Fortran, Python and R, a C example, and a cross-library benchmark against pyvinecopulib, rvinecopulib and torchvine.

docs.title: Python package
docs.text:
The fortvine Python package lets you use the library from Python with NumPy arrays. It is a binding, not a port: every density, h-function, fit, family selection, vine selection, Rosenblatt transform and simulation is computed by the compiled Fortran library through its C interface. Python converts arrays and family names into the layout the C routines expect and wraps what they return in two classes, Bicop and Vinecop. The class and method names follow pyvinecopulib, so code written for it needs few changes.

Besides the fv_* routines of src/fortvine.f90, the package calls src/fortvine_capi.f90 (the fvc_* routines), a C interface to the typed Fortran API (fortvine_api). Through it the Python package has everything the Fortran API offers: observation weights, discrete and mixed margins, the nonparametric families tll and bernstein, every selection control (select_trunc_lvl, select_threshold, fast_mle, ...), non-simplified vines (relax), pdf_grid, the fit cache, the abort flag, parameter bounds and gen_flip. Nothing is recomputed in Python.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install fortvine

The wheels on PyPI (Linux x86_64, macOS arm64 and x86_64, Windows x86_64) contain the compiled library, so no compiler is needed. Elsewhere pip builds the package from the source distribution, which needs gfortran on the PATH (set FC to choose another compiler).

From a clone of the repository, or straight from GitHub, the package is always compiled from the Fortran sources in src/:

pip install ./python
pip install "git+https://github.com/Bluerrror/fortvine#subdirectory=python"

The build compiles src/fortvine_ad.f90, src/fortvine.f90, src/fortvine_api.f90 and src/fortvine_capi.f90 with -O3 -fopenmp, without -march=native, so the library runs on any CPU of the platform. It is placed in fortvine/_lib/. On Windows the gfortran, OpenMP, quadmath and winpthread runtimes are linked statically into libfortvine.dll, which then depends only on system DLLs and loads in a fresh virtual environment. On Linux and macOS the library uses the compiler's runtime libraries; the wheels bundle them (auditwheel, delocate). FORTVINE_LIB points the package at a library built elsewhere.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

cop = fv.Bicop("clayton", rotation=0, parameters=[2.0])
u = cop.simulate(2000, seed=1)          # (2000, 2) array in (0, 1)
cop.pdf(u[:5]), cop.hfunc1(u[:5]), cop.cdf(u[:5])

est = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u)        # maximum likelihood
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=["gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank"])

x = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((1000, 4)).cumsum(axis=1)
v = fv.to_pseudo_obs(x)
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(v, criterion="bic", trunc_lvl=2, num_threads=4)
print(vc)
vc.loglik(v), vc.npars, vc.simulate(500, seed=2)

Data are copula data: an (n, d) array with values in \((0, 1)\), one row per observation. Because the C interface keeps observations in the last Fortran dimension, such a C-order array is passed to Fortran without a copy. Families are given by name (case-insensitive, as fv_fam_name spells them, e.g. "bb1" or "Archimax(gamma|HuslerReiss)") or by integer code, including the generic codes 10000 and up. fv.families() lists all 111.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Python does C routine Bicop(family, rotation, parameters, aux=None) pair copula; family, family_code, rotation, parameters, npars, aux, is_nonparametric .pdf(u), .logpdf(u) density, log-density on u of shape \((n, 2)\) fv_bicop_eval; fvc_bicop_eval for tll / bernstein .cdf(u) distribution function fvc_bicop_eval .hfunc1(u), .hfunc2(u) \(h_1 = P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1)\), \(h_2 = P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2)\) as .pdf .hinv1(u), .hinv2(u) inverses in the second / first argument as .pdf .loglik(u=None), .aic(u=None), .bic(u=None) log-likelihood on u, or of the last fit; AIC, BIC with npars as .pdf .fit(u, method, ..., weights=None) estimate the parameters (tll / bernstein: the estimate aux) of the current family and rotation fvc_bicop_fit .select(u, family_set, criterion, ..., weights=None) choose family, rotation and parameters fvc_bicop_fit .parameters_lower_bounds, .parameters_upper_bounds the parameter box fvc_par_bounds .simulate(n, seed) \(u_2 = h_1^{-1}(w \mid u_1)\) for uniform \(u_1, w\) as .pdf Vinecop(d, var_types=None) empty vine: d, trunc, order, st, fam, rot, par, edge_ll, aux, disc, threshold .set_dvine(order), .set_cvine(order) fixed D- or C-vine structure fvc_vine_structure Vinecop.from_data(u, ...), .select(u, ..., weights, var_types, select_trunc_lvl, select_threshold) select structure (unless fixed), families, parameters fvc_vine_select .pdf(u), .loglik(u=None), .aic(u=None), .bic(u=None) vine density; log-likelihood; AIC, BIC fvc_vine_eval .pdf_grid(ug, target) density on a prediction grid fvc_vine_pdf_grid .rosenblatt(u, randomize_discrete=True, seed=1), .inverse_rosenblatt(w) Rosenblatt transform and its inverse fvc_vine_eval .simulate(n, seed) inverse Rosenblatt transform of uniforms fvc_vine_eval .relax(u, target=0, mode="test", ..., weights=None), .unrelax() non-simplified edges; nrel, relaxed_edges, erel, wa, wk, pk fvc_vine_relax .rel_params(u) parameters (n, nrel, 3) of the relaxed edges at the samples u fvc_vine_rel_params .matrix, .families, .rotations, .parameters, .npars, .var_types R-vine matrix; pair copulas per tree; parameter count; variable types fvc_vine_matrix .get_pair_copula(t, e), .set_pair_copula(t, e, bicop) one edge as a Bicop to_pseudo_obs(x), kendall_tau(x, y) ranks / \((n + 1)\); Kendall's \(\tau_b\) fv_pseudo_obs, fv_kendall_tau families(), family_group(name) the family list; the codes of a family group fvc_families par_bounds(family), gen_flip(family, parameters) parameter box; the transposed generic copula fvc_par_bounds, fvc_gen_flip fitcache_enable(capacity), fitcache_clear(), fitcache_disable(), fitcache_stats() the pair-fit cache fvc_fitcache set_abort(flag=True) the abort flag of running fits and selections fvc_set_abort cite(), __version__, NAUX, NK the citation; the version; length of a tll / bernstein estimate; anchors of a relaxed edge fvc_naux, fvc_nk

The options of select are those of fv_controls: family_set (default: the fv_controls default, codes 0 to 22), criterion ("loglik", "aic", "bic", "mbic", "mbicv"), method ("mle", "itau"), preselect, allow_rotations, fast_mle, tau_mode ("auto", "exact", "approx"), psi0 and num_threads (default: the environment variable FORTVINE_THREADS, otherwise half the logical CPUs — the same rule as the Fortran library), and the keyword-only weights; for vines also tree_criterion ("tau", "rho", "joe", "hoeffd", "xi", "mi", "ferreira"), tree_algorithm ("prim", "kruskal"), trunc_lvl, threshold, fixed and the keyword-only var_types, select_trunc_lvl and select_threshold. The pyvinecopulib and Fortran spellings are accepted too: selection_criterion, parametric_method, tree_crit, tree_algo, preselect_families, select_trunc. fit takes method, fast_mle, tau_mode, num_threads and weights.

A family_set is a list of family names, codes or group names; a single name or group is accepted as well. The groups (family_group(name) returns their codes):

group codes Fortran "default" 0 to 22, every parametric hand-coded family except tev fv_controls default "parametric" 0 to 11 FV_PARAMETRIC "all_parametric" 0 to 23 FV_ALL "nonparametric" 24 (tll), 25 (bernstein) FV_NONPAR "all" 0 to 25 FV_NCLASSIC families "one_par" 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 FV_ONE_PAR "generic" the 85 generic codes 10000 and up fv_generic_families()

In a Vinecop the arrays are indexed [tree, edge] from 0, the transpose of the Fortran fam(edge, tree): edge e of tree t joins variables order[e] and order[st[t, e] - 1] (the labels in order and st are 1-based, as in Fortran). par is (d, d, 3), aux is (d, d, naux) with naux = NAUX when the vine has a tll or bernstein edge and 1 otherwise, and disc is a (d,) boolean array of the discrete variables. Seeds make simulate reproducible; the uniforms come from NumPy, so the draws differ from Fortran's simulate with the same seed. Bicop and Vinecop hold only NumPy arrays and numbers, so they pickle (and copy) like any Python object, including their estimates, discreteness flags and non-simplified edges.

Vine selection and relax run in a worker thread when they are called from the main thread, so Ctrl-C (KeyboardInterrupt) interrupts them: the package sets the abort flag, waits until the Fortran code returns (a few milliseconds), clears the flag and re-raises.

docs.title: Observation weights
docs.text:
weights (one value per row) is accepted by Bicop.fit, Bicop.select, Vinecop.select and Vinecop.relax. The weighted log-likelihood is maximised and weighted Kendall taus build the trees. With integer weights a weighted fit is the fit to the sample with rows repeated:

import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

u = fv.Bicop("clayton", parameters=[2.0]).simulate(1000, seed=1)
w = np.random.default_rng(2).integers(1, 3, len(u))           # weights 1 or 2
a = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u, weights=w)
b = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(np.repeat(u, w, axis=0))           # rows repeated w times
print("weighted fit   :", a.parameters, round(a.loglik(), 4))
print("duplicated rows:", b.parameters, round(b.loglik(), 4))

x = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((1000, 4)).cumsum(axis=1)
v = fv.to_pseudo_obs(x)
recent = 0.998 ** np.arange(len(v))[::-1]                      # time-decay weights
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(v, weights=recent, family_set=["gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank"])
print(vc.families, round(vc.loglik(), 2))

weighted fit   : [1.87015409] 549.3913
duplicated rows: [1.87015409] 549.3913
[['gaussian', 'gaussian', 'gaussian'], ['clayton', 'clayton'], ['clayton']] 663.87

loglik() without data returns the weighted log-likelihood of the fit.

Time-decay weights on a sample whose dependence strengthens over time: 2000 observations, the $i$-th drawn from a Clayton copula with $\theta$ rising linearly from 0.5 to 6. (a) The sample in normal scores, coloured by the weight $2^{-(n - i)/200}$. (b) The Clayton parameter fitted with `fit(u, weights=w)` against the half-life of the weights: short half-lives track the latest $\theta = 6$ (5.95 at half-life 50), long ones approach the unweighted fit (2.73), which describes the whole period.

docs.title: Discrete and mixed margins
docs.text:
Discrete variables follow pyvinecopulib's convention (Discrete data explains the likelihood). var_types gives "c" or "d" per variable, and with \(k\) discrete variables the data are an \((n, d + k)\) array: the first \(d\) columns hold \(F(x)\) of every variable, the last \(k\) columns \(F(x^-)\) of the discrete ones, in their order. An \((n, 2d)\) array with \(F(x^-)\) of every variable in columns \(d, \dots, 2d - 1\) is accepted too (only the discrete columns are read). The vine keeps the flags (disc, var_types), and pdf, loglik, rosenblatt and pdf_grid then expect data of the same form.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import poisson
import fortvine as fv

# a Gaussian D-vine 1-2-3; variable 2 is observed as a Poisson(2) count
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
truth.fam[0, :2] = 1                       # gaussian
truth.par[0, :2, 0] = [0.7, 0.5]
v = truth.simulate(2000, seed=1)
k = poisson.ppf(v[:, 1], 2.0)              # the counts
# F(x) of the three variables, then F(x-) of the discrete one: an (n, d + 1) array
u = np.column_stack([v[:, 0], poisson.cdf(k, 2.0), v[:, 2], poisson.cdf(k - 1, 2.0)])

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, var_types=["c", "d", "c"], family_set=["indep", "gaussian", "frank"])
print(vc)
print("var_types:", vc.var_types, "  loglik %.2f" % vc.loglik(u))
r = vc.rosenblatt(u, seed=3)               # Brockwell's randomised transform
print("Rosenblatt means", r.mean(axis=0).round(4), " variances", r.var(axis=0).round(4))

fortvine vine copula: d = 3, trunc = 2
order: 1 2 3
discrete: 2
  tree 1 edge 1: gaussian     rot   0 par 0.6995
  tree 1 edge 2: gaussian     rot   0 par 0.5155
  tree 2 edge 1: indep        rot   0 par 
var_types: ['c', 'd', 'c']   loglik 894.19
Rosenblatt means [0.4933 0.5008 0.5083]  variances [0.0846 0.0829 0.0854]

Both latent correlations (0.7 and 0.5) are recovered from a count with a handful of values, and the randomised Rosenblatt transform has the mean \(1/2\) and variance \(1/12\) of uniforms. rosenblatt(u, randomize_discrete=False) returns \(F(x_k \mid \dots)\) itself; seed (non-zero) selects the randomisation. inverse_rosenblatt and simulate return the copula sample on the continuous scale; apply the marginal quantile functions to get discrete data. The test suite rebuilds such a vine in pyvinecopulib and finds the same discrete density to \(10^{-6}\) relative. relax is not available for vines with discrete variables, and a Bicop has no discrete margins (use a two-dimensional Vinecop).

The example above. (a) Variable 2 is a Poisson(2) count driven by a latent Gaussian dependence on variable 1. (b) The non-randomised Rosenblatt transform (`randomize_discrete=False`) of the count is not uniform: it is $F(x_2 \mid x_1)$ at the upper end of each jump. (c) Brockwell's randomised transform (`rosenblatt(u, seed=3)`) is uniform under the fitted model, as a goodness-of-fit residual should be.

docs.title: Nonparametric families
docs.text:
tll (24) and bernstein (25) (Nonparametric pair copulas) are fitted like any other family. Their estimate is the vector aux (NAUX = 933 values); their parameters are empty, rotation is ignored, and npars is the effective number of parameters of the estimate, the penalty that AIC and BIC use. They are not in the default family set: name them or use the "nonparametric" or "all" group.

import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

# an equal mixture of a Clayton and a 90-degree Gumbel copula
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
a = fv.Bicop("clayton", parameters=[4.0]).simulate(3000, seed=1)
b = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 90, [3.0]).simulate(3000, seed=2)
u = np.where(rng.random((3000, 1)) < 0.5, a, b)

tll = fv.Bicop("tll").fit(u)
print(tll, " loglik %.2f" % tll.loglik(), " aux", tll.aux.shape)
print("density at (0.1,0.1), (0.5,0.5), (0.9,0.1):", tll.pdf(np.array([[.1, .1], [.5, .5], [.9, .1]])).round(3))
for crit in ("bic", "aic"):
    best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=["parametric", "nonparametric"], criterion=crit)
    print(crit, "->", best.family, " loglik %.2f  npars %.2f" % (best.loglik(), best.npars))

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(np.column_stack([u, rng.random(3000)]), family_set=["indep", "gaussian", "tll"])
print(vc)
print("npars %.2f" % vc.npars, " aux", vc.aux.shape)

Bicop(family='tll', npars=142.21)  loglik 1009.79  aux (933,)
density at (0.1,0.1), (0.5,0.5), (0.9,0.1): [2.81  1.835 1.688]
bic -> student  loglik 520.45  npars 2.00
aic -> tll  loglik 1009.79  npars 142.21
fortvine vine copula: d = 3, trunc = 2
order: 1 2 3
  tree 1 edge 1: tll          edf 142.21
  tree 1 edge 2: indep        rot   0 par 
  tree 2 edge 1: indep        rot   0 par 
npars 142.21  aux (3, 3, 933)

TLL nearly doubles the log-likelihood of the best parametric family (Student), but with 142 effective parameters: BIC keeps the Student copula, AIC takes TLL. Every evaluation (pdf, h-functions and their inverses, cdf, the vine methods) uses the stored estimate, and get_pair_copula / set_pair_copula carry it between a vine and a Bicop. In families() the two families have npars = -1.

The mixture sample of the example (3000 points, normal scores) with the density contours of (a) the TLL estimate and (b) the Student copula that BIC prefers. TLL follows both arms of the mixture, the Clayton lower tail along the diagonal and the rotated Gumbel tail in the upper-left corner; the Student copula can only spread its mass symmetrically.

docs.title: Truncation, thresholding and other controls
docs.text:
select_trunc_lvl=True lets mBICv choose the truncation level and select_threshold=True the threshold below which edges are set to independence, as vinecopulib's options of the same names (the threshold found is in vc.threshold):

import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

rng = np.random.default_rng(4)                 # a Gaussian AR(1) chain: only tree 1 matters
z = np.zeros((2000, 6))
z[:, 0] = rng.standard_normal(2000)
for j in range(1, 6):
    z[:, j] = 0.7 * z[:, j - 1] + np.sqrt(0.51) * rng.standard_normal(2000)
u = fv.to_pseudo_obs(z)

full = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)
trunc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, select_trunc_lvl=True)
thr = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, select_threshold=True, criterion="mbicv")
print("full      : trunc", full.trunc, " npars", full.npars, " loglik %.2f" % full.loglik())
print("mBICv trunc: trunc", trunc.trunc, " npars", trunc.npars, " loglik %.2f" % trunc.loglik())
print("mBICv thr : threshold %.4f" % thr.threshold, " npars", thr.npars, " loglik %.2f" % thr.loglik())
alt = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, tree_crit="rho", tree_algo="kruskal", parametric_method="itau",
                           fast_mle=True, preselect=False, allow_rotations=False, trunc_lvl=2)
print("rho/kruskal/itau, 2 trees:", alt.families)

full      : trunc 5  npars 5  loglik 3264.58
mBICv trunc: trunc 1  npars 5  loglik 3264.58
mBICv thr : threshold 0.3167  npars 5  loglik 3264.58
rho/kruskal/itau, 2 trees: [['gaussian', 'gaussian', 'gaussian', 'gaussian', 'gaussian'], ['indep', 'indep', 'indep', 'indep']]

BIC already sets every edge above the first tree to independence; with select_trunc_lvl the vine is also cut after tree 1.

A second chain, $d = 8$, in which each variable depends on the two before it ($z_j = 0.5 z_{j-1} + 0.35 z_{j-2} + 0.6\,\varepsilon_j$, $n = 2000$), fitted with every fixed `trunc_lvl` from 1 to 7. (a) The log-likelihood jumps from tree 1 to tree 2 and is flat after it. (b) BIC with the number of parameters at each point; `select_trunc_lvl=True` (mBICv) stops at 2. BIC itself is lowest at level 6, by 1.2 units for one extra parameter; mBICv's prior against dependence in high trees removes such an edge.

docs.title: Non-simplified vines
docs.text:
relax(u, target=0, mode="test") lets the parameters of edges of trees \(t \ge 2\) vary with their conditioning variables (see relax): target is the variable label whose edges may be relaxed (0: any), mode="test" relaxes the edges whose constant-conditional-correlation test rejects at 5 %, mode="all" every eligible edge; method, fast_mle, tau_mode, num_threads and weights control the local fits. The relaxed edges are stored in the vine (nrel, relaxed_edges as 0-based (tree, edge), and the Fortran arrays erel ((nrel, 2): edge, tree, 1-based), wa ((nrel, d)), wk ((nrel, NK)) and pk ((nrel, NK, 3))). pdf, loglik and pdf_grid use them; rosenblatt, inverse_rosenblatt and simulate use par (the middle-anchor values), as in Fortran. unrelax() deletes the records, and select starts from a simplified vine again.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
import fortvine as fv

# the copula of (U1, U3) given U2 changes with U2: not a simplified vine
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
u2, w1, w3 = rng.random(n), rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
x1 = fv.Bicop("clayton", parameters=[2.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u2, w1]))
rho = -0.6 + 1.4 * u2
v3 = norm.cdf(rho * norm.ppf(w1) + np.sqrt(1 - rho**2) * norm.ppf(w3))
x3 = fv.Bicop("frank", parameters=[5.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u2, v3]))
u = np.column_stack([x1, u2, x3])

vc = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3]).select(u, family_set=["indep", "gaussian", "clayton", "frank"])
print("simplified    : loglik %.2f  npars %d" % (vc.loglik(), vc.npars))
vc.relax(u, target=0, mode="test")
print("non-simplified: loglik %.2f  npars %d  relaxed edges %s" % (vc.loglik(), vc.npars, vc.relaxed_edges))
print("check: sum log pdf = %.2f" % vc.loglik(u))
print(vc)
print("anchors wk:", vc.wk.round(3), " loadings wa:", vc.wa.round(3))

# predictive density of variable 3 on a grid, for the first two samples
g = np.repeat(u[:2, None, :], 5, axis=1)
g[:, :, 2] = [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]
print(vc.pdf_grid(g, target=3).round(4))

simplified    : loglik 1342.48  npars 3
non-simplified: loglik 1521.02  npars 7  relaxed edges [(1, 0)]
check: sum log pdf = 1521.02
fortvine vine copula: d = 3, trunc = 2
order: 3 2 1
  tree 1 edge 1: frank        rot   0 par 5.0930
  tree 1 edge 2: clayton      rot   0 par 1.9290
  tree 2 edge 1: frank        rot   0 par 0.3364
  non-simplified tree 2 edge 1: first parameter at the w anchors -2.5260 -1.2442 0.3364 2.0974 3.9420
anchors wk: [[-1.249 -0.51  -0.004  0.506  1.305]]  loadings wa: [[0. 1. 0.]]
[[0.8766 1.6637 2.1001 1.5994 0.8216]
 [0.0397 0.1    0.2134 0.2932 0.1411]]

The test relaxes the single second-tree edge; its Frank parameter now runs from \(-2.5\) to \(3.9\) across the anchors of \(w = \Phi^{-1}(u_2)\), and the log-likelihood gains 179 for four extra parameter sets.

The non-simplified example. (a) Conditional Kendall's $\tau$ of $(U_1, U_3)$ given $U_2 = u_2$: the truth (Gaussian, $\rho = -0.6 + 1.4\,u_2$), the single Frank copula of the simplified vine ($\tau = 0.06$), and the relaxed Frank edge at its five anchors (parameters `pk`, at $u_2 = \Phi(w_k)$, converted to $\tau$ by simulation; constant beyond the outer anchors). (b) The predictive density of $u_3$ from `pdf_grid` at $u_1 = 0.8$ and three values of $u_2$, relaxed (solid) and simplified (dotted): the two agree at $u_2 = 0.5$, where the relaxed parameter is close to the constant one, and differ where the conditional dependence has changed sign or strength.

docs.title: Prediction grids
docs.text: pdf_grid(ug, target) evaluates the vine density on ug of shape (n, bins, d): for each of the n samples, bins points that differ only in variable target (1-based label, as in order). It returns (n, bins), the same values as pdf at those points, but edges that do not involve target are evaluated once per sample (the example above). With discrete variables the last axis is d + k (or 2d), as for pdf. After relax(target=0) the conditioning values of relaxed edges are taken from the first bin of each sample, which is exact when no relaxed edge conditions on target (see the note in relax).

docs.title: Fit cache, abort flag, bounds
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

u = fv.to_pseudo_obs(np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal((1500, 5)).cumsum(axis=1))
fv.fitcache_enable(20000)
a = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)
print("after the first select :", fv.fitcache_stats())
b = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)
print("after the second select:", fv.fitcache_stats(), " same loglik:", a.loglik() == b.loglik())
fv.fitcache_disable()

fv.set_abort(True)                      # e.g. from another thread or a GUI callback
print("aborted select: trunc", fv.Vinecop.from_data(u).trunc)
fv.set_abort(False)

print(fv.par_bounds("bb1"))
print(fv.gen_flip("tawn-asymmixed", [0.5, 0.5]))

after the first select : FitCacheStats(hits=0, misses=260, used=260)
after the second select: FitCacheStats(hits=260, misses=260, used=260)  same loglik: True
aborted select: trunc 0
(array([0., 1.]), array([7., 7.]))
(10011, array([0.625     , 0.42105263]))

The fit cache is shared by every fit and selection while it is enabled; fitcache_clear() empties it and resets the counters. With the abort flag set, fits return at once and a selection stops (its result is to be discarded); the flag stays set until set_abort(False). par_bounds is the MLE search box of a family, and gen_flip the generic family and parameters of the transposed copula \(C(u_2, u_1)\) (other families are returned unchanged).

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
This is the program of the Quick start in Python (example/python/python_quickstart.py in the repository): a Gumbel pair copula that is evaluated, simulated, fitted and selected, then a four-dimensional C-vine with Clayton pairs that is simulated, selected from the sample and simulated again.

import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n = 1000

# one pair copula: Gumbel with theta = 1.5 (Kendall tau = 1 - 1/theta = 1/3)
cop = fv.Bicop("gumbel", parameters=[1.5])
g = np.array([0.1, 0.5, 0.95])
print("density c(u,u)   :", cop.pdf(np.column_stack([g, g])).round(4))
print("h1(u | u)        :", cop.hfunc1(np.column_stack([g, g])).round(4))

u12 = cop.simulate(n, seed=42)                       # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
print("sample Kendall tau: %.4f" % fv.kendall_tau(u12[:, 0], u12[:, 1]))

est = fv.Bicop("gumbel").fit(u12)
print("Gumbel MLE theta : %.4f   loglik %.3f" % (est.parameters[0], est.loglik()))
best = fv.Bicop().select(u12)
print("BIC selection    :", best)

# a 4-dimensional vine: a C-vine with Clayton pairs as the truth
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_cvine([1, 2, 3, 4])
truth.fam[0, :3] = 3; truth.par[0, :3, 0] = 3.0      # tree 1: Clayton(3)
truth.fam[1, :2] = 3; truth.par[1, :2, 0] = 1.0      # tree 2: Clayton(1)
u = truth.simulate(n, seed=1)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)                         # structure, families, parameters
print(vc)
print("loglik %.2f   (truth %.2f)   parameters %d" % (vc.loglik(u), truth.loglik(u), vc.npars))
print("five draws from the fitted vine:")
print(vc.simulate(5, seed=2).round(4))

Output (Windows, Python 3.14, gfortran 16):

density c(u,u)   : [1.8518 1.2196 4.5946]
h1(u | u)        : [0.2052 0.5282 0.7701]
sample Kendall tau: 0.3683
Gumbel MLE theta : 1.5544   loglik 202.420
BIC selection    : Bicop(family='gumbel', rotation=0, parameters=[1.55436957060358])
fortvine vine copula: d = 4, trunc = 3
order: 2 3 1 4
  tree 1 edge 1: joe          rot 180 par 3.9498
  tree 1 edge 2: joe          rot 180 par 4.1778
  tree 1 edge 3: clayton      rot   0 par 3.1232
  tree 2 edge 1: clayton      rot   0 par 0.3395
  tree 2 edge 2: clayton      rot   0 par 0.6397
  tree 3 edge 1: clayton      rot   0 par 0.5037
loglik 2296.80   (truth 2308.14)   parameters 6
five draws from the fitted vine:
[[0.0767 0.0961 0.1321 0.0919]

The density and h-function values match the Fortran quick start digit for digit: both call the same compiled routines. The samples differ, because Python draws its uniforms with NumPy.

quantity \(n\) Kendall \(\hat\tau\) \(\hat\theta\) log-likelihood Gumbel pair, \(\theta = 1.5\), \(\tau = 1/3\) 1000 0.368 1.554 202.42

The selected vine is not the true one edge for edge. Its first tree is the path 2-3-1-4 rather than the star around variable 4, two of its edges are survival Joe (joe rotated by 180 degrees, which has lower tail dependence like Clayton), and the third tree picks up a little dependence. Its log-likelihood is still within 12 units of the truth's, with six parameters where the truth has five. The Fortran quick start lands on the same structure.

(a) Density of the selected Gumbel copula (colour scale clipped at 3) with 200 of the simulated pairs. (b) Variables 1 and 4 of the C-vine sample (blue) and of a simulation of the same size from the fitted vine (green). (c) The Rosenblatt transform of the sample under the fitted vine, all four coordinates pooled: close to the uniform density (gold line), as expected for a well-specified model (the pairwise Kendall \(\tau\) of the transformed coordinates are all below 0.05).

The figure is drawn by the same script: python example/python/python_quickstart.py docs/assets/python_example.png.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
python/tests/test_basic.py checks that \(h_1^{-1}(h_1(u))\) is the identity, that densities integrate to 1, that fitting recovers parameters, that selection finds the true family, that a vine's log-likelihood equals the sum of its log-densities, that the Rosenblatt transform round-trips, and that a generic family works. For the features of the typed API it checks that a weighted fit equals the fit to the sample with duplicated rows (pair copula and vine), that tll and bernstein densities are positive and integrate to 1 and their h-inverses round-trip, that a discrete vine has the density pyvinecopulib computes for the same model, that relax relaxes the non-simplified edge of a known example and keeps loglik() equal to the sum of the log-densities, that pdf_grid equals pdf, that select_trunc_lvl truncates a Markov chain, that the fit cache counts hits, that the abort flag and Ctrl-C stop a selection, that gen_flip transposes asymmetric generic copulas, and that all objects pickle. When pyvinecopulib is installed, a few densities and h-functions are compared with it (they agree to \(10^{-6}\) relative).

pip install ./python pytest scipy
pytest python/tests

docs.text:
If you use fortvine in published work, please cite

Shojaeezadeh, S. A. (2026). fortvine: a complete compendium to work on vine copula modeling. In preparation.

@unpublished{shojaeezadeh2026fortvine,
  author = {Shojaeezadeh, Shahab Aldin},
  title  = {fortvine: a complete compendium to work on vine copula modeling},
  year   = {2026},
  note   = {In preparation. Software: https://github.com/Bluerrror/fortvine}
}

fortvine.cite() prints this reference and returns it as a string.

docs.title: R package
docs.text: The R package fortvine lets you use the library from R. It is a binding, not a port: every density, distribution function, h-function, fit, family selection, vine selection, Rosenblatt transform and pseudo-observation is computed by the Fortran code through its C interface (the fvc_* routines of fortvine_capi, the C interface to the typed API). The R functions only check and convert their arguments (an n x d R matrix becomes the u(d, n) array of the C routines, family names become integer codes) and wrap the results in R objects with print, summary and logLik methods. The function names follow rvinecopulib, so code written for it needs few changes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
The package compiles the library from source with R's own toolchain, so you need a Fortran compiler that R can use:

platform what to install Windows Rtools matching your R version (Rtools43 for R 4.3, Rtools44 for R 4.4, ...). It contains gfortran. Linux gfortran, e.g. sudo apt-get install gfortran (Debian, Ubuntu) or sudo dnf install gcc-gfortran (Fedora) macOS the gfortran build that CRAN recommends for your R version (mac.r-project.org/tools)

Then, from R:

install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Bluerrror/fortvine", subdir = "r")

or, from a clone of the repository:

R CMD INSTALL r

OpenMP is used when R's compiler supports it; otherwise the library runs on one thread and gives the same results. The cores argument of each function sets the number of threads (default 1, as CRAN expects of R packages). Selection over large family sets is several times faster with more threads, e.g. cores = parallel::detectCores() %/% 2.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
A pair copula: build a model, evaluate the density and the h-function, simulate, fit and select.

library(fortvine)
cop <- bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)
u <- rbind(c(0.1, 0.1), c(0.5, 0.5), c(0.9, 0.9))
dbicop(u, cop)
#> [1] 5.370177 1.481004 2.157801
hbicop(u, 1, cop)
#> [1] 0.3562217 0.4319594 0.7703349
pbicop(u, cop)                                              # distribution function C(u1, u2)
#> [1] 0.07088812 0.37796447 0.82502865

set.seed(42)
x <- rbicop(2000, cop)
bicop(x, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0)$parameters   # fit one family and rotation
#> [1] 1.974684
bicop(x, family_set = "all")                                # select among families 0-22
#> Bivariate copula ('bicop_dist'): family = clayton (3), rotation = 0, parameters = 1.975

Families are given by their fortvine name (any case; "t" also means "student") or code. fortvine_families() lists the 111 families with their codes and numbers of parameters, read from the library. The generic families (codes \(\ge 10000\)) work everywhere a family is accepted:

fam <- fortvine_families()
table(generic = fam$code >= 10000)
#> generic
#> FALSE  TRUE
#>    26    85
bicop(x, family_set = "generic", cores = 2)
#> Bivariate copula ('bicop_dist'): family = Arch(gamma.Sibuya) (11700), rotation = 0, parameters = 1.936, 1.064

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
R function what it does computed by bicop_dist(family, rotation, parameters) pair-copula model object (checks only) dbicop(u, model, log = FALSE) density \(c(u_1, u_2)\) or \(\log c\) fvc_bicop_eval pbicop(u, model) distribution function \(C(u_1, u_2)\) fvc_bicop_eval hbicop(u, cond_var, model, inverse = FALSE) \(h_1 = \partial C / \partial u_1\), \(h_2 = \partial C / \partial u_2\) and their inverses fvc_bicop_eval rbicop(n, model) simulation \(\big(u_1, h_1^{-1}(u_1, w)\big)\) fvc_bicop_eval bicop(data, family_set, selcrit, rotation = NULL, weights, ...) select family, rotation and parameters; or, with rotation, fit one family fvc_bicop_fit bicop_par_bounds(family) parameter box of a family fvc_par_bounds gen_flip(model) generic family of the transposed copula \(C(u_2, u_1)\) fvc_gen_flip dvine_structure(order, trunc_lvl), cvine_structure(order, trunc_lvl) D-vine and C-vine structures fvc_vine_structure as_rvine_matrix(x) R-vine matrix of a structure or a vine, in original labels fvc_vine_matrix vinecop_dist(pair_copulas, structure, var_types) vine model object from pair copulas (checks only) vinecop(data, family_set, structure, selcrit, trunc_lvl, threshold, var_types, weights, ...) Dissmann selection, or families on a fixed structure fvc_vine_select dvinecop(u, vinecop) vine density fvc_vine_eval dvinecop_grid(u, vinecop, tgt, grid) vine density on a grid of one variable fvc_vine_pdf_grid rosenblatt(x, model), inverse_rosenblatt(u, model) Rosenblatt transform and its inverse fvc_vine_eval rvinecop(n, vinecop) simulation: inverse Rosenblatt of uniforms fvc_vine_eval vinecop_relax(vinecop, data, tgt, mode) non-simplified (relaxed) edges fvc_vine_relax vinecop_rel_params(vinecop, u), vinecop_unrelax(vinecop, data) parameters of the relaxed edges at given points; delete the relaxed edges fvc_vine_rel_params, (R) fitcache_enable(capacity), fitcache_clear(), fitcache_disable(), fitcache_stats() the fit cache fvc_fitcache pseudo_obs(x) ranks / \((n + 1)\), ties averaged fv_pseudo_obs fortvine_families() the 111 families: code, name, number of parameters fvc_families, fvc_fam_name logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), print(), summary() methods for fitted bicop_dist and vinecop_dist objects (stored results)

family_set takes names, codes and four groups: "all" (codes 0-22, the default set of the library), "parametric" (0-11, the parametric families of vinecopulib), "nonparametric" ("tll" and "bernstein", codes 24 and 25) and "generic" (the 85 generic families); a list combines them, e.g. list("all", "nonparametric"). selcrit is one of "loglik", "aic", "bic", "mbic" and "mbicv".

The controls are arguments of bicop() and vinecop(), with the defaults of fv_controls:

argument control values par_method method "mle", "itau" selcrit, psi0 selcrit, psi0 see above; psi0 in \((0, 1)\) presel, allow_rotations, fast_mle preselect, allow_rotations, fast_mle TRUE / FALSE tau_mode tau_mode "exact" (default), "approx", "auto" weights observation weights n non-negative numbers tree_crit, tree_algorithm (vines) tree_crit, tree_algo "tau", "rho", "joe", "hoeffd", "xi", "mi", "ferreira"; "mst_prim", "mst_kruskal" trunc_lvl (vines) trunc_lvl; NA sets select_trunc a number, Inf (all trees) or NA threshold (vines) threshold; NA sets select_threshold in \([0, 1]\), or NA var_types (vines) discrete variables "c" or "d" per variable cores nthreads number of threads, default 1

As in rvinecopulib, trunc_lvl = NA and threshold = NA let the data choose the truncation level and the threshold (by mBICv, see Truncation and Thresholding).

Random numbers. rbicop() and rvinecop() draw their uniforms with R's runif(), so set.seed() makes them reproducible. They do not use the counter-based generator behind the seed argument of fv_vinecop%simulate, so the same seed gives different samples in R and in Fortran. The randomised Rosenblatt transform of discrete variables takes its seed from R's generator, so it follows set.seed() too.

Not exposed. The abort flag (fvc_set_abort) has no R function: R cannot run code while the library computes, so there is nothing to call it from. Everything else of the Fortran API has an R function, including vinecop_rel_params() (the per-sample parameters of relaxed edges) and vinecop_unrelax().

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Daily log returns of four European stock indices, 1991-1998 (EuStockMarkets, shipped with R): first a pair copula for DAX and CAC, then a vine for all four indices.

library(fortvine)
x <- diff(log(EuStockMarkets))          # daily log returns of DAX, SMI, CAC, FTSE
u <- pseudo_obs(x)
dim(u)
#> [1] 1859    4

pair <- bicop(u[, c("DAX", "CAC")], family_set = "all", cores = 2)
summary(pair)
#>   family code rotation    parameters npars   loglik
#> 1    bb1    7      180 0.3035, 1.771     2 709.9664
c(AIC = AIC(pair), BIC = BIC(pair))
#>       AIC       BIC
#> -1415.933 -1404.877

The DAX-CAC pair is a survival BB1 copula (rotation 180), which has a stronger lower tail than upper tail: large joint losses are more common than large joint gains. The vine:

fit <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", cores = 2)
fit
#> Vine copula ('vinecop_dist'): d = 4, trunc_lvl = 3, order = 2 1 3 4
#>   npars = 11, loglik = 2038.51 (n = 1859)
#>  tree edge conditioned conditioning   family rotation    parameters
#>     1    1    SMI, DAX                   bb3        0 1.577, 0.2891
#>     1    2    DAX, CAC                   bb1      180 0.3035, 1.771
#>     1    3   CAC, FTSE                   bb1      180 0.2627, 1.607
#>     2    1    SMI, CAC          DAX  student        0 0.2101,  11.9
#>     2    2   DAX, FTSE          CAC  student        0 0.3204, 10.88
#>     3    1   SMI, FTSE     DAX, CAC plackett        0          1.87

Tree 1 is the path SMI - DAX - CAC - FTSE. summary(fit) returns the same table as a data frame, with the log-likelihood of each edge. The vine log-likelihood is the sum of the edge log-likelihoods, and the density routine reproduces it:

c(loglik = fit$loglik, sum_log_density = sum(log(dvinecop(u, fit))), npars = fit$npars)
#>          loglik sum_log_density           npars
#>        2038.507        2038.507          11.000

If the model fits, the Rosenblatt transform \(w = T(u)\) has independent uniform columns, and the inverse transform recovers \(u\):

w <- rosenblatt(u, fit)
round(cor(w, method = "kendall"), 3)
#>       [,1]   [,2]  [,3]   [,4]
#> [1,] 1.000  0.008 0.011  0.003
#> [2,] 0.008  1.000 0.007 -0.004
#> [3,] 0.011  0.007 1.000  0.002
#> [4,] 0.003 -0.004 0.002  1.000
max(abs(inverse_rosenblatt(w, fit) - u))
#> [1] 6.448175e-13

set.seed(1)
round(rvinecop(3, fit), 4)
#>        [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
#> [1,] 0.2132 0.6958 0.6235 0.0618
#> [2,] 0.2926 0.1680 0.4114 0.2060
#> [3,] 0.3630 0.6858 0.3562 0.1766

The figure is drawn by tools/r_example.R with the package. Panel (a) is the density of the selected DAX-CAC pair copula in normal scores, \(c\big(\Phi(z_1), \Phi(z_2)\big)\, \varphi(z_1)\varphi(z_2)\); panel (b) compares the DAX-FTSE returns with a sample of the same size simulated from the vine (DAX and FTSE are not neighbours in tree 1, so this pair is modelled through the higher trees); panel (c) shows two columns of the Rosenblatt transform.

The EuStockMarkets vine fitted from R: (a) the selected DAX-CAC pair copula, (b) data and vine simulation, (c) Rosenblatt-transformed data.

docs.title: Nonparametric families and weights
docs.text:
TLL and Bernstein copulas are fitted like any other family. Their estimate is kept in the model ($aux, 933 numbers) and used by every function that evaluates it; npars is the effective number of degrees of freedom, which logLik(), AIC() and BIC() use. For the DAX-CAC pair the parametric BB1 copula is preferred:

tl <- bicop(u[, c("DAX", "CAC")], family_set = "tll")
tl
#> Bivariate copula ('bicop_dist'): family = tll (24), rotation = 0, parameters = none (nonparametric, edf 65.1)
c(edf = tl$npars, loglik = tl$loglik, AIC = AIC(tl))
#>        edf     loglik        AIC
#>    65.0559   743.3251 -1356.5385
bicop(u[, c("DAX", "CAC")], family_set = list("all", "nonparametric"), cores = 2)$family
#> [1] "bb1"

Observation weights enter every pair fit (and the weighted tree criteria of vinecop()); here the second half of the sample counts three times:

wts <- rep(c(1, 3), c(930, 929))
bicop(u[, c("DAX", "CAC")], family_set = "student", rotation = 0, weights = wts)$parameters
#> [1] 0.7342719 6.6380788
bicop(u[, c("DAX", "CAC")], family_set = "student", rotation = 0)$parameters
#> [1] 0.7226908 6.4391172

docs.title: Structures, truncation and thresholding
docs.text:
as_rvine_matrix() gives the R-vine matrix of vinecopulib in original labels: the anti-diagonal holds order, and row t of column e the partner of order[e] in tree t. cvine_structure(order) makes the last element of order the root of the first tree, as set_cvine does (and as rvinecopulib's cvine_structure). With a fixed structure only the families and parameters are selected:

as_rvine_matrix(fit)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
#> [1,]    1    3    4    4
#> [2,]    3    4    3    0
#> [3,]    4    1    0    0
#> [4,]    2    0    0    0
cv <- cvine_structure(c(4, 3, 2, 1))      # DAX (variable 1) is the root of tree 1
fc <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", structure = cv, cores = 2)
summary(fc)[, c("tree", "conditioned", "conditioning", "family")]
#>   tree conditioned conditioning   family
#> 1    1    CAC, DAX                   bb1
#> 2    1    SMI, DAX                   bb3
#> 3    1   DAX, FTSE                   bb1
#> 4    2    CAC, SMI          DAX  student
#> 5    2   SMI, FTSE          DAX plackett
#> 6    3   CAC, FTSE     DAX, SMI plackett

trunc_lvl = NA and threshold = NA select both by mBICv. On these returns the sparse vine keeps tree 1 only:

sp <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", selcrit = "mbicv", trunc_lvl = NA, threshold = NA, cores = 2)
c(trunc = sp$trunc, threshold = sp$threshold, npars = sp$npars, loglik = sp$loglik)
#>        trunc    threshold        npars       loglik
#>    1.0000000    0.4370411    6.0000000 1846.5384662

docs.title: Discrete margins
docs.text:
Discrete variables follow rvinecopulib: var_types marks each variable "c" or "d", and the data have d + k columns, the d columns \(F_j(x_j)\) followed by the columns \(F_j(x_j^-)\) of the k discrete variables (see Discrete and mixed data). The flags are stored in the model ($var_types), and dvinecop(), rosenblatt() and dvinecop_grid() of that model expect the same layout. A latent Gaussian vector whose third variable is observed only as a count with four levels:

set.seed(2)
z <- matrix(rnorm(3000), 1000, 3) %*% chol(matrix(c(1, .7, .5, .7, 1, .6, .5, .6, 1), 3))
cnt <- findInterval(z[, 3], c(-1, 0, 1))       # variable 3 observed as a count 0..3
Fc <- ecdf(cnt)
xd <- cbind(pseudo_obs(z[, 1:2]), Fc(cnt) * 1000 / 1001, Fc(cnt - 1) * 1000 / 1001)
vd <- vinecop(xd, family_set = "parametric", var_types = c("c", "c", "d"))
vd
#> Vine copula ('vinecop_dist'): d = 3, trunc_lvl = 2, order = 1 2 3
#>   npars = 3, loglik = 560.78 (n = 1000)
#>   discrete variables: 3
#>  tree edge conditioned conditioning   family rotation parameters
#>     1    1        1, 2              gaussian        0     0.7211
#>     1    2        2, 3              gaussian        0     0.6013
#>     2    1        1, 3            2   gumbel        0      1.085
c(loglik = vd$loglik, sum_log_density = sum(log(dvinecop(xd, vd))))
#>          loglik sum_log_density
#>        560.7824        560.7824

rosenblatt() returns Brockwell's randomised transform for the discrete columns, so every column is uniform under the model (mean \(1/2\), variance \(1/12 \approx 0.0833\)); randomize_discrete = FALSE returns \(F(x \mid \cdot)\) instead:

set.seed(3)
r <- rosenblatt(xd, vd)
round(rbind(mean = colMeans(r), var = apply(r, 2, var)), 4)
#>        [,1]   [,2]   [,3]
#> mean 0.5016 0.4991 0.5014
#> var  0.0813 0.0840 0.0831

inverse_rosenblatt() and rvinecop() work on the copula scale; discrete observations follow from the marginal quantile functions.

docs.title: Density on a grid
docs.text:
dvinecop_grid(u, vinecop, tgt, grid) evaluates the density at every row of u with variable tgt replaced by each grid value (pdf_grid of the library, which evaluates the edges that do not involve tgt once per row instead of once per point). The values are those of dvinecop() at the same points:

grid <- c(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95)
dvinecop_grid(u[1:2, ], fit, tgt = 4, grid = grid)
#>          [,1]     [,2]      [,3]      [,4]       [,5]
#> [1,] 1.578372 1.308332 0.5737784 0.2176129 0.04716697
#> [2,] 7.241727 1.895510 0.6856401 0.2816178 0.07218052
dvinecop(cbind(u[1, 1], u[1, 2], u[1, 3], grid), fit)
#> [1] 1.57837176 1.30833193 0.57377844 0.21761289 0.04716697

For a discrete tgt, pass the \(F(x^-)\) values of the grid as grid_minus.

docs.title: Non-simplified vines
docs.text:
vinecop_relax(vinecop, data, tgt, mode) lets the parameters of edges in trees \(t \ge 2\) vary with their conditioning variables (see Non-simplified edges). mode = 1 relaxes only the edges whose test of constant conditional correlation rejects; mode = 2 relaxes every eligible edge. The relaxed edges are stored in $relaxed and used by dvinecop() and dvinecop_grid(); the Rosenblatt transforms and rvinecop() use the middle-anchor parameters, as the library does. Each relaxed edge counts its parameters at four more anchors in npars. On the stock returns the test relaxes nothing, and relaxing all three eligible edges raises the log-likelihood by 14 for 20 more parameters, which AIC does not support:

is.null(vinecop_relax(fit, u, tgt = 0, mode = 1)$relaxed)
#> [1] TRUE
rel <- vinecop_relax(fit, u, tgt = 0, mode = 2)
rel$relaxed$erel                                 # edge (row 1) and tree (row 2)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    2    1
#> [2,]    2    2    3
c(loglik = rel$loglik, npars = rel$npars, sum_log_density = sum(log(dvinecop(u, rel))))
#>          loglik           npars sum_log_density
#>        2052.445          31.000        2052.445
c(AIC_simplified = AIC(fit), AIC_relaxed = AIC(rel))
#> AIC_simplified    AIC_relaxed
#>      -4055.014      -4042.889

Relaxing is not available for vines with discrete variables.

docs.title: Fit cache and parameter bounds
docs.text:
The fit cache stores every pair fit, so repeated selections on the same data reuse them, here a second selection with another tree criterion:

fitcache_enable(20000)
f1 <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", cores = 2)
f2 <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", tree_crit = "rho", cores = 2)
fitcache_stats()
#>   hits misses   used
#>    148    254    254
fitcache_disable()
bicop_par_bounds("bb1")
#>       [,1] [,2]
#> lower    0    1
#> upper    7    7

docs.title: From rvinecopulib
docs.text:
The names and the main arguments are those of rvinecopulib, including var_types with the d + k data layout for discrete variables, weights, and trunc_lvl = NA / threshold = NA for automatic selection. The differences:

  • families use fortvine names and codes (fortvine_families()), and family_set = "all" means the hand-coded parametric families 0-22;
  • vine structures are stored in the natural-order arrays of fortvine (order, struct_array[edge, tree], see Vine copulas); as_rvine_matrix() converts them to an R-vine matrix, but an R-vine matrix cannot be passed as structure;
  • bicop() accepts rotation to fit a single family with a fixed rotation, and has no var_types (fit a two-dimensional vine for a pair with discrete margins);
  • vinecop_relax(), dvinecop_grid() and the fit cache have no rvinecopulib counterpart.

docs.title: Citing
docs.text:
If you use fortvine, from R or otherwise, please cite:

Shojaeezadeh, S. A. (2026). fortvine: a complete compendium to work on vine copula modeling. In preparation. Software: https://github.com/Bluerrror/fortvine

In R, citation("fortvine") prints this reference and a BibTeX entry.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
This section lists every public entity of the Fortran module fortvine_api with its exact signature. For explanations, defaults in context and worked examples see the User manual; for the bind(C) routines see the C interface.

use fortvine_api

All reals are real(kind(1.0d0)) (written real(dp) below). Array arguments are assumed-shape. Data matrices are u(n, d) with one row per observation.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text: page entities fv_bicop the pair-copula type: fields; pdf, logpdf, cdf, hfunc1, hfunc2, hinv1, hinv2, fit, select, npars, npars_eff fv_vinecop the vine-copula type: fields; init, set_dvine, set_cvine, select, pdf, pdf_grid, loglik, rosenblatt, inverse_rosenblatt, simulate, npars, npars_eff, matrix, print, relax, unrelax, rel_params fv_controls the options record Functions fv_threads, fv_kendall_tau, fv_dependence, fv_tau_mat, fv_pseudo_obs_nd, fv_par_bounds, fv_fam_name, fv_generic_families, fam_is_np, gen_is, gen_valid, gen_dup, gen_npar, gen_exch, gen_lt, gen_ut, gen_flip, fv_fitcache_enable, fv_fitcache_capacity, fv_fitcache_clear, fv_fitcache_disable, fv_fitcache_stats Family codes and constants FV_* family codes, family sets, FV_NFAM, FV_NCLASSIC, NAUX, selection criteria, methods, tree criteria, tree algorithms, tau modes

docs.title: Reading the argument tables
docs.text:
Each routine is documented with its Fortran interface, then a table with one row per dummy argument:

column content name dummy-argument name, usable as a keyword (call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed=.false.)) type declared type and rank, e.g. real(dp)(:, :) intent in, out, inout; optional arguments are marked description meaning, shape requirements, defaults

For type-bound procedures the passed object (self) is omitted from the table: call cop%pdf(u1, u2, out) passes cop as self.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text: The library does not return error codes from evaluation routines. Inputs outside \((0, 1)\) are clamped to \([10^{-10}, 1 - 10^{-10}]\), parameters outside a family's domain are clipped to the nearest admissible value, and failed likelihood terms are replaced by a very small log-density. fv_vinecop%select has an optional info output, and fv_vinecop%rosenblatt stops with error stop if a vine with discrete variables is called without u_minus. Array extents are not checked beyond what the compiler does; pass output arrays of the documented shape.

docs.title: Thread safety
docs.text:
The routines keep no hidden state, with two exceptions:

  • the fit cache (fv_fitcache_*) is a single global table. Concurrent fits share it safely (lookups and stores are serialised), but enabling, clearing or disabling it while fits run elsewhere is not safe;
  • fv_vinecop%simulate draws from the intrinsic random_number generator and, with seed, reseeds it, which affects the rest of the program and other threads using that generator.

docs.title: fv_bicop
docs.text:
A bivariate (pair) copula. Manual: Pair copulas.

type, public :: fv_bicop
  integer  :: family   = FV_INDEP
  integer  :: rotation = 0
  real(dp) :: par(3)   = 0.0_dp
  real(dp) :: loglik   = 0.0_dp
  real(dp), allocatable :: aux(:)        ! nonparametric estimate (tll, bernstein)
contains
  procedure :: pdf, logpdf, cdf, hfunc1, hfunc2, hinv1, hinv2
  procedure :: fit, select, npars, npars_eff
end type fv_bicop

docs.title: Fields
docs.text: name type default description family integer FV_INDEP family code, see constants and the catalogue rotation integer 0 0, 90, 180 or 270; ignored by rotationless families par real(dp)(3) 0 parameters, first npars() used loglik real(dp) 0 log-likelihood of the last fit / select (weighted if weights were given) aux real(dp), allocatable (:) unallocated TLL / Bernstein estimate. Allocated by fit (length NAUX for TLL / Bernstein, else 1) and select (length NAUX if the family set contains 24 or 25, else 1)

docs.title: pdf
docs.text:
subroutine pdf(self, u1, u2, out)
  class(fv_bicop), intent(in) :: self
  real(dp), intent(in)  :: u1(:), u2(:)
  real(dp), intent(out) :: out(:)
name type intent description u1, u2 real(dp)(:) in evaluation points, same length \(m\) out real(dp)(:) out copula density \(c(u_1, u_2)\), length \(m\); never below tiny(1.0_dp) 
call cop%pdf([0.2_dp, 0.8_dp], [0.3_dp, 0.9_dp], dens)

docs.title: logpdf
docs.text:
subroutine logpdf(self, u1, u2, out)

Same arguments as pdf; out \(= \log c(u_1, u_2)\), computed directly in log space (no floor).

docs.title: cdf
docs.text:
subroutine cdf(self, u1, u2, out)

Same arguments as pdf; out \(= C(u_1, u_2)\). Closed form for every family except the Student copula (Gauss-Legendre quadrature of \(h_1\), accuracy about \(10^{-6}\)). Runs on the OpenMP default team.

docs.title: hfunc1, hfunc2
docs.text:
subroutine hfunc1(self, u1, u2, out)
subroutine hfunc2(self, u1, u2, out)
name type intent description u1, u2 real(dp)(:) in points out real(dp)(:) out hfunc1: \(\partial C/\partial u_1 = P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1)\); hfunc2: \(\partial C/\partial u_2 = P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2)\)

docs.title: hinv1, hinv2
docs.text:
subroutine hinv1(self, u1, u2, out)
subroutine hinv2(self, u1, u2, out)
name type intent description u1 real(dp)(:) in hinv1: conditioning value \(u_1\); hinv2: level \(w\) u2 real(dp)(:) in hinv1: level \(w\); hinv2: conditioning value \(u_2\) out real(dp)(:) out hinv1: \(v\) with \(h_1(u_1, v) = w\); hinv2: \(v\) with \(h_2(v, u_2) = w\) 
call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
call cop%hinv1(u1, w, u2)          ! (u1, u2) is a sample of the copula

docs.title: fit
docs.text:
subroutine fit(self, u1, u2, ctl, weights)
  class(fv_bicop), intent(inout) :: self
  real(dp), intent(in) :: u1(:), u2(:)
  type(fv_controls), intent(in), optional :: ctl
  real(dp), intent(in), optional :: weights(:)

Estimates par (and aux for TLL / Bernstein) for the current family and rotation.

name type intent description u1, u2 real(dp)(:) in pseudo-observations, length \(n\) ctl type(fv_controls) in, optional uses method, fast_mle, tau_mode, nthreads; default fv_controls() weights real(dp)(:) in, optional observation weights, length \(n\)

Sets par, loglik, aux. FV_ITAU is only meaningful for families 0 to 6; see the warning in the manual.

cop%family = FV_BB1; cop%rotation = 0
call cop%fit(u1, u2)

docs.title: select
docs.text:
subroutine select(self, u1, u2, ctl, weights)
  class(fv_bicop), intent(inout) :: self
  real(dp), intent(in) :: u1(:), u2(:)
  type(fv_controls), intent(in), optional :: ctl
  real(dp), intent(in), optional :: weights(:)

Chooses family, rotation and par among ctl%family_set(1:ctl%nfam).

name type intent description u1, u2 real(dp)(:) in pseudo-observations, length \(n\) ctl type(fv_controls) in, optional uses family_set, nfam, selcrit, psi0, method, fast_mle, preselect, allow_rotations, tau_mode, nthreads weights real(dp)(:) in, optional observation weights, length \(n\)

Sets family, rotation, par, loglik and aux.

type(fv_controls) :: ctl
ctl%selcrit = FV_AIC
call cop%select(u1, u2, ctl)

docs.title: npars
docs.text:
integer function npars(self)

Number of parameters of family: 0 (independence), 1, 2 or 3 (for generic codes gen_npar); for TLL / Bernstein the rounded effective degrees of freedom.

docs.title: npars_eff
docs.text:
real(dp) function npars_eff(self)

As npars, as a real number; for TLL / Bernstein the unrounded effective degrees of freedom aux(2) (0 before a fit).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
type(fv_bicop) :: cop
real(dp) :: d(1)
cop%family = FV_JOE; cop%rotation = 90; cop%par(1) = 2.5_dp
call cop%pdf([0.9_dp], [0.1_dp], d)

A complete program is in the manual.

docs.title: Family codes and constants
docs.text: All constants are integer, parameter, public in fortvine_api unless stated otherwise.

docs.title: Hand-coded families
docs.text:
constant code name (FV_FAMILY_NAME) parameters rotations FV_INDEP 0 indep 0 no FV_GAUSSIAN 1 gaussian 1 no FV_STUDENT 2 student 2 no FV_CLAYTON 3 clayton 1 yes FV_GUMBEL 4 gumbel 1 yes FV_FRANK 5 frank 1 no FV_JOE 6 joe 1 yes FV_BB1 7 bb1 2 yes FV_BB6 8 bb6 2 yes FV_BB7 9 bb7 2 yes FV_BB8 10 bb8 2 yes FV_TAWN 11 tawn 3 yes FV_PLACKETT 12 plackett 1 no FV_FGM 13 fgm 1 no FV_AMH 14 amh 1 no FV_GALAMBOS 15 galambos 1 yes FV_HUSLER_REISS 16 husler_reiss 1 yes FV_BB2 17 bb2 2 yes FV_BB3 18 bb3 2 yes FV_BB5 19 bb5 2 yes FV_BB9 20 bb9 2 yes FV_BB10 21 bb10 2 yes FV_BB4 22 bb4 2 yes FV_TEV 23 tev 2 yes FV_TLL 24 tll effective df no FV_BERNSTEIN 25 bernstein effective df no

Codes 0 to 11 are the parametric families that vinecopulib also provides (FV_PARAMETRIC). The parameter order and boxes are in the catalogue and in Pair copulas.

character(len=12), parameter, public :: FV_FAMILY_NAME(0:25)

Lower-case names of codes 0 to 25. For any code, including generic ones, use fv_fam_name.

docs.title: Generic families
docs.text:
Codes \(\ge 10000\) are built by the generic engine:

\[ \texttt{fam} = 10000\,k + 100\,\text{og} + \text{ie}, \]

with \(k \in \{1, 2\}\) (plain / Khoudraji), og the outer generator (0 to 7, 11 to 26) and ie the inner Pickands function (0 to 13). There is no named constant per generic code; fv_generic_families returns the list.

docs.title: Family sets and sizes
docs.text:
constant value meaning FV_ALL [0, 1, ..., 23] (24 codes) every hand-coded parametric family FV_PARAMETRIC [0, 1, ..., 11] (12 codes) vinecopulib's parametric set FV_NONPAR [24, 25] TLL and Bernstein FV_ONE_PAR [1, 3, 4, 5, 6] the one-parameter families with closed-form fits and Kendall's \(\tau\) inversion FV_NCLASSIC 26 number of hand-coded codes (0 to 25) FV_NFAM 192 capacity of fv_controls%family_set NAUX 933 length of the aux vector of TLL / Bernstein (\(3 + 30 + 30 \cdot 30\))

The default family set of fv_controls is family_set(1:23) = [0, ..., 22], that is FV_ALL without t-EV.

docs.title: Selection criteria (fv_controls%selcrit)
docs.text: constant value FV_LOGLIK 0 FV_AIC 1 FV_BIC 2 FV_MBIC 3 FV_MBICV 4

docs.title: Estimation methods (fv_controls%method)
docs.text: constant value FV_MLE 0 maximum likelihood FV_ITAU 1 Kendall's \(\tau\) inversion (families 0 to 6)

docs.title: Tree criteria (fv_controls%tree_crit, fv_dependence)
docs.text: constant value measure FV_TREE_TAU 0 Kendall's \(\tau\) FV_TREE_RHO 1 Spearman's \(\rho\) FV_TREE_JOE 2 \(-\tfrac12\log(1 - r^2)\) of the normal scores FV_TREE_HOEFFD 3 Hoeffding's \(D\) FV_TREE_XI 4 symmetrised Chatterjee \(\xi\) FV_TREE_MI 5 mutual information (KSG) FV_TREE_FERREIRA 6 Ferreira's tail-dependence coefficient

docs.title: Tree algorithms (fv_controls%tree_algo)
docs.text: constant value FV_PRIM 0 FV_KRUSKAL 1

docs.title: Tau modes (fv_controls%tau_mode)
docs.text: constant value FV_TAU_AUTO 0 exact for \(n < 800\), approximate above FV_TAU_EXACT 1 exact \(\tau_b\) FV_TAU_APPROX 2 \(\tfrac2\pi\arcsin\) of the normal-score correlation

docs.title: Rotations
docs.text: Rotations are plain integers: 0, 90, 180, 270 (degrees, counter-clockwise). There are no named constants. See Rotations and asymmetry.

docs.title: Kernel module
docs.text: The kernel module fortvine additionally exports fv_abort (logical, public, volatile, default .false.), the host abort flag described in Fitting. It is not re-exported by fortvine_api; use fortvine, only: fv_abort to reach it.

docs.title: fv_controls
docs.text:
Options of fitting and selection. Manual: Controls.

type, public :: fv_controls
  integer  :: family_set(FV_NFAM) = [FV_ALL, FV_NONPAR, spread(0, 1, FV_NFAM - FV_NCLASSIC)]
  integer  :: nfam = size(FV_ALL) - 1        ! 23: codes 0..22
  integer  :: selcrit = FV_BIC
  integer  :: method = FV_MLE
  integer  :: tree_crit = FV_TREE_TAU
  integer  :: tree_algo = FV_PRIM
  integer  :: tau_mode = FV_TAU_EXACT
  integer  :: trunc_lvl = -1                 ! -1 = d - 1
  integer  :: nthreads = 0                   ! 0 = FORTVINE_THREADS or half the logical CPUs
  logical  :: preselect = .true.
  logical  :: allow_rotations = .true.
  logical  :: fast_mle = .false.
  real(dp) :: threshold = 0.0_dp

real(dp) function fv_dependence(x, y, kind, weights)
  real(dp), intent(in) :: x(:), y(:)
  integer, intent(in) :: kind
  real(dp), intent(in), optional :: weights(:)
name type intent description x, y real(dp)(:) in pseudo-observations of equal length \(n\) kind integer in FV_TREE_TAU, FV_TREE_RHO, FV_TREE_JOE, FV_TREE_HOEFFD, FV_TREE_XI, FV_TREE_MI, FV_TREE_FERREIRA weights real(dp)(n) in, optional observation weights; used by \(\tau\), \(\rho\) and Joe only

The absolute value of the dependence measure that vine selection uses as edge weight, see tree_crit. Returns 0 for \(n \le 10\).

program funcs_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 1000
  real(dp) :: x(n, 3), u(n, 3), tm(3, 3)
  character(len=8) :: kinds(0:6) = [character(len=8) :: 'tau', 'rho', 'joe', 'hoeffd', 'xi', 'mi', 'ferreira']
  integer :: k, i

  call random_seed(put=[(7 * i, i = 1, 33)])
  call random_number(x)
  x(:, 2) = x(:, 1) + 0.3_dp * x(:, 2)              ! monotone dependence
  x(:, 3) = (x(:, 1) - 0.5_dp)**2 + 0.02_dp * x(:, 3)   ! non-monotone dependence
  call fv_pseudo_obs_nd(x, u)
  call fv_tau_mat(u, tm)
  print '(a,3f8.3)', 'tau matrix row 1:', tm(1, :)
  do k = 0, 6
    print '(a8,a,f7.3,a,f7.3)', kinds(k), '  (1,2):', fv_dependence(u(:, 1), u(:, 2), k), &
      '   (1,3):', fv_dependence(u(:, 1), u(:, 3), k)
  end do
end program funcs_demo

Output:

tau matrix row 1:   1.000   0.818  -0.087
tau       (1,2):  0.818   (1,3):  0.087
rho       (1,2):  0.961   (1,3):  0.098
joe       (1,2):  1.005   (1,3):  0.003
hoeffd    (1,2):  0.724   (1,3):  0.214
xi        (1,2):  0.753   (1,3):  0.892
mi        (1,2):  1.321   (1,3):  2.389
ferreira  (1,2):  0.855   (1,3):  0.103

The pair (1, 3) is a noisy parabola: strongly dependent but almost unconcordant. Kendall's \(\tau\), Spearman's \(\rho\) and the Gaussian measure joe barely see it; Chatterjee's \(\xi\), mutual information and Hoeffding's \(D\) do.

type, public :: fv_vinecop
  integer :: d = 0

  integer, intent(in), optional :: trunc
