docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Every example is a complete, short program in the repository's example/ directory. The first four also come as Python and R scripts (example/python/, example/r/) that use the Python and R packages; each page shows the three versions in language tabs. The Fortran programs are compiled by

bash build.sh examples        # -> build/ex01_pair_copula, build/ex02_vine, ...

and run from anywhere (./build/ex02_vine); the scripts with python example/python/ex02_vine.py and Rscript example/r/ex02_vine.R. The outputs shown on these pages are copied from real runs on Windows 11 with gfortran 16.1 (WinLibs), OMP_NUM_THREADS=4, Python 3.14 and R 4.3.2.

Page Program What it shows Pair copula basics example/ex01_pair_copula.f90, python/ex01_pair_copula.py, r/ex01_pair_copula.R density, simulation by inverse h-function, MLE of a given family, family selection by BIC Vine copula workflow example/ex02_vine.f90, python/ex02_vine.py, r/ex02_vine.R simulate from a known D-vine, select a regular vine, density, Rosenblatt transform, new samples Generic families example/ex03_generic_families.f90, python/ex03_generic_families.py, r/ex03_generic_families.R the 85 generic family codes, an Archimax copula, an asymmetric Khoudraji copula, selection among all 109 parametric families Tail dependence and asymmetry example/ex04_tails.f90, python/ex04_tails.py, r/ex04_tails.R tail coefficients from family formulas, from the copula CDF at finite levels and from samples; what BIC selects Weighted and discrete data example/ex05_weights_discrete.f90 observation weights (time decay, duplicated rows) and a vine with a Poisson count variable Calling fortvine from Python and C example/python/fortvine_ctypes.py, example/c/bicop.c the bind(C) API through ctypes + numpy, and from a C program

Random numbers and reproducibility

Every program fixes its seeds (random_seed(put=...) or the seed= argument of fv_vinecop%simulate in Fortran, np.random.default_rng(seed) and seed= in Python, set.seed() in R), so it prints the same numbers every time with the same compiler and package. The three languages draw their uniforms from different generators, though, so the numbers that depend on a simulated sample differ between the Fortran, Python and R versions of an example; deterministic quantities (densities, h-functions, exact tail coefficients) agree to the printed digits.

The remaining programs in example/ (bench.f90, famspeed.f90, fitspeed.f90, selspeed.f90) are timing drivers used for the benchmarks.

docs.title: Generic families
docs.text:
Program: example/ex03_generic_families.f90, example/python/ex03_generic_families.py, example/r/ex03_generic_families.R  ·  Topics: generic family codes, fv_generic_families, fv_par_bounds, gen_npar, Archimax copulas, Khoudraji asymmetrisation, selection over all families.

Besides the 26 hand-coded families (codes 0-25), fortvine contains a generic engine that assembles pair copulas from building blocks: an outer generator, an inner (Pickands) function, and optionally a Khoudraji asymmetrisation. It contributes 85 families that are not available under another code, which brings the total to 111. This program lists some of them, fits two, and runs a selection over everything.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
! ex03_generic_families -- the generic engine (codes 10000+): list the families, use an Archimax
! copula and an asymmetric Khoudraji copula, and select among classic + generic families.
program ex03_generic_families
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer :: ns
  integer, allocatable :: seed(:)
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 3000
  type(fv_bicop) :: truth, fitted, chosen
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  integer, allocatable :: codes(:)
  real(dp) :: u1(n), w(n), u2(n), lo(3), hi(3)
  integer :: k

  codes = fv_generic_families()                      ! the 85 new families (duplicates excluded)
  print '(a,i0,a)', 'generic families: ', size(codes), '; the first five:'
  do k = 1, 5
    call fv_par_bounds(codes(k), lo, hi)
    print '(i7,2x,a40,a,i0,a)', codes(k), fv_fam_name(codes(k)), '  (', gen_npar(codes(k)), ' parameters)'
  end do

  ! Archimax(gamma | Husler-Reiss) = code 10203: gamma (Clayton) generator, Husler-Reiss Pickands
  truth%family = 10203; truth%par = [1.0_dp, 1.5_dp, 0.0_dp]
  call random_seed(size=ns); allocate(seed(ns)); seed = 20261116; call random_seed(put=seed)   ! reproducible sample
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  call truth%hinv1(u1, w, u2)
  fitted%family = 10203
  call fitted%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,a,a,2f8.3)', 'fitted ', trim(fv_fam_name(fitted%family)), ':', fitted%par(1:2)

  ! Khoudraji-Clayton = code 20200: asymmetric, C(u,v) = u^(1-a) v^(1-b) Clayton(u^a, v^b)
  truth%family = 20200; truth%par = [2.0_dp, 0.6_dp, 0.95_dp]
  call truth%hinv1(u1, w, u2)
  fitted%family = 20200
  call fitted%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,3f8.3)', 'fitted Khoudraji-Clayton (theta, a, b):', fitted%par

  ! selection among every parametric family + every generic family
  ctl%nfam = 24 + size(codes); ctl%family_set = 0
  ctl%family_set(1:24) = FV_ALL; ctl%family_set(25:ctl%nfam) = codes
  call chosen%select(u1, u2, ctl)
  print '(a,a,a,i0)', 'selected among all families: ', trim(fv_fam_name(chosen%family)), '  rotation ', chosen%rotation
end program ex03_generic_families

"""ex03_generic_families -- the generic engine (codes 10000+): list the families, use an Archimax
copula and an asymmetric Khoudraji copula, and select among classic + generic families.

The Python version of example/ex03_generic_families.f90 (pip install ./python).
"""
import numpy as np

import fortvine as fv

n = 3000

codes = [f.code for f in fv.families() if f.code >= 10000]     # the 85 new families
print(f"generic families: {len(codes)}; the first five:")
for f in fv.families():
    if f.code in codes[:5]:
        print(f"{f.code:7d}  {f.name:<40s}  ({f.npars} parameters)")

# Archimax(gamma | Husler-Reiss) = code 10203: gamma (Clayton) generator, Husler-Reiss Pickands
rng = np.random.default_rng(20261116)                          # reproducible sample
u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
truth = fv.Bicop(10203, 0, [1.0, 1.5])
u = np.column_stack([u1, truth.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))])
fitted = fv.Bicop(10203).fit(u)
print(f"fitted {fitted.family}:" + "".join(f"{p:8.3f}" for p in fitted.parameters))

# Khoudraji-Clayton = code 20200: asymmetric, C(u,v) = u^(1-a) v^(1-b) Clayton(u^a, v^b)
truth = fv.Bicop(20200, 0, [2.0, 0.6, 0.95])
u = np.column_stack([u1, truth.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))])
fitted = fv.Bicop(20200).fit(u)
print("fitted Khoudraji-Clayton (theta, a, b):" + "".join(f"{p:8.3f}" for p in fitted.parameters))

# selection among every parametric family + every generic family
chosen = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=list(range(24)) + codes, num_threads=4)
print(f"selected among all families: {chosen.family}  rotation {chosen.rotation}")

# ex03_generic_families -- the generic engine (codes 10000+): list the families, use an Archimax
# copula and an asymmetric Khoudraji copula, and select among classic + generic families.
# The R version of example/ex03_generic_families.f90 (R CMD INSTALL r).
library(fortvine)
n <- 3000

fam <- fortvine_families()
gen <- fam[fam$code >= 10000, ]                                # the 85 new families
cat("generic families: ", nrow(gen), "; the first five:\n", sep = "")
for (k in 1:5)
  cat(sprintf("%7d  %-40s  (%d parameters)\n", gen$code[k], gen$name[k], gen$npars[k]))

# Archimax(gamma | Husler-Reiss) = code 10203: gamma (Clayton) generator, Husler-Reiss Pickands
set.seed(20261116)                                             # reproducible sample
u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
truth <- bicop_dist(10203, 0, c(1.0, 1.5))
u <- cbind(u1, hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, truth, inverse = TRUE))
fitted <- bicop(u, family_set = 10203, rotation = 0)
cat("fitted ", fitted$family, ":", sprintf("%8.3f", fitted$parameters), "\n", sep = "")

# Khoudraji-Clayton = code 20200: asymmetric, C(u,v) = u^(1-a) v^(1-b) Clayton(u^a, v^b)
truth <- bicop_dist(20200, 0, c(2.0, 0.6, 0.95))
u <- cbind(u1, hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, truth, inverse = TRUE))
fitted <- bicop(u, family_set = 20200, rotation = 0)
cat("fitted Khoudraji-Clayton (theta, a, b):", sprintf("%8.3f", fitted$parameters), "\n", sep = "")

# selection among every parametric family + every generic family
chosen <- bicop(u, family_set = c(0:23, gen$code), cores = 4)
cat("selected among all families: ", chosen$family, "  rotation ", chosen$rotation, "\n", sep = "")

docs.title: How generic codes are built
docs.text:
A generic code reads

\[ \text{code} = 10000\,k + 100\,o + i, \] Digit group Values \(k\) (construction) 1 plain family; 2 Khoudraji asymmetrisation with two extra parameters \(a, b \in (0, 1]\) \(o\) (outer generator \(\psi\)) 0 none, \(\psi(s) = e^{-s}\); 1 positive stable, 2 gamma, 3 Sibuya, 4 logarithmic series; 5 tilted positive stable, 6 generalised Sibuya, 7 negative binomial (two parameters); 11-26 compositions \(\psi_p(-\log \zeta_q)\) of two one-parameter Laplace transforms \(i\) (inner Pickands function \(A\)) 0 independence, \(A \equiv 1\) (Archimedean); 1 logistic, 2 negative logistic, 3 Hüsler-Reiss, 4 symmetric mixed, 5 asymmetric logistic, 6/7 its types 1/2, 8 asymmetric negative logistic, 9/10 its types 1/2, 11 asymmetric mixed, 12 Khoudraji-Hüsler-Reiss, 13 Khoudraji-mixed

All of them share one formula (Capéraà, Fougères & Genest 2000; Charpentier et al. 2014):

\[ C(u, v) = \psi\bigl(\ell(\varphi(u), \varphi(v))\bigr), \qquad \varphi = \psi^{-1}, \qquad \ell(s, t) = (s + t)\, A\!\left(\frac{t}{s + t}\right), \]

with \(\psi\) the Laplace transform of the outer generator and \(A\) a Pickands dependence function. With \(A \equiv 1\) (\(i = 0\)) the copula is Archimedean; with \(\psi(s) = e^{-s}\) (\(o = 0\)) it is an extreme-value copula; with both it is an Archimax copula. The parameters are stored in the order outer, inner, Khoudraji, at most three in all.

Codes that would repeat a hand-coded family (for instance 10100, positive stable generator = Gumbel, or 10200, gamma generator = Clayton) are valid and are used by the test suite to check the engine against the hand-coded formulas, but fv_generic_families() leaves them out; fv_generic_families(.false.) includes them. The complete list with bounds is the family catalogue.

fv_fam_name returns a readable name for any code, gen_npar the number of parameters of a generic code, and fv_par_bounds the box in which maximum likelihood searches. The first five codes are extreme-value copulas (\(o = 0\)) with Tawn's mixed model and the asymmetric (negative) logistic models.

docs.title: An Archimax copula
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
truth%family = 10203; truth%par = [1.0_dp, 1.5_dp, 0.0_dp]

truth = fv.Bicop(10203, 0, [1.0, 1.5])

truth <- bicop_dist(10203, 0, c(1.0, 1.5))

Code 10203 combines the gamma Laplace transform \(\psi(s) = (1 + s)^{-1/\theta}\) (the Clayton generator, here \(\theta = 1\)) with the Hüsler-Reiss Pickands function

\[ A(w) = w\, \Phi\!\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} + \frac{\lambda}{2} \log\frac{w}{1 - w}\right) + (1 - w)\, \Phi\!\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{\lambda}{2} \log\frac{w}{1 - w}\right), \qquad \lambda = 1.5 . \]

The outer gamma part gives lower tail dependence, the extreme-value inner part gives upper tail dependence, so this one family has both. Data are simulated with hinv1 exactly as for a hand-coded family (generic inverse h-functions use the safeguarded Newton iteration with the exact density), and fit recovers \((\hat\theta, \hat\lambda) \approx (1.00, 1.51)\) from 3000 observations.

Pickands dependence functions $A(w)$, all computed from fortvine's copula distribution function. Every $A$ lies in the shaded triangle between $\max(w, 1 - w)$ (comonotonicity) and 1 (independence). (a) The inner function of the Archimax copula 10203, recovered from $C$ itself as $A(w) = \varphi\bigl(C(\psi(1 - w), \psi(w))\bigr)$ with the gamma generator, at the true $(\theta, \lambda) = (1, 1.5)$ and at the fitted $(\hat\theta, \hat\lambda) = (0.995, 1.514)$; the circles are the hand-coded Hüsler-Reiss copula (family 16) with $\lambda = 1.5$, $A(w) = -\log C(e^{-(1-w)}, e^{-w})$, which agrees to all printed digits: the outer generator does not alter the inner function. (b) The five extreme-value codes listed by the program, at the parameters shown; types 1 and 2 of Tawn's model are mirror images, $A_{10007}(w) = A_{10006}(1 - w)$, and asymmetry in $A$ is what makes these copulas non-exchangeable.

docs.title: A Khoudraji copula
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
truth%family = 20200; truth%par = [2.0_dp, 0.6_dp, 0.95_dp]

truth = fv.Bicop(20200, 0, [2.0, 0.6, 0.95])

truth <- bicop_dist(20200, 0, c(2.0, 0.6, 0.95))

Khoudraji's device (Khoudraji 1995; Genest, Ghoudi & Rivest 1998) makes any copula \(C_0\) asymmetric:

\[ C(u, v) = u^{1 - a}\, v^{1 - b}\, C_0\bigl(u^{a}, v^{b}\bigr), \qquad a, b \in (0, 1]. \]

With \(a \neq b\) the copula is not exchangeable, \(C(u, v) \neq C(v, u)\): the dependence is stronger in one direction than the other. Code 20200 applies it to Clayton (outer gamma, no inner); the three parameters are \((\theta, a, b)\). The fit recovers them to within a few hundredths of \(a\) and \(b\) and about 0.1 of \(\theta\).

True and fitted densities of the two examples in normal scores (dotted: the diagonal). The Archimax copula 10203 (left pair) is exchangeable, with a lower tail from the gamma generator and an upper tail from the Hüsler-Reiss inner function. The Khoudraji-Clayton copula 20200 (right pair) with $a = 0.6 \ne b = 0.95$ is not exchangeable: its density is not symmetric about the diagonal. Each fit uses the 3000 draws of the program.

When an asymmetric family sits on a vine edge whose orientation is reversed, fortvine transposes it exactly (\(a \leftrightarrow b\) for Khoudraji, swapped asymmetry parameters or type 1 ↔ type 2 codes for the Pickands families); the test suite checks this identity for every asymmetric code (Validation).

docs.title: Selecting among all 109 parametric families
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
ctl%nfam = 24 + size(codes); ctl%family_set = 0
ctl%family_set(1:24) = FV_ALL; ctl%family_set(25:ctl%nfam) = codes
call chosen%select(u1, u2, ctl)

chosen = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=list(range(24)) + [f.code for f in gen])

chosen <- bicop(u, family_set = list(0:23, "generic"))      # "generic": the 85 generic codes

FV_ALL holds the 24 parametric hand-coded codes 0-23 (including independence and t-EV), codes the 85 generic ones: 109 candidates, each with its admissible rotations. The selection fits them all to the Khoudraji-Clayton sample and BIC picks the true family. The whole selection takes about a second for 3000 observations: candidate fits are raced, i.e. a fit is abandoned as soon as a bound on the log-likelihood it can still reach shows that it cannot beat the best criterion found so far. In vine selection the generic candidates of each edge are, in addition, pre-screened by a quick fit on a subsample, and only the best few are fitted on all the data.

When to use the generic families

The default family set (hand-coded families 0-22) covers most data. Add the generic codes when you suspect tail dependence in both corners with different strengths, or asymmetric (non-exchangeable) dependence; the tail dependence example shows a case where only the generic set contains the right model. See The generic engine for the formulas of every building block.

docs.title: Calling fortvine from Python and C
docs.text:
Programs: example/python/fortvine_ctypes.py, example/c/bicop.c  ·  Topics: the shared library, the bind(C) interface of src/fortvine.f90, array layout, ctypes + numpy, linking a C program.

Every computational kernel in src/fortvine.f90 has a C-interoperable entry point (bind(C, name="fv_...")). bash build.sh links them into the shared library build/libfortvine.so (Linux), libfortvine.dylib (macOS) or libfortvine.dll (Windows), which any language with a C foreign-function interface can load. No wrapper code has to be compiled.

docs.title: The conventions
docs.text:
• Scalars (integer(c_int), real(c_double)) declared with value are passed by value; output scalars (ll, fam, rot, info) are passed by reference.
  • Arrays are passed by pointer and must be contiguous double / int32 buffers.
  • Observations are the last Fortran dimension. u(2, n) for a pair, u(d, n) for a vine: one observation's values are adjacent in memory. In C or numpy that is a row-major array of shape (n, 2) or (n, d), so ordinary C-ordered numpy arrays are passed as they are.
  • Vine structure arrays st, fam, rot are Fortran (edge, tree) arrays of size d x d, which in row-major languages are [tree][edge]; parameters par(3, edge, tree) are [tree][edge][k], i.e. numpy shape (d, d, 3). Indices of trees and edges start at 0 on the C side; order holds 1-based variable labels.
  • nthreads is an explicit OpenMP thread count (use 1 or more).

The C prototypes of the routines used below (see the C interface for all of them):

int    fv_version(void);
void   fv_bicop_eval(int fam, int rot, const double *par, int n, const double *u,
                     int what, double *out, int nthreads);   /* what: 0 logpdf 1 pdf 2 h1 3 h2 4 hinv1 5 hinv2 */
void   fv_bicop_fit(int n, const double *u, int fam, int rot, const int *ci,
                    double *par, double *ll, int nthreads);
void   fv_bicop_select(int n, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset, const int *ci,
                       double psi0, int *fam, int *rot, double *par, double *ll, int nthreads);
double fv_kendall_tau(int n, const double *x, const double *y);
void   fv_tau_matrix(int n, int d, const double *x, double *tau, int nthreads);
void   fv_pseudo_obs(int n, int d, const double *x, double *u, int nthreads);
void   fv_vine_select(int n, int d, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset,
                      const int *ci, const double *cr, int *order, const int *st_in,
                      int *st, int *fam, int *rot, double *par, double *edge_ll,
                      int nthreads, int *info);
void   fv_vine_pdf(int nsamp, int bins, int d, int tgt, const double *u, const int *order,
                   int trunc, const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot,
                   const double *par, double *out, int nthreads);
void   fv_vine_rosenblatt(int n, int d, const double *u, const int *order, int trunc,
                          const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot,
                          const double *par, double *out, int nthreads);
void   fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt(int n, int d, const double *u, const int *order, int trunc,
                                  const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot,
                                  const double *par, double *out, int nthreads);

The integer control vector ci mirrors fv_controls:

Index \(j\) of ci[j] Meaning Default 0 selection criterion: 0 log-likelihood, 1 AIC, 2 BIC, 3 mBIC, 4 mBICv 2 1 method: 0 maximum likelihood, 1 inversion of Kendall's \(\tau\) 0 2 preselect families (1 = yes) 1 3 allow rotations (1 = yes) 1 4 fast one-parameter fits (\(\tau\) inversion only) 0 5 \(\tau\) estimator: 0 automatic, 1 exact, 2 approximate 1 6 (vine only) tree criterion: 0 Kendall's \(\tau\), 1 Spearman's \(\rho\), 2 Joe, 3 Hoeffding, ... 0 7 (vine only) spanning-tree algorithm: 0 Prim, 1 Kruskal 0 8 (vine only) truncation level, \(-1\) = none \(-1\) 9 (vine only) structure given in order/st_in (1) or to be selected (0) 0

and cr = {threshold, psi0} (default {0, 0.9}).

The C interface covers unweighted, continuous data with the parametric families. Weights, discrete variables, the nonparametric families and the mBICv-based truncation search are reached through the Fortran API (fortvine_api).

docs.title: Python with ctypes
docs.text:
"""fortvine_ctypes.py -- call the fortvine shared library from Python (ctypes + numpy).

Build the library first (bash build.sh), then run

    python example/python/fortvine_ctypes.py

The library is looked up in build/ next to this repository (or at $FORTVINE_LIB).

Array convention of the C API: observations are the LAST Fortran dimension, i.e. one
observation's values are contiguous.  A numpy array of shape (n, k) in C order is exactly
the Fortran array (k, n) the kernels expect -- no transposes, no copies.
"""
import ctypes as ct
import os
import shutil
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

FAMILY = ['indep', 'gaussian', 'student', 'clayton', 'gumbel', 'frank', 'joe', 'bb1', 'bb6', 'bb7',
          'bb8', 'tawn', 'plackett', 'fgm', 'amh', 'galambos', 'husler_reiss', 'bb2', 'bb3', 'bb5',
          'bb9', 'bb10', 'bb4', 'tev', 'tll', 'bernstein']


def load_library():
    root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
    name = {'win32': 'libfortvine.dll', 'darwin': 'libfortvine.dylib'}.get(sys.platform, 'libfortvine.so')
    path = Path(os.environ.get('FORTVINE_LIB', root / 'build' / name))
    if sys.platform == 'win32':
        # the DLL needs the MinGW runtime (libgomp-1.dll, libquadmath-0.dll, libwinpthread-1.dll)
        gfortran = shutil.which('gfortran')
        if gfortran:
            os.add_dll_directory(str(Path(gfortran).parent))
    return ct.CDLL(str(path))


lib = load_library()
I, D = ct.c_int, ct.c_double
dptr = np.ctypeslib.ndpointer(dtype=np.float64, flags='C_CONTIGUOUS')
iptr = np.ctypeslib.ndpointer(dtype=np.int32, flags='C_CONTIGUOUS')
Iref, Dref = ct.POINTER(I), ct.POINTER(D)

# signatures of the bind(C) routines in src/fortvine.f90 (scalars by value unless marked out)
lib.fv_version.restype = I
lib.fv_kendall_tau.argtypes = [I, dptr, dptr]
lib.fv_kendall_tau.restype = D
lib.fv_bicop_eval.argtypes = [I, I, dptr, I, dptr, I, dptr, I]           # fam, rot, par(3), n, u(n,2), what, out(n), nthreads
lib.fv_bicop_fit.argtypes = [I, dptr, I, I, iptr, dptr, Dref, I]          # n, u, fam, rot, ci(6), par(3), ll, nthreads
lib.fv_bicop_select.argtypes = [I, dptr, I, iptr, iptr, D, Iref, Iref, dptr, Dref, I]
lib.fv_pseudo_obs.argtypes = [I, I, dptr, dptr, I]                        # n, d, x(n,d), out(n,d), nthreads
lib.fv_tau_matrix.argtypes = [I, I, dptr, dptr, I]                        # n, d, x(n,d), tau(d,d), nthreads
lib.fv_vine_select.argtypes = [I, I, dptr, I, iptr, iptr, dptr, iptr, iptr, iptr, iptr, iptr, dptr, dptr, I, Iref]
lib.fv_vine_pdf.argtypes = [I, I, I, I, dptr, iptr, I, iptr, iptr, iptr, dptr, dptr, I]
lib.fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt.argtypes = [I, I, dptr, iptr, I, iptr, iptr, iptr, dptr, dptr, I]
for f in (lib.fv_bicop_eval, lib.fv_bicop_fit, lib.fv_bicop_select, lib.fv_pseudo_obs, lib.fv_tau_matrix,
          lib.fv_vine_select, lib.fv_vine_pdf, lib.fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt):
    f.restype = None

NTH = 4
# ci(1:6): selection criterion (2 = BIC), method (0 = MLE), preselect, allow rotations,
#          fast one-parameter fits, tau estimator (1 = exact) -- the fv_controls defaults
CI6 = np.array([2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1], dtype=np.int32)
PARAMETRIC = np.arange(23, dtype=np.int32)          # families 0..22 (the default set: no tev, tll, bernstein)


def bicop_eval(fam, rot, par, u, what):
    """what: 0 log-density, 1 density, 2 h1, 3 h2, 4 h1 inverse, 5 h2 inverse; u has shape (n, 2)."""
    u = np.ascontiguousarray(u, dtype=np.float64)
    out = np.empty(len(u))
    lib.fv_bicop_eval(fam, rot, np.asarray(par, dtype=np.float64), len(u), u, what, out, NTH)
    return out


# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ one pair
print('fortvine C API version', lib.fv_version())
par = np.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0])                      # Clayton, theta = 2
g = np.array([0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
print('Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:', bicop_eval(3, 0, par, np.column_stack([g, g]), 1).round(4))

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
u2 = bicop_eval(3, 0, par, np.column_stack([u1, w]), 4)      # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
u = np.column_stack([u1, u2])
print('empirical Kendall tau: %.3f' % lib.fv_kendall_tau(n, u1, u2))

est, ll = np.zeros(3), D()
lib.fv_bicop_fit(n, u, 3, 0, CI6, est, ct.byref(ll), NTH)
print('fitted theta: %.4f   log-likelihood: %.2f' % (est[0], ll.value))

fam, rot = I(), I()
lib.fv_bicop_select(n, u, len(PARAMETRIC), PARAMETRIC, CI6, 0.9, ct.byref(fam), ct.byref(rot), est, ct.byref(ll), NTH)
print('selected:', FAMILY[fam.value], 'rotation', rot.value, 'par', est.round(3))

# ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ a vine
# 4-dimensional data with a Gaussian dependence, turned into pseudo-observations
d, n = 4, 3000
corr = 0.6 ** np.abs(np.subtract.outer(np.arange(d), np.arange(d)))   # AR(1) correlation
x = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(d), corr, size=n)
u = np.empty((n, d))
lib.fv_pseudo_obs(n, d, x, u, NTH)

# ci(1:10) = CI6, tree criterion (0 tau), tree algorithm (0 Prim), truncation (-1 = none),
# structure given (0 = select it); cr = threshold, psi0
ci10 = np.concatenate([CI6, [0, 0, -1, 0]]).astype(np.int32)
cr = np.array([0.0, 0.9])
order = np.zeros(d, dtype=np.int32)
st_in = np.zeros((d, d), dtype=np.int32)
st, fam, rot = (np.zeros((d, d), dtype=np.int32) for _ in range(3))    # [tree, edge]
vpar, edge_ll = np.zeros((d, d, 3)), np.zeros((d, d))                   # [tree, edge, k], [tree, edge]
info = I()
lib.fv_vine_select(n, d, u, len(PARAMETRIC), PARAMETRIC, ci10, cr, order, st_in, st, fam, rot, vpar, edge_ll,
                   NTH, ct.byref(info))
assert info.value == 0
print('\nvine order:', order)
for t in range(d - 1):
    print('  tree %d:' % (t + 1), ', '.join('%s(%.3f)' % (FAMILY[fam[t, e]], vpar[t, e, 0]) for e in range(d - 1 - t)))

trunc = d - 1
dens = np.empty(n)                                   # density: one bin per sample, tgt = -1
lib.fv_vine_pdf(n, 1, d, -1, u, order, trunc, st, fam, rot, vpar, dens, NTH)
print('log-likelihood: %.2f  (sum of edge log-likelihoods %.2f)' % (np.log(dens).sum(), edge_ll.sum()))

# simulation = inverse Rosenblatt transform of independent uniforms
sim = np.empty((n, d))
lib.fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt(n, d, rng.random((n, d)), order, trunc, st, fam, rot, vpar, sim, NTH)
t_data, t_sim = np.empty((d, d)), np.empty((d, d))
lib.fv_tau_matrix(n, d, u, t_data, NTH)
lib.fv_tau_matrix(n, d, sim, t_sim, NTH)
print('Kendall tau, data      :', t_data[0].round(3))
print('Kendall tau, simulated :', t_sim[0].round(3))

docs.title: What the script does
docs.text:
• Loading. ctypes.CDLL opens the library. On Windows the DLL imports the MinGW runtime DLLs (libgomp-1.dll, libquadmath-0.dll, libwinpthread-1.dll), so the script adds the directory of gfortran on PATH with os.add_dll_directory first.
  • Signatures. Declaring argtypes with numpy.ctypeslib.ndpointer(..., flags='C_CONTIGUOUS') makes ctypes check every array's type and layout, so a wrongly shaped or Fortran-ordered array raises an error instead of producing garbage.
  • One pair. fv_bicop_eval with what = 1 gives the same Clayton densities as the Fortran pair copula example; what = 4 (inverse \(h_1\)) simulates; fv_bicop_fit and fv_bicop_select fit and select with the default controls.
  • A vine. Four-dimensional data with the correlation matrix \(0.6^{|i-j|}\) (a Gaussian AR(1) process) are converted to pseudo-observations by fv_pseudo_obs, and fv_vine_select chooses the structure. The answer is the one theory predicts: the Gaussian AR(1) process is Markov, so the D-vine 1-2-3-4 with Gaussian pairs of correlation 0.6 in tree 1 and independence in all higher trees is exact. The estimates 0.57-0.60 match, and BIC sets the three higher edges to independence.
  • Density and simulation. fv_vine_pdf with one bin per sample and tgt = -1 returns the ordinary vine density (the bins/tgt arguments serve the fast prediction-grid evaluation of pdf_grid); its log-sum equals the sum of the edge log-likelihoods returned by the selection. fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt maps uniform noise to a new sample whose Kendall taus reproduce those of the data.
  • Truncation. fv_vine_select does not return a truncation level; with no truncation requested (ci[8] = -1) it is d - 1, the value passed to the other routines.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
/* bicop.c -- one pair copula through the fortvine C API: evaluate, simulate, fit, select.
 *
 * Build the shared library (bash build.sh), then from the repository root:
 *   Linux:   gcc -O2 example/c/bicop.c -Lbuild -lfortvine -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/build" -o build/bicop_c
 *   macOS:   gcc -O2 example/c/bicop.c -Lbuild -lfortvine -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/build" -o build/bicop_c
 *   Windows (MinGW-w64): gcc -O2 example/c/bicop.c build/libfortvine.dll -o build/bicop_c.exe
 *
 * Arrays follow the kernels' convention: observations in the last Fortran dimension, so the
 * pair (u1, u2) of observation i sits at u[2*i], u[2*i+1] (a row-major n x 2 array).
 */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* bind(C) routines of src/fortvine.f90 (integer = int, real(c_double) = double) */
int fv_version(void);
void fv_bicop_eval(int fam, int rot, const double *par, int n, const double *u, int what,
                   double *out, int nthreads);
void fv_bicop_fit(int n, const double *u, int fam, int rot, const int *ci, double *par,
                  double *ll, int nthreads);
void fv_bicop_select(int n, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset, const int *ci,
                     double psi0, int *fam, int *rot, double *par, double *ll, int nthreads);
double fv_kendall_tau(int n, const double *x, const double *y);

enum { CLAYTON = 3, N = 2000, NTH = 4 };
enum { LOGPDF = 0, PDF = 1, HFUNC1 = 2, HFUNC2 = 3, HINV1 = 4, HINV2 = 5 };

/* uniform in (0, 1) from a 64-bit xorshift generator (deterministic) */
static double unif(unsigned long long *s) {
  *s ^= *s << 13; *s ^= *s >> 7; *s ^= *s << 17;
  return ((*s >> 11) + 0.5) / 9007199254740992.0;
}

int main(void) {
  static const char *name[] = {"indep", "gaussian", "student", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank",
    "joe", "bb1", "bb6", "bb7", "bb8", "tawn", "plackett", "fgm", "amh", "galambos",
    "husler_reiss", "bb2", "bb3", "bb5", "bb9", "bb10", "bb4"};
  /* ci: criterion (2 BIC), method (0 MLE), preselect, rotations, fast fits, exact tau */
  const int ci[6] = {2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1};
  double par[3] = {2.0, 0.0, 0.0}, est[3], ll, diag[6] = {0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.9, 0.9}, dens[3];
  double *uw = malloc(2 * N * sizeof *uw), *u = malloc(2 * N * sizeof *u), *v = malloc(N * sizeof *v);
  double *x = malloc(N * sizeof *x), *y = malloc(N * sizeof *y);
  int famset[23], fam, rot, i;
  unsigned long long seed = 88172645463325252ULL;

  printf("fortvine C API version %d\n", fv_version());
  fv_bicop_eval(CLAYTON, 0, par, 3, diag, PDF, dens, 1);
  printf("Clayton(2) density on the diagonal: %.4f %.4f %.4f\n", dens[0], dens[1], dens[2]);

  /* simulate: u2 = h1^-1(w | u1) for independent uniforms (u1, w) */
  for (i = 0; i < N; i++) { uw[2 * i] = unif(&seed); uw[2 * i + 1] = unif(&seed); }
  fv_bicop_eval(CLAYTON, 0, par, N, uw, HINV1, v, NTH);
  for (i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    u[2 * i] = x[i] = uw[2 * i];
    u[2 * i + 1] = y[i] = v[i];
  }
  printf("empirical Kendall tau: %.3f\n", fv_kendall_tau(N, x, y));

  fv_bicop_fit(N, u, CLAYTON, 0, ci, est, &ll, NTH);
  printf("fitted theta: %.4f   log-likelihood: %.2f\n", est[0], ll);

  for (i = 0; i < 23; i++) famset[i] = i;          /* families 0..22 */
  fv_bicop_select(N, u, 23, famset, ci, 0.9, &fam, &rot, est, &ll, NTH);
  printf("selected: %s rotation %d par %.3f %.3f %.3f\n", name[fam], rot, est[0], est[1], est[2]);

  free(uw); free(u); free(v); free(x); free(y);
  return 0;
}

Compile against the shared library and run (from the repository root):

Linux / macOSWindows (MinGW-w64) 
gcc -O2 example/c/bicop.c -Lbuild -lfortvine -Wl,-rpath,"$PWD/build" -o build/bicop_c
./build/bicop_c

gcc -O2 example/c/bicop.c build/libfortvine.dll -o build/bicop_c.exe
PATH="$PWD/build:$PATH" ./build/bicop_c.exe

MinGW's linker can link directly against a DLL. At run time the DLL must be found on PATH (or next to the executable), together with the MinGW runtime DLLs it imports.

Output:

fortvine C API version 1
Clayton(2) density on the diagonal: 5.3702 1.4810 2.1578
empirical Kendall tau: 0.504
fitted theta: 2.0611   log-likelihood: 879.27
selected: clayton rotation 0 par 2.061 0.000 0.000

The program declares the prototypes itself, so no header file is needed. The pairs are stored as a row-major n x 2 array (u[2*i], u[2*i+1]), which is the Fortran u(2, n) the kernel expects. A small xorshift generator makes the run reproducible.

docs.title: Same numbers in every language
docs.text:
(a) Twelve pair copulas (Gaussian, Student t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, BB1, Clayton rotated 90°, Tawn, Hüsler-Reiss, Archimax 10203, Khoudraji-Joe 20300) evaluated at the same 500 points from Fortran (`fv_bicop%pdf`), from Python through ctypes and from C through `fv_bicop_eval`. All 18 000 values of $c$, $h_1$ and $h_1^{-1}$ agree bit for bit: the bindings pass the same doubles to the same kernel (`tools/example_interop.f90` and `tools/example_interop.c`). (b) The Python demo above: the Kendall $\hat\tau_{ij}$ of the four-dimensional data against those of a sample drawn from the vine that `fv_vine_select` fitted; the differences are sampling noise of one simulated sample (averaged over 20 simulations, every pair agrees with the data within 0.006).

Linking statically from C

build/libfortvine.a can also be linked into a C program, but then the Fortran and OpenMP runtimes must be linked too. The simplest way is to let gfortran drive the link: gcc -c prog.c && gfortran -fopenmp prog.o build/libfortvine.a -o prog (add -static on Windows for a self-contained executable). With gcc as the driver, use gcc -fopenmp prog.o build/libfortvine.a -lgfortran -lquadmath -lm -o prog.

docs.title: Pair copula basics
docs.text:
Program: example/ex01_pair_copula.f90, example/python/ex01_pair_copula.py, example/r/ex01_pair_copula.R  ·  Topics: fv_bicop, density, inverse h-function, simulation, maximum likelihood, BIC family selection.

The program works with one bivariate copula from start to finish: it evaluates a Clayton copula, draws a sample from it, refits the parameter, and finally lets fortvine choose the family without being told.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
! ex01_pair_copula -- one bivariate copula: evaluate, simulate, fit a known family, select a family.
program ex01_pair_copula
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer :: ns
  integer, allocatable :: seed(:)
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 2000
  type(fv_bicop) :: truth, fitted, chosen
  real(dp) :: u1(n), w(n), u2(n), dens(3)

  ! a Clayton copula with theta = 2 (Kendall's tau = theta / (theta + 2) = 0.5)
  truth%family = FV_CLAYTON; truth%par = [2.0_dp, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp]

  ! density at three points
  call truth%pdf([0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp], [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp], dens)
  print '(a,3f10.4)', 'Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:', dens

  ! simulate by inverse Rosenblatt: u2 = h^-1(w | u1) with independent uniforms u1, w
  call random_seed(size=ns); allocate(seed(ns)); seed = 20261116; call random_seed(put=seed)   ! reproducible sample
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  call truth%hinv1(u1, w, u2)
  print '(a,f7.3)', 'empirical Kendall tau:', fv_kendall_tau(u1, u2)

  ! maximum likelihood fit of a given family
  fitted%family = FV_CLAYTON
  call fitted%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,f8.4,a,f10.2)', 'fitted theta:', fitted%par(1), '   log-likelihood:', fitted%loglik

  ! family selection by BIC over the default family set (with rotations)
  call chosen%select(u1, u2)
  print '(a,a,a,i0,a,3f8.3)', 'selected: ', trim(fv_fam_name(chosen%family)), '  rotation ', chosen%rotation, &
    '  par', chosen%par
end program ex01_pair_copula

"""ex01_pair_copula -- one bivariate copula: evaluate, simulate, fit a known family, select a family.

The Python version of example/ex01_pair_copula.f90 (pip install ./python).
"""
import numpy as np

import fortvine as fv

n = 2000

# a Clayton copula with theta = 2 (Kendall's tau = theta / (theta + 2) = 0.5)
truth = fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [2.0])

# density at three points
g = np.array([0.1, 0.5, 0.9])
dens = truth.pdf(np.column_stack([g, g]))
print("Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:" + "".join(f"{x:10.4f}" for x in dens))

# simulate by inverse Rosenblatt: u2 = h^-1(w | u1) with independent uniforms u1, w
rng = np.random.default_rng(20261116)                # reproducible sample
u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
u2 = truth.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))
u = np.column_stack([u1, u2])
print(f"empirical Kendall tau:{fv.kendall_tau(u1, u2):7.3f}")

# maximum likelihood fit of a given family
fitted = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u)
print(f"fitted theta:{fitted.parameters[0]:8.4f}   log-likelihood:{fitted.loglik():10.2f}")

# family selection by BIC over the default family set (with rotations)
chosen = fv.Bicop().select(u)
par = np.zeros(3); par[:chosen.npars] = chosen.parameters
print(f"selected: {chosen.family}  rotation {chosen.rotation}  par" + "".join(f"{p:8.3f}" for p in par))

# ex01_pair_copula -- one bivariate copula: evaluate, simulate, fit a known family, select a family.
# The R version of example/ex01_pair_copula.f90 (R CMD INSTALL r).
library(fortvine)
n <- 2000

# a Clayton copula with theta = 2 (Kendall's tau = theta / (theta + 2) = 0.5)
truth <- bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)

# density at three points
g <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)
dens <- dbicop(cbind(g, g), truth)
cat("Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:", sprintf("%10.4f", dens), "\n", sep = "")

# simulate by inverse Rosenblatt: u2 = h^-1(w | u1) with independent uniforms u1, w
set.seed(20261116)                                   # reproducible sample
u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
u2 <- hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, truth, inverse = TRUE)
u <- cbind(u1, u2)
cat(sprintf("empirical Kendall tau:%7.3f\n", cor(u1, u2, method = "kendall")))

# maximum likelihood fit of a given family
fitted <- bicop(u, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0)
cat(sprintf("fitted theta:%8.4f   log-likelihood:%10.2f\n", fitted$parameters, fitted$loglik))

# family selection by BIC over the default family set (with rotations)
chosen <- bicop(u, family_set = "all", selcrit = "bic")
par <- c(chosen$parameters, 0, 0, 0)[1:3]
cat("selected: ", chosen$family, "  rotation ", chosen$rotation, "  par",
    sprintf("%8.3f", par), "\n", sep = "")

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:    5.3702    1.4810    2.1578
empirical Kendall tau:  0.514
fitted theta:  2.0422   log-likelihood:    892.73
selected: clayton  rotation 0  par   2.042   0.000   0.000

Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:    5.3702    1.4810    2.1578
empirical Kendall tau:  0.517
fitted theta:  2.0239   log-likelihood:    915.66
selected: clayton  rotation 0  par   2.024   0.000   0.000

Clayton(2) density on the diagonal:    5.3702    1.4810    2.1578
empirical Kendall tau:  0.502
fitted theta:  1.9733   log-likelihood:    824.55
selected: clayton  rotation 0  par   1.973   0.000   0.000

The first line is deterministic and the same in all three languages. The other three depend on the random sample. Each program fixes its seed (random_seed(put=seed) in Fortran, np.random.default_rng(seed) in Python, set.seed() in R), so its output is reproducible, but the three generators produce different uniforms and so slightly different values around the same truth. Another Fortran compiler has another intrinsic generator as well. The numbers in the walk-through are those of the Fortran run.

docs.title: Defining a copula
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
truth%family = FV_CLAYTON; truth%par = [2.0_dp, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp]

truth = fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [2.0])        # family, rotation, parameters

truth <- bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)         # family, rotation, parameters

An fv_bicop is a plain derived type: family is an integer code (named constants FV_GAUSSIAN, FV_CLAYTON, ... in fortvine_api), rotation is 0, 90, 180 or 270, and par(3) holds up to three parameters with unused slots left at 0. Nothing has to be initialised or allocated. In Python and R the family is given by its name (as fv_fam_name spells it, any case) or its integer code, and only as many parameters as the family has. The Clayton copula has the distribution function and density

\[ C(u, v) = \bigl(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1\bigr)^{-1/\theta}, \qquad c(u, v) = (1 + \theta)\,(uv)^{-1-\theta} \bigl(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1\bigr)^{-2 - 1/\theta}, \]

with Kendall's \(\tau = \theta / (\theta + 2)\), i.e. \(\tau = 0.5\) for \(\theta = 2\).

docs.title: Evaluating the density
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call truth%pdf([0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp], [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp], dens)

dens = truth.pdf([[0.1, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5], [0.9, 0.9]])      # one point per row

dens <- dbicop(rbind(c(0.1, 0.1), c(0.5, 0.5), c(0.9, 0.9)), truth)   # one point per row

All evaluation routines take arrays of points (Fortran: two vectors; Python and R: an \(n \times 2\) array): here the three diagonal points \((0.1, 0.1)\), \((0.5, 0.5)\), \((0.9, 0.9)\). At the centre the formula gives \(3 \cdot 0.25^{-3} \cdot 7^{-5/2} = 1.4810\), as printed. The density is largest near the origin (5.37 at \((0.1, 0.1)\)) because Clayton has lower tail dependence, \(\lambda_L = 2^{-1/\theta} \approx 0.71\); at \((0.9, 0.9)\) it is smaller (2.16) since \(\lambda_U = 0\). The same calling pattern serves logpdf, cdf, hfunc1, hfunc2, hinv1 and hinv2 (in R: dbicop(u, b, log = TRUE), pbicop(u, b) and hbicop(u, 1 or 2, b, inverse =)). Long arrays (more than 4096 points) are evaluated in parallel.

docs.title: Simulating
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
call truth%hinv1(u1, w, u2)

u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
u2 = truth.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))
u = np.column_stack([u1, u2])                # the same in one call: truth.simulate(n, seed=...)

u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
u2 <- hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, truth, inverse = TRUE)
u <- cbind(u1, u2)                           # the same in one call: rbicop(n, truth)

hinv1(u1, w, u2) returns the \(v\) that solves \(h_1(v \mid u_1) = w\), where \(h_1(v \mid u) = \partial C(u, v)/\partial u\) is the conditional distribution of \(V\) given \(U = u\). If \(u_1\) and \(w\) are independent uniforms, \((u_1, u_2)\) is a draw from the copula: the inverse Rosenblatt transform in two dimensions. For Clayton, fortvine uses the closed form

\[ h_1^{-1}(w \mid u) = \Bigl(1 + u^{-\theta}\bigl(w^{-\theta/(1+\theta)} - 1\bigr)\Bigr)^{-1/\theta}, \]

written so that the factor \(w^{-\theta/(1+\theta)} - 1\) is computed with expm1 and nothing cancels for small \(u\).

The conditional distribution behind the simulation, for the Clayton copula with $\theta = 2$. (a) $h_1(v \mid u)$ for $u = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9$ (lines) and the points $\bigl(h_1^{-1}(w \mid u), w\bigr)$ returned by `hinv1` for $w = 0.05, 0.10, \ldots, 0.95$ (circles), which fall on the curves: over a 401-point grid $|h_1^{-1}(h_1(v \mid u) \mid u) - v| \le 3 \times 10^{-14}$. (b) The conditional density $c(u, v) = \partial h_1(v \mid u) / \partial v$: for small $u$ the mass of $V$ piles up near 0, the lower tail dependence of Clayton.

The empirical Kendall tau of the 2000 draws (0.514 with the fixed seed) scatters around the theoretical 0.5 with a standard error of roughly 0.01.

docs.title: Fitting a known family
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
fitted%family = FV_CLAYTON
call fitted%fit(u1, u2)

fitted = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u)          # fitted.parameters, fitted.loglik()

fitted <- bicop(u, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0)   # fitted$parameters, logLik(fitted)

fit keeps family and rotation and estimates par by maximum likelihood; the maximised log-likelihood goes to fitted%loglik. In R, bicop() fits a single family when family_set holds one family and rotation is given; without rotation it selects. Internally the start value comes from inverting Kendall's tau, and the likelihood is maximised by Fisher-scoring steps with exact parameter scores (see Exact parameter scores). Passing an fv_controls with method = FV_ITAU instead returns the tau-inversion estimate itself (method="itau" in Python, par_method = "itau" in R), and weights= gives observation weights (weights= in Python and R; example).

The program's sample, $n = 2000$ draws from the Clayton copula with $\theta = 2$ ($\tau = 0.5$). (a) In copula scale the lower tail dependence shows as the dense cluster at $(0, 0)$. (b) In normal scores $z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$, with the contours of the fitted density ($\hat\theta = 2.042$, solid) and of the true density ($\theta = 2$, dashed): the two are indistinguishable at this sample size.

docs.title: Selecting a family
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call chosen%select(u1, u2)

chosen = fv.Bicop().select(u)                # chosen.family, chosen.rotation, chosen.parameters

chosen <- bicop(u)                           # family_set = "all", selcrit = "bic"

select with no controls tries the default candidate set: the 23 hand-coded parametric families 0..22 (every parametric family except the slow-to-fit t-EV). A rotatable family is tried in the two rotations that match the sign of the sample's Kendall tau (0 and 180 degrees for positive dependence, 90 and 270 for negative). With preselect on (the default), the correlations of the normal scores in the lower and the upper part of the sample are compared, as in vinecopulib, and a rotation whose tail sits on the weaker side is dropped before fitting. Every remaining candidate is fitted and the one with the smallest BIC, \(-2\ell + k \log n\), wins. The data came from Clayton, and Clayton without rotation is recovered with the same parameter as the dedicated fit.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
Restrict or extend the candidates with a control object (keyword arguments in Python and R). See Controls for every field.

FortranPythonR 
type(fv_controls) :: ctl
ctl%nfam = 5; ctl%family_set(1:5) = FV_ONE_PAR     ! gaussian, clayton, gumbel, frank, joe
ctl%selcrit = FV_AIC
call chosen%select(u1, u2, ctl)

chosen = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=["gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank", "joe"],
                           criterion="aic")

chosen <- bicop(u, family_set = c("gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank", "joe"),
                selcrit = "aic")

Evaluate a rotated copula: set the rotation to 90 before calling pdf/hinv1; a 90 or 270 degree rotation of Clayton models negative dependence with a tail in an off-diagonal corner (Rotations and asymmetry).

FortranPythonR 
truth%rotation = 90

truth = fv.Bicop("clayton", 90, [2.0])

truth <- bicop_dist("clayton", 90, 2)

The distribution function \(C\) itself is in closed form for every family except the Gaussian and Student ones, which are integrated by Gauss-Legendre quadrature over their exact h-function.

FortranPythonR 
call truth%cdf(u1, u2, out)

out = truth.cdf(u)

out <- pbicop(u, truth)

docs.title: Tail dependence and asymmetry
docs.text:
Program: example/ex04_tails.f90, example/python/ex04_tails.py, example/r/ex04_tails.R  ·  Topics: tail dependence coefficients, cdf, rotations, Tawn and Khoudraji asymmetric families, BIC selection with and without the generic families.

Two copulas can have the same Kendall tau and behave completely differently in the corners. This program takes five copulas with very different tails and measures their tail dependence three ways:

  1. the limit \(\lambda_L\) or \(\lambda_U\) from the family's formula;
  2. the exact finite-level coefficient from the copula distribution function, $$ \lambda_L(q) = \frac{C(q, q)}{q}, \qquad \lambda_U(q) = \frac{1 - 2(1 - q) + C(1 - q, 1 - q)}{q}, $$ at \(q = 10^{-2}\) and \(q = 10^{-4}\) (here \(q\) is the distance from the corner);
  3. the empirical coefficient: the fraction of a 200 000-point sample in the corner square of side \(q = 0.01\), divided by \(q\).

It then asks which family BIC selects from 2000 observations of each copula.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
! ex04_tails -- tail dependence of five pair copulas, three ways: the limit from the family
! formula, the exact coefficient at a finite level from the copula CDF, and the empirical
! coefficient of a simulated sample.  Then: which family does BIC select from each sample?
!
!   lower tail  lambda_L(q) = C(q, q) / q                      -> lambda_L as q -> 0
!   upper tail  lambda_U(q) = (1 - 2 q + C(q, q)) / (1 - q)    -> lambda_U as q -> 1
program ex04_tails
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 200000, m = 2000, nc = 5
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop(nc), chosen
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp), allocatable :: u1(:), w(:), u2(:)   ! large samples: heap, not stack (-fopenmp)
  real(dp) :: lim(2, nc), th, a, b
  integer, allocatable :: gen(:)
  integer :: k

  allocate(u1(n), w(n), u2(n))
  ! the five copulas (par = family parameters, unused slots 0)
  cop(1)%family = FV_GUMBEL;  cop(1)%par = [2.0_dp, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp]
  cop(2)%family = FV_CLAYTON; cop(2)%par = [2.0_dp, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp]
  cop(3)%family = FV_CLAYTON; cop(3)%par = [2.0_dp, 0.0_dp, 0.0_dp]; cop(3)%rotation = 180
  cop(4)%family = FV_TAWN;    cop(4)%par = [0.4_dp, 0.9_dp, 3.0_dp]     ! psi1, psi2, theta
  cop(5)%family = 20300;      cop(5)%par = [3.0_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp]     ! Khoudraji-Joe: theta, a, b

  ! limits (lambda_L, lambda_U) from the family formulas
  th = 2.0_dp
  lim(:, 1) = [0.0_dp, 2.0_dp - 2.0_dp**(1.0_dp / th)]                 ! Gumbel
  lim(:, 2) = [2.0_dp**(-1.0_dp / th), 0.0_dp]                         ! Clayton
  lim(:, 3) = [0.0_dp, 2.0_dp**(-1.0_dp / th)]                         ! survival Clayton
  a = 0.4_dp; b = 0.9_dp; th = 3.0_dp
  lim(:, 4) = [0.0_dp, a + b - (a**th + b**th)**(1.0_dp / th)]         ! Tawn
  a = 0.5_dp; b = 0.9_dp; th = 3.0_dp
  lim(:, 5) = [0.0_dp, a + b - (a**th + b**th)**(1.0_dp / th)]         ! Khoudraji-Joe

  print '(a)', '                        |      lower tail lambda_L(q)         |      upper tail lambda_U(q)'
  print '(a)', 'copula              rot |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample'
  do k = 1, nc
    call simulate(cop(k), 1000 + k)
    print '(a20,i3,a,4f8.3,a,4f8.3)', fv_fam_name(cop(k)%family), cop(k)%rotation, ' |   ', &
      lim(1, k), lam_lower(cop(k), 1.0e-2_dp), lam_lower(cop(k), 1.0e-4_dp), &
      count(u1 < 1.0e-2_dp .and. u2 < 1.0e-2_dp) / (n * 1.0e-2_dp), ' |   ', &
      lim(2, k), lam_upper(cop(k), 1.0e-2_dp), lam_upper(cop(k), 1.0e-4_dp), &
      count(u1 > 1 - 1.0e-2_dp .and. u2 > 1 - 1.0e-2_dp) / (n * 1.0e-2_dp)
  end do

  ! BIC selection from the first m rows of each sample: default family set (hand-coded
  ! parametric families with rotations), then the same plus every generic family
  gen = fv_generic_families()
  print '(/,a)', 'BIC selection from 2000 observations:'
  do k = 1, nc
    call simulate(cop(k), 1000 + k)
    call chosen%select(u1(1:m), u2(1:m))
    write(*, '(2x,a14,a,a10,a,i3)', advance='no') fv_fam_name(cop(k)%family), ' default set: ', &
      fv_fam_name(chosen%family), ' rot', chosen%rotation
    ctl%nfam = 24 + size(gen); ctl%family_set = 0
    ctl%family_set(1:24) = FV_ALL; ctl%family_set(25:ctl%nfam) = gen
    call chosen%select(u1(1:m), u2(1:m), ctl)
    print '(a,a14,a,i3)', '   + generic families: ', fv_fam_name(chosen%family), ' rot', chosen%rotation
  end do

contains

  ! n draws of (u1, u2) from c by the inverse Rosenblatt transform, reproducible from seed
  subroutine simulate(c, seed)
    type(fv_bicop), intent(in) :: c
    integer, intent(in) :: seed
    integer :: ns, j
    integer, allocatable :: s(:)
    call random_seed(size=ns)
    s = [(seed + 7919 * j, j = 1, ns)]
    call random_seed(put=s)
    call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
    call c%hinv1(u1, w, u2)               ! u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
  end subroutine simulate

  real(dp) function lam_lower(c, q)
    type(fv_bicop), intent(in) :: c
    real(dp), intent(in) :: q
    real(dp) :: cq(1)
    call c%cdf([q], [q], cq)
    lam_lower = cq(1) / q
  end function lam_lower

  real(dp) function lam_upper(c, q)       ! q is the distance from 1
    type(fv_bicop), intent(in) :: c
    real(dp), intent(in) :: q
    real(dp) :: cq(1)
    call c%cdf([1 - q], [1 - q], cq)
    lam_upper = (2 * q - 1 + cq(1)) / q
  end function lam_upper
end program ex04_tails

"""ex04_tails -- tail dependence of five pair copulas, three ways: the limit from the family
formula, the exact coefficient at a finite level from the copula CDF, and the empirical
coefficient of a simulated sample.  Then: which family does BIC select from each sample?

    lower tail  lambda_L(q) = C(q, q) / q                      -> lambda_L as q -> 0
    upper tail  lambda_U(q) = (2 q - 1 + C(1-q, 1-q)) / q      -> lambda_U as q -> 0

The Python version of example/ex04_tails.f90 (pip install ./python).
"""
import numpy as np

import fortvine as fv

n, m = 200000, 2000

# the five copulas (parameters as in the Fortran program)
cops = [fv.Bicop("gumbel", 0, [2.0]),
        fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [2.0]),
        fv.Bicop("clayton", 180, [2.0]),
        fv.Bicop("tawn", 0, [0.4, 0.9, 3.0]),            # psi1, psi2, theta
        fv.Bicop(20300, 0, [3.0, 0.5, 0.9])]             # Khoudraji-Joe: theta, a, b

# limits (lambda_L, lambda_U) from the family formulas
th = 2.0
lim = [(0.0, 2 - 2 ** (1 / th)),                         # Gumbel
       (2 ** (-1 / th), 0.0),                            # Clayton
       (0.0, 2 ** (-1 / th))]                            # survival Clayton
for a, b, th in [(0.4, 0.9, 3.0), (0.5, 0.9, 3.0)]:      # Tawn, Khoudraji-Joe
    lim.append((0.0, a + b - (a ** th + b ** th) ** (1 / th)))


def simulate(c, seed, size=n):
    """size draws of (u1, u2) from c by the inverse Rosenblatt transform, reproducible from seed"""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    u1, w = rng.random(size), rng.random(size)
    return np.column_stack([u1, c.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))])   # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)


def lam_lower(c, q):
    return c.cdf([[q, q]])[0] / q


def lam_upper(c, q):                                      # q is the distance from 1
    return (2 * q - 1 + c.cdf([[1 - q, 1 - q]])[0]) / q


f8 = lambda xs: "".join(f"{x:8.3f}" for x in xs)
print("                        |      lower tail lambda_L(q)         |      upper tail lambda_U(q)")
print("copula              rot |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample")
for k, c in enumerate(cops):
    u = simulate(c, 1000 + k + 1)
    low = np.mean((u[:, 0] < 0.01) & (u[:, 1] < 0.01)) / 0.01
    upp = np.mean((u[:, 0] > 0.99) & (u[:, 1] > 0.99)) / 0.01
    print(f"{c.family:<20s}{c.rotation:3d} |   "
          + f8([lim[k][0], lam_lower(c, 1e-2), lam_lower(c, 1e-4), low]) + " |   "
          + f8([lim[k][1], lam_upper(c, 1e-2), lam_upper(c, 1e-4), upp]))

# BIC selection from m observations of each copula: default family set (hand-coded parametric
# families with rotations), then the same plus every generic family
allfam = list(range(24)) + [f.code for f in fv.families() if f.code >= 10000]
print("\nBIC selection from 2000 observations:")
for k, c in enumerate(cops):
    u = simulate(c, 1000 + k + 1)[:m]
    d = fv.Bicop().select(u, num_threads=4)
    g = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=allfam, num_threads=4)
    print(f"  {c.family:<14s} default set: {d.family:<10s} rot{d.rotation:3d}"
          f"   + generic families: {g.family:<14s} rot{g.rotation:3d}")

# ex04_tails -- tail dependence of five pair copulas, three ways: the limit from the family
# formula, the exact coefficient at a finite level, and the empirical coefficient of a simulated
# sample.  Then: which family does BIC select from each sample?
# The R version of example/ex04_tails.f90 (R CMD INSTALL r).
#
# The R package has no copula distribution function C (the C interface does not export it), so
# the finite-level coefficients are computed from the h-function h1(s, v) = dC(s, v)/ds:
#   lower tail  lambda_L(q) = C(q, q) / q = (1/q) * integral_0^q h1(s, q) ds
#   upper tail  lambda_U(q) = P(U1 > 1-q, U2 > 1-q) / q = (1/q) * integral_{1-q}^1 (1 - h1(s, 1-q)) ds
library(fortvine)
n <- 200000; m <- 2000

# the five copulas (parameters as in the Fortran program)
cops <- list(bicop_dist("gumbel", 0, 2),
             bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2),
             bicop_dist("clayton", 180, 2),
             bicop_dist("tawn", 0, c(0.4, 0.9, 3)),       # psi1, psi2, theta
             bicop_dist(20300, 0, c(3, 0.5, 0.9)))        # Khoudraji-Joe: theta, a, b

# limits (lambda_L, lambda_U) from the family formulas
th <- 2
lim <- list(c(0, 2 - 2^(1 / th)),                         # Gumbel
            c(2^(-1 / th), 0),                            # Clayton
            c(0, 2^(-1 / th)),                            # survival Clayton
            c(0, 0.4 + 0.9 - (0.4^3 + 0.9^3)^(1 / 3)),    # Tawn
            c(0, 0.5 + 0.9 - (0.5^3 + 0.9^3)^(1 / 3)))    # Khoudraji-Joe

# n draws of (u1, u2) from cop by the inverse Rosenblatt transform, reproducible from seed
simulate <- function(cop, seed, size = n) {
  set.seed(seed)
  u1 <- runif(size); w <- runif(size)
  cbind(u1, hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, cop, inverse = TRUE))  # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
}

h1 <- function(s, v, cop) hbicop(cbind(s, v), 1, cop)
lam_lower <- function(cop, q)
  integrate(h1, 0, q, v = q, cop = cop, rel.tol = 1e-10)$value / q
lam_upper <- function(cop, q)                              # q is the distance from 1
  integrate(function(s) 1 - h1(s, 1 - q, cop), 1 - q, 1, rel.tol = 1e-10)$value / q

f8 <- function(x) paste(sprintf("%8.3f", x), collapse = "")
cat("                        |      lower tail lambda_L(q)         |      upper tail lambda_U(q)\n")
cat("copula              rot |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample |      limit  q=1e-2  q=1e-4  sample\n")
for (k in seq_along(cops)) {
  cop <- cops[[k]]
  u <- simulate(cop, 1000 + k)
  low <- mean(u[, 1] < 0.01 & u[, 2] < 0.01) / 0.01
  upp <- mean(u[, 1] > 0.99 & u[, 2] > 0.99) / 0.01
  cat(sprintf("%-20s%3d |   ", cop$family, cop$rotation),
      f8(c(lim[[k]][1], lam_lower(cop, 1e-2), lam_lower(cop, 1e-4), low)), " |   ",
      f8(c(lim[[k]][2], lam_upper(cop, 1e-2), lam_upper(cop, 1e-4), upp)), "\n", sep = "")
}

# BIC selection from m observations of each copula: default family set (hand-coded parametric
# families with rotations), then the same plus every generic family
cat("\nBIC selection from 2000 observations:\n")
for (k in seq_along(cops)) {
  cop <- cops[[k]]
  u <- simulate(cop, 1000 + k)[1:m, ]
  d <- bicop(u, family_set = "all", cores = 4)
  g <- bicop(u, family_set = list(0:23, "generic"), cores = 4)
  cat(sprintf("  %-14s default set: %-10s rot%3d   + generic families: %-14s rot%3d\n",
              cop$family, d$family, d$rotation, g$family, g$rotation))
}

The distribution function in R

The R script computes the finite-level coefficients from the h-function of the library: \(C(q, q) = \int_0^q h_1(s, q)\, ds\) and \(P(U_1 > 1 - q, U_2 > 1 - q) = \int_{1-q}^1 \bigl(1 - h_1(s, 1 - q)\bigr)\, ds\), by adaptive quadrature (integrate). The values agree with the CDF of the Fortran and Python programs to the printed digits. pbicop(u, cop) evaluates \(C\) directly and gives the same values, e.g. pbicop(cbind(q, q), cop) / q for \(\lambda_L(q)\).

All samples use fixed seeds, so each output is reproducible (the Fortran program takes about 4 seconds, mostly the two selections over 109 families per copula). The limits and the finite-level columns are exact and the same in all three languages. The "sample" columns and the selections depend on the random draws, which differ between Fortran, NumPy and R: on the Python samples BIC picks survival Joe (also lower-tail dependent) for the Clayton data, and with the generic families Joe-asymneglogistic (another asymmetric extreme-value-type upper tail) for the Tawn data. The discussion below refers to the Fortran run.

docs.title: The five copulas and their tail formulas
docs.text:
Copula Parameters Tail formula \(\lambda_L\) \(\lambda_U\) Gumbel \(\theta = 2\) \(\lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) 0 0.586 Clayton \(\theta = 2\) \(\lambda_L = 2^{-1/\theta}\) 0.707 0 Clayton rotated 180° (survival Clayton) \(\theta = 2\) \(\lambda_U = 2^{-1/\theta}\) 0 0.707 Tawn (asymmetric logistic) \((\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta) = (0.4, 0.9, 3)\) \(\lambda_U = \psi_1 + \psi_2 - (\psi_1^\theta + \psi_2^\theta)^{1/\theta}\) 0 0.374 Khoudraji-Joe (code 20300) \((\theta, a, b) = (3, 0.5, 0.9)\) \(\lambda_U = a + b - (a^\theta + b^\theta)^{1/\theta}\) 0 0.451

The last two formulas follow from the tail behaviour of extreme-value-type copulas. Near \((1, 1)\) any copula with upper tail dependence behaves like \(C(1 - x, 1 - y) \approx 1 - \ell(x, y)\) with the stable tail dependence function \(\ell\), and \(\lambda_U = 2 - \ell(1, 1)\). For an extreme-value copula with Pickands function \(A\), \(\ell(x, y) = (x + y) A(y / (x + y))\), so \(\lambda_U = 2(1 - A(1/2))\). Tawn's model has \(A(w) = (1 - \psi_1)(1 - w) + (1 - \psi_2) w + [(\psi_1 (1 - w))^\theta + (\psi_2 w)^\theta]^{1/\theta}\), which gives the formula in the table. For the Khoudraji construction \(C(u, v) = u^{1-a} v^{1-b} C_0(u^a, v^b)\), expanding each factor at \((1 - x, 1 - y)\) gives \(\ell(x, y) = (1 - a)x + (1 - b)y + \ell_0(ax, by)\); with Joe's \(\ell_0(x, y) = (x^\theta + y^\theta)^{1/\theta}\) this yields \(\lambda_U = a + b - \ell_0(a, b)\), the same expression as for Tawn: Khoudraji-Joe and Tawn share their upper tail structure but not their bodies.

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
The finite-level coefficients converge, at very different speeds. For Clayton, \(\lambda_L(q) = (2 - q^{\theta})^{-1/\theta}\), so the lower tail coefficient is already 0.707 at \(q = 0.01\). For the zero limits, the convergence can be slow: Gumbel's lower tail coefficient is 0.148 at \(q = 0.01\) and still 0.022 at \(q = 10^{-4}\), since \(C(q, q)/q = q^{2^{1/\theta} - 1}\) decays only like \(q^{0.41}\). A finite sample never reaches the limit; an empirical tail coefficient estimates the finite-level value, as the "sample" columns show (0.150 against 0.148, 0.565 against 0.589, and so on, within the binomial noise of roughly \(\pm 0.02\) for about 1000-1500 corner points).

Finite-level tail dependence $\lambda_L(q)$ (a) and $\lambda_U(q)$ (b) from the copula distribution function, for $10^{-6} \le q \le 0.5$ (lines). Dashed: the limits $\lambda_L$, $\lambda_U$ of the table above (the grey dashed line is the common limit 0). Circles: empirical coefficients of the program's 200 000-point samples at $q = 10^{-3}, \ldots, 0.4$; at $q = 10^{-3}$ the corner square holds only $200\,000\, q\, \lambda(q) \le 140$ points, hence the scatter. Dotted: a Gaussian copula with the same $\tau = 0.5$ ($\rho = 0.707$), whose $\lambda_U(q)$ decays to 0 slowly, like Gumbel's lower tail. Clayton reaches its limit almost at once; the zero limits are approached only as a power of $q$.

The rotation swaps the tails. Survival Clayton has exactly the numbers of Clayton with the two tails exchanged, because \(C_{180}(u, v) = u + v - 1 + C(1 - u, 1 - v)\).

Asymmetric families keep their tail where the formula says. Tawn and Khoudraji-Joe have no lower tail dependence and upper tail coefficients 0.374 and 0.451, reproduced by the CDF to three decimals at \(q = 10^{-4}\).

Khoudraji copulas lose the base copula's lower tail

The catalogue flags Khoudraji-Clayton (20200) as a lower-tail family because its base copula is one, and the flag is used to decide which rotations to try. Unless \(a = b = 1\) the construction actually has \(\lambda_L = 0\): with \(a \le b\), \(C(t, t) \le t^{2 - a - b}\, t^{b} = t^{2 - a}\), so \(C(t, t)/t \to 0\). Only the upper tail survives the asymmetrisation, as in this example.

docs.title: Which family does BIC select?
docs.text:
• Gumbel → Galambos. Gumbel and Galambos are both extreme-value copulas, with Pickands functions that are nearly indistinguishable for comparable dependence. With 2000 observations the data cannot separate them; BIC takes the one with the marginally higher likelihood. Both have \(\lambda_L = 0\) and a positive \(\lambda_U\), so tail inference is not affected.
  • Clayton and survival Clayton are recovered with the correct rotation. Rotation selection is driven by the sign of Kendall's tau (0 or 180 for positive dependence) and by which half of the data is more strongly correlated in normal scores.
  • Tawn is recovered by both family sets.
  • Khoudraji-Joe is not in the default family set, so the default selection settles for the closest available model, Tawn, which has the same kind of asymmetric upper tail. Once the generic families are added, BIC picks the true family.

Tail dependence in a model matters for joint exceedance probabilities. A Gaussian copula with the same Kendall tau as the Gumbel copula above (\(\tau = 0.5\), \(\rho = 0.707\)) has \(\lambda_U(q) = 0.273\) at \(q = 10^{-2}\) and \(0.103\) at \(q = 10^{-4}\), against Gumbel's 0.589 and 0.586: at the 1-in-10 000 level the Gaussian model underestimates the chance of a joint extreme almost sixfold. Selecting among families with the right tail behaviour, including the generic ones when asymmetry is suspected, is the point of having many families.

See also Rotations and asymmetry, Extreme-value families and Khoudraji asymmetrisation.

docs.title: Vine copula workflow
docs.text:
Program: example/ex02_vine.f90, example/python/ex02_vine.py, example/r/ex02_vine.R  ·  Topics: fv_vinecop, set_dvine, simulate, select (Dissmann's algorithm), loglik, npars, pdf, rosenblatt, print, fv_controls%nthreads.

The program builds a five-dimensional D-vine by hand, draws 3000 observations from it, forgets the model, selects a new regular vine from the sample, and then uses the fitted model: its density, its Rosenblatt transform and new simulations.

What a vine sample looks like: 1500 draws from a four-dimensional D-vine with Clayton, Gumbel and Tawn pairs in the first tree, Frank and Gaussian in the second and a Student t in the third (`tools/vine_sample.f90`), shown in normal scores. Below the diagonal: scatter plots; above: empirical Kendall's tau.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
! ex02_vine -- a 5-dimensional vine copula: simulate from a known D-vine, select a new vine from
! the sample (structure, families, parameters), then density, Rosenblatt transform and simulation.
program ex02_vine
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 3000, d = 5
  type(fv_vinecop) :: truth, vc
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u(n, d), w(n, d), dens(n), sim(10, d)
  integer :: e, t

  ! a D-vine 1-2-3-4-5 with Gumbel pairs in tree 1 and Frank pairs in tree 2, independence above
  call truth%set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
  do e = 1, d - 1
    truth%fam(e, 1) = FV_GUMBEL; truth%par(1, e, 1) = 2.0_dp
  end do
  do e = 1, d - 2
    truth%fam(e, 2) = FV_FRANK; truth%par(1, e, 2) = 3.0_dp
  end do
  call truth%simulate(n, u, seed=42)

  ! select a regular vine: Dissmann's algorithm, all parametric families, BIC
  ctl%nthreads = 4
  call vc%select(u, ctl)
  call vc%print()
  print '(a,f12.2,a,i0)', 'log-likelihood:', vc%loglik(u), '   parameters:', vc%npars()

  ! density, Rosenblatt transform (independent uniforms if the model is right) and new samples
  call vc%pdf(u, dens)
  call vc%rosenblatt(u, w)
  print '(a,f8.4)', 'Kendall tau of the first two Rosenblatt columns (should be ~0):', &
    fv_kendall_tau(w(:, 1), w(:, 2))
  call vc%simulate(10, sim, seed=7)
  print '(a,5f8.4)', 'first simulated row:', sim(1, :)
  do t = 1, 2
    print '(a,i0,a,*(1x,a))', 'tree ', t, ' families:', (trim(fv_fam_name(vc%fam(e, t))), e = 1, d - t)
  end do
end program ex02_vine

"""ex02_vine -- a 5-dimensional vine copula: simulate from a known D-vine, select a new vine from
the sample (structure, families, parameters), then density, Rosenblatt transform and simulation.

The Python version of example/ex02_vine.f90 (pip install ./python).
"""
import numpy as np

import fortvine as fv

n, d = 3000, 5

# a D-vine 1-2-3-4-5 with Gumbel pairs in tree 1 and Frank pairs in tree 2, independence above
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
for e in range(d - 1):
    truth.set_pair_copula(0, e, fv.Bicop("gumbel", 0, [2.0]))
for e in range(d - 2):
    truth.set_pair_copula(1, e, fv.Bicop("frank", 0, [3.0]))
u = truth.simulate(n, seed=42)

# select a regular vine: Dissmann's algorithm, all parametric families, BIC
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, num_threads=4)
print(vc)
print(f"log-likelihood:{vc.loglik(u):12.2f}   parameters:{vc.npars}")

# density, Rosenblatt transform (independent uniforms if the model is right) and new samples
dens = vc.pdf(u)
w = vc.rosenblatt(u)
print("Kendall tau of the first two Rosenblatt columns (should be ~0):"
      f"{fv.kendall_tau(w[:, 0], w[:, 1]):8.4f}")
sim = vc.simulate(10, seed=7)
print("first simulated row:" + "".join(f"{x:8.4f}" for x in sim[0]))
for t in range(2):
    print(f"tree {t + 1} families: " + " ".join(vc.families[t]))

# ex02_vine -- a 5-dimensional vine copula: simulate from a known D-vine, select a new vine from
# the sample (structure, families, parameters), then density, Rosenblatt transform and simulation.
# The R version of example/ex02_vine.f90 (R CMD INSTALL r).
library(fortvine)
n <- 3000; d <- 5

# a D-vine 1-2-3-4-5 with Gumbel pairs in tree 1 and Frank pairs in tree 2, independence above
pcs <- list(rep(list(bicop_dist("gumbel", 0, 2)), d - 1),
            rep(list(bicop_dist("frank", 0, 3)), d - 2))
truth <- vinecop_dist(pcs, dvine_structure(1:d))
set.seed(42)
u <- rvinecop(n, truth)

# select a regular vine: Dissmann's algorithm, all parametric families, BIC
vc <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", selcrit = "bic", cores = 4)
print(vc)
cat(sprintf("log-likelihood:%12.2f   parameters:%d\n", sum(log(dvinecop(u, vc))), vc$npars))

# density, Rosenblatt transform (independent uniforms if the model is right) and new samples
dens <- dvinecop(u, vc)
w <- rosenblatt(u, vc)
cat(sprintf("Kendall tau of the first two Rosenblatt columns (should be ~0):%8.4f\n",
            cor(w[, 1], w[, 2], method = "kendall")))
set.seed(7)
sim <- rvinecop(10, vc)
cat("first simulated row:", sprintf("%8.4f", sim[1, ]), "\n", sep = "")
for (t in 1:2)
  cat("tree ", t, " families: ",
      paste(vapply(vc$pair_copulas[[t]], function(b) b$family, ""), collapse = " "), "\n", sep = "")
