Each sample is drawn with a fixed seed (seed=42 in Fortran and Python, set.seed(42) in R), so each output is reproducible. The three languages draw different uniforms, though, so the three samples differ, and with them the selected vines. The walk-through discusses the Fortran run. The R sample leads to the same first tree, the path 4-2-1-3-5; on the Python sample it is yet another path, 1-2-4-5-3. Neither is the true path 1-2-3-4-5, for the reason explained below.

docs.title: Building a vine by hand
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call truth%set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
truth%fam(e, 1) = FV_GUMBEL; truth%par(1, e, 1) = 2.0_dp     ! tree 1
truth%fam(e, 2) = FV_FRANK;  truth%par(1, e, 2) = 3.0_dp     ! tree 2

truth = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
for e in range(4):
    truth.set_pair_copula(0, e, fv.Bicop("gumbel", 0, [2.0]))   # tree 1
for e in range(3):
    truth.set_pair_copula(1, e, fv.Bicop("frank", 0, [3.0]))    # tree 2
u = truth.simulate(3000, seed=42)

pcs <- list(rep(list(bicop_dist("gumbel", 0, 2)), 4),        # tree 1
            rep(list(bicop_dist("frank", 0, 3)), 3))         # tree 2
truth <- vinecop_dist(pcs, dvine_structure(1:5))
set.seed(42)
u <- rvinecop(3000, truth)

set_dvine(order) allocates a vine for d = size(order) variables with the D-vine (path) structure along order, and every pair copula set to independence. Edge e of tree t is then configured through fam(e, t), rot(e, t) and par(1:3, e, t). In Python the same arrays are indexed [t, e] from 0 (vc.fam[t - 1, e - 1]), or set one Bicop at a time with set_pair_copula; in R a vine is built from a list of trees, each a list of bicop_dist objects, and a structure from dvine_structure(). In this D-vine, tree 1 holds the pairs \((1,2), (2,3), (3,4), (4,5)\), each a Gumbel copula with \(\theta = 2\) (\(\tau = 0.5\), upper tail dependence \(\lambda_U = 2 - \sqrt 2 \approx 0.59\)); tree 2 holds \((1,3 \mid 2)\), \((2,4 \mid 3)\), \((3,5 \mid 4)\), Frank copulas with \(\theta = 3\) (\(\tau \approx 0.31\)). Trees 3 and 4 stay independent, so the truth has \(4 + 3 = 7\) parameters.

simulate(n, u, seed=42) fills u(n, d) by applying the inverse Rosenblatt transform to uniforms drawn from a generator seeded with 42.

docs.title: Selecting a vine
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
ctl%nthreads = 4
call vc%select(u, ctl)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, num_threads=4)

vc <- vinecop(u, cores = 4)

vc has no structure yet, so select runs the full Dissmann et al. (2013) algorithm: tree by tree it builds a maximum spanning tree on \(|\hat\tau|\), then selects family, rotation and parameters for every edge by BIC among the default 23 parametric families, and computes the conditional pseudo-observations for the next tree. Independent edges are fitted in parallel on the requested 4 threads. (The Python and R functions use one thread unless num_threads or cores says otherwise; the Fortran default is half the logical CPUs.)

docs.title: Why the selected vine differs from the truth
docs.text:
The selected model has 15 parameters and log-likelihood 5271.6, although the true model reaches 5429.4 with 7. The reason is visible in the sample's Kendall tau matrix (fv_tau_mat(u, tm)):

   1.000   0.502   0.506   0.402   0.362
   0.502   1.000   0.494   0.503   0.389
   0.506   0.494   1.000   0.500   0.512
   0.402   0.503   0.500   1.000   0.498
   0.362   0.389   0.512   0.498   1.000

The Frank copulas in tree 2 add so much dependence between second neighbours that \(\hat\tau_{13} = 0.506\) and \(\hat\tau_{35} = 0.512\) exceed the true tree-1 pair \(\hat\tau_{23} = 0.494\). The maximum spanning tree takes the stronger pairs, the first tree is no longer the path 1-2-3-4-5, and higher trees have to mop up the dependence that the first tree misplaced (hence BB1, Plackett and Student copulas in trees 2-4 instead of Frank and independence). Greedy tree selection is a heuristic; it is very good when the strongest dependence really sits in the first tree and can be fooled otherwise.

Why Dissmann's algorithm picks another first tree. (a) The empirical Kendall $\hat\tau_{ij}$ of the 3000 draws; solid green squares mark the pairs of the true tree 1 (the path 1-2-3-4-5), dashed gold squares those of the selected tree 1. (b) The ten pairs ranked by $\hat\tau_{ij}$: the maximum spanning tree takes the four strongest pairs, which already connect all five variables, while three of the true pairs, (3,4), (4,5) and (2,3), rank only fifth to seventh, within the sampling error of about $\pm 0.01$.

The true vine (left) and the vine selected from the sample (right), tree by tree. Nodes of tree $T_t$ are the edges of $T_{t-1}$, written as conditioned pair | conditioning set; every edge is labelled with its pair-copula family and the Kendall $\tau$ of that pair copula. Gold edges in the selected $T_1$ are pairs that the true $T_1$ does not contain; the selected vine compensates with dependence in all higher trees (15 parameters, $\ell = 5271.6$) where the truth is independent from $T_3$ on (7 parameters, $\ell = 5429.4$).

When the structure is known, fixing it avoids the problem. With

FortranPythonR 
call vc%set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
call vc%select(u, ctl)            ! only families and parameters are selected

vc = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
vc.select(u, num_threads=4)       # only families and parameters are selected

vc <- vinecop(u, structure = dvine_structure(1:5), cores = 4)   # families and parameters only

fortvine selects Gumbel in all four tree-1 edges (\(\hat\theta\) from 1.98 to 2.03), Frank in all three tree-2 edges (\(\hat\theta\) from 2.90 to 3.06), independence above, 7 parameters and log-likelihood 5431.45, slightly above the truth's 5429.45 as a maximum-likelihood fit should be. (The fitted vine is stored with the order reversed, 5 4 3 2 1, which describes the same D-vine.)

docs.title: Using the fitted model
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
print *, vc%loglik(u), vc%npars()
call vc%pdf(u, dens)
call vc%rosenblatt(u, w)
call vc%simulate(10, sim, seed=7)

print(vc.loglik(u), vc.npars)
dens = vc.pdf(u)
w = vc.rosenblatt(u)
sim = vc.simulate(10, seed=7)

print(c(loglik = sum(log(dvinecop(u, vc))), npars = vc$npars))
dens <- dvinecop(u, vc)
w <- rosenblatt(u, vc)
set.seed(7)
sim <- rvinecop(10, vc)
  • loglik(u) is \(\sum_i \log c(u_i)\) and npars() the number of parameters, the two ingredients of an information criterion (\(\mathrm{BIC} = -2 \cdot 5271.6 + 15 \log 3000\)).
  • pdf(u, dens) returns the vine density at every row; it is a product of 10 pair-copula densities evaluated along the trees (computed as a sum of logs).
  • rosenblatt(u, w) maps the data to what should be independent uniforms if the model is right. The Kendall tau between the first two transformed columns, \(-0.0145\), is well within the sampling noise of \(\pm 0.012\) (one standard error at \(n = 3000\)), as expected since the selected vine fits the data well even with the "wrong" structure.
  • simulate(10, sim, seed=7) draws ten new rows from the fitted model.

The fam array is indexed (edge, tree), so the last loop prints the families of tree 1 and tree 2 by name with fv_fam_name (in Python vc.families[t], in R the family of each bicop_dist in vc$pair_copulas[[t]]).

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• ctl%select_trunc = .true. lets the mBICv choose a truncation level; ctl%trunc_lvl = 2 truncates after tree 2 by fiat.
  • ctl%tree_crit = FV_TREE_RHO (or FV_TREE_HOEFFD, FV_TREE_XI, FV_TREE_MI, ...) changes the edge weights of the spanning trees; ctl%tree_algo = FV_KRUSKAL the algorithm.
  • vc%matrix() returns the R-vine matrix in the original variable labels, the format used by vinecopulib and VineCopula.
FortranPythonR 
ctl%select_trunc = .true.         ! mBICv chooses the truncation level
ctl%trunc_lvl = 2                 ! or: stop after tree 2
ctl%tree_crit = FV_TREE_RHO       ! Spearman's rho as edge weight
ctl%tree_algo = FV_KRUSKAL        ! Kruskal instead of Prim
call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed=.false.)
m = vc%matrix()                   ! R-vine matrix, original labels

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, select_trunc_lvl=True)   # mBICv chooses the truncation level
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, trunc_lvl=2, tree_criterion="rho", tree_algorithm="kruskal")
m = vc.matrix                     # R-vine matrix, original labels

vc <- vinecop(u, trunc_lvl = NA)  # mBICv chooses the truncation level
vc <- vinecop(u, trunc_lvl = 2, tree_crit = "rho", tree_algorithm = "mst_kruskal")
m <- as_rvine_matrix(vc)          # R-vine matrix, original labels

See Vine copulas and Fitting and selection.

docs.title: Weighted and discrete data
docs.text:
Program: example/ex05_weights_discrete.f90  ·  Topics: the weights= argument of fit/select, the discrete= and u_minus= arguments of fv_vinecop%select, pdf, loglik and rosenblatt, randomised Rosenblatt residuals.

Two features that real data often need:

  1. Observation weights. Every fitting and selection routine accepts weights(n). The weighted log-likelihood \(\sum_i w_i \log c(u_i; \theta)\) is maximised, and weighted Kendall taus drive the vine structure.
  2. Discrete variables. Counts, classes and other discrete margins are supported inside a vine following the convention of vinecopulib: each discrete variable is passed as \(u = F(x)\) together with \(u^- = F(x^-)\), the margin's distribution function just below the observed value.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
! ex05_weights_discrete -- (1) observation weights: a time-decay weighted fit that follows a
! change in dependence, and integer weights = duplicated rows; (2) a vine with a discrete
! (Poisson count) variable, passed as u = F(x) and u_minus = F(x-) with discrete = .true.
program ex05_weights_discrete
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 3000, d = 3
  real(dp), parameter :: LAM = 2.0_dp                ! Poisson mean of the count variable
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop, fit
  type(fv_vinecop) :: truth, vd, vn
  real(dp), allocatable :: u1(:), u2(:), w(:), wt(:), x1(:), x2(:)
  real(dp), allocatable :: z(:, :), u(:, :), um(:, :), umid(:, :), r(:, :), dens(:)
  integer :: i, k, cnt

  ! ---------------------------------------------------------------- (1) weights
  allocate(u1(n), u2(n), w(n), wt(n), x1(2 * n), x2(2 * n))
  call seed_rng(11)
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  cop%family = FV_CLAYTON
  cop%par(1) = 1.0_dp; call cop%hinv1(u1(1:n/2), w(1:n/2), u2(1:n/2))           ! old regime: tau 1/3
  cop%par(1) = 4.0_dp; call cop%hinv1(u1(n/2+1:), w(n/2+1:), u2(n/2+1:))       ! recent regime: tau 2/3

  fit%family = FV_CLAYTON
  call fit%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,f7.3)', 'Clayton fit, equal weights:          theta =', fit%par(1)
  wt = [(0.998_dp**(n - i), i = 1, n)]                ! exponential time decay, half-life ~350 rows
  call fit%fit(u1, u2, weights=wt)
  print '(a,f7.3,a,f7.1,a)', 'Clayton fit, time-decay weights:     theta =', fit%par(1), &
    '   (effective n =', sum(wt)**2 / sum(wt**2), ')'

  ! integer weights are the same as repeating rows
  call random_number(wt)
  wt = merge(2.0_dp, 1.0_dp, wt > 0.5_dp)
  k = 0
  do i = 1, n
    do cnt = 1, nint(wt(i))
      k = k + 1; x1(k) = u1(i); x2(k) = u2(i)
    end do
  end do
  call fit%fit(u1, u2, weights=wt)
  print '(a,f12.8,a,f12.4)', 'weights 1/2:     theta =', fit%par(1), '  loglik =', fit%loglik
  call fit%fit(x1(1:k), x2(1:k))
  print '(a,f12.8,a,f12.4)', 'duplicated rows: theta =', fit%par(1), '  loglik =', fit%loglik

  ! ---------------------------------------------------------------- (2) a discrete variable
  ! D-vine 1-2-3: gaussian(0.7) and clayton(2) in tree 1, frank(2) in tree 2
  allocate(z(n, d), u(n, d), um(n, d), umid(n, d), r(n, d), dens(n))
  call truth%set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
  truth%fam(1:2, 1) = [FV_GAUSSIAN, FV_CLAYTON]
  truth%par(1, 1, 1) = 0.7_dp; truth%par(1, 2, 1) = 2.0_dp
  truth%fam(1, 2) = FV_FRANK; truth%par(1, 1, 2) = 2.0_dp
  call truth%simulate(n, z, seed=5)

  ! variable 2 becomes a Poisson(2) count x = F^-1(z); the copula data are F(x) and F(x-)
  u = z; um = z                                      ! continuous columns: u_minus is not used
  do i = 1, n
    k = qpois(z(i, 2))
    u(i, 2) = ppois(k); um(i, 2) = ppois(k - 1)
  end do
  print '(/,a,i0,a,i0,a,f6.3)', 'count variable: ', count(um(:, 2) == 0.0_dp), ' zeros, maximum ', &
    maxval([(qpois(z(i, 2)), i = 1, n)]), ', mean ', sum([(qpois(z(i, 2)), i = 1, n)]) / real(n, dp)

  ! (a) the discrete-aware fit on the fixed D-vine structure
  call vd%set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
  call vd%select(u, discrete=[.false., .true., .false.], u_minus=um)
  ! (b) a naive fit that treats the count as continuous (mid-point of its CDF jump)
  umid = u; umid(:, 2) = 0.5_dp * (u(:, 2) + um(:, 2))
  call vn%set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
  call vn%select(umid)
  ! select may store the same D-vine in the reverse order, so edges are found by their pair
  print '(a)', 'tree-1 pair      truth             discrete-aware    naive'
  do k = 1, 2
    print '(a,i0,a,i0,a,3(a10,f7.3,1x))', '  (', k, ',', k + 1, ')    ', &
      fv_fam_name(truth%fam(edge(truth, k, k + 1), 1)), truth%par(1, edge(truth, k, k + 1), 1), &
      fv_fam_name(vd%fam(edge(vd, k, k + 1), 1)), vd%par(1, edge(vd, k, k + 1), 1), &
      fv_fam_name(vn%fam(edge(vn, k, k + 1), 1)), vn%par(1, edge(vn, k, k + 1), 1)
  end do

  ! log-likelihood of the mixed data (density in x1, x3 times probability mass in x2)
  truth%disc = [.false., .true., .false.]
  print '(a,f10.2,a,f10.2)', 'loglik of the mixed data: truth', truth%loglik(u, um), &
    '   discrete-aware fit', vd%loglik(u, um)
  call vd%pdf(u(1:3, :), dens(1:3), u_minus=um(1:3, :))
  print '(a,3es11.3)', 'first three mixed densities:', dens(1:3)

  ! randomised Rosenblatt transform (Brockwell 2007): iid uniform when the model is right
  call vd%rosenblatt(u, r, u_minus=um, seed=1)
  print '(a,3f8.4)', 'Rosenblatt column means (1/2):       ', sum(r, 1) / n
  print '(a,3f8.4)', 'Rosenblatt column variances (1/12):  ', &
    [(sum((r(:, k) - sum(r(:, k)) / n)**2) / n, k = 1, d)]
  print '(a,3f8.4)', 'Kendall tau (1,2) (1,3) (2,3), ~0:   ', fv_kendall_tau(r(:, 1), r(:, 2)), &
    fv_kendall_tau(r(:, 1), r(:, 3)), fv_kendall_tau(r(:, 2), r(:, 3))

contains

  ! index of the tree-1 edge joining variables a and b: edge e joins m(d-e+1, e) and m(1, e)
  integer function edge(v, a, b)
    type(fv_vinecop), intent(in) :: v
    integer, intent(in) :: a, b
    integer :: m(v%d, v%d), e
    m = v%matrix()
    do e = 1, v%d - 1
      edge = e
      if (minval([m(v%d - e + 1, e), m(1, e)]) == min(a, b) .and. maxval([m(v%d - e + 1, e), m(1, e)]) == max(a, b)) &
        return
    end do
    edge = 0
  end function edge

  subroutine seed_rng(seed)
    integer, intent(in) :: seed
    integer :: ns, j
    integer, allocatable :: s(:)
    call random_seed(size=ns)
    s = [(seed + 7919 * j, j = 1, ns)]
    call random_seed(put=s)
  end subroutine seed_rng

  ! Poisson(LAM) distribution function F(k) and quantile min{k : F(k) >= p}
  pure real(dp) function ppois(k)
    integer, intent(in) :: k
    real(dp) :: p
    integer :: j
    ppois = 0.0_dp
    if (k < 0) return
    p = exp(-LAM); ppois = p
    do j = 1, k
      p = p * LAM / j; ppois = ppois + p
    end do
  end function ppois

  pure integer function qpois(p)
    real(dp), intent(in) :: p
    qpois = 0
    do while (ppois(qpois) < p)
      qpois = qpois + 1
    end do
  end function qpois
end program ex05_weights_discrete

# ex05_weights_discrete.py -- the Python version of example/ex05_weights_discrete.f90:
# (1) observation weights: a time-decay weighted fit that follows a change in dependence, and
# integer weights = duplicated rows; (2) a vine with a discrete (Poisson count) variable.
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import poisson
import fortvine as fv

n, LAM = 3000, 2.0
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- (1) weights
u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
u2 = np.concatenate([fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [1.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w])[: n // 2]),   # tau 1/3
                     fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [4.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w])[n // 2:])])   # tau 2/3
u = np.column_stack([u1, u2])
fit = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u)
print("Clayton fit, equal weights:          theta = %6.3f" % fit.parameters[0])
wt = 0.998 ** (n - 1 - np.arange(n))              # exponential time decay, half-life ~350 rows
fit = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u, weights=wt)
print("Clayton fit, time-decay weights:     theta = %6.3f   (effective n = %6.1f)"
      % (fit.parameters[0], wt.sum() ** 2 / (wt ** 2).sum()))

wt = np.where(rng.random(n) > 0.5, 2.0, 1.0)      # integer weights = repeated rows
fit = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(u, weights=wt)
print("weights 1/2:     theta = %.8f  loglik = %.4f" % (fit.parameters[0], fit.loglik()))
fit = fv.Bicop("clayton").fit(np.repeat(u, wt.astype(int), axis=0))
print("duplicated rows: theta = %.8f  loglik = %.4f" % (fit.parameters[0], fit.loglik()))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- (2) a discrete variable
# D-vine 1-2-3: gaussian(0.7) and clayton(2) in tree 1, frank(2) in tree 2
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
truth.fam[0, :2] = [1, 3]; truth.par[0, 0, 0], truth.par[0, 1, 0] = 0.7, 2.0
truth.fam[1, 0] = 5; truth.par[1, 0, 0] = 2.0
z = truth.simulate(n, seed=5)

# variable 2 becomes a Poisson(2) count; the data are F(x) of all three, then F(x-) of the count
k = poisson.ppf(z[:, 1], LAM)
u = np.column_stack([z[:, 0], poisson.cdf(k, LAM), z[:, 2], poisson.cdf(k - 1, LAM)])
print("\ncount variable: %d zeros, maximum %d, mean %.3f" % ((k == 0).sum(), k.max(), k.mean()))

vd = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3]).select(u, var_types=["c", "d", "c"])   # discrete-aware
umid = u[:, :3].copy(); umid[:, 1] = 0.5 * (u[:, 1] + u[:, 3])                # naive: mid-point
vn = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3]).select(umid)
print("discrete-aware fit:\n%s\nnaive fit:\n%s" % (vd, vn))

truth.var_types = ["c", "d", "c"]
print("loglik of the mixed data: truth %9.2f   discrete-aware fit %9.2f" % (truth.loglik(u), vd.loglik(u)))
print("first three mixed densities:", np.array2string(vd.pdf(u[:3]), precision=3))

r = vd.rosenblatt(u, seed=1)                      # randomised Rosenblatt transform (Brockwell 2007)
print("Rosenblatt column means (1/2):      ", r.mean(axis=0).round(4))
print("Rosenblatt column variances (1/12): ", r.var(axis=0).round(4))
print("Kendall tau (1,2) (1,3) (2,3), ~0:  ", np.round([fv.kendall_tau(r[:, 0], r[:, 1]),
      fv.kendall_tau(r[:, 0], r[:, 2]), fv.kendall_tau(r[:, 1], r[:, 2])], 4))

# ex05_weights_discrete.R -- the R version of example/ex05_weights_discrete.f90:
# (1) observation weights: a time-decay weighted fit that follows a change in dependence, and
# integer weights = duplicated rows; (2) a vine with a discrete (Poisson count) variable.
library(fortvine)
n <- 3000; LAM <- 2
set.seed(11)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- (1) weights
u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n); h <- 1:(n / 2)
u2 <- c(hbicop(cbind(u1, w)[h, ], 1, "clayton", 0, 1, inverse = TRUE),      # tau 1/3
        hbicop(cbind(u1, w)[-h, ], 1, "clayton", 0, 4, inverse = TRUE))     # tau 2/3
u <- cbind(u1, u2)
fit <- bicop(u, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0)
cat(sprintf("Clayton fit, equal weights:          theta = %6.3f\n", fit$parameters))
wt <- 0.998^(n - seq_len(n))                     # exponential time decay, half-life ~350 rows
fit <- bicop(u, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0, weights = wt)
cat(sprintf("Clayton fit, time-decay weights:     theta = %6.3f   (effective n = %6.1f)\n",
            fit$parameters, sum(wt)^2 / sum(wt^2)))

wt <- ifelse(runif(n) > 0.5, 2, 1)               # integer weights = repeated rows
fit <- bicop(u, family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0, weights = wt)
cat(sprintf("weights 1/2:     theta = %.8f  loglik = %.4f\n", fit$parameters, fit$loglik))
fit <- bicop(u[rep(seq_len(n), wt), ], family_set = "clayton", rotation = 0)
cat(sprintf("duplicated rows: theta = %.8f  loglik = %.4f\n", fit$parameters, fit$loglik))

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- (2) a discrete variable
# D-vine 1-2-3: gaussian(0.7) and clayton(2) in tree 1, frank(2) in tree 2
pcs <- list(list(bicop_dist("gaussian", 0, 0.7), bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)),
            list(bicop_dist("frank", 0, 2)))
truth <- vinecop_dist(pcs, dvine_structure(1:3))
set.seed(5)
z <- rvinecop(n, truth)

# variable 2 becomes a Poisson(2) count; the data are F(x) of all three, then F(x-) of the count
k <- qpois(z[, 2], LAM)
u <- cbind(z[, 1], ppois(k, LAM), z[, 3], ppois(k - 1, LAM))
cat(sprintf("\ncount variable: %d zeros, maximum %d, mean %.3f\n", sum(k == 0), max(k), mean(k)))

vd <- vinecop(u, structure = dvine_structure(1:3), var_types = c("c", "d", "c"))   # discrete-aware
umid <- u[, 1:3]; umid[, 2] <- (u[, 2] + u[, 4]) / 2                               # naive: mid-point
vn <- vinecop(umid, structure = dvine_structure(1:3))
cat("discrete-aware fit:\n"); print(summary(vd)[, c("tree", "conditioned", "family", "parameters")])
cat("naive fit:\n"); print(summary(vn)[, c("tree", "conditioned", "family", "parameters")])

truth <- vinecop_dist(pcs, dvine_structure(1:3), var_types = c("c", "d", "c"))
cat(sprintf("loglik of the mixed data: truth %9.2f   discrete-aware fit %9.2f\n",
            sum(log(dvinecop(u, truth))), vd$loglik))
cat("first three mixed densities:", signif(dvinecop(u[1:3, ], vd), 4), "\n")

set.seed(1)
r <- rosenblatt(u, vd)                            # randomised Rosenblatt transform (Brockwell 2007)
cat("Rosenblatt column means (1/2):      ", round(colMeans(r), 4), "\n")
cat("Rosenblatt column variances (1/12): ", round(apply(r, 2, var), 4), "\n")
tc <- cor(r, method = "kendall")
cat("Kendall tau (1,2) (1,3) (2,3), ~0:  ", round(tc[cbind(c(1, 1, 2), c(2, 3, 3))], 4), "\n")

docs.title: Following a change in dependence
docs.text:
The 3000 observations are generated in two regimes: the first half from Clayton with \(\theta = 1\) (\(\tau = 1/3\)), the second half from Clayton with \(\theta = 4\) (\(\tau = 2/3\)). An ordinary fit treats all rows alike and lands in between (\(\hat\theta = 1.88\)). Weights that decay exponentially with age,

\[ w_i = 0.998^{\,n - i}, \qquad n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_i w_i)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2} \approx 994, \]

concentrate the fit on the recent regime: \(\hat\theta = 3.48\), close to the current value 4 (the oldest weights still pull it down a little). This is the usual way to obtain a time-varying dependence estimate from a rolling sample.

wt = [(0.998_dp**(n - i), i = 1, n)]
call fit%fit(u1, u2, weights=wt)

(a) The 3000 observations in normal scores, coloured by their weight $w_i = 0.998^{\,n - i}$: the recent regime ($\theta = 4$, dark) is the tighter cloud. (b) The Clayton log-likelihood per unit weight, $\ell_w(\theta) / \sum_i w_i$, each curve shifted to a maximum of 0, with equal weights (grey) and with the time-decay weights (blue); the triangles mark the estimates $\hat\theta = 1.88$ and $\hat\theta = 3.48$. Fitted to each regime alone, the same data give $\hat\theta = 1.03$ and $\hat\theta = 3.81$.

docs.title: Weights as frequencies
docs.text:
With integer weights, a weighted fit is exactly the fit to a sample in which observation \(i\) is repeated \(w_i\) times. The program draws weights 1 or 2 at random, builds the expanded sample, and fits both: the estimates agree to all printed digits (\(\hat\theta = 1.87489409\)) and so do the log-likelihoods. The test suite checks the same identity for the weighted Kendall tau and for a two-parameter family (Validation).

Weights are accepted by fv_bicop%fit, fv_bicop%select and fv_vinecop%select; for a vine they also enter the weighted tau that builds the spanning trees, and with select_threshold the effective sample size \(n_{\text{eff}}\) replaces \(n\) in the mBICv.

docs.title: Part 2: a vine with a count variable
Making the data
docs.text:
A three-dimensional D-vine 1-2-3 is simulated (Gaussian \(\rho = 0.7\) on (1,2), Clayton \(\theta = 2\) on (2,3), Frank \(\theta = 2\) on (1,3 | 2)), and variable 2 is turned into a Poisson(2) count through its quantile function, \(x_2 = F_{\text{Pois}}^{-1}(u_2)\). The copula of \((U_1, X_2, U_3)\) is still the D-vine; only the second margin is now discrete, with 389 zeros among the 3000 values.

For the discrete column the program stores

u(i, 2)  = ppois(k)       ! F(x)   with k = x_i2
um(i, 2) = ppois(k - 1)   ! F(x-)  = F(x - 1) for integer data

and for the continuous columns um = u (the values are not used). Here the Poisson distribution function is known; with real data the empirical distribution function of the counts plays its role.

The mixed data. (a, b) The count $x_2$ (jittered horizontally for display only) against the normal scores of the continuous variables: Gaussian dependence with $\rho = 0.7$ on $(1, 2)$ and Clayton dependence with $\theta = 2$ on $(2, 3)$, whose lower tail shows as the tight cluster at $x_2 = 0$. (c) On the copula scale an observed count only says that $u_2$ lies in the interval $[F(x_2^-), F(x_2)]$ (blue segments, first 150 rows); the discrete-aware likelihood integrates over that interval, the naive fit replaces it by its mid-point (gold).

docs.title: Fitting with and without the discrete information
docs.text:
call vd%set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
call vd%select(u, discrete=[.false., .true., .false.], u_minus=um)

With discrete= and u_minus=, every pair copula that involves a discrete argument is evaluated as a probability of a rectangle instead of a density. For a pair (continuous \(u_1\), discrete \(x_2\)) the likelihood contribution is

\[ h_1\bigl(F(x_2) \mid u_1\bigr) - h_1\bigl(F(x_2^-) \mid u_1\bigr), \]

and for two discrete arguments it is the copula mass of the cell \(C(u_1, u_2) - C(u_1^-, u_2) - C(u_1, u_2^-) + C(u_1^-, u_2^-)\) (Panagiotelis, Czado & Joe 2012). Conditional distributions for the next tree are formed from the same differences, so the whole vine sweep carries both \(F(x)\) and \(F(x^-)\) for discrete nodes.

The naive alternative pretends the count is continuous by placing each value in the middle of its jump, \(u = (F(x) + F(x^-))/2\). The table compares the tree-1 pairs:

Pair Truth \(\theta\) Discrete-aware \(\hat\theta\) Naive (mid-point) \(\hat\theta\) \((1, 2)\) Gaussian 0.700 Gaussian 0.714 Gaussian 0.706 \((2, 3)\) Clayton 2.000 Clayton 2.119 BB8 3.407

(\(\theta\) is the first parameter of each family: \(\rho\) for the Gaussian copula.)

The discrete-aware fit recovers both families. The naive one keeps the Gaussian pair but mistakes the Clayton pair: the ties at only ten distinct values destroy the fine structure of the lower tail that identifies Clayton, and BIC prefers a different family. The size of such distortions depends on how coarse the discrete variable is; with only a handful of categories they can be severe.

Edges are identified by their variables

select may store a fixed D-vine in the reverse order (3 2 1 instead of 1 2 3, which is the same vine). The program therefore locates the tree-1 edge that joins two given variables through vc%matrix(): in the R-vine matrix m, edge e of tree 1 joins m(d-e+1, e) and m(1, e).

docs.title: Density, likelihood and residuals
docs.text:
print *, truth%loglik(u, um), vd%loglik(u, um)
call vd%pdf(u, dens, u_minus=um)
call vd%rosenblatt(u, r, u_minus=um, seed=1)
  • loglik(u, um) is the log of a mixed density: a density in \(u_1\) and \(u_3\) times a probability mass in \(x_2\). The fit (2246.6) exceeds the truth (2241.2) by a few units, as a maximum-likelihood fit with 3 parameters should.
  • pdf(u, dens, u_minus=um) returns those mixed densities per row. The truth's discrete flags are set by hand (truth%disc = [.false., .true., .false.]) because it was not produced by select.
  • rosenblatt(u, r, u_minus=um) returns Brockwell's (2007) randomised transform: for the discrete coordinate the conditional distribution has a jump from \(F(x^-\mid\cdot)\) to \(F(x \mid \cdot)\), and a uniform point \(W F(x \mid \cdot) + (1 - W)F(x^- \mid \cdot)\) inside the jump is returned, with \(W\) drawn reproducibly from seed. Under the model the result is i.i.d. uniform: here the column means are 0.49-0.50 (expected 1/2), the variances 0.082-0.084 (expected \(1/12 = 0.0833\)), and the pairwise Kendall taus are at most 0.006 in absolute value. Pass randomize=.false. to get \(F(x \mid \cdot)\) itself, with out_minus= receiving \(F(x^- \mid \cdot)\).
Histograms (20 bins) of the randomised Rosenblatt residuals $r_1, r_2, r_3$ of the discrete-aware fit, $n = 3000$. The shaded band is the uniform density 1 plus or minus two binomial standard errors per bin; all three columns scatter about 1 with the expected spread. For the discrete variable, the non-randomised $F(x_2 \mid x_1)$ (gold outline) is far from uniform: it is the upper end of each conditional jump and therefore piles up towards 1, which is why the randomisation is needed before any uniformity check.

See Discrete and mixed data for the full interface, including pdf_grid with discrete variables.

docs.title: Copula families
docs.text: fortvine offers 111 pair-copula families: 26 hand-coded families with codes 0 to 25, and 85 families produced by a single generic engine with codes from 10000 up. This section describes them by construction. Every page gives the copula, its density and h-functions, the parameter box fortvine uses, Kendall's tau, the tail dependence coefficients and the symmetry properties; the complete catalogue lists every code with its name and box in one table.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
Throughout, \((u, v) \in (0, 1)^2\) and

  • \(C(u, v)\) is the copula and \(c(u, v) = \partial^2 C / \partial u\, \partial v\) its density;
  • \(h_1(v \mid u) = \partial C(u, v) / \partial u\) is the conditional distribution of \(V\) given \(U = u\), and \(h_2(u \mid v) = \partial C(u, v) / \partial v\) that of \(U\) given \(V = v\) (fortvine's hfunc1 and hfunc2); their inverses (hinv1, hinv2) drive simulation and the inverse Rosenblatt transform;
  • \(\tau\) is Kendall's tau, \(\tau = 4\,\mathrm{E}\,C(U, V) - 1\);
  • \(\lambda_L = \lim_{t \to 0} C(t, t)/t\) and \(\lambda_U = \lim_{t \to 1} \big(1 - 2t + C(t, t)\big)/(1 - t)\) are the lower and upper tail dependence coefficients;
  • a copula is exchangeable if \(C(u, v) = C(v, u)\);
  • parameters are written in the order in which they are stored in par(1:3).

Rotations. Most families describe positive dependence only. fortvine extends them by rotating the data counter-clockwise, as vinecopulib does: with \(c_0\) the unrotated density,

rotation density effect 0 \(c_0(u, v)\) as defined 90 \(c_0(v, 1 - u)\) negative dependence 180 \(c_0(1 - u, 1 - v)\) survival copula: lower and upper tails swap 270 \(c_0(1 - v, u)\) negative dependence

The families that already cover both signs, or are radially symmetric (independence, Gaussian, Student t, Frank, Plackett, FGM, AMH and the two nonparametric families), have no rotations. Details are in the manual.

docs.title: Constructions
docs.text:
Construction General form Hand-coded Generic Page Independence \(C(u, v) = uv\) 1 — — Elliptical \(F_\rho\big(F^{-1}(u), F^{-1}(v)\big)\) 2 — Elliptical Archimedean \(\psi\big(\varphi(u) + \varphi(v)\big)\), \(\psi\) a Laplace transform 13 6 Archimedean Extreme-value \(\exp\!\big(-(x + y)\, A\big(\tfrac{y}{x + y}\big)\big)\), \(x = -\log u\) 5 (+ Gumbel) 9 Extreme-value Archimax \(\psi\big(\ell(\varphi(u), \varphi(v))\big)\) 1 67 Archimax Khoudraji \(u^{1-a} v^{1-b} C_0(u^a, v^b)\) — 3 Khoudraji Other parametric Plackett, FGM 2 — Other Nonparametric TLL, Bernstein 2 — Nonparametric Total 26 85

Elliptical. The Gaussian and Student t copulas: the dependence of an elliptical distribution with its margins made uniform. Symmetric in every sense; the t copula has equal tail dependence in both corners.

Archimedean. A single decreasing convex function \(\psi\), the generator, with inverse \(\varphi\). fortvine draws every generator from seven Laplace-transform families (positive stable, gamma, Sibuya, logarithmic series, tilted positive stable, generalised Sibuya, negative binomial) and from compositions \(\psi_o(-\log\zeta(s))\) of two of them. The hand-coded members are Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, AMH and BB1, BB2, BB3, BB6, BB7, BB8, BB9, BB10; the generic engine adds six new compositions. Gumbel is counted here even though it is also extreme-value.

Extreme-value. Max-stable copulas, determined by a convex Pickands function \(A\) on \([0, 1]\). Positive dependence and upper-tail dependence only. Hand-coded: Tawn's asymmetric logistic, Galambos, Hüsler–Reiss, BB5 and the t-EV copula (plus Gumbel); the generic engine adds the symmetric and asymmetric mixed models, the one-weight Tawn types, Joe's asymmetric negative logistic and its types, and Khoudraji versions of Hüsler–Reiss and the mixed model.

Archimax. Capéraà, Fougères & Genest's (2000) combination of an Archimedean generator and a Pickands function, \(\ell(s, t) = (s + t) A(t/(s + t))\). It contains both previous classes and gives the only non-exchangeable families with dependence in both tails. BB4 is hand-coded; BB1, BB5 and BB6 are also Archimax copulas.

Khoudraji. An asymmetrisation that turns any copula into a non-exchangeable one with two extra exponents. Applied to Clayton, Joe and Frank it gives three new families; applied to extreme-value bases it gives the asymmetric EV models listed above.

Other parametric and nonparametric. Plackett and Farlie–Gumbel–Morgenstern belong to no construction above. TLL (transformation local likelihood) and the Bernstein copula estimate the copula density directly from the data.

docs.title: Generic families: fam = 10000 k + 100 og + ie
docs.text:
A generic code is read as three digits groups. Take 10206 as an example: k = 1, og = 02, ie = 06, an Archimax copula with the gamma generator and the type-1 asymmetric logistic Pickands function, parameters \((\theta, \theta_\ell, \psi_1)\).

field values meaning k 1 the copula as built from og and ie 2 its Khoudraji asymmetrisation, two more parameters \((a, b)\) og 0 no generator, \(\psi(s) = e^{-s}\): the copula is extreme-value 1–4 positive stable, gamma, Sibuya, log series (one parameter) 5–7 tilted positive stable, generalised Sibuya, negative binomial (two parameters) 11–26 composition po.pin: outer po and inner pin from 1–4, og = 10 + 4(po - 1) + pin (two parameters) ie 0 independence inner, \(\ell(s, t) = s + t\): the copula is Archimedean 1–4 logistic, negative logistic, Hüsler–Reiss, symmetric mixed (one parameter) 6, 7, 9, 10, 11 asymmetric logistic types 1/2, asymmetric negative logistic types 1/2, asymmetric mixed (two parameters) 5, 8, 12, 13 asymmetric logistic, asymmetric negative logistic, Khoudraji–HR, Khoudraji–mixed (three parameters)

Parameters are stored in the order generator, Pickands function, Khoudraji exponents, with at most three in total. The generic engine accepts a code only if it is well defined and identifiable (gen_valid):

  • at most three parameters;
  • not the independence copula (og = 0, ie = 0) and not Gumbel written as positive stable plus logistic (10101);
  • not a composition that collapses to one transform (PS.PS, Sibuya.Sibuya) or that is not accurate in double precision (a log-series inner under a positive stable, Sibuya or log-series outer);
  • no Pickands function together with a gamma-inner composition (BB2, BB3, BB7 and logseries.gamma type generators);
  • no Khoudraji wrapper around an already asymmetric Pickands function (ie ≥ 5).

Of the valid codes, those that duplicate a hand-coded family or another generic code (gen_dup: for example 10200 = Clayton, 10202 = BB4, 20100 = Tawn) stay usable for cross-checks but are left out of fv_generic_families(). The 85 codes it returns are 6 Archimedean, 9 extreme-value, 67 Archimax and 3 Khoudraji families.

FortranPythonR 
integer, allocatable :: codes(:)
codes = fv_generic_families()          ! the 85 new codes
print *, trim(fv_fam_name(10206))      ! Archimax(gamma|asymlogistic1)
print *, gen_npar(10206)               ! 3

codes = [f.code for f in fv.families() if f.code >= 10000]   # the 85 new codes
cop = fv.Bicop(10206, 0, [1.5, 0.5, 2.0])
print(cop.family)                      # Archimax(gamma|asymlogistic1)
print(cop.npars)                       # 3

fam <- fortvine_families()
codes <- fam$code[fam$code >= 10000]   # the 85 new codes
fam[fam$code == 10206, ]               # Archimax(gamma|asymlogistic1), npars 3

Unrotated families; the 180° rotation swaps \(\lambda_L\) and \(\lambda_U\), and the 90°/270° rotations move the tail dependence to the off-diagonal corners.

For the generic families the rules are short:

generic class \(\lambda_L\) \(\lambda_U\) extreme-value (og = 0) 0 \(2(1 - A(1/2))\) Archimedean compositions from a gamma part only from a positive stable or Sibuya part Archimax \((2A(1/2))^{-1/k}\) with a gamma outer part, else 0 \(2 - (2A(1/2))^{1/m}\), positive unless \(A \equiv 1\) Khoudraji 0 unless \(a = b = 1\) \(a + b - \ell_0(a, b)\)

The exponents \(k\) and \(m\) and the per-family formulas are on the Archimedean and Archimax pages. The lower tail and upper tail columns of the catalogue record which tails a family can have somewhere in its parameter box; they are what fortvine's preselection uses.

Where the families sit in the tail plane. For each family at Kendall's $ au = 0.5$ (Tawn: $ au = 0.4$), the finite-level coefficients $\lambda_L(q) = C(q, q)/q$ and $\lambda_U(q) = \{2q - 1 + C(1 - q, 1 - q)\}/q$ from fortvine's `cdf`, followed from $q = 10^{-1}$ (open circle) to $q = 10^{-8}$ (filled). Clayton ends on the $\lambda_L$ axis, the extreme-value and Joe copulas on the $\lambda_U$ axis (Gumbel, Galambos and Hüsler-Reiss on top of each other), BB1, BB7 and BB4 inside the plane with both tails, the Student t copula ($ u = 4$) on the diagonal at 0.397 (its limit $\lambda_L = \lambda_U$; its path runs under those of the Gaussian and Frank copulas), Frank at the origin. The Gaussian copula is still at 0.017 at $q = 10^{-8}$: its limit is 0, but it is approached only logarithmically.

docs.title: Choosing a family set
docs.text:
The family set is the list of candidates that select compares for each pair (or vine edge), held in ctl%family_set(1:ctl%nfam). Some guidelines:

  • Default. fv_controls starts with the 23 parametric families 0–22. Setting ctl%nfam = 24 adds the t-EV copula, which is slow to fit, and ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC (26) adds the two nonparametric families as well.
  • vinecopulib parity. FV_PARAMETRIC (codes 0–11) is the set used by vinecopulib and pyvinecopulib, convenient for comparisons.
  • Fast first pass. FV_ONE_PAR (Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe) plus independence. With ctl%method = FV_ITAU (tau inversion instead of maximum likelihood) only codes 0–6 are considered.

  • Adding generic families. Append fv_generic_families() (85 codes) or a hand-picked subset; family_set holds up to 192 codes.

    integer, allocatable :: g(:)
g = fv_generic_families()
ctl%family_set = 0
ctl%family_set(1:24) = FV_ALL                       ! hand-coded 0..23
ctl%family_set(25:24 + size(g)) = g
ctl%nfam = 24 + size(g)

  • What the extra families buy. Asymmetry (Tawn and its types, the asymmetric EV models, Khoudraji and the asymmetric Archimax codes) and both-tail dependence with separate control of each tail (BB1, BB4, BB7, gamma.Sibuya 11700, gamma-generator Archimax). Families that differ only in fine detail add run time but rarely change a selection: at equal Kendall's tau, Gumbel, Galambos, Hüsler–Reiss and t-EV are nearly indistinguishable.

  • Penalties and sample size. With BIC, every extra parameter must earn its keep, so three-parameter families win only on large samples with clear asymmetry. On small samples a short list of one- and two-parameter families is both faster and more stable.
  • Preselection (ctl%preselect, on by default) drops rotations and families whose tail pattern contradicts the data, using the correlation of the normal scores in the two opposite quadrants, so a large family set costs less than its length suggests.

How alike Gumbel, Galambos and Hüsler-Reiss are. (a) The family that BIC selects from all 24 parametric families on 100 samples of 1000 points from a Gumbel copula with $\theta = 2$: Gumbel 71 times, Galambos 23, Hüsler-Reiss 3. (b) On the same samples, the BIC of each alternative fitted on its own, relative to the Gumbel fit (symmetric log scale): Galambos is within a few units either way, the two-parameter families pay their extra $\log n$, and Joe, whose upper tail is shaped differently, is far behind.

See fitting and selection for the selection criteria and the generic engine for how the 85 codes are evaluated.

docs.title: Archimax families
docs.text:
Archimax copulas (Capéraà, Fougères & Genest 2000) join the two previous constructions. An Archimedean generator \(\psi\) (with inverse \(\varphi\)) supplies the body and the lower tail, an extreme-value Pickands function \(A\) supplies the shape of the upper tail and, if wanted, asymmetry:

\[ C(u, v) = \psi\Big( \ell\big(\varphi(u), \varphi(v)\big) \Big), \qquad \ell(s, t) = (s + t)\, A\!\left(\frac{t}{s + t}\right). \]

The two special cases are the familiar ones. With \(A \equiv 1\), \(\ell(s, t) = s + t\) and \(C\) is Archimedean; with \(\psi(s) = e^{-s}\), \(\varphi(u) = -\log u\) and \(C\) is an extreme-value copula. In fortvine the generator is any of the Laplace transforms (or a composition of two) and \(A\) is any of the Pickands functions; one formula in src/families_gen.inc evaluates them all.

Archimax copulas at Kendall's \(\tau \approx 0.5\). BB4 and gamma–Hüsler–Reiss (left two) are exchangeable with both tails; gamma with the asymmetric logistic type 1 (top right) adds asymmetry to both-tail dependence.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
With \(S = \varphi(u)\), \(T = \varphi(v)\), \(w = T/(S + T)\) and \(L = \ell(S, T)\), the partial derivatives of \(\ell\) are

\[ \ell_s = A(w) - w A'(w), \qquad \ell_t = A(w) + (1 - w) A'(w), \qquad \ell_{st} = -\frac{w(1 - w)}{S + T}\, A''(w) \le 0, \]

and the density and h-functions are

\[ c(u, v) = \frac{\psi''(L)\, \ell_s \ell_t + \big(-\psi'(L)\big)\big(-\ell_{st}\big)}{\psi'(S)\, \psi'(T)}, \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{\psi'(L)\, \ell_s}{\psi'(S)}, \qquad h_2(u \mid v) = \frac{\psi'(L)\, \ell_t}{\psi'(T)} . \]

Both terms of the density numerator are non-negative, and fortvine adds them in log space. The Pickands argument \(w\) is computed from \(\log S\) and \(\log T\), so it stays exact even when \(S\) and \(T\) differ by many orders of magnitude.

Kendall's tau separates into the two ingredients (Capéraà, Fougères & Genest 2000):

\[ \tau = \tau_A + (1 - \tau_A)\, \tau_\psi , \]

where \(\tau_A = \int_0^1 w(1-w) A''(w)/A(w)\, dw\) is the tau of the EV copula with Pickands function \(A\), and \(\tau_\psi\) is the tau of the Archimedean copula with generator \(\psi\). The formula was checked with fortvine's own quadrature: gamma generator \(\theta = 1\) (\(\tau_\psi = 1/3\)) with Hüsler–Reiss \(\lambda = 2\) (\(\tau_A = 0.5387\)) gives \(0.6925\) both ways.

Tail dependence combines the midpoint value \(A(1/2)\) with the end behaviour of \(\psi\) used on the Archimedean page. If \(1 - \psi(s)\) behaves like \(s^{1/m}\) at zero (\(m = 1\) when \(\psi'(0)\) is finite) and \(\psi(s)\) like \(s^{-1/k}\) at infinity, then

\[ \lambda_U = 2 - \big(2A(1/2)\big)^{1/m}, \qquad \lambda_L = \big(2A(1/2)\big)^{-1/k}, \]

and \(\lambda_L = 0\) when \(\psi\) decays faster than any power. For the generators in fortvine:

outer generator \(m\) (upper tail) \(k\) (lower tail) positive stable (\(\theta\)) \(\theta\) none (\(\lambda_L = 0\)) gamma (\(\theta\)) 1 \(\theta\) Sibuya (\(\theta\)) \(\theta\) none log series, tilted PS, generalised Sibuya (\(\delta < 1\)), negative binomial 1 none PS.Sibuya (\(\theta, \delta\)) \(\theta\delta\) none gamma.PS (\(\theta, \delta\)) \(\delta\) \(\theta\delta\) gamma.Sibuya (\(\theta, \delta\)) \(\delta\) \(\theta\) gamma.logseries (\(\theta, \delta\)) 1 \(\theta\) Sibuya.PS (\(\theta, \delta\)) \(\theta\delta\) none logseries.PS, logseries.Sibuya (\(\theta, \delta\)) \(\delta\) none

So an Archimax copula has lower-tail dependence exactly when its generator contains the gamma transform as the outer part, and with \(m = 1\) its upper tail coefficient equals that of the Pickands function alone, \(2 - 2A(1/2)\). These values were confirmed numerically for one member of each row.

Symmetry and rotations. The generator is symmetric, so an Archimax copula is exchangeable exactly when \(A\) is (\(A(w) = A(1 - w)\), i.e. Pickands codes 1 to 4). A vine edge flip transposes the inner Pickands function as described on the extreme-value page. All Archimax codes accept the 90°, 180° and 270° rotations.

Parameter order. Outer generator parameters first (one or two), then the Pickands parameters, at most three in total. Hence a two-parameter generator can only be combined with a one-parameter Pickands function (codes 1–4).

docs.title: Named members
docs.text:
Several classical two-parameter families are Archimax copulas. fortvine keeps the hand-coded versions and marks the generic codes as duplicates:

Family Generator Pickands function Hand code Generic code BB1 gamma logistic 7 10201 BB4 gamma negative logistic 22 10202 BB5 positive stable negative logistic 19 10102 BB6 Sibuya logistic 8 10301 logseries.PS log series logistic — 10401 (= 12300) Gumbel positive stable logistic 4 (rejected)

The last two rows illustrate a general rule: combining any generator with the logistic Pickands function gives the Archimedean copula of the composition "generator stopped positive stable", because \(\psi\big((S^\delta + T^\delta)^{1/\delta}\big)\) is Archimedean with generator \(s \mapsto \psi(s^{1/\delta})\).

docs.title: BB4
docs.text:
Property Value Code 22 (FV_BB4); generic 10202 Parameters, box \(\theta \in [0.01, 15]\) (gamma), \(\delta \in [0.01, 15]\) (negative logistic) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(\tau_{\text{Galambos}}(\delta) + \big(1 - \tau_{\text{Galambos}}(\delta)\big)\, \frac{\theta}{\theta + 2}\); \(\tau \in [0, 0.992]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(\left(2 - 2^{-1/\delta}\right)^{-1/\theta}\), \(2^{-1/\delta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ C(u, v) = \left( u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1 - \left[ (u^{-\theta} - 1)^{-\delta} + (v^{-\theta} - 1)^{-\delta} \right]^{-1/\delta} \right)^{-1/\theta}. \]

BB4 (Joe & Hu 1996) has both tails, each with its own parameter. With \(x = u^{-\theta} - 1\), \(y = v^{-\theta} - 1\), \(S = (x^{-\delta} + y^{-\delta})^{-1/\delta}\), \(W = 1 + x + y - S\) and \(p = (S/x)^{\delta+1}\), \(q = (S/y)^{\delta+1}\) (both below one):

\[ c(u, v) = (uv)^{-\theta - 1}\, W^{-1/\theta - 2} \left[ (1 + \theta)(1 - p)(1 - q) + \theta(1 + \delta)\, \frac{W p q}{S} \right], \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = W^{-1/\theta - 1} (1 - p)\, u^{-\theta - 1}. \]

For BB1, BB5 and BB6 see the Archimedean and extreme-value pages.

docs.text:
The code is 10000 + 100 og + ie with og the generator and ie the Pickands function. The table lists every code that fv_generic_families() returns; "—" marks a combination that is either a duplicate (see above) or not allowed.

Pickands columns: lg logistic (1), nl negative logistic (2), HR Hüsler–Reiss (3), mx symmetric mixed (4), al1/al2 asymmetric logistic types 1/2 (6/7), anl1/anl2 asymmetric negative logistic types 1/2 (9/10), amx asymmetric mixed (11).

One-parameter generators (3 parameters with a two-parameter Pickands function):

generator (og) lg nl HR mx al1 al2 anl1 anl2 amx positive stable (1) — — 10103 10104 10106 10107 10109 10110 10111 gamma (2) — — 10203 10204 10206 10207 10209 10210 10211 Sibuya (3) — 10302 10303 10304 10306 10307 10309 10310 10311 log series (4) — 10402 10403 10404 10406 10407 10409 10410 10411

Two-parameter generators (only the one-parameter Pickands functions fit in three parameters):

generator (og) lg nl HR mx tilted positive stable (5) 10501 10502 10503 10504 generalised Sibuya (6) 10601 10602 10603 10604 negative binomial (7) 10701 10702 10703 10704 PS.Sibuya (13) 11301 11302 11303 11304 gamma.PS (15) — 11502 11503 11504 gamma.Sibuya (17) 11701 11702 11703 11704 gamma.logseries (18) 11801 11802 11803 11804 Sibuya.PS (19) — 11902 11903 11904 logseries.PS (23) — 12302 12303 12304 logseries.Sibuya (25) 12501 12502 12503 12504

That is \(7 + 7 + 8 + 8 = 30\) codes with one-parameter generators and \(10 \times 4 - 3 = 37\) with two-parameter generators. Parameter boxes are those of the parts: generator boxes as on the Archimedean page, Pickands boxes as on the extreme-value page; the catalogue lists each code's box.

Reading the table by tails:

  • Row positive stable — these are all extreme-value copulas (see positive stable Archimax): upper tail only, \(\lambda_U = 2 - (2A(1/2))^{1/\theta}\).
  • Rows gamma, gamma.PS, gamma.Sibuya, gamma.logseries — dependence in both tails. With an asymmetric Pickands function (10206 to 10211) these are the only non-exchangeable families in fortvine with lower and upper tail dependence.
  • All other rows — upper tail only, of the Pickands function's strength (\(m = 1\)) or stronger (\(m > 1\) for Sibuya, PS.Sibuya, Sibuya.PS, logseries.PS, logseries.Sibuya).

Three combinations are reparametrisations of two-parameter families

By the logistic rule above, a generator that already ends in a positive stable inner part absorbs the logistic exponent: 11501 (gamma.PS with logistic) is BB1\((\theta, \delta\theta_\ell)\), 11901 (Sibuya.PS with logistic) is BB6\((\theta, \delta\theta_\ell)\) and 12301 (logseries.PS with logistic) is 12300\((\theta, \delta\theta_\ell)\), where \(\theta_\ell\) is the logistic parameter. Only the product \(\delta\theta_\ell\) is identified, so these three codes add a flat direction to the likelihood without adding any shape; their densities agree with the two-parameter families to machine precision. gen_dup therefore marks them as duplicates: they remain valid codes for cross-checks but are not returned by fv_generic_families().

docs.title: Excluded combinations
docs.text:
• A logistic inner with a one-parameter generator duplicates a hand-coded or Archimedean code (BB1, BB6, 12300), and positive stable with logistic is Gumbel itself.
  • Three-parameter Pickands functions (asymmetric logistic 5, asymmetric negative logistic 8, Khoudraji–Hüsler–Reiss 12, Khoudraji–mixed 13) would need four or more parameters with any generator; fortvine stores at most three per pair copula. The one-weight types 6/7 and 9/10 carry the asymmetry instead.
  • Generators with a gamma inner part (BB3-type og 12, BB2-type og 16, BB7-type og 20 and logseries.gamma og 24) are not combined with any Pickands function: such combinations did not pass fortvine's numerical consistency tests (gen_valid rejects them). They remain available as Archimedean copulas.
  • The generators excluded on the Archimedean page (PS.PS, Sibuya.Sibuya and the log-series inner compositions) are excluded here as well.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Capéraà, P., Fougères, A.-L. and Genest, C. (2000). Bivariate distributions with given extreme value attractor. Journal of Multivariate Analysis 72, 30–49.
  • Joe, H. and Hu, T. (1996). Multivariate distributions from mixtures of max-infinitely divisible distributions. Journal of Multivariate Analysis 57, 240–265.
  • Joe, H. (2014). Dependence Modeling with Copulas. Chapman & Hall/CRC, §3.18.

docs.title: Archimedean families
docs.text:
An Archimedean copula is built from a single univariate function. Take a generator \(\psi : [0, \infty) \to (0, 1]\) that starts at \(\psi(0) = 1\), decreases to \(0\) and is convex, and let \(\varphi = \psi^{-1}\) be its inverse. Then

\[ C(u, v) = \psi\big(\varphi(u) + \varphi(v)\big). \]

Every generator fortvine uses is the Laplace transform of a positive random variable \(M\), \(\psi(s) = \mathrm{E}\, e^{-sM}\). This gives the family a mixing ("frailty") reading: draw a common factor \(M\), then draw \(U\) and \(V\) independently given \(M\) with \(P(U \le u \mid M) = \exp(-M \varphi(u))\). The heavier the variation of \(M\), the stronger the dependence (Marshall & Olkin 1988).

Hand-coded Archimedean families at Kendall's \(\tau = 0.5\), density contours in normal scores (parameters in brackets, in fortvine's order).

docs.title: The general formulas
docs.text:
With \(s = \varphi(u) + \varphi(v)\), every quantity fortvine needs follows from \(\psi\) and its first two derivatives:

\[ c(u, v) = \frac{\psi''(s)}{\psi'(\varphi(u))\, \psi'(\varphi(v))}, \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{\psi'(s)}{\psi'(\varphi(u))}, \qquad h_2(u \mid v) = \frac{\psi'(s)}{\psi'(\varphi(v))}. \]

All Archimedean copulas are exchangeable. In two dimensions a convex, decreasing \(\psi\) is enough for \(C\) to be a copula; complete monotonicity (the Laplace-transform property) is what lets the same generator work in any dimension, and it is what makes the compositions below valid. fortvine evaluates \(\log\psi\), \(\log(-\psi')\) and \(\log\psi''\) directly, so \(C\) itself never has to be formed and nothing cancels.

Kendall's tau has a one-dimensional representation (Genest & MacKay 1986; Joe 2014, §3.3):

\[ \tau = 1 - 4 \int_0^\infty s\, \big[\psi'(s)\big]^2 \, ds = 1 + 4 \int_0^1 \frac{\varphi(t)}{\varphi'(t)}\, dt . \]

Tail dependence depends only on the behaviour of \(\psi\) at the two ends of its domain:

\[ \lambda_L = \lim_{s \to \infty} \frac{\psi(2s)}{\psi(s)}, \qquad \lambda_U = 2 - \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{1 - \psi(2s)}{1 - \psi(s)} . \]

So a generator with a power-law right tail, \(\psi(s) \sim c\, s^{-1/k}\), gives \(\lambda_L = 2^{-1/k}\), and one with \(1 - \psi(s) \sim c\, s^{1/m}\) near zero (\(m > 1\)) gives \(\lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/m}\). A generator that decays exponentially has \(\lambda_L = 0\); one with a finite slope \(\psi'(0)\) has \(\lambda_U = 0\).

Rotations. The Archimedean families with a positive parameter range model positive dependence only. The 90° and 270° rotations give negative dependence and the 180° rotation (the survival copula) swaps the two tails; see rotations. Frank and Ali–Mikhail–Haq cover negative dependence through their parameter and are not rotated.

docs.title: The seven Laplace transforms
docs.text:
The generic engine (codes 10000+, see the index) builds every Archimedean and Archimax family from seven Laplace-transform families. Each one, used alone, is the generator of a classical copula:

og Laplace transform \(\psi(s)\) \(\varphi(u) = \psi^{-1}(u)\) Copula Hand code 1 positive stable \(e^{-s^{1/\theta}}\), \(\theta \ge 1\) \((-\log u)^\theta\) Gumbel 4 2 gamma \((1+s)^{-1/\theta}\), \(\theta > 0\) \(u^{-\theta} - 1\) Clayton 3 3 Sibuya \(1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\), \(\theta \ge 1\) \(-\log\big(1 - (1-u)^\theta\big)\) Joe 6 4 logarithmic series \(-\frac{1}{\theta}\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-\theta}) e^{-s}\big)\), \(\theta > 0\) \(-\log\frac{1 - e^{-\theta u}}{1 - e^{-\theta}}\) Frank (\(\theta > 0\)) 5 5 exponentially tilted positive stable \(\exp\big(\delta^{-1} - (\delta^{-\theta} + s)^{1/\theta}\big)\) \((\delta^{-1} - \log u)^\theta - \delta^{-\theta}\) BB9 20 6 generalised Sibuya \(\delta^{-1}\big[1 - (1 - \eta e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\big]\), \(\eta = 1 - (1-\delta)^\theta\) \(-\log\frac{1 - (1 - \delta u)^\theta}{\eta}\) BB8 10 7 shifted negative binomial \(\left(\frac{1 - \pi}{e^s - \pi}\right)^{1/\theta}\) \(\log\big((1-\pi) u^{-\theta} + \pi\big)\) BB10 21

The generic codes of these seven Archimedean copulas, 10100 to 10700, are valid and are used for cross-checks against the hand-coded versions, but fv_generic_families() leaves them out because they duplicate codes 3–6, 10, 20 and 21.

For implementers, the derivatives fortvine evaluates (in log form) are:

LT \(-\psi'(s)\) \(\psi''(s)\) positive stable (\(q = s^{1/\theta}\)) \(\frac{q}{\theta s} e^{-q}\) \(\frac{q}{\theta s^2} e^{-q} \left(\frac{q}{\theta} + 1 - \frac{1}{\theta}\right)\) gamma \(\frac{1}{\theta} (1+s)^{-1/\theta - 1}\) \(\frac{1}{\theta}\left(\frac{1}{\theta} + 1\right)(1+s)^{-1/\theta - 2}\) Sibuya (\(w = 1 - e^{-s}\)) \(\frac{1}{\theta} w^{1/\theta - 1} e^{-s}\) \(\frac{1}{\theta} w^{1/\theta - 2} e^{-s} \left(1 - \frac{e^{-s}}{\theta}\right)\) log series (\(z = (1 - e^{-\theta}) e^{-s}\)) \(\frac{z}{\theta (1 - z)}\) \(\frac{z}{\theta (1 - z)^2}\) tilted PS (\(r = \delta^{-\theta} + s\), \(q = r^{1/\theta}\)) \(\psi(s) \frac{q}{\theta r}\) \(\psi(s) \frac{q}{\theta r^2}\left(\frac{q}{\theta} + 1 - \frac{1}{\theta}\right)\) gen. Sibuya (\(z = \eta e^{-s}\)) \(\frac{z (1-z)^{1/\theta - 1}}{\delta\theta}\) \(\frac{z (1-z)^{1/\theta - 2}}{\delta\theta}\left(1 - \frac{z}{\theta}\right)\) neg. binomial (\(e = e^{-s}\)) \(\frac{\psi(s)}{\theta (1 - \pi e)}\) \(\frac{\psi(s)}{(1 - \pi e)^2} \left(\frac{1}{\theta^2} + \frac{\pi e}{\theta}\right)\)

docs.title: Clayton
docs.text:
Property Value Code 3 (FV_CLAYTON); generic duplicate 10200 Generator gamma LT, \(\psi(s) = (1 + s)^{-1/\theta}\) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [10^{-10}, 28]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(\theta / (\theta + 2)\), so \(\tau \in (0, 0.933]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\theta}\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ C(u, v) = \left(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1\right)^{-1/\theta}, \qquad c(u, v) = (1 + \theta)(uv)^{-1-\theta}\left(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1\right)^{-2-1/\theta}, \] \[ h_1(v \mid u) = u^{-1-\theta}\left(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} - 1\right)^{-1-1/\theta}, \qquad h_1^{-1}(p \mid u) = \left[1 + u^{-\theta}\left(p^{-\theta/(1+\theta)} - 1\right)\right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

Clayton (1978) is the canonical lower-tail family. The negative-parameter branch \(\theta \in [-1, 0)\) of the literature is left out: there the density vanishes on a region of positive area, which breaks likelihood fitting (see other families); negative dependence comes from the 90° and 270° rotations instead.

docs.title: Gumbel
docs.text:
Property Value Code 4 (FV_GUMBEL); generic duplicate 10100 (and 10001 as an EV copula) Generator positive stable LT, \(\psi(s) = \exp(-s^{1/\theta})\) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [1, 50]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 - 1/\theta\), \(\tau \in [0, 0.98]\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270

With \(x = -\log u\), \(y = -\log v\) and \(m = (x^\theta + y^\theta)^{1/\theta}\):

\[ C(u, v) = e^{-m}, \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{e^{-m}}{uv}\, (xy)^{\theta - 1} \left(x^\theta + y^\theta\right)^{1/\theta - 2} (\theta - 1 + m), \] \[ h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{e^{-m}}{u}\, x^{\theta - 1} \left(x^\theta + y^\theta\right)^{1/\theta - 1}. \]

Gumbel (1960) is the only copula that is both Archimedean and extreme-value; its Pickands function is the logistic model of the extreme-value page. The h-inverse has no closed form; fortvine solves the equivalent scalar equation \(d + (\theta - 1)\log(1 + d/x) = -\log p\) for \(d = m - x\) by a Newton iteration that is monotone from its starting point, so it never needs bracketing.

docs.title: Frank
docs.text:
Property Value Code 5 (FV_FRANK); generic duplicate 10400 (positive branch only) Generator logarithmic-series LT (for \(\theta > 0\)) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [-35, 35]\), \(\theta = 0\) is independence Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 - \frac{4}{\theta} + \frac{4}{\theta^2}\int_0^\theta \frac{t}{e^t - 1}\,dt\), \(\tau \in [-0.891, 0.891]\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes, and radially symmetric Rotations none (\(\theta < 0\) gives negative dependence) \[ C(u, v) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\log\left(1 + \frac{(e^{-\theta u} - 1)(e^{-\theta v} - 1)}{e^{-\theta} - 1}\right), \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{-\theta\,(e^{-\theta} - 1)\, e^{-\theta(u + v)}}{\big[(e^{-\theta} - 1) + (e^{-\theta u} - 1)(e^{-\theta v} - 1)\big]^2}, \] \[ h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{e^{-\theta u}\,(e^{-\theta v} - 1)}{(e^{-\theta} - 1) + (e^{-\theta u} - 1)(e^{-\theta v} - 1)}, \qquad h_1^{-1}(p \mid u) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\log\left(1 + \frac{p\,(e^{-\theta} - 1)}{e^{-\theta u} - p\,(e^{-\theta u} - 1)}\right). \]

Frank (1979) is the standard "no tail dependence, symmetric" family. The integral in \(\tau\) is the first Debye function; fortvine evaluates it numerically and inverts \(\tau\) by Newton's method with the analytic derivative. For \(\theta < 0\) the generator is no longer a Laplace transform, but it stays convex, so the formula is a valid two-dimensional copula.

docs.title: Joe
docs.text:
Property Value Code 6 (FV_JOE); generic duplicate 10300 Generator Sibuya LT, \(\psi(s) = 1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [1, 30]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 + \frac{2}{2 - \theta}\big[\Psi(2) - \Psi(2/\theta + 1)\big]\) (\(\Psi\) = digamma function), \(\tau \in [0, 0.936]\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270

With \(\bar u = 1 - u\), \(\bar v = 1 - v\) and \(S = \bar u^\theta + \bar v^\theta - \bar u^\theta \bar v^\theta\):

\[ C(u, v) = 1 - S^{1/\theta}, \qquad c(u, v) = S^{1/\theta - 2}\, (\bar u \bar v)^{\theta - 1}\, (\theta - 1 + S), \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = \bar u^{\theta - 1} (1 - \bar v^\theta)\, S^{1/\theta - 1}. \]

Joe (1993) has a stronger upper tail than Gumbel at the same \(\tau\). The \(\tau\) formula has a removable singularity at \(\theta = 2\) (where \(\tau = 2 - \pi^2/6\)); fortvine expands it there. As for Gumbel, the h-inverse is found by a monotone scalar Newton iteration.

docs.title: Ali–Mikhail–Haq (AMH)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 14 (FV_AMH) Generator \(\psi(s) = (1 - \theta)/(e^s - \theta)\): for \(\theta \in [0, 1)\) the LT of a geometric distribution Parameter, box \(\theta \in [-1, 0.9999]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 - \frac{2\left[\theta + (1 - \theta)^2 \log(1 - \theta)\right]}{3\theta^2}\), \(\tau \in [-0.182, 1/3)\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) (inside the box) Exchangeable yes Rotations none (\(\theta < 0\) gives negative dependence) \[ C(u, v) = \frac{uv}{1 - \theta(1-u)(1-v)}, \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{1 + \theta\big[(1+u)(1+v) - 3\big] + \theta^2 (1-u)(1-v)}{\big[1 - \theta(1-u)(1-v)\big]^3}, \] \[ h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{v\,\big[1 - \theta(1 - v)\big]}{\big[1 - \theta(1-u)(1-v)\big]^2}. \]

Ali, Mikhail & Haq (1978). AMH is a weak-dependence family: even at \(\theta \to 1\) Kendall's \(\tau\) only reaches \(1/3\). The geometric LT is the negative-binomial LT of BB10 with exponent one, so AMH is the \(\theta = 1\) slice of BB10, with AMH's parameter in the role of \(\pi\). Its lower tail coefficient jumps to \(1/2\) exactly at the excluded end point \(\theta = 1\).

docs.title: BB9
docs.text:
Property Value Code 20 (FV_BB9); generic duplicate 10500 Generator exponentially tilted positive stable LT Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 10]\), \(\delta \in [0.01, 30]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.893]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ C(u, v) = \exp\left\{ \frac{1}{\delta} - \left[ \left(\frac{1}{\delta} - \log u\right)^\theta + \left(\frac{1}{\delta} - \log v\right)^\theta - \delta^{-\theta} \right]^{1/\theta} \right\}. \]

BB9 is Crowder's (1989) copula. Tilting gives the generator a finite slope at zero, so the upper tail dependence of Gumbel disappears for every finite \(\delta\); as \(\delta \to \infty\) the family tends to Gumbel(\(\theta\)). The power-variance-function (PVF) frailty copula and the inverse-Gaussian frailty copula of other software are reparametrisations of BB9.

docs.title: BB8
docs.text:
Property Value Code 10 (FV_BB8); generic duplicate 10600 Generator generalised Sibuya LT Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 8]\), \(\delta \in [10^{-4}, 1]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.783]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) for \(\delta < 1\); \(\lambda_U = 2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) at \(\delta = 1\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270

With \(\eta = 1 - (1 - \delta)^\theta\):

\[ C(u, v) = \frac{1}{\delta}\left( 1 - \left[ 1 - \frac{\big(1 - (1 - \delta u)^\theta\big)\big(1 - (1 - \delta v)^\theta\big)}{\eta} \right]^{1/\theta} \right). \]

At \(\delta = 1\) BB8 is the Joe copula; \(\theta = 1\) gives independence. The parameter \(\delta\) therefore dials between a tail-dependent and a tail-free shape at fixed \(\theta\).

docs.title: BB10
docs.text:
Property Value Code 21 (FV_BB10); generic duplicate 10700 Generator shifted negative binomial LT Parameters, box \(\theta \in [0.01, 30]\), \(\pi \in [0, 1]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.943]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ C(u, v) = uv \left[ 1 - \pi (1 - u^\theta)(1 - v^\theta) \right]^{-1/\theta}, \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{\big(1 - \pi\bar v_\theta + \pi\theta v^\theta\big) D - (1 + \theta)\pi\,(1 - \pi\bar v_\theta)\, v^\theta \bar u_\theta}{D^{2 + 1/\theta}}, \]

with \(\bar u_\theta = 1 - u^\theta\), \(\bar v_\theta = 1 - v^\theta\) and \(D = 1 - \pi \bar u_\theta \bar v_\theta\). \(\pi = 0\) is independence and \(\theta = 1\) is AMH(\(\pi\)). Like AMH it is a moderate-dependence family without tail dependence.

docs.title: Compositions: \(\psi\) stopped \(\zeta\)
docs.text:
New Laplace transforms can be made by composing two old ones. If \(\zeta\) is a Laplace transform such that \(g = -\log\zeta\) is increasing and concave with \(g(0) = 0\) (it is a Bernstein function when \(\zeta\) belongs to an infinitely divisible distribution), then

\[ \psi(s) = \psi_{o}\big(g(s)\big) = \psi_o\big(-\log \zeta(s)\big) \]

is again a generator. Joe (2014, Appendix A.1.2) calls this "\(\psi\) stopped \(\zeta\)"; in the frailty picture the outer frailty is replaced by a compound one. Its derivatives

\[ \psi'(s) = \psi_o'(g)\, g', \qquad \psi''(s) = \psi_o''(g)\, g'^2 + \psi_o'(g)\, g'' \]

are sums of non-negative terms (since \(\psi_o' < 0\) and \(g'' \le 0\)), which is how fortvine keeps them in log space. The inverse is \(\varphi(u) = g^{-1}\big(\varphi_o(u)\big)\).

The generic engine uses the four one-parameter transforms both as outer generator \(\psi_o(\,\cdot\,;\theta)\) and as inner Bernstein function \(g(\,\cdot\,;\delta)\). The parameter order is always (outer \(\theta\), inner \(\delta\)). The inner functions are:

inner \(g(s; \delta)\) \(g^{-1}(x; \delta)\) box of \(\delta\) in a composition positive stable \(s^{1/\delta}\) \(x^\delta\) \([1, 10]\) gamma \(\delta^{-1}\log(1 + s)\) \(e^{\delta x} - 1\) \([10^{-3}, 15]\) Sibuya \(-\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\delta}\big)\) \(-\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-x})^\delta\big)\) \([1, 10]\) log series \(-\log\left[-\delta^{-1}\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-\delta})e^{-s}\big)\right]\) \(\log(1 - e^{-\delta}) - \log\big(1 - e^{-\delta e^{-x}}\big)\) \([10^{-3}, 30]\)

The outer parameter boxes in a composition are the same as the inner ones: \([1, 10]\) for positive stable and Sibuya, \([10^{-3}, 15]\) for gamma, \([10^{-3}, 30]\) for log series.

docs.title: The sixteen combinations
docs.text:
The outer-generator code of a composition is og = 10 + 4 (po - 1) + pin, where po and pin number the outer and inner transform as 1 positive stable, 2 gamma, 3 Sibuya, 4 log series. The Archimedean code is then 10000 + 100 og.

outer \(\downarrow\) / inner \(\rightarrow\) positive stable gamma Sibuya log series positive stable og 11: excluded, equals Gumbel(\(\theta\delta\)) og 12: BB3 (hand code 18) og 13: new, 11300 og 14: excluded (numerics) gamma og 15: BB1 (hand code 7) og 16: BB2 (hand code 17) og 17: new, 11700 og 18: new, 11800 Sibuya og 19: BB6 (hand code 8) og 20: BB7 (hand code 9) og 21: excluded, equals Joe(\(\theta\delta\)) og 22: excluded (numerics) log series og 23: new, 12300 og 24: new, 12400 og 25: new, 12500 og 26: excluded (numerics)

Why some cells are missing:

  • Closed under composition. Positive stable after positive stable is positive stable with exponent \(\theta\delta\), and Sibuya after Sibuya is Sibuya with \(\theta\delta\): \(1 - \big(1 - e^{-g}\big)^{1/\theta}\) with \(e^{-g} = 1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\delta}\) collapses to \(1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/(\theta\delta)}\). Both parameters would not be identifiable.
  • Numerically unreliable. A log-series inner under a positive-stable, Sibuya or log-series outer does not reach the accuracy fortvine requires in double precision, so those three codes are rejected (gen_valid returns false; compare the remarks in Joe 2014, Appendix A.1.2). Under a gamma outer the same inner is accurate, which is why 11800 is offered.
  • Already hand-coded. The five BB cells are valid generic codes (11200, 11500, 11600, 11900, 12000), useful for cross-checking, but fv_generic_families() omits them as duplicates.

The six new compositions at \(\tau = 0.5\) (outer \(\theta\) tuned, inner \(\delta\) fixed).

docs.title: Tail behaviour of a composition
docs.text: The two ends of \(\psi_o \circ g\) combine the two ends of the parts. Near \(s = 0\), positive stable and Sibuya behave like a power, \(1 - \psi(s) \approx s^{1/\theta}\), while gamma and log series are linear; near \(s = \infty\) only the gamma transform has a power-law tail, and a gamma inner turns \(s\) into \(\log s\), so the outer tail is read on a logarithmic scale. The resulting coefficients are listed in each family below; they agree with numerical limits of \(C(t,t)/t\) computed with fortvine.

docs.title: BB1
docs.text:
Property Value Code 7 (FV_BB1); generic 11500 (gamma outer, positive-stable inner) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [0, 7]\), \(\delta \in [1, 7]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 - \dfrac{2}{\delta(\theta + 2)}\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/(\theta\delta)}\), \(2 - 2^{1/\delta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ \psi(s) = \left(1 + s^{1/\delta}\right)^{-1/\theta}, \qquad C(u, v) = \left\{ 1 + \left[ (u^{-\theta} - 1)^\delta + (v^{-\theta} - 1)^\delta \right]^{1/\delta} \right\}^{-1/\theta}. \]

BB1 (Joe & Hu 1996) has dependence in both tails with two separate controls; \(\delta = 1\) is Clayton(\(\theta\)) and \(\theta \to 0\) gives Gumbel(\(\delta\)). It is also the Archimax copula of a gamma generator with the logistic Pickands function (see Archimax).

docs.title: BB2
docs.text:
Property Value Code 17 (FV_BB2); generic 11600 (gamma outer, gamma inner) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [0.01, 30]\), \(\delta \in [0.01, 30]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.997]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(1\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ \psi(s) = \left(1 + \delta^{-1}\log(1 + s)\right)^{-1/\theta}, \qquad C(u, v) = \left[ 1 + \frac{1}{\delta}\log\!\left( e^{\delta(u^{-\theta} - 1)} + e^{\delta(v^{-\theta} - 1)} - 1 \right) \right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

The generator decays only like a power of \(\log s\), which makes the lower tail coefficient equal to one for every parameter value: the lower tail is as heavy as possible without being singular. Nelsen's (2006) families 4.2.19 and 4.2.20 are the slices \(\theta = 1\) and \(\delta = 1\) of BB2.

docs.title: BB3
docs.text:
Property Value Code 18 (FV_BB3); generic 11200 (positive-stable outer, gamma inner) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 10]\), \(\delta \in [0.01, 30]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.956]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(1\) if \(\theta > 1\), \(2^{-1/\delta}\) if \(\theta = 1\); \(2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ \psi(s) = \exp\!\left( -\left[\delta^{-1}\log(1 + s)\right]^{1/\theta} \right), \qquad C(u, v) = \exp\!\left( -\left[ \frac{1}{\delta}\log\!\left( e^{\delta x^\theta} + e^{\delta y^\theta} - 1 \right) \right]^{1/\theta} \right), \]

with \(x = -\log u\), \(y = -\log v\). At \(\theta = 1\) BB3 is Clayton(\(\delta\)).

docs.title: BB6
docs.text:
Property Value Code 8 (FV_BB6); generic 11900 (Sibuya outer, positive-stable inner) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 6]\), \(\delta \in [1, 8]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.965]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/(\theta\delta)}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ \psi(s) = 1 - \left(1 - e^{-s^{1/\delta}}\right)^{1/\theta}, \qquad C(u, v) = 1 - \left(1 - \exp\!\left\{ -\left[ \big(-\log(1 - \bar u^\theta)\big)^\delta + \big(-\log(1 - \bar v^\theta)\big)^\delta \right]^{1/\delta} \right\}\right)^{1/\theta}. \]

\(\theta = 1\) is Gumbel(\(\delta\)) and \(\delta = 1\) is Joe(\(\theta\)). BB6 is the Archimax copula of the Sibuya generator and the logistic Pickands function.

docs.title: BB7
docs.text:
Property Value Code 9 (FV_BB7); generic 12000 (Sibuya outer, gamma inner) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 6]\), \(\delta \in [0.01, 25]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.863]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\delta}\), \(2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ \psi(s) = 1 - \left[1 - (1 + s)^{-1/\delta}\right]^{1/\theta}, \qquad C(u, v) = 1 - \left( 1 - \left[ (1 - \bar u^\theta)^{-\delta} + (1 - \bar v^\theta)^{-\delta} - 1 \right]^{-1/\delta} \right)^{1/\theta}. \]

BB7 ("Joe–Clayton") separates the two tails cleanly: \(\delta\) sets the lower tail and \(\theta\) the upper. \(\theta = 1\) is Clayton(\(\delta\)); \(\delta \to 0\) gives Joe(\(\theta\)).

docs.title: PS.Sibuya (11300)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 11300 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 10]\) (positive stable), \(\delta \in [1, 10]\) (Sibuya) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.961]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/(\theta\delta)}\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = \exp\!\left( -\left[-\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\delta}\big)\right]^{1/\theta} \right), \qquad \varphi(u) = -\log\!\left(1 - \left[1 - e^{-(-\log u)^\theta}\right]^{\delta}\right). \]

An upper-tail family that interpolates between Gumbel (\(\delta = 1\)) and Joe (\(\theta = 1\)), the mirror image of BB6 (which puts Sibuya outside and positive stable inside).

docs.title: gamma.Sibuya (11700)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 11700 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 15]\) (gamma), \(\delta \in [1, 10]\) (Sibuya) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.897]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\theta}\), \(2 - 2^{1/\delta}\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = \left[ 1 - \log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\delta}\big) \right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

A both-tails family like BB1 and BB7, with the lower tail set by \(\theta\) alone and the upper tail by \(\delta\) alone. \(\delta = 1\) is Clayton(\(\theta\)) and \(\theta \to 0\) tends to Joe(\(\delta\)).

docs.title: gamma.logseries (11800)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 11800 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 15]\) (gamma), \(\delta \in [10^{-3}, 30]\) (log series) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.901]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\theta}\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = \left[ 1 - \log\!\left( -\frac{1}{\delta}\log\big(1 - (1 - e^{-\delta})e^{-s}\big) \right) \right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

A lower-tail family with a Frank-like body: \(\delta \to 0\) gives Clayton(\(\theta\)) and \(\theta \to 0\) gives Frank(\(\delta\)).

docs.title: logseries.PS (12300)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 12300 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 30]\) (log series), \(\delta \in [1, 10]\) (positive stable) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.987]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/\delta}\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\log\!\left( 1 - (1 - e^{-\theta})\, e^{-s^{1/\delta}} \right). \]

\(\delta = 1\) is Frank(\(\theta\)); \(\theta \to 0\) gives Gumbel(\(\delta\)). It is also the Archimax copula of the log-series generator with the logistic Pickands function.

docs.title: logseries.gamma (12400)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 12400 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 30]\) (log series), \(\delta \in [10^{-3}, 15]\) (gamma) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.882]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\delta}\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\log\!\left( 1 - (1 - e^{-\theta})(1 + s)^{-1/\delta} \right). \]

The lower-tail counterpart of 11800 with the roles of the two transforms swapped: \(\theta \to 0\) gives Clayton(\(\delta\)) and \(\delta \to 0\) gives Frank(\(\theta\)).

docs.title: logseries.Sibuya (12500)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 12500 (generic only) Parameters, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 30]\) (log series), \(\delta \in [1, 10]\) (Sibuya) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.987]\) in the box \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(2 - 2^{1/\delta}\) Exchangeable yes \[ \psi(s) = -\frac{1}{\theta}\log\!\left( 1 - (1 - e^{-\theta})\left[1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\delta}\right] \right). \]

\(\delta = 1\) is Frank(\(\theta\)); \(\theta \to 0\) gives Joe(\(\delta\)).

docs.title: Elliptical families
docs.text:
An elliptical copula is the dependence structure left over when the margins of an elliptically contoured distribution are transformed to uniform. If \(F_\rho\) is the bivariate distribution function with correlation \(\rho\) and \(F\) is its univariate margin, then

\[ C(u, v) = F_\rho\big(F^{-1}(u),\, F^{-1}(v)\big). \]

Both elliptical families in fortvine are exchangeable and radially symmetric: the lower and upper tails behave alike, and the 180° rotation gives back the same copula. Negative dependence needs no rotation, because \(\rho\) can be negative. fortvine therefore registers no rotations for these two families.

Throughout, \(x = F^{-1}(u)\) and \(y = F^{-1}(v)\) are the scores of the two arguments, and \(h_1(v \mid u) = \partial C / \partial u\) is the conditional distribution of \(V\) given \(U = u\).

Density contours of the copula with standard normal margins. Left and middle: the same Kendall's \(\tau = 0.5\); the Student t puts more mass in both corners. Right: a Student t copula with \(\rho = 0\) is uncorrelated but not independent.

docs.title: Gaussian
docs.text:
Property Value Code 1 (FV_GAUSSIAN) Parameter \(\rho\) (correlation) Box in fortvine \([-1, 1]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(\frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\rho\), any value in \((-1, 1)\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) (for \(\lvert\rho\rvert < 1\)) Exchangeable yes Rotations none (radially symmetric; \(\rho < 0\) gives negative dependence)

With \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function, \(x = \Phi^{-1}(u)\), \(y = \Phi^{-1}(v)\):

\[ C(u, v) = \Phi_2(x, y; \rho), \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}} \exp\!\left( -\frac{\rho^2 (x^2 + y^2) - 2 \rho x y}{2 (1 - \rho^2)} \right). \]

The h-function and its inverse are both closed:

\[ h_1(v \mid u) = \Phi\!\left( \frac{y - \rho x}{\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}} \right), \qquad h_1^{-1}(p \mid u) = \Phi\!\left( \rho x + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, \Phi^{-1}(p) \right), \]

and \(h_2\) is the same expression with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) exchanged.

Dependence measures. Kendall's \(\tau = \frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin\rho\) and Spearman's \(\rho_S = \frac{6}{\pi}\arcsin(\rho/2)\). fortvine uses the first relation to start the fit (\(\rho = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\)) and for the FV_ITAU method.

Notes.

  • The Gaussian copula is asymptotically independent in both tails: however strong \(\rho\) is, \(\lambda_L = \lambda_U = 0\) (Sibuya 1960). Joint extremes still occur more often than under independence, but at a rate that vanishes in the limit.
  • fortvine evaluates \(C\) itself (needed for discrete margins) by Gauss–Legendre quadrature of the exact h-function, since the bivariate normal integral has no elementary form.
  • At \(\rho = \pm 1\) the copula is singular (the comonotone or countermonotone copula); the box boundary is never reached in practice because the likelihood diverges there.
