docs.title: Extreme-value families
docs.text:
Extreme-value (EV) copulas are the possible dependence structures of componentwise maxima in the limit of many observations. They are exactly the copulas that are max-stable, \(C(u^t, v^t) = C(u, v)^t\) for all \(t > 0\), and in two dimensions every one of them can be written with a single function of one variable, the Pickands dependence function \(A\) (Pickands 1981):

\[ C(u, v) = \exp\!\big(-\ell(x, y)\big), \qquad \ell(x, y) = (x + y)\, A\!\left(\frac{y}{x + y}\right), \qquad x = -\log u,\; y = -\log v . \]

\(A : [0, 1] \to [1/2, 1]\) is convex with \(\max(w, 1 - w) \le A(w) \le 1\). The lower bound \(A(w) = \max(w, 1 - w)\) is the comonotone copula and the upper bound \(A \equiv 1\) is independence. \(\ell\) is called the stable tail dependence function.

Orientation of the Pickands argument

In fortvine, \(w = y/(x + y) = \log v / \log(uv)\) is the share of the second argument. Some software (for example the R package evd) uses the share of the first argument, which replaces \(A(w)\) by \(A(1 - w)\). For exchangeable families the two conventions agree; for the asymmetric ones the parameters attached to the first and second margins swap.

Top row: the four exchangeable EV families at Kendall's \(\tau = 0.5\); they are very close to one another. Bottom row: asymmetric EV families at \(\tau \approx 0.4\). Tawn (11) and Tawn type 2 (10007) with the same \(\theta\) and the weight 0.5 on opposite margins are mirror images.

docs.title: General formulas
docs.text:
Write \(A'\), \(A''\) for the derivatives of \(A\) at \(w\) and

\[ \ell_x = A - w A', \qquad \ell_y = A + (1 - w) A', \qquad \ell_{xy} = -\frac{w (1 - w)}{x + y}\, A'' \;(\le 0). \]

Then

\[ c(u, v) = \frac{C(u, v)}{uv}\,\big[\ell_x \ell_y - \ell_{xy}\big], \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{C(u, v)}{u}\, \ell_x, \qquad h_2(u \mid v) = \frac{C(u, v)}{v}\, \ell_y . \]

The bracket is a sum of two non-negative terms, which is how fortvine keeps the log-density free of cancellation. No EV family has a closed-form h-inverse. fortvine reduces Gumbel's to a monotone scalar equation and inverts all the others with a bracketed Newton iteration that uses the density as the exact derivative; for asymmetric families \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) are inverted separately.

Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho are one-dimensional integrals of \(A\) (Hürlimann 2003; Gudendorf & Segers 2010):

\[ \tau = \int_0^1 \frac{w (1 - w)}{A(w)}\, A''(w)\, dw, \qquad \rho_S = 12 \int_0^1 \frac{dw}{\big(1 + A(w)\big)^2} - 3 . \]

Tails. The upper tail coefficient is read off at the midpoint,

\[ \lambda_U = 2\big(1 - A(1/2)\big), \]

and every EV copula other than the comonotone one has \(\lambda_L = 0\): near the origin the copula behaves like \(u^{2A(1/2)}\) along the diagonal, which goes to zero faster than \(u\).

Positive dependence only. An EV copula always satisfies \(C(u, v) \ge uv\) (positive quadrant dependence), so \(\tau \ge 0\) and \(\rho_S \ge 0\). Negative dependence and lower-tail dependence are obtained by rotation: 90° and 270° for negative association, 180° to move the tail dependence to the lower-left corner (see rotations).

Symmetry. An EV copula is exchangeable exactly when \(A(w) = A(1 - w)\). For the asymmetric families, swapping the two arguments (which a vine does when it flips an edge) replaces \(A(w)\) by \(A(1 - w)\); fortvine maps this to an exact change of parameters (or of code), listed per family.

Codes. The hand-coded EV families are Gumbel (4), Tawn (11), Galambos (15), Hüsler–Reiss (16), BB5 (19) and t-EV (23). The generic engine adds nine EV codes 100ie (outer generator og = 0, \(\psi(s) = e^{-s}\)), with ie the Pickands function below. The generic codes of the logistic, negative logistic, Hüsler–Reiss and asymmetric logistic models (10001, 10002, 10003, 10005) are kept for cross-checks but left out of fv_generic_families().

docs.text:

docs.title: Logistic (Gumbel)
docs.text:
Property Value Codes 4 (hand-coded, see Archimedean); generic 10001 Parameter, box \(\theta \in [1, 50]\) (code 4), \([1, 20]\) (generic) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(1 - 1/\theta\) \(\lambda_U\) \(2 - 2^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes \[ A(w) = \left(w^\theta + (1 - w)^\theta\right)^{1/\theta}, \qquad \ell(x, y) = \left(x^\theta + y^\theta\right)^{1/\theta}. \]

The logistic model (Gumbel 1960) is the benchmark EV family; \(\theta = 1\) is independence and \(\theta \to \infty\) the comonotone copula.

docs.title: Negative logistic (Galambos)
docs.text:
Property Value Codes 15 (FV_GALAMBOS); generic 10002 Parameter, box \(\theta \in [0.01, 30]\) (code 15), \([0.01, 20]\) (generic) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.967]\) in the box \(\lambda_U\) \(2^{-1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ A(w) = 1 - \left(w^{-\theta} + (1 - w)^{-\theta}\right)^{-1/\theta}, \qquad C(u, v) = uv\, \exp\!\left\{ \left(x^{-\theta} + y^{-\theta}\right)^{-1/\theta} \right\}. \]

Galambos (1975). The second form makes the structure visible: the copula is the independence copula times a correction that only matters when both \(x\) and \(y\) are small, i.e. in the upper corner. fortvine evaluates \(A\), \(A'\), \(A''\) in log space through the two shares \(r_p = w^{-\theta}/m\) and \(r_q = (1-w)^{-\theta}/m\), \(m = w^{-\theta} + (1-w)^{-\theta}\), which sum to one, so nothing cancels even for large \(\theta\).

docs.title: Hüsler–Reiss
docs.text:
Property Value Codes 16 (FV_HUSLER_REISS); generic 10003 Parameter, box \(\lambda \in [0.01, 30]\) (code 16), \([0.01, 20]\) (generic) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.963]\) in the box \(\lambda_U\) \(2\big(1 - \Phi(1/\lambda)\big)\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ A(w) = w\, \Phi(z_1) + (1 - w)\, \Phi(z_2), \qquad z_{1,2} = \frac{1}{\lambda} \pm \frac{\lambda}{2}\log\frac{w}{1 - w}, \]

with derivatives \(A'(w) = \Phi(z_1) - \Phi(z_2)\) (the density terms cancel because \(w\,\phi(z_1) = (1 - w)\,\phi(z_2)\)) and \(A''(w) = \lambda\,\phi(z_1) / \big(2 w (1-w)^2\big)\).

Hüsler & Reiss (1989) obtained this copula as the limit of maxima of bivariate normal samples whose correlation tends to one at a suitable rate. Larger \(\lambda\) means stronger dependence: \(\lambda \to 0\) is independence and \(\lambda \to \infty\) comonotonicity. For the log-density fortvine uses \(\ell_x = \Phi(z_2)\) and \(\ell_y = \Phi(z_1)\), evaluated as \(\log\Phi\) with an asymptotic series far in the lower tail.

docs.title: Symmetric mixed (Tawn)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 10004 (generic only) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [0, 1]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(\dfrac{8 \arctan\sqrt{\theta/(4 - \theta)}}{\sqrt{\theta(4 - \theta)}} - 2\), so \(\tau \in [0, 0.418]\) \(\lambda_U\) \(\theta / 2\) Exchangeable yes \[ A(w) = 1 - \theta\, w (1 - w), \qquad \ell(x, y) = x + y - \theta\,\frac{xy}{x + y}. \]

The mixed model (Tawn 1988) has the simplest possible Pickands function, a quadratic. It is a weak-dependence family: even at \(\theta = 1\) Kendall's tau stays below \(0.42\). The R package copula calls this model tawnCopula; it is not the same as fortvine's tawn (code 11), which is the asymmetric logistic model.

docs.title: Asymmetric logistic (Tawn)
docs.text:
Property Value Codes 11 (FV_TAWN); generic 10005 Parameters, box \((\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta) \in [0, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [1, 60]\) (code 11); \([0.01, 1]^2 \times [1, 20]\) (generic) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.983]\) in the box of code 11 \(\lambda_U\) \(\psi_1 + \psi_2 - \left(\psi_1^\theta + \psi_2^\theta\right)^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable only if \(\psi_1 = \psi_2\) Rotations 90, 180, 270 Edge flip swap \(\psi_1 \leftrightarrow \psi_2\) \[ A(w) = (1 - \psi_1)(1 - w) + (1 - \psi_2)\, w + \left[ \big(\psi_1 (1 - w)\big)^\theta + (\psi_2 w)^\theta \right]^{1/\theta}, \] \[ \ell(x, y) = (1 - \psi_1)\, x + (1 - \psi_2)\, y + \left[ (\psi_1 x)^\theta + (\psi_2 y)^\theta \right]^{1/\theta}. \]

Tawn (1988). The stable tail function reads as a mixture of three sources of extremes: a share \(1 - \psi_1\) of the first variable's extremes that is independent of everything, a share \(1 - \psi_2\) of the second's, and the remaining shares \(\psi_1\), \(\psi_2\) that are tied together by a logistic (Gumbel) dependence. Unequal weights make the copula non-exchangeable. \(\psi_1 = \psi_2 = 1\) is Gumbel(\(\theta\)); either weight at \(0\) gives independence. This is also the Khoudraji asymmetrisation of the Gumbel copula with \(a = \psi_1\), \(b = \psi_2\).

Parameter order. fortvine stores Tawn as \((\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta)\), the weights first, in both the hand-coded and the generic version; \(\psi_1\) is attached to the first argument \(u\).

Two-parameter sub-models. With one weight fixed at one, the asymmetric logistic model keeps its asymmetry with one parameter less, which BIC rewards when the data support only one-sided asymmetry:

Code Name Parameters, box Fixed 10006 Tawn type 1 \((\theta, \psi_1) \in [1, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) \(\psi_2 = 1\) 10007 Tawn type 2 \((\theta, \psi_2) \in [1, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) \(\psi_1 = 1\)

Note the parameter order of the types: \(\theta\) comes first. An edge flip maps type 1 to type 2 with the same parameter values (fortvine changes the code). For the type numbering used by other packages, compare the formulas rather than the names.

docs.title: Asymmetric negative logistic (Joe)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 10008 (generic only) Parameters, box \((\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta) \in [0.01, 1]^2 \times [0.01, 20]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.952]\) in the box \(\lambda_U\) \(\left(\psi_1^{-\theta} + \psi_2^{-\theta}\right)^{-1/\theta}\) Exchangeable only if \(\psi_1 = \psi_2\) Edge flip swap \(\psi_1 \leftrightarrow \psi_2\) \[ A(w) = 1 - \left[ \big(\psi_1 (1 - w)\big)^{-\theta} + (\psi_2 w)^{-\theta} \right]^{-1/\theta}. \]

Joe (1990). This is to Galambos what the asymmetric logistic is to Gumbel, and it is likewise the Khoudraji asymmetrisation of the Galambos copula with \(a = \psi_1\), \(b = \psi_2\). \(\psi_1 = \psi_2 = 1\) recovers Galambos(\(\theta\)). The one-weight sub-models are

Code Name Parameters, box Fixed 10009 asymmetric negative logistic, type 1 \((\theta, \psi_1) \in [0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) \(\psi_2 = 1\) 10010 asymmetric negative logistic, type 2 \((\theta, \psi_2) \in [0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) \(\psi_1 = 1\)

Asymmetric lower-tail dependence

The upper tail of the asymmetric negative logistic is that of a Khoudraji-transformed survival Clayton copula. Rotated by 180°, code 10008 therefore gives a non-exchangeable copula with lower-tail dependence \(\left(\psi_1^{-\theta} + \psi_2^{-\theta}\right)^{-1/\theta}\), something Khoudraji-Clayton itself cannot provide.

docs.title: Asymmetric mixed (Tawn)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 10011 (generic only) Parameters, box \((\theta, \kappa) \in [0, 1]^2\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.418]\) \(\lambda_U\) \(\theta/2 + 3\phi/4\) Exchangeable only if \(\phi = 0\) Edge flip \((\theta, \phi) \to (\theta + 3\phi, -\phi)\), then \(\kappa\) recomputed \[ A(w) = 1 - (\theta + \phi)\, w + \theta\, w^2 + \phi\, w^3 . \]

Tawn (1988) gives the admissible region of the cubic as \(\theta \ge 0\), \(\theta + 3\phi \ge 0\), \(\theta + \phi \le 1\) and \(\theta + 2\phi \le 1\). A box is much easier for an optimiser than four linear constraints, so fortvine replaces \(\phi\) by a share \(\kappa \in [0, 1]\):

\[ \phi = -\frac{\theta}{3} + \kappa \left( \frac{1 - \theta}{2} + \frac{\theta}{3} \right). \]

\(\kappa = 0\) puts \(\phi\) on the edge \(\theta + 3\phi = 0\) and \(\kappa = 1\) on the edge \(\theta + 2\phi = 1\); every \((\theta, \kappa)\) in the unit square is admissible and every admissible \((\theta, \phi)\) is reached. The symmetric mixed model is the slice \(\phi = 0\). Since \(w\) is the share of the second argument, \(A(1 - w)\) is again a cubic of the same form, with \(\theta' = \theta + 3\phi\) and \(\phi' = -\phi\); that is the transposition fortvine applies when a vine edge is flipped. Like the symmetric model, the asymmetric mixed model is limited to weak and moderate dependence.

docs.title: Khoudraji–Hüsler–Reiss and Khoudraji–mixed
docs.text:
Property Khoudraji–HR Khoudraji–mixed Code 10012 10013 Parameters, box \((\lambda, a, b) \in [0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]^2\) \((\theta, a, b) \in [0, 1] \times [0.01, 1]^2\) Kendall's \(\tau\) range in the box \([0, 0.945]\) \([0, 0.418]\) \(\lambda_U\) \((a + b)\left[1 - A_{HR}\!\left(\frac{b}{a+b}\right)\right]\) \(\dfrac{\theta\, a b}{a + b}\) Exchangeable only if \(a = b\) only if \(a = b\) Edge flip swap \(a \leftrightarrow b\) swap \(a \leftrightarrow b\)

The Khoudraji construction \(C_K(u, v) = u^{1-a} v^{1-b} C_0(u^a, v^b)\) (see the Khoudraji page) maps an EV copula to another EV copula. In terms of the stable tail function, \(\ell_K(x, y) = (1 - a)x + (1 - b)y + \ell_0(ax, by)\), so the new Pickands function is

\[ A_K(w) = (1 - a)(1 - w) + (1 - b)\, w + v\, A_0\!\left(\frac{b w}{v}\right), \qquad v = a (1 - w) + b w, \]

with \(A_K''(w) = a^2 b^2 A_0''(bw/v) / v^3\). fortvine provides it for the two symmetric bases whose asymmetric versions are not already in the list: Hüsler–Reiss and the symmetric mixed model. Applied to Gumbel or Galambos the same construction gives the asymmetric logistic and asymmetric negative logistic models above, so those are not repeated.

docs.title: t-EV (Student extreme value)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 23 (FV_TEV) Parameters, box \(( ho, u) \in [-0.95, 0.99] imes [1, 30]\) Kendall's \( au\) no closed form; \( au \in [0, 0.894]\) in the box \(\lambda_U\) \(2\, T_{ u+1}\!\left(-\sqrt{( u+1) rac{1- ho}{1+ ho}} ight)\), the same as the t copula Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ A(w) = w\, T_{ u+1}(z_1) + (1 - w)\, T_{ u+1}(z_2), \qquad z_1 = k\left[\left( rac{w}{1-w} ight)^{1/ u} - ho ight], \quad z_2 = k\left[\left( rac{1-w}{w} ight)^{1/ u} - ho ight], \quad k = \sqrt{ rac{ u + 1}{1 - ho^2}} . \]

The t-EV copula (Demarta & McNeil 2005) is the extreme-value limit of the Student t copula; in the joint limit \( u o \infty\), \( ho o 1\) it contains Hüsler–Reiss. Its parameters are poorly separated: quite different \(( ho, u)\) pairs give almost the same \(A\), along a ridge that is nearly straight in \(( ho, \log u)\). The t distribution function has no elementary derivative in its degrees of freedom, so fortvine first locates the optimum on a subsample by profiling \(\log u\) (with \( ho\) solved by Newton on its exact score), then refines \(( ho, u)\) jointly on all data with a dedicated \( u\)-derivative of the t distribution function. Even so, code 23 is the slowest family to fit, which is why the default family set leaves it out.

docs.title: BB5
docs.text:
Property Value Code 19 (FV_BB5); generic 10102 Parameters, box \(\theta \in [1, 10]\), \(\delta \in [0.01, 30]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [0, 0.997]\) in the box \(\lambda_U\) \(2 - \left(2 - 2^{-1/\delta}\right)^{1/\theta}\) Exchangeable yes Rotations 90, 180, 270 \[ C(u, v) = \exp\!\left\{ -\left[ x^\theta + y^\theta - \left(x^{-\theta\delta} + y^{-\theta\delta}\right)^{-1/\delta} \right]^{1/\theta} \right\}, \qquad A(w) = \left[ w^\theta + (1 - w)^\theta - \left(w^{-\theta\delta} + (1 - w)^{-\theta\delta}\right)^{-1/\delta} \right]^{1/\theta}. \]

BB5 (Joe & Hu 1996) combines a logistic and a negative logistic part: \(\delta \to 0\) leaves Gumbel(\(\theta\)) and \(\theta = 1\) gives Galambos(\(\delta\)). It is the Archimax copula of the positive stable generator with the negative logistic Pickands function.

docs.title: More extreme-value copulas: positive stable Archimax
docs.text:
Any Archimax copula whose outer generator is the positive stable transform, \(\psi(s) = e^{-s^{1/\theta}}\), is again an EV copula, because \(C(u, v) = \exp\{-\ell_0(x^\theta, y^\theta)^{1/\theta}\}\) is max-stable. Its Pickands function is

\[ A^*(w) = \left[ \big((1 - w)^\theta + w^\theta\big)\; A_0\!\left( \frac{w^\theta}{(1 - w)^\theta + w^\theta} \right) \right]^{1/\theta}, \]

and its Kendall's tau is \(\tau_{A_0} + (1 - \tau_{A_0})(1 - 1/\theta)\). So the seven codes 10103, 10104, 10106, 10107, 10109, 10110 and 10111 (positive stable with Hüsler–Reiss, mixed, the asymmetric logistic types, the asymmetric negative logistic types and the asymmetric mixed model) extend the EV list with three-parameter members. They are documented with the Archimax families.

docs.title: Khoudraji asymmetrisation
docs.text:
Most parametric copulas are exchangeable: swapping the two variables changes nothing. Khoudraji's device (Khoudraji 1995; Genest, Ghoudi & Rivest 1998) turns any copula \(C_0\) into a non-exchangeable one with two extra parameters \(a, b \in [0, 1]\):

\[ C_K(u, v) = u^{1 - a}\, v^{1 - b}\, C_0\big(u^a, v^b\big). \]

The three Khoudraji families in fortvine at Kendall's \(\tau = 0.35\), parameters \((\theta, a, b)\). The unequal exponents bend the density away from the diagonal.

docs.title: Intuition: a shared and a private component
docs.text:
The construction has a simple stochastic reading. Let \((X_1, Y_1)\) be independent uniforms and \((X_2, Y_2)\) a pair with copula \(C_0\), independent of the first pair. Put

\[ U = \max\big(X_1^{1/(1 - a)},\, X_2^{1/a}\big), \qquad V = \max\big(Y_1^{1/(1 - b)},\, Y_2^{1/b}\big). \]

Then \(P(U \le u, V \le v) = P(X_1 \le u^{1-a})\,P(Y_1 \le v^{1-b})\,P(X_2 \le u^a, Y_2 \le v^b)\), which is exactly \(C_K(u, v)\). Each variable is the larger of a private component, unrelated to the other variable, and a shared component that carries the dependence of \(C_0\). The exponent \(a\) is the weight of the shared component in \(U\), and \(b\) its weight in \(V\):

  • \(a = b = 1\): no private parts, \(C_K = C_0\);
  • \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\): one variable is purely private, \(C_K\) is the independence copula;
  • \(a \ne b\): one variable is more "driven" by the common factor than the other, and the copula is no longer symmetric in its arguments.

docs.title: Formulas
docs.text:
Write \(x = u^a\), \(y = v^b\), and let \(C_0\), \(\partial_1 C_0\), \(\partial_2 C_0\) and \(c_0\) be the base copula, its two partial derivatives and its density, all at \((x, y)\). Then

\[ c_K(u, v) = (1 - a)(1 - b)\, u^{-a} v^{-b}\, C_0 + a (1 - b)\, v^{-b}\, \partial_1 C_0 + (1 - a)\, b\, u^{-a}\, \partial_2 C_0 + a b\, c_0 , \] \[ h_1(v \mid u) = v^{1 - b}\left[ (1 - a)\, u^{-a} C_0 + a\, \partial_1 C_0 \right], \qquad h_2(u \mid v) = u^{1 - a}\left[ (1 - b)\, v^{-b} C_0 + b\, \partial_2 C_0 \right]. \]

All four density terms are non-negative, so fortvine forms the log-density as a log-sum of four logs without cancellation. The base quantities come from the generic engine, which already returns \(\log C_0\), \(\log \partial_1 C_0\), \(\log \partial_2 C_0\) and \(\log c_0\) for every member. Neither h-function has a closed-form inverse; fortvine inverts each of them by a bracketed Newton iteration.

docs.title: Tail dependence
docs.text:
Upper tail. Suppose the base copula has a stable tail dependence function \(\ell_0\) at the upper corner, \(1 - C_0(1 - sx, 1 - sy) \approx s\, \ell_0(x, y)\) as \(s \to 0\). Then

\[ \lambda_U(C_K) = a + b - \ell_0(a, b). \]

For an extreme-value base, \(\ell_0(a, b) = (a + b) A_0\big(b/(a + b)\big)\), which gives

\[ \lambda_U(C_K) = (a + b)\left[ 1 - A_0\!\left(\frac{b}{a + b}\right) \right]. \]

With \(a = b\) the coefficient is simply \(a\, \lambda_U(C_0)\). For the Joe base, whose upper corner behaves like Gumbel's, \(\ell_0(x, y) = (x^\theta + y^\theta)^{1/\theta}\) and \(\lambda_U = a + b - (a^\theta + b^\theta)^{1/\theta}\). For Clayton and Frank, \(\ell_0(x, y) = x + y\) and \(\lambda_U = 0\).

Lower tail. Lower-tail dependence does not survive the transformation unless \(a = b = 1\). Along the diagonal, \(C_K(t, t) = t^{2 - a - b}\, C_0(t^a, t^b)\), and the Fréchet bound \(C_0(t^a, t^b) \le \min(t^a, t^b) = t^{\max(a, b)}\) gives

\[ \frac{C_K(t, t)}{t} \le t^{\,1 - \min(a, b)} \longrightarrow 0 \quad (t \to 0) \]

as soon as either exponent is below one: the private components dominate the joint small values. Khoudraji-Clayton therefore has \(\lambda_L = 0\) everywhere except at the corner \(a = b = 1\) of its box, where it is Clayton. (The tail flags in the catalogue say which tails a family can have anywhere in its box, so they mark Khoudraji-Clayton as lower-tail.)

For asymmetric lower-tail dependence use the 180° rotation of an asymmetric family with an upper tail, for example the asymmetric negative logistic model (code 10008, see the tip on the extreme-value page).

docs.title: Codes in fortvine
docs.text:
Khoudraji codes are 20000 + 100 og + ie: the base family's generic code plus 10000. The base parameters come first, then \(a\) and \(b\).

Code Base Parameters, box \(\tau\) range in box \(\lambda_L\) \(\lambda_U\) 20200 Clayton (gamma LT) \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 20]\), \(a, b \in [0.01, 1]\) \([0, 0.909]\) \(2^{-1/\theta}\) only at \(a = b = 1\) \(0\) 20300 Joe (Sibuya LT) \(\theta \in [1, 20]\), \(a, b \in [0.01, 1]\) \([0, 0.906]\) \(0\) \(a + b - (a^\theta + b^\theta)^{1/\theta}\) 20400 Frank (log-series LT, \(\theta > 0\)) \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 35]\), \(a, b \in [0.01, 1]\) \([0, 0.891]\) \(0\) \(0\)

All three are non-exchangeable for \(a \ne b\), positive-dependence families (negative dependence through the 90° and 270° rotations), and accept all rotations.

Edge flips. Transposing a Khoudraji copula with an exchangeable base just swaps the two exponents, \(C_K(v, u)\) with \((a, b)\) equals \(C_K(u, v)\) with \((b, a)\). fortvine applies this swap exactly when a vine flips an edge, so no refit is needed.

Identifiability. When \(a\) or \(b\) is close to zero the copula is nearly independent whatever the base parameter, and when both are near one the exponents hardly matter. Between these regimes the three parameters are well identified, but expect wide confidence intervals on \(a\) and \(b\) for weakly dependent pairs.

docs.title: Why only three codes?
docs.text:
The generic engine could wrap any member, but most wraps are either duplicates or exceed fortvine's limit of three parameters per pair copula:

  • Gumbel base. \(C_K\) with a Gumbel base is Tawn's asymmetric logistic model with \(\psi_1 = a\), \(\psi_2 = b\), already available as code 11 (and 10005). The code 20100 is therefore marked as a duplicate.
  • Extreme-value bases. The Khoudraji transform of an EV copula is again EV (its stable tail function is \((1 - a)x + (1 - b)y + \ell_0(ax, by)\)). The wraps of Gumbel-EV, Galambos, Hüsler–Reiss and the mixed model (20001 to 20004) are the Pickands functions ie = 5, 8, 12, 13 of the extreme-value page: asymmetric logistic, asymmetric negative logistic, Khoudraji–Hüsler–Reiss and Khoudraji–mixed. They are offered there, under their EV codes.
  • Two-parameter bases (BB families, compositions, Archimax) plus \(a, b\) would need four or more parameters.
  • Already asymmetric inner functions (ie 5 and above) are rejected: they are asymmetric by construction and would exceed three parameters.
  • Elliptical bases (Gaussian, Student t) are not part of the generic engine, which is built on Laplace-transform generators and Pickands functions.

docs.title: Nonparametric families
docs.text:
Two families let the data decide the shape of a pair copula instead of a parametric formula. Their estimate is not a parameter vector but a table stored with the pair copula (the aux component of fv_bicop and of each vine edge). This page summarises what they are; the manual page on nonparametric families covers estimation, smoothing choices and usage in detail.

Property TLL Bernstein Code 24 (FV_TLL) 25 (FV_BERNSTEIN) Estimate density on a \(30 \times 30\) grid in normal scores cell weights on an \(m \times m\) grid, \(m \le 15\) Smoothing bandwidth \(\propto n^{-1/3}\), shaped by the correlation of the normal scores order \(m\) chosen by AIC Complexity reported by npars / npars_eff effective degrees of freedom \((m - 1)^2\) Exchangeable, tails whatever the data show (no tail dependence in the limit sense) same Rotations none (not needed) none

Both families are excluded from the default family set; they are added with ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC or by listing FV_TLL / FV_BERNSTEIN in ctl%family_set.

docs.title: TLL: transformation local likelihood
docs.text:
The transformation estimator (Geenens, Charpentier & Paindaveine 2017) avoids the boundary bias of kernel smoothing on the unit square by working in normal scores. With \(z_1 = \Phi^{-1}(u)\), \(z_2 = \Phi^{-1}(v)\) and \(f\) a kernel estimate of the density of \((z_1, z_2)\),

\[ c(u, v) = \frac{f\big(\Phi^{-1}(u), \Phi^{-1}(v)\big)}{\phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(u)\big)\, \phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(v)\big)} . \]

fortvine follows vinecopulib's local-constant variant: a Gaussian kernel whose bandwidth matrix is \(n^{-1/3}\) times a matrix built from the correlation of the normal scores (adjusted by a maximal-correlation estimate), the density evaluated on a \(30 \times 30\) grid of normal scores in \([-3.25, 3.25]\), and the margins of the gridded copula renormalised to uniform. Between grid points the density is interpolated bilinearly; the h-functions integrate the interpolant exactly, and so does the distribution function. The reported number of parameters is the effective degrees of freedom of the smoother, so AIC and BIC can compare TLL with parametric families.

docs.title: Bernstein copula
docs.text:
The empirical Bernstein copula (Sancetta & Satchell 2004) smooths a two-dimensional histogram with Bernstein polynomials. Count the (weighted) observations in the cells of an \(m \times m\) grid, rebalance the cell masses \(W_{ij}\) by iterative proportional fitting so that every row and every column holds exactly \(1/m\) (which makes the result a proper copula), and set

\[ c(u, v) = m^2 \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{m} W_{ij}\; b_{i-1, m-1}(u)\; b_{j-1, m-1}(v), \qquad b_{k, n}(t) = \binom{n}{k} t^k (1 - t)^{n - k}. \]

The h-functions follow in closed form from binomial tail probabilities. The order \(m\) runs from 1 (the independence copula) to 15 and is chosen by AIC with \((m - 1)^2\) free cell weights; orders with \((m - 1)^2 \ge n/4\) are not tried.

docs.title: How they compare
docs.text: Density estimates in normal scores from 2000 points of an equal mixture of a Clayton ($\theta = 4$) and a 90-degree Gumbel ($\theta = 3$) copula. TLL recovers both arms (effective degrees of freedom 114); the Bernstein copula (order $m = 11$, 100 free cell weights) only hints at them, because a polynomial of moderate order cannot form the sharp tails; the best parametric family by BIC (Student t) is symmetric by construction. The same mixture at training sizes 250 to 8000 (mean of four samples each). (a) Log-likelihood per observation on 20 000 independent test points: TLL approaches the true density (dashed) as $n$ grows, the Bernstein copula follows more slowly and saturates when its order reaches the cap $m = 15$, and the best parametric family stays at the level of the wrong shape. (b) Effective number of parameters, which AIC and BIC charge: it grows with $n$ for both estimators; Bernstein's is $(m - 1)^2$, at most 196.

docs.title: Other parametric families
docs.text:
Two hand-coded families belong to none of the constructions on the previous pages: Plackett and Farlie–Gumbel–Morgenstern. Both are exchangeable, radially symmetric, free of tail dependence and cover negative dependence through their own parameter, so fortvine registers no rotations for them. The Ali–Mikhail–Haq copula (code 14) is Archimedean and is described on the Archimedean page, together with BB10 (code 21), which contains it.

The second half of this page explains which families from the literature fortvine leaves out on purpose, and why.

Plackett at \(\tau = 0.5\), and the strongest positive members of FGM (\(\theta = 1\)) and AMH (\(\theta = 0.95\)), density contours in normal scores. FGM and AMH cannot reach strong dependence.

docs.title: Plackett
docs.text:
Property Value Code 12 (FV_PLACKETT) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [10^{-3}, 10^3]\); \(\theta = 1\) is independence, \(\theta < 1\) negative dependence Kendall's \(\tau\) no closed form; \(\tau \in [-0.926, 0.926]\) in the box Spearman's \(\rho_S\) \(\dfrac{\theta + 1}{\theta - 1} - \dfrac{2\theta\log\theta}{(\theta - 1)^2}\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes, and radially symmetric Rotations none

With \(s = 1 + (\theta - 1)(u + v)\) and \(D = s^2 - 4\theta(\theta - 1)\, uv\):

\[ C(u, v) = \frac{s - \sqrt{D}}{2(\theta - 1)}, \qquad c(u, v) = \frac{\theta\,\big[1 + (\theta - 1)(u + v - 2uv)\big]}{D^{3/2}}, \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = \frac{1}{2}\left[ 1 - \frac{s - 2\theta v}{\sqrt{D}} \right]. \]

Plackett (1965) built the family from a constant cross-product ratio: for every point \((u, v)\),

\[ \frac{P(U \le u, V \le v)\; P(U > u, V > v)}{P(U \le u, V > v)\; P(U > u, V \le v)} = \theta , \]

so \(\theta\) is a global odds ratio, the continuous analogue of the odds ratio of a 2×2 table. It reaches strong dependence of both signs without any tail dependence, which makes it a symmetric alternative to Frank with a somewhat different body shape. fortvine inverts the h-function numerically.

docs.title: Farlie–Gumbel–Morgenstern (FGM)
docs.text:
Property Value Code 13 (FV_FGM) Parameter, box \(\theta \in [-1, 1]\) Kendall's \(\tau\) \(2\theta/9\), so \(\lvert\tau\rvert \le 2/9\) Spearman's \(\rho_S\) \(\theta / 3\) \(\lambda_L\), \(\lambda_U\) \(0\), \(0\) Exchangeable yes, and radially symmetric Rotations none \[ C(u, v) = uv\,\big[1 + \theta (1 - u)(1 - v)\big], \qquad c(u, v) = 1 + \theta (1 - 2u)(1 - 2v), \qquad h_1(v \mid u) = v\,\big[1 + \theta (1 - v)(1 - 2u)\big]. \]

The FGM copula (Morgenstern 1956; Gumbel 1960; Farlie 1960) is the independence copula plus a single product perturbation. That makes it the simplest possible model for weak dependence, and also limits it: \(\lvert\tau\rvert \le 2/9\) and \(\lvert\rho_S\rvert \le 1/3\). In vines it is useful in the higher trees, where the conditional dependence is often weak and a one-parameter family with a polynomial density is cheap to fit.

docs.title: Families not implemented
docs.text: fortvine's family list is meant for likelihood-based fitting and selection inside vines. That rules out several well-known copulas. The reasons fall into four groups.

docs.title: Singular families
docs.text:
A copula with a singular component puts positive probability on a curve of zero area. Such a copula has no density on that part of its mass, so the product of densities that a vine likelihood is made of does not describe the model, and an observation on the curve has no finite likelihood contribution. Left out for this reason:

  • Marshall–Olkin (Marshall & Olkin 1967) and its one-parameter case Cuadras–Augé (Cuadras & Augé 1981): mass on the curve \(u^\alpha = v^\beta\) (the diagonal for Cuadras–Augé);
  • Fréchet and Mardia families, mixtures of the comonotone, independence and countermonotone copulas: mass on the two diagonals;
  • Lévy-frailty, Durante–Salvadori and similar shock-model constructions;
  • Archimedean copulas with a non-strict generator (\(\varphi(0) < \infty\)), for example Nelsen's (2006) families 4.2.2, 4.2.7, 4.2.8 and 4.2.18: they carry mass \(-\varphi(0)/\varphi'(0^+)\) on their zero curve \(\varphi(u) + \varphi(v) = \varphi(0)\).

The Raftery copula (Raftery 1984) is sometimes listed as singular. It is not: it is absolutely continuous, with a density that has a kink along the diagonal. It is simply not implemented (see the candidates below).

docs.title: Families with a zero-density region
docs.text:
Some absolutely continuous copulas have a density that is exactly zero on a region of positive area. One pseudo-observation in that region sends the log-likelihood to \(-\infty\), and because the region moves with the parameter the likelihood is discontinuous. In a vine, the conditional pseudo-observations of the higher trees fill the whole unit square, so such regions are hit sooner or later. Left out for this reason:

  • Nelsen's (2006) families 4.2.11, 4.2.15, 4.2.21 and 4.2.22;
  • the negative-parameter branch of Clayton (\(-1 \le \theta < 0\)), whose density vanishes wherever \(u^{-\theta} + v^{-\theta} < 1\) (negative dependence comes from rotating Clayton instead);
  • the Pearson type II copula, whose elliptical support excludes the corners of the square.

docs.title: Families that need special functions per evaluation
docs.text:
Every log-density evaluation in a fit is repeated for every observation and every optimiser step, and fortvine differentiates it exactly with dual numbers. Families whose density needs an inverse special function with a parameter-dependent shape at every point are therefore very expensive, and their exact parameter derivatives need implicit differentiation of that inverse:

  • the GB2 (generalised beta of the second kind) copula (Yang, Frees & Zhang 2011): two inverse regularised incomplete beta functions per observation;
  • the Joe–Ma integrated positive stable copula (Joe & Ma 2000), with generator \(\psi(s) = Q(1/\alpha, s^\alpha)\) (the regularised upper incomplete gamma function): an inverse incomplete gamma per observation;
  • the inverse-gamma Laplace transform generator, \(\psi(s) = 2 s^{\alpha/2} K_\alpha(2\sqrt{s}) / \Gamma(\alpha)\): a modified Bessel function of parameter-dependent order, inverted numerically for every observation;
  • skew-normal and skew-t copulas: no closed-form quantile function of the margins, and the Azzalini–Capitanio skew-t copula needs four parameters, above fortvine's limit of three per pair.

docs.title: Weak polynomial families
docs.text: Copulas of the form "independence plus a bounded polynomial perturbation" (Huang–Kotz, Bekrizadeh, Bozkurt, Lai–Xie and similar FGM extensions) are absolutely continuous and cheap, but their attainable dependence is small (\(\lvert\rho_S\rvert\) around \(0.4\) at most), so they add little beyond FGM. The Durrleman cubic family has \(\tau = \rho_S = 0\) for all parameter values.

docs.title: Candidates for future versions
docs.text:
These absolutely continuous families with at most three parameters are not in fortvine yet but would fit its framework:

Family Parameters What it would add Raftery (1984) 1 closed \(\tau = 2\theta/(3 - \theta)\) and \(\lambda_L = 2\theta/(1 + \theta)\), a lower tail stronger than Clayton's at equal \(\tau\) Gumbel–Barnett (Nelsen 4.2.9) 1 weak negative dependence, \(\tau \in [-0.361, 0]\) Nelsen 4.2.16 1 \(\lambda_L = 1/2\) for every parameter, everything in closed form Cubic-section copulas (Nelsen, Quesada-Molina & Rodríguez-Lallena 1997) 2 the strongest smooth FGM-type family, \(\lvert\rho_S\rvert \le 0.577\), non-monotone shapes Roch & Alegre (2006) 2 Gumbel with an extra body parameter Bilogistic (Smith 1990), negative bilogistic (Coles & Tawn 1994) 2 two-parameter asymmetric EV families; each needs a scalar root per observation

docs.text:
Many families in the literature are reparametrisations of families fortvine already has:

Family as published Equals power-variance-function (PVF) and inverse-Gaussian frailty copulas BB9 (code 20) Nelsen 4.2.12 and 4.2.14 BB1 with \(\theta = 1\), and with \((\theta, \delta) = (1/\theta', \theta')\) Nelsen 4.2.13 with \(\theta \ge 1\) BB9 with \(\delta = 1\) Nelsen 4.2.19 and 4.2.20 BB2 with \(\theta = 1\), and with \(\delta = 1\) Kimeldorf–Sampson, Cook–Johnson, Burr Clayton (or its survival copula) Koehler–Symanowski Khoudraji-Clayton (code 20200) Khoudraji-Gumbel Tawn's asymmetric logistic (code 11) Khoudraji-Galambos asymmetric negative logistic (code 10008)

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
This page collects the theory needed to use fortvine with confidence: what a copula is, how data are brought to the copula scale, how dependence is summarised, which functions of a pair copula a vine needs, and how vines glue pair copulas into a \(d\)-dimensional model. The notation follows the code: a pair copula is evaluated at \((u_1, u_2)\), a vine at a row \(u = (u_1, \dots, u_d)\).

For book-length treatments see Joe (1997, 2014), Nelsen (2006) and Czado (2019) in the references.

docs.title: Copulas and Sklar's theorem
docs.text:
A \(d\)-dimensional copula \(C\) is the distribution function of a random vector \((U_1, \dots, U_d)\) whose components are each uniform on \((0, 1)\). Copulas matter because of the theorem of Sklar (1959): for any joint distribution function \(F\) with margins \(F_1, \dots, F_d\) there is a copula \(C\) with

\[ F(x_1, \dots, x_d) = C\bigl(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\bigr), \]

and \(C\) is unique on the product of the ranges of the margins (in particular everywhere when all margins are continuous). Conversely, any copula combined with any margins in this way gives a valid joint distribution. The margins carry everything about each variable on its own; the copula carries everything about how the variables move together.

With continuous margins and densities \(f_j\), differentiating gives the density factorisation that all likelihood computations rest on:

\[ f(x_1, \dots, x_d) = c\bigl(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\bigr) \prod_{j=1}^d f_j(x_j), \qquad c(u) = \frac{\partial^d C(u)}{\partial u_1 \cdots \partial u_d}. \]

The log-likelihood therefore splits into a sum of marginal terms and a copula term, which is why the dependence model can be estimated separately from the margins.

Some reference copulas:

Copula \(C(u_1, u_2)\) Meaning independence \(\Pi\) \(u_1 u_2\) no dependence (fortvine family 0) comonotonicity \(M\) \(\min(u_1, u_2)\) perfect positive dependence (upper Fréchet bound) countermonotonicity \(W\) \(\max(u_1 + u_2 - 1, 0)\) perfect negative dependence (lower Fréchet bound, \(d = 2\))

Every bivariate copula lies between them: \(W \le C \le M\).

docs.title: Pseudo-observations
docs.text:
In practice the margins are unknown. The standard remedy is to replace each observation by its scaled rank within its column,

\[ \hat u_{ij} = \frac{R_{ij}}{n + 1}, \qquad R_{ij} = \text{rank of } x_{ij} \text{ among } x_{1j}, \dots, x_{nj}, \]

so that the transformed data live in \((0, 1)\) and are approximately uniform. Dividing by \(n + 1\) instead of \(n\) keeps the values away from the boundary, where many copula densities are infinite. These pseudo-observations are what fv_pseudo_obs_nd(x, u) computes; tied values receive their average rank. Fitting a parametric copula to pseudo-observations by maximum likelihood is the semiparametric (canonical) maximum-likelihood method of Genest, Ghoudi & Rivest (1995). If the margins have been modelled parametrically instead, the probability integral transforms \(\hat F_j(x_{ij})\) can be used directly.

From data to the copula scale. (a) 800 draws with a log-normal and a gamma margin and a Gumbel copula ($\theta = 2$). (b) Their pseudo-observations (`to_pseudo_obs`): the margins are gone and only the ranks remain; the upper-right cluster is the Gumbel upper tail. (c) The same points in normal scores $\Phi^{-1}(\hat u)$, the scale used for every density plot on this site, with the density of a Gumbel copula fitted to the pseudo-observations.

fortvine never sees raw data: every routine expects copula data in \((0, 1)\). Values are clamped internally to \([10^{-10}, 1 - 10^{-10}]\) (see Numerics).

Discrete variables

For a discrete margin the probability integral transform is not uniform and the copula is not unique. fortvine follows the convention of Panagiotelis, Czado & Joe (2012) and vinecopulib: for each discrete variable pass both \(u = F(x)\) and \(u^- = F(x^-)\) (the distribution function just below \(x\)). See Discrete and mixed data and the example.

docs.title: Kendall's tau
docs.text:
Two observations \((x_1, y_1)\) and \((x_2, y_2)\) are concordant if both coordinates move in the same direction and discordant otherwise. Kendall's tau is the probability of concordance minus the probability of discordance for two independent draws. It depends on the copula only:

\[ \tau = 4 \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1 C(u_1, u_2)\, \mathrm dC(u_1, u_2) - 1 \in [-1, 1]. \]

For many one-parameter families \(\tau\) is a simple function of the parameter, which is used for starting values and for estimation by inversion of tau (method = FV_ITAU):

Family \(\tau(\theta)\) Gaussian, Student \(t\) \(\tfrac{2}{\pi} \arcsin \rho\) Clayton \(\theta / (\theta + 2)\) Gumbel \(1 - 1/\theta\) Frank \(1 - \tfrac{4}{\theta}\bigl(1 - D_1(\theta)\bigr)\), \(D_1(\theta) = \tfrac{1}{\theta}\int_0^\theta \tfrac{t}{e^t - 1}\,\mathrm dt\) Archimedean with generator \(\varphi\) \(1 + 4 \int_0^1 \varphi(t) / \varphi'(t)\, \mathrm dt\) Extreme-value with Pickands \(A\) \(\int_0^1 \tfrac{t(1 - t)}{A(t)}\, \mathrm dA'(t)\)

The sample version, fv_kendall_tau(x, y), is the tau-b statistic, which corrects for ties,

\[ \hat\tau_b = \frac{n_c - n_d}{\sqrt{(n_0 - n_x)(n_0 - n_y)}}, \qquad n_0 = \tbinom{n}{2}, \]

with \(n_c, n_d\) the concordant and discordant pairs and \(n_x, n_y\) the pairs tied in \(x\) or in \(y\). fortvine computes it in \(O(n \log n)\) operations with the merge-sort algorithm of Knight (1966); fv_tau_mat fills the whole \(d \times d\) matrix in parallel. Absolute Kendall taus are the default edge weights of vine structure selection; other weights (Spearman's rho, Hoeffding's D, Chatterjee's xi, mutual information, ...) are selected by fv_controls%tree_crit.

docs.title: Tail dependence
docs.text:
Rank correlations average over the whole unit square. Risk applications care about the corners, which the tail dependence coefficients measure:

\[ \lambda_L = \lim_{q \downarrow 0} P(U_2 \le q \mid U_1 \le q) = \lim_{q \downarrow 0} rac{C(q, q)}{q}, \qquad \lambda_U = \lim_{q \uparrow 1} P(U_2 > q \mid U_1 > q) = \lim_{q \uparrow 1} rac{1 - 2q + C(q, q)}{1 - q}. \]

A family with \(\lambda_U > 0\) lets very large values of both variables occur together far more often than a Gaussian model with the same correlation, whose tail coefficients are 0.

Family \(\lambda_L\) \(\lambda_U\) Gaussian (\(\lvert ho vert < 1\)) 0 0 Student \(t\) (\( ho\), \( u\)) \(2\, t_{ u+1}\!\left(-\sqrt{( u + 1)(1 - ho)/(1 + ho)} ight)\) same Clayton \(2^{-1/ heta}\) 0 Gumbel, Joe 0 \(2 - 2^{1/ heta}\) Frank, Plackett, FGM, AMH 0 0 BB1 (\( heta\), \(\delta\)) \(2^{-1/( heta\delta)}\) \(2 - 2^{1/\delta}\) extreme-value with Pickands \(A\) 0 (unless \(C = M\)) \(2 igl(1 - A(1/2) igr)\)

A rotation by 180 degrees exchanges \(\lambda_L\) and \(\lambda_U\). The tail dependence example compares these limits with the exact finite-level values and with empirical estimates, and shows how slowly some of them are approached.

docs.title: Conditional distributions: h-functions
docs.text:
Vines never need the bivariate copula \(C\) itself as much as its partial derivatives, the conditional distribution functions

\[ h_1(u_2 \mid u_1) = \frac{\partial C(u_1, u_2)}{\partial u_1} = P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1), \qquad h_2(u_1 \mid u_2) = \frac{\partial C(u_1, u_2)}{\partial u_2} = P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2). \]

In fortvine hfunc1(u1, u2, out) returns \(h_1(u_2 \mid u_1)\) (it conditions on the first argument) and hfunc2 returns \(h_2(u_1 \mid u_2)\). Both are distribution functions in the free argument, increasing from 0 to 1, and their derivatives in that argument are the density:

\[ \frac{\partial h_1(u_2 \mid u_1)}{\partial u_2} = \frac{\partial h_2(u_1 \mid u_2)}{\partial u_1} = c(u_1, u_2). \]

For exchangeable copulas, \(C(u_1, u_2) = C(u_2, u_1)\), the two coincide after swapping the arguments; for asymmetric families (Tawn, Khoudraji, asymmetric logistic, ...) they do not.

The inverse h-functions solve \(h_1(v \mid u_1) = w\) and \(h_2(v \mid u_2) = w\) for \(v\): hinv1(u1, w, out) and hinv2(w, u2, out). They are closed-form for the elliptical, Clayton and Frank families and use specialised monotone Newton iterations for Gumbel and Joe; every other family is inverted by a safeguarded Newton iteration whose derivative is the exact density, falling back to bisection inside a maintained bracket.

The conditional functions of a Clayton copula ($\theta = 2$, $\tau = 0.5$) for five conditioning values $u$. (a) $h_1(v \mid u)$ rises from 0 to 1 in $v$; it is steep for small $u$ because Clayton concentrates mass in the lower tail. (b) Its slope in $v$ is the density $c(u, v)$ (log scale). (c) The inverse $h_1^{-1}(w \mid u)$: feeding it uniform $w$ draws $V$ given $U = u$, which is how every simulation in fortvine works. All curves are `hfunc1`, `pdf` and `hinv1` of `fv.Bicop("clayton", parameters=[2])`.

docs.title: Rotations
docs.text:
Many families can only express positive dependence, and many have a tail in one corner only. Rotating the copula density by 90, 180 or 270 degrees creates the missing variants. With \((A, B)\) distributed as the unrotated copula \(C_0\), fortvine's rotations (counter-clockwise, the convention of vinecopulib) are

rotation point passed to \(C_0\) density distribution function 0 \((u_1, u_2)\) \(c_0(u_1, u_2)\) \(C_0(u_1, u_2)\) 90 \((u_2,\ 1 - u_1)\) \(c_0(u_2, 1 - u_1)\) \(u_2 - C_0(u_2, 1 - u_1)\) 180 \((1 - u_1,\ 1 - u_2)\) \(c_0(1 - u_1, 1 - u_2)\) \(u_1 + u_2 - 1 + C_0(1 - u_1, 1 - u_2)\) 270 \((1 - u_2,\ u_1)\) \(c_0(1 - u_2, u_1)\) \(u_1 - C_0(1 - u_2, u_1)\)

The 180-degree rotation is the survival copula: it moves a lower tail to the upper corner. Rotations by 90 and 270 degrees turn positive into negative dependence, placing the tail of \(C_0\) in the \((1, 0)\) or \((0, 1)\) corner respectively. Families that are already radially symmetric and cover negative dependence (Gaussian, Student, Frank, Plackett, FGM, AMH) are not rotated; for the rest, family selection tries the rotations that match the sign of the empirical tau. See Rotations and asymmetry.

A Gumbel copula ($\theta = 2$) in the four rotations, density in normal scores. The upper tail of the unrotated copula moves to the lower-left corner under 180 degrees (the survival copula) and to the off-diagonal corners under 90 and 270 degrees, where the dependence becomes negative.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Few parametric \(d\)-dimensional copulas are flexible enough for real data: most impose one kind of dependence on all pairs. A pair-copula construction (Joe 1996; Bedford & Cooke 2002; Aas et al. 2009) instead builds the density from \(d(d-1)/2\) bivariate copulas, some of which act on conditional distributions. For three variables, one such decomposition is

\[ c(u_1, u_2, u_3) = c_{12}(u_1, u_2)\; c_{23}(u_2, u_3)\; c_{13;2}\bigl(h_1(u_1 \mid u_2),\ h_1(u_3 \mid u_2)\bigr), \]

where \(c_{13;2}\) is the copula of \(U_1\) and \(U_3\) given \(U_2\), evaluated at their two conditional distribution functions. Each factor is an ordinary pair copula from any family, so a 10-dimensional model can mix 45 different families, rotations and tail behaviours.

docs.title: Regular vines
docs.text:
Which pairs are allowed is organised by a regular vine (R-vine): a sequence of trees \(T_1, \dots, T_{d-1}\) in which

  1. \(T_1\) is a tree on the \(d\) variables;
  2. the edges of \(T_k\) are the nodes of \(T_{k+1}\);
  3. (proximity) two nodes of \(T_{k+1}\) may be joined only if, as edges of \(T_k\), they share a node.

Each edge \(e\) of tree \(T_k\) is labelled by a conditioned pair \(\{a, b\}\) and a conditioning set \(D\) with \(|D| = k - 1\), and carries the pair copula \(c_{a,b;D}\). The vine density is the product over all edges:

\[ c(u) = \prod_{k=1}^{d-1} \prod_{e \in T_k} c_{a_e, b_e; D_e}\bigl(u_{a_e \mid D_e},\ u_{b_e \mid D_e}\bigr), \qquad u_{a \mid D} = F(u_a \mid u_D). \]

The conditional arguments are themselves h-functions of edges in the tree below, through the recursion (Joe 1996)

\[ F(u_a \mid u_D) = h\bigl(F(u_a \mid u_{D \setminus j}) \,\big|\, F(u_j \mid u_{D \setminus j})\bigr), \qquad j \in D, \]

where \(h\) is the h-function of the pair copula of \((a, j; D \setminus j)\). Evaluating a vine is therefore one sweep through the trees: every edge needs one density evaluation and at most two h-function evaluations per observation. fortvine stores the structure in a compact natural-order array (st(edge, tree) with the variable order); vc%matrix() returns the equivalent R-vine matrix in the original variable labels. The number of distinct R-vine structures grows super-exponentially, \(\tfrac{d!}{2}\, 2^{\binom{d-2}{2}}\) (Morales-Nápoles 2011), which is why structures are selected greedily.

Two special shapes have their own constructors:

  • C-vine (canonical): every tree is a star; one variable, the root, is linked to all others in \(T_1\), the next root to all remaining ones in \(T_2\), and so on. Natural when one variable drives the rest. set_cvine(order).
  • D-vine (drawable): every tree is a path; \(T_1\) links neighbours in order, and later trees follow. Natural for ordered variables such as time lags. set_dvine(order).

The four trees of a five-dimensional C-vine (`set_cvine([5, 4, 3, 2, 1])`, roots 1, 2, 3 in turn) and D-vine (`set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])`), read from fortvine's structure arrays. Nodes of tree $T_{k+1}$ are the edges of $T_k$, labelled by conditioned pair | conditioning set; in path-shaped trees each edge is also labelled with the pair copula it carries. Both vines satisfy the proximity condition: nodes joined in $T_{k+1}$ share a node of $T_k$.

docs.title: Structure selection
docs.text:
fortvine selects a vine with the sequential method of Dissmann et al. (2013):

  1. compute the edge weights of all admissible pairs (default \(|\hat\tau|\));
  2. find the maximum spanning tree (Prim's or Kruskal's algorithm);
  3. for every edge choose family, rotation and parameters by the selection criterion and compute the pseudo-observations of the next tree with the fitted h-functions;
  4. repeat on the pairs allowed by the proximity condition, until \(T_{d-1}\).

The procedure is greedy: putting the strongest dependence into the first trees is a good heuristic, not a guarantee of the best global vine (the vine example shows a case where it misses the true structure). With a structure fixed by set_cvine/set_dvine only steps 3-4 run.

docs.title: The simplifying assumption
docs.text: In general the copula of \((U_a, U_b)\) given \(U_D = u_D\) depends on the value \(u_D\). Vines used in practice assume it does not: \(c_{a,b;D}\) is one fixed copula applied to the conditional distribution functions. This simplifying assumption (Hobæk Haff, Aas & Frigessi 2010) is what makes estimation feasible; it is exact for Gaussian and Student vines and a good approximation in many applications. fortvine can relax it for selected edges (parameters varying with the conditioning variables, after Acar, Craiu & Yao 2011, with a constant-conditional-correlation test following Kurz & Spanhel 2022) through vc%relax.

docs.title: Truncation and thresholding
docs.text: High trees often carry little dependence. A vine truncated at level \(k\) sets every pair copula in trees \(k+1, \dots, d-1\) to independence, which removes their parameters and their evaluation cost. A threshold sets an edge to independence when its weight is below a cut-off. Both can be fixed (trunc_lvl, threshold) or chosen automatically by the modified BIC for vines (mBICv, Nagler, Bumann & Czado 2019) with select_trunc and select_threshold.

docs.title: Selection criteria
docs.text:
Given the maximised log-likelihood \(\ell\), the number of parameters \(k\) and the sample size \(n\), family selection compares

\[ \mathrm{AIC} = -2\ell + 2k, \qquad \mathrm{BIC} = -2\ell + k \log n, \]

and, for vines, the mBICv, which adds to the BIC of each tree \(t\) a prior that the pair copulas of tree \(t\) are non-independent with probability \(\psi_0^t\) (fv_controls%psi0, default 0.9):

\[ \mathrm{mBICv} = -2\ell + k \log n - 2 \sum_{t} \Bigl[ q_t \log \psi_0^t + (d - t - q_t) \log(1 - \psi_0^t) \Bigr], \]

with \(q_t\) the number of non-independence edges in tree \(t\). The prior favours sparse vines, increasingly so in higher trees. For the nonparametric families (TLL, Bernstein) \(k\) is the effective number of parameters of the smoother.

docs.title: The Rosenblatt transform
docs.text:
The Rosenblatt transform (Rosenblatt 1952) maps a \(d\)-dimensional observation to independent uniforms by successive conditioning:

\[ w_1 = u_1, \quad w_2 = F(u_2 \mid u_1), \quad \dots, \quad w_d = F(u_d \mid u_1, \dots, u_{d-1}). \]

If \(u\) follows the model, \(w\) is uniform on \((0, 1)^d\) with independent components. In a vine every conditional distribution is a chain of h-functions, so the transform costs about the same as one density evaluation (vc%rosenblatt). Applied to data it produces model-based residuals for goodness-of-fit checks: their columns should be uniform and mutually independent. The conditioning order is the vine's variable order, so the first transformed column is the variable with the empty conditioning set.

For discrete variables the conditional distribution has jumps and \(w\) is not uniform; fortvine then returns Brockwell's (2007) randomised transform \(W F(x_k \mid \cdot) + (1 - W) F(x_k^- \mid \cdot)\) with independent uniforms \(W\), which is again i.i.d. uniform under the model.

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
Inverting the Rosenblatt transform turns independent uniforms into a sample from the model:

\[ u_1 = w_1, \quad u_2 = F^{-1}(w_2 \mid u_1), \quad \dots, \quad u_d = F^{-1}(w_d \mid u_1, \dots, u_{d-1}), \]

and in a vine each conditional quantile is a chain of inverse h-functions, taken from the top tree down. vc%inverse_rosenblatt(w, u) does exactly this, and vc%simulate(n, u, seed) draws the uniforms first. For a single pair it reduces to \(u_2 = h_1^{-1}(w \mid u_1)\), i.e. cop%hinv1(u1, w, u2). Simulated copula data are mapped to any margins with the marginal quantile functions, \(x_{ij} = F_j^{-1}(u_{ij})\).

docs.title: Estimation
docs.text: For a single pair copula fortvine maximises the log-likelihood \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_i w_i \log c(u_{i1}, u_{i2}; \theta)\) (observation weights \(w_i\) default to 1) inside the family's parameter box. One-parameter families can instead be estimated by inverting Kendall's tau. The maximisation uses exact parameter scores from dual-number arithmetic and Fisher-scoring steps; see Exact parameter scores. A vine is estimated edge by edge, tree by tree (sequential estimation), each edge on the pseudo-observations produced by the trees below; this is the standard estimator of vinecopulib and VineCopula and is consistent, although not fully efficient compared with a joint maximisation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: fortvine is plain modern Fortran with OpenMP directives. It has no dependencies beyond the compiler: no BLAS, no LAPACK, no CMake, no Python. You can compile it with the bundled shell script, with the Fortran Package Manager, or by hand with three compiler calls.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
What Version Notes gfortran 10 or newer Tested up to GCC 16. Other Fortran 2008 compilers with a C preprocessor should work but are not tested. OpenMP the one that ships with gfortran (libgomp) Optional. Without it the library runs on one thread and gives the same results. A POSIX shell bash Only for build.sh. On Windows, Git Bash or the MSYS2 shell.

Supported platforms:

LinuxmacOSWindows

Any distribution's gfortran works:

sudo apt-get install gfortran        # Debian / Ubuntu
sudo dnf install gcc-gfortran        # Fedora / RHEL

Homebrew's GCC contains gfortran and libgomp:

brew install gcc
export FC=gfortran-14                # the versioned name Homebrew installs

Apple's clang has no Fortran compiler; the shared library is built as libfortvine.dylib.

Use a MinGW-w64 gfortran, for example one of these:

  • WinLibs (standalone GCC + MinGW-w64, unpack and add mingw64\bin to PATH),
  • MSYS2 (pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc-fortran),
  • any other MinGW-w64 distribution of GCC 10+.

Run build.sh from Git Bash or the MSYS2 shell. The script detects MinGW / MSYS / Cygwin and links the example and test programs statically (see Troubleshooting).

docs.title: Building with build.sh
docs.text:
From the repository root:

bash build.sh

This compiles the three source files (src/fortvine_ad.f90, src/fortvine.f90, src/fortvine_api.f90; the .inc files are pulled in by the preprocessor) and writes, in build/:

File Purpose libfortvine.a static library for Fortran programs libfortvine.so / libfortvine.dylib / libfortvine.dll shared library for C, C++, Python, Julia, R, ... fortvine_api.mod, fortvine.mod, fortvine_ad*.mod module files the compiler needs for use fortvine_api

Extra targets can be appended in any combination:

bash build.sh test                 # build and run test/test_fortvine and test/test_genfam
bash build.sh examples             # build every example/*.f90 into build/<name>
bash build.sh bench                # build bench/fv_bench (driven by bench/run_bench.py)
bash build.sh test examples bench  # all of them

bash build.sh test must end with the two lines ALL TESTS PASSED and ALL GENERIC FAMILY TESTS PASSED; see Validation for what the suites check. A full bash build.sh test examples takes about half a minute on a laptop.

docs.title: Compiler and flags
docs.text:
Two environment variables control the build:

Variable Default Meaning FC gfortran the Fortran compiler FFLAGS -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fno-math-errno -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp compile flags

build.sh always adds -cpp -I ../src -fPIC itself, so FFLAGS only has to carry optimisation and OpenMP choices. -ffree-line-length-none is required: a few source lines are longer than the standard 132 columns.

FC=gfortran-13 bash build.sh test
FFLAGS="-O2 -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" bash build.sh test examples   # what CI uses
FFLAGS="-O2 -ffree-line-length-none" bash build.sh                           # serial build

Portable binaries

-march=native tunes the code for the CPU that compiles it. A library built this way can crash with illegal instruction on an older machine. If you distribute binaries, replace it by a baseline such as -march=x86-64-v2 (or -march=x86-64-v3 for AVX2 machines), or leave it out:

FFLAGS="-O3 -march=x86-64-v2 -funroll-loops -fno-math-errno -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" bash build.sh

docs.title: Building with fpm
docs.text:
The repository is also a Fortran Package Manager package. fpm.toml declares the library in src/, turns on the C preprocessor ([preprocess.cpp], needed for the .inc family files), disables implicit typing, and discovers the tests in test/ and the examples in example/ automatically.

fpm does not know about the long source lines or about OpenMP, so pass the flags explicitly:

fpm build --profile release --flag "-ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" --link-flag "-fopenmp"
fpm test  --profile release --flag "-ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" --link-flag "-fopenmp"
fpm run --example ex01_pair_copula --profile release --flag "-ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" --link-flag "-fopenmp"

To use fortvine as a dependency of your own fpm project:

[dependencies]
fortvine = { git = "https://github.com/Bluerrror/fortvine" }

Note

The fpm route has not been exercised by the continuous integration (which runs build.sh); if your fpm version does not preprocess .f90 files, add -cpp to --flag.

docs.title: Linking your own program
docs.text:
A Fortran program needs the module files at compile time and the static library at link time:

hello_vine.f90
program hello_vine
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop
  real(kind(1d0)) :: c(1)
  cop%family = FV_FRANK; cop%par(1) = 5.0d0
  call cop%pdf([0.3d0], [0.4d0], c)
  print *, 'Frank(5) density at (0.3, 0.4):', c(1)
end program hello_vine
Linux / macOSWindows (MinGW-w64) 
gfortran -O3 -fopenmp -I path/to/fortvine/build hello_vine.f90 \
         path/to/fortvine/build/libfortvine.a -o hello_vine

gfortran -O3 -fopenmp -I path/to/fortvine/build hello_vine.f90 \
         path/to/fortvine/build/libfortvine.a -static -o hello_vine.exe

Rules of thumb:

  • Compile your program with the same compiler (and preferably the same version) as the library: .mod files are not portable between compilers or major gfortran versions.
  • If the library was built with OpenMP, link with -fopenmp too, or the linker reports undefined GOMP_* / omp_* symbols. A serial library links without it.
  • The library must come after your source or object files on the command line.

docs.title: The shared library (C, C++, Python, ...)
docs.text:
build.sh also produces build/libfortvine.so (Linux), .dylib (macOS) or .dll (Windows). Every kernel of src/fortvine.f90 with a bind(C, name="fv_...") interface is exported under that name, e.g. fv_bicop_eval, fv_bicop_fit, fv_bicop_select, fv_vine_select, fv_vine_pdf, fv_vine_rosenblatt, fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt, fv_kendall_tau, fv_tau_matrix, fv_pseudo_obs.

  • C and C++: declare the prototypes and link against the library, see Calling fortvine from Python and C and the C interface.
  • Python: load it with ctypes (or cffi) and pass numpy arrays; a complete script is in example/python/fortvine_ctypes.py.

On Windows the DLL is linked with -static-libgfortran -static-libgcc, so it does not need libgfortran, but it still imports libgomp-1.dll, libquadmath-0.dll and libwinpthread-1.dll. Those ship with every MinGW-w64 gfortran: keep its bin directory on PATH (or call os.add_dll_directory in Python), or copy the three DLLs next to libfortvine.dll.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Error: Line truncated or Unterminated character constant

-ffree-line-length-none is missing from FFLAGS. If you set FFLAGS yourself, keep that flag.

undefined reference to GOMP_parallel / omp_get_num_procs

The library was compiled with -fopenmp but your program was linked without it. Add -fopenmp to the link command, or rebuild the library serially (FFLAGS="-O3 -ffree-line-length-none" bash build.sh).

OpenMP is not available on my compiler

Build without -fopenmp as above. Every routine still works, on one thread. Densities, h-functions and log-likelihood sums do not depend on the number of threads (sums are accumulated over a fixed set of blocks in a fixed order). Family selection races candidate fits against each other when several threads are available, so a near-tie between two candidates can occasionally be decided differently; see Performance and threads.

Illegal instruction on another machine

The library was built with -march=native on a newer CPU. Rebuild with a baseline architecture (see the tip under Compiler and flags).

Windows: the program starts and exits silently, or complains about missing DLLs

A dynamically linked executable needs libgfortran-5.dll, libgomp-1.dll, libquadmath-0.dll, libwinpthread-1.dll and libgcc_s_seh-1.dll at run time. Either link with -static (what build.sh does for the tests and examples) or put the MinGW-w64 bin directory on PATH.

Windows: a program with big arrays exits silently (exit code 127 in Git Bash)

With -fopenmp, gfortran also implies -frecursive, which places local arrays, even those of the main program, on the stack, and the default Windows stack is 2 MB. Make large arrays allocatable (as example/ex04_tails.f90 does) or enlarge the stack at link time with -Wl,--stack,268435456.

Fatal Error: Cannot read module file 'fortvine_api.mod' ... created by a different version

Rebuild fortvine with the compiler you use for your program.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page takes about five minutes. It assumes the library is built (bash build.sh, see Installation), or the Python or R package installed, and walks through one complete program: a pair copula that is evaluated, simulated, fitted and selected, followed by a four-dimensional vine that is selected from data, scored and simulated. Pick a language in the tabs; the choice applies to every code example on the site.

Everything goes through one module, fortvine_api, and two derived types:

  • fv_bicop, a bivariate (pair) copula: family, rotation, par(3), loglik;
  • fv_vinecop, a vine copula: structure, one fv_bicop-like edge per tree and position.

The Python package wraps them as the classes Bicop and Vinecop; the R package as the model objects bicop_dist and vinecop_dist with functions in the style of rvinecopulib (dbicop, hbicop, bicop, vinecop, ...).

Data are copula data: numbers in \((0, 1)\), one column per variable, typically pseudo-observations (scaled ranks) of the raw data. fv_pseudo_obs_nd(x, u) turns raw data x(n, d) into u(n, d) (fv.to_pseudo_obs(x) in Python, pseudo_obs(x) in R).

docs.title: The program
docs.text:
FortranPythonR quickstart.f90
program quickstart
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 1000
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop, est, best
  type(fv_vinecop) :: truth, vc
  real(dp) :: u1(n), w(n), u2(n), c(3), h(3)
  real(dp), allocatable :: u(:, :), sim(:, :)
  integer :: ns, k

  ! ---- one pair copula: Gumbel with theta = 1.5 (Kendall tau = 1 - 1/theta = 1/3)
  cop%family = FV_GUMBEL
  cop%par(1) = 1.5_dp
  call cop%pdf([0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.95_dp], [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.95_dp], c)
  call cop%hfunc1([0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.95_dp], [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.95_dp], h)
  print '(a,3f9.4)', 'density c(u,u)   :', c
  print '(a,3f9.4)', 'h1(u | u)        :', h

  ! simulate n pairs: u2 = h1^-1(w | u1) with independent uniforms u1, w
  call random_seed(size=ns)
  call random_seed(put=[(42 + k, k = 1, ns)])
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  call cop%hinv1(u1, w, u2)
  print '(a,f8.4)', 'sample Kendall tau:', fv_kendall_tau(u1, u2)

  ! maximum likelihood for a known family, then family selection by BIC
  est%family = FV_GUMBEL
  call est%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,f8.4,a,f9.3)', 'Gumbel MLE theta :', est%par(1), '   loglik', est%loglik
  call best%select(u1, u2)
  print '(3a,i0,a,2f8.4)', 'BIC selection    : ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), ', rotation ', &
    best%rotation, ', par', best%par(1:2)

  ! ---- a 4-dimensional vine: a C-vine with Clayton pairs as the truth
  allocate(u(n, 4), sim(5, 4))
  call truth%set_cvine([1, 2, 3, 4])
  truth%fam(1:3, 1) = FV_CLAYTON; truth%par(1, 1:3, 1) = 3.0_dp     ! tree 1
  truth%fam(1:2, 2) = FV_CLAYTON; truth%par(1, 1:2, 2) = 1.0_dp     ! tree 2
  call truth%simulate(n, u, seed=1)

  call vc%select(u)                        ! structure, families, parameters
  call vc%print()
  print '(a,f10.2,a,f10.2,a,i0)', 'loglik', vc%loglik(u), '   (truth', truth%loglik(u), ')   parameters ', vc%npars()
  call vc%simulate(5, sim, seed=2)
  print '(a)', 'five draws from the fitted vine:'
  print '(4f9.4)', (sim(k, :), k = 1, 5)
end program quickstart
quickstart.py
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n = 1000

# ---- one pair copula: Gumbel with theta = 1.5 (Kendall tau = 1 - 1/theta = 1/3)
cop = fv.Bicop("gumbel", parameters=[1.5])
g = np.array([0.1, 0.5, 0.95])
print("density c(u,u)   :", cop.pdf(np.column_stack([g, g])).round(4))
print("h1(u | u)        :", cop.hfunc1(np.column_stack([g, g])).round(4))

u12 = cop.simulate(n, seed=42)                       # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
print("sample Kendall tau: %.4f" % fv.kendall_tau(u12[:, 0], u12[:, 1]))

est = fv.Bicop("gumbel").fit(u12)                    # maximum likelihood, fixed family
print("Gumbel MLE theta : %.4f   loglik %.3f" % (est.parameters[0], est.loglik()))
best = fv.Bicop().select(u12)                        # family and rotation by BIC
print("BIC selection    :", best)

# ---- a 4-dimensional vine: a C-vine with Clayton pairs as the truth
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_cvine([1, 2, 3, 4])
truth.fam[0, :3] = 3; truth.par[0, :3, 0] = 3.0      # tree 1: Clayton(3)
truth.fam[1, :2] = 3; truth.par[1, :2, 0] = 1.0      # tree 2: Clayton(1)
u = truth.simulate(n, seed=1)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)                         # structure, families, parameters
print(vc)
print("loglik %.2f   (truth %.2f)   parameters %d" % (vc.loglik(u), truth.loglik(u), vc.npars))
print("five draws from the fitted vine:")
print(vc.simulate(5, seed=2).round(4))
quickstart.R
library(fortvine)
n <- 1000

# ---- one pair copula: Gumbel with theta = 1.5 (Kendall tau = 1 - 1/theta = 1/3)
cop <- bicop_dist("gumbel", 0, 1.5)
g <- c(0.1, 0.5, 0.95)
cat("density c(u,u)   :", sprintf("%9.4f", dbicop(cbind(g, g), cop)), "\n", sep = "")
cat("h1(u | u)        :", sprintf("%9.4f", hbicop(cbind(g, g), 1, cop)), "\n", sep = "")

set.seed(42)
u12 <- rbicop(n, cop)                                  # u2 = h1^-1(w | u1)
cat(sprintf("sample Kendall tau: %.4f\n", cor(u12[, 1], u12[, 2], method = "kendall")))

est <- bicop(u12, family_set = "gumbel", rotation = 0)  # maximum likelihood, fixed family
cat(sprintf("Gumbel MLE theta : %.4f   loglik %.3f\n", est$parameters, est$loglik))
best <- bicop(u12, family_set = "all", selcrit = "bic") # family and rotation by BIC
best

# ---- a 4-dimensional vine: a C-vine with Clayton pairs as the truth
pcs <- list(rep(list(bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 3)), 3),  # tree 1: Clayton(3)
            rep(list(bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 1)), 2))  # tree 2: Clayton(1)
truth <- vinecop_dist(pcs, cvine_structure(1:4))
set.seed(1)
u <- rvinecop(n, truth)

vc <- vinecop(u)                                       # structure, families, parameters
vc
cat(sprintf("loglik %.2f   (truth %.2f)   parameters %d\n",
            sum(log(dvinecop(u, vc))), sum(log(dvinecop(u, truth))), vc$npars))
cat("five draws from the fitted vine:\n")
set.seed(2)
round(rvinecop(5, vc), 4)

The Fortran program is compiled and run like any program that uses the library:

gfortran -O3 -fopenmp -I build quickstart.f90 build/libfortvine.a -o quickstart   # add -static on Windows
./quickstart

The scripts run with python quickstart.py and Rscript quickstart.R.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text:
Evaluating. A copula is defined by setting family (a code such as FV_GUMBEL, see Family codes and constants) and the parameters par(1:3); unused slots stay 0. All evaluation methods are vectorised: pdf, logpdf, cdf, hfunc1, hfunc2, hinv1, hinv2 take two arrays of equal length and fill a third (in Python and R they take an \(n \times 2\) array and return a vector). The density of the Gumbel copula grows towards \((1, 1)\) (4.59 at \(u = v = 0.95\)) because the family has upper tail dependence.

Simulating. hinv1(u1, w, u2) inverts the conditional distribution \(h_1(v \mid u) = \partial C(u, v) / \partial u\) in \(v\). Feeding it independent uniforms \((u_1, w)\) yields a sample from the copula: this inverse Rosenblatt construction is how every simulation in fortvine works, including Bicop.simulate and rbicop. The sample's Kendall tau (0.36) is close to the theoretical \(1 - 1/\theta = 1/3\).

Fitting. fit maximises the likelihood of the family already stored in est%family (and est%rotation), here giving \(\hat\theta = 1.536\). The maximum log-likelihood is stored in est%loglik. In R, bicop() fits a single family when it is given one family and a rotation.

Selecting. select fits every family of the candidate set in every admissible rotation and keeps the one with the best criterion (BIC by default). On the Fortran sample it picked the Galambos copula rather than Gumbel (the Python and R samples give Gumbel): both are extreme-value copulas with nearly identical Pickands functions, and from 1000 observations the two cannot be told apart, so the choice between them is close to a coin flip. That is normal behaviour, not an error; the candidate set and criterion are configured with an fv_controls argument (keyword arguments in Python and R).

The pair-copula part of the Python run. (a) The 1000 simulated pairs in normal scores with the density contours of the fitted ($\hat\theta = 1.554$) and of the true Gumbel copula ($\theta = 1.5$), which nearly coincide. (b) BIC of every family of the default set, each fitted in its best rotation and shown relative to the selected one (the 12 best of 23): Galambos trails Gumbel by less than one BIC unit, which is why the Fortran sample, drawn with different uniforms, ends up with Galambos.

A vine. set_cvine and set_dvine create a fixed C- or D-vine structure whose edge families and parameters are then filled in by hand (fam(edge, tree), par(1:3, edge, tree); in Python fam[tree, edge]); simulate draws from it. vc%select(u) runs the whole Dissmann et al. (2013) procedure on the sample: it chooses the tree structure with maximum spanning trees on \(|\tau|\), then a family, rotation and parameters for every edge, tree by tree. The selected vine is not the true one edge for edge (survival Joe and Clayton have similar lower tails, and the third tree absorbs a small amount of dependence that the second tree's choice left over), but its log-likelihood (2329.6) is within 12 units of the truth's (2341.6), using six parameters where the truth has five.

The vine of the Python run, tree by tree: the true C-vine (a star around variable 4 with Clayton($\theta = 3$) edges, Clayton(1) in tree 2, independence in tree 3) and the vine that `Vinecop.from_data` selects from its sample. Each edge shows its family and its Kendall's $\tau$; tree-1 edges that are not in the true vine are gold. The selection replaces the star by the path 2-3-1-4 and two Clayton edges by survival Joe, yet its log-likelihood is within 12 units of the truth's.

print lists every edge, loglik and npars give what an information criterion needs, and simulate(m, out, seed=) draws new observations reproducibly.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Concepts: the theory behind h-functions, rotations, vines and the Rosenblatt transform.
  • Examples: fully explained programs, including tail dependence, weighted and discrete data, and calling the library from Python and C.
  • Pair copulas and Vine copulas in the manual; the API reference lists every argument.
  • The Python package and the R package: installation and the full list of functions of the bindings.

docs.title: User manual
docs.text: This manual explains how fortvine is organised and how its pieces fit together. The API reference lists every routine and argument; the manual is where the behaviour behind those signatures is described: which defaults are used, what the fitting code actually does, and which options interact.

docs.title: Two levels of interface
docs.text:
fortvine ships two Fortran modules:

module file what it is for fortvine_api src/fortvine_api.f90 the typed interface: derived types with type-bound procedures, Fortran-natural array layout u(n, d). This is what Fortran users should use. fortvine src/fortvine.f90 the kernels: evaluation, fitting, selection, Rosenblatt transforms, the generic family engine and the bind(C) entry points. Arrays have observations in the last dimension (u(d, n)).

Everything a Fortran program needs is re-exported by fortvine_api, including the family constants, the fit cache controls and the gen_* helpers of the generic families. The kernel module is only of direct interest if you call the library from another language (see the C interface).

docs.title: The three types
docs.text: fv_bicop One bivariate (pair) copula: a family code, a rotation, up to three parameters, the log-likelihood of the last fit and, for the two nonparametric families, an estimate vector aux. Methods evaluate the density, distribution function, both h-functions and their inverses, fit parameters for a given family, or select the family. See Pair copulas. fv_vinecop A regular vine copula in d dimensions, stored as a structure (an order vector plus a natural-order structure array) and one pair copula per edge. Methods select structure, families and parameters (Dissmann et al. 2013), and evaluate the density, the Rosenblatt transform and its inverse, and simulate. See Vine copulas. fv_controls A plain record of options shared by every fit and selection: family set, selection criterion, estimation method, tree criterion, truncation, thresholding, threads. Every field has a default, so type(fv_controls) :: ctl is a valid configuration. See Controls.

docs.title: A typical session
docs.text:
The usual sequence is: transform the data to the copula scale, select a model, then use it.

FortranPythonR workflow.f90
program workflow
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 1500, d = 4
  real(dp) :: z(n, d), x(n, d), u(n, d), sim(5, d)
  type(fv_vinecop) :: vc
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  integer :: i

  ! 1. raw data with arbitrary margins (here: a skewed, dependent toy sample)
  call random_seed(put=[(17 * i, i = 1, 33)])
  call random_number(z)
  z = -log(z)                                   ! exponential noise
  x(:, 1) = z(:, 1)
  x(:, 2) = z(:, 1) + z(:, 2)
  x(:, 3) = sqrt(x(:, 2)) + 0.5_dp * z(:, 3)
  x(:, 4) = exp(-z(:, 4)) * x(:, 1)

  ! 2. pseudo-observations: ranks / (n + 1), column by column
  call fv_pseudo_obs_nd(x, u)

  ! 3. structure, families and parameters in one call
  ctl%nthreads = 4
  call vc%select(u, ctl)
  call vc%print()

  ! 4. use the fitted model
  print '(a,f10.2,a,i0)', 'log-likelihood', vc%loglik(u), '   parameters ', vc%npars()
  call vc%simulate(5, sim, seed=1)
  print '(a,4f8.4)', 'first simulated row:', sim(1, :)
end program workflow

The raw data are random draws, so the three programs work on different samples and select slightly different vines. The Fortran program is compiled against the built library (see Installation):

gfortran -O2 -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp -I build workflow.f90 build/libfortvine.a -o workflow

Copula scale

Every routine expects data on the unit square or cube. fortvine does not model margins: use fv_pseudo_obs_nd (ranks) or your own fitted marginal distributions to map the data to \((0,1)\) first. Values are clamped internally to \([10^{-10}, 1-10^{-10}]\), so exact 0 or 1 do not crash, but they carry no information.

docs.title: Conventions used throughout
docs.text:
• Array layout (Fortran API). Data matrices are u(n, d): rows are observations, columns are variables. Pair data are two vectors u1(n), u2(n).
  • h-functions. hfunc1(u1, u2) \(= P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1) = \partial C/\partial u_1\), hfunc2(u1, u2) \(= P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2) = \partial C/\partial u_2\). Details in Pair copulas.
  • Rotations are counter-clockwise rotations of the data by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees, following vinecopulib. See Rotations and asymmetry.
  • Family codes are integers: 0 to 25 for the hand-coded families, \(\ge 10000\) for the generic engine. The constants are listed in Family codes and constants and the full list in the catalogue.
  • Variable labels in a vine are 1-based and refer to the columns of u.
  • Threads. Every heavy routine runs on OpenMP threads; the count comes from fv_controls%nthreads, an optional nthreads argument, the FORTVINE_THREADS environment variable or half the logical CPUs, in that order. See Performance.
