docs.title: Pair copulas (fv_bicop)
docs.text:
fv_bicop holds one bivariate copula \(C(u_1, u_2)\). It is the building block of every vine edge, but it is also useful on its own: to evaluate a known copula, to fit one family, or to let fortvine choose the family and rotation for a pair of variables.

FortranPythonR 
use fortvine_api
type(fv_bicop) :: cop
cop%family = FV_CLAYTON; cop%par(1) = 2.0_dp     ! a Clayton copula with theta = 2

import fortvine as fv
cop = fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [2.0])              # a Clayton copula with theta = 2

library(fortvine)
cop <- bicop_dist("clayton", 0, 2)               # a Clayton copula with theta = 2

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
field type default meaning family integer FV_INDEP (0) family code: 0 to 25 for the hand-coded families, \(\ge 10000\) for the generic engine. See the catalogue. rotation integer 0 0, 90, 180 or 270 (counter-clockwise, in degrees). Ignored by rotationless families, see Rotations. par(3) real(dp) 0 parameters; only the first npars() entries are used. The order is the one of the catalogue. loglik real(dp) 0 log-likelihood (weighted if weights were given) of the last fit or select. Not updated by evaluation methods. aux(:) real(dp), allocatable unallocated estimate of the nonparametric families FV_TLL / FV_BERNSTEIN (length NAUX = 933). Allocated by fit and select. See Nonparametric families.

The fields are public: you may set family, rotation and par directly and then evaluate. No validation happens at assignment; evaluation clips parameters to the range in which the formulas are defined (for example Gaussian \(\rho\) to \(\pm 0.999999\), Student \(\nu\) to \([2, 100]\)), so out-of-range values give the density of the nearest admissible copula rather than an error.

docs.title: Methods at a glance
docs.text:
method kind result pdf(u1, u2, out) subroutine density \(c(u_1, u_2)\) logpdf(u1, u2, out) subroutine \(\log c(u_1, u_2)\) (computed directly in log space) cdf(u1, u2, out) subroutine distribution function \(C(u_1, u_2)\) hfunc1(u1, u2, out) subroutine \(h_1 = \partial C / \partial u_1 = P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1)\) hfunc2(u1, u2, out) subroutine \(h_2 = \partial C / \partial u_2 = P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2)\) hinv1(u1, u2, out) subroutine the \(v\) with \(h_1(u_1, v) = u_2\) hinv2(u1, u2, out) subroutine the \(v\) with \(h_2(v, u_2) = u_1\) fit(u1, u2 [, ctl, weights]) subroutine maximum-likelihood (or tau-inversion) parameters for the current family and rotation select(u1, u2 [, ctl, weights]) subroutine family, rotation and parameters chosen by a criterion npars() integer function number of parameters npars_eff() real function number of parameters, or the effective degrees of freedom of a nonparametric estimate

All evaluation methods take three arrays of the same length: u1(:), u2(:) (input) and out(:) (output). Signatures with argument tables are in the API reference. The Python class Bicop has the same methods (cop.pdf(u), cop.cdf(u), cop.hfunc1(u), ... on an \(n \times 2\) array, cop.npars); in R they are dbicop(u, cop), dbicop(u, cop, log = TRUE), pbicop(u, cop), hbicop(u, 1, cop), hbicop(u, 2, cop), hbicop(u, 1, cop, inverse = TRUE), hbicop(u, 2, cop, inverse = TRUE) and cop$npars. In both bindings npars is the value of npars_eff: the effective degrees of freedom for a nonparametric estimate (see the Python and R pages).

No generic eval

The typed object has one method per quantity instead of a single eval with a selector. The selector-style routine exists in the kernel and C interface (fv_bicop_eval, with what = 0 logpdf, 1 pdf, 2 hfunc1, 3 hfunc2, 4 hinv1, 5 hinv2), see the C interface.

docs.title: Density and distribution function
docs.text:
pdf returns \(\max(e^{\log c}, \text{tiny})\), so it never returns exactly zero; logpdf returns the logarithm without that floor. The density of every family is written in log space, which keeps it finite deep in the tails and for strong dependence (see Numerics).

cdf is available for every family. It is in closed form wherever one exists: the Archimedean and extreme-value families directly, the Gaussian through a bivariate-normal integral routine, TLL as the exact integral of its bilinear interpolant, Bernstein as a sum of binomial terms. The Student copula has no closed form; its CDF is computed as \(C(u_1, u_2) = \int_0^{u_1} h_1(s, u_2)\, ds\) with 16-point Gauss-Legendre rules on 8 equal panels. Its accuracy is of the order of \(10^{-6}\) (for \(\rho = 0.7\), \(\nu = 4\) the largest deviation of \(\partial C/\partial u_1\) from \(h_1\) on a \(9 \times 9\) grid is \(2.4 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and \(C(1, 0.3) = 0.2999991\)), which is ample for probabilities but worth knowing if you difference the CDF over very small rectangles.

The copula of the example below, a Gumbel copula with $\theta = 1.8$ rotated by 180 degrees. (a) `pdf` on a grid in normal scores $z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$, with 400 draws from `hinv1`; the rotation puts the tail dependence in the lower-left corner. (b) `cdf` (blue) at the levels $0.1, \ldots, 0.9$, against the independence copula $C = u_1 u_2$ (dashed), and the three points evaluated in the example with their values.

docs.title: h-functions and their inverses
docs.text:
The two h-functions are the conditional distribution functions of one margin given the other:

\[ h_1(u_1, u_2) = \frac{\partial C(u_1,u_2)}{\partial u_1} = P(U_2 \le u_2 \mid U_1 = u_1), \qquad h_2(u_1, u_2) = \frac{\partial C(u_1,u_2)}{\partial u_2} = P(U_1 \le u_1 \mid U_2 = u_2). \]

The numeral names the conditioning argument. The inverses keep the conditioning value in the same slot as the h-function they invert:

call solves for conditioning value level hinv1(u1, w, v) \(v\) with \(h_1(u_1, v) = w\) first argument second argument hinv2(w, u2, v) \(v\) with \(h_2(v, u_2) = w\) second argument first argument

This is the vinecopulib convention, and it is what makes hinv1 a sampler: if \(U_1\) and \(W\) are independent uniforms then \((U_1, h_1^{-1}(U_1, W))\) has distribution \(C\).

Closed-form inverses are used for the Gaussian, Student, Clayton and Frank families, and a monotone Newton iteration in a transformed variable for Gumbel and Joe; other families use a bracketed Newton iteration on the exact h-function with the density as its derivative. The result is clipped to \([0, 1]\).

Round trips are exact to rounding

hfunc1(u1, hinv1(u1, w)) reproduces w to about \(10^{-14}\) for the parametric families (see the example below), which is what makes Rosenblatt transforms and simulation in a vine reliable.

(a) $h_1(u_1, u_2)$ as a function of $u_2$ for $u_1 = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9$ (lines) and the points $\big(h_1^{-1}(u_1, w), w\big)$ returned by `hinv1` for $w = 0.1, \ldots, 0.9$ (dots), for the rotated Gumbel copula of the example. (b) The same for $h_2$ as a function of $u_1$ and `hinv2`. (c) The largest error of the round trips $h_1(u_1, h_1^{-1}(u_1, w))$ and $h_2(h_2^{-1}(w, u_2), u_2)$ over a $60 \times 60$ grid of $(u, w)$ in $[0.001, 0.999]^2$, for sixteen families including the generic codes 10203 (Archimax) and 20200 (Khoudraji-Clayton): every error is below $10^{-12}$.

docs.title: Fitting a given family
docs.text:
fit estimates the parameters of the family and rotation already stored in the object:

FortranPythonR 
cop%family = FV_GUMBEL; cop%rotation = 180
call cop%fit(u1, u2)          ! cop%par, cop%loglik updated

cop = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 180).fit(u)              # cop.parameters, cop.loglik() updated

cop <- bicop(u, family_set = "gumbel", rotation = 180)   # cop$parameters, cop$loglik

What happens inside (details in Fitting and selection):

  1. The data are rotated, and Kendall's \(\tau\) of the rotated pair is computed (ctl%tau_mode; weighted \(\tau\) if weights are given).
  2. A start value and a search box are derived. For the one-parameter families Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Joe, and for the Student, the start is the \(\tau\)-inversion and the box is narrowed to the parameters of \(\tau \pm 0.1\) (as vinecopulib does). Other families start from family-specific grids inside the full box of fv_par_bounds.
  3. The maximum-likelihood estimate in that box is found with exact parameter scores (Fisher scoring with BFGS refinement; closed-form or one-dimensional Newton for the five one-parameter families). For \(n > 1800\) the search runs on a stride subsample first and is then polished on all observations.

The controls that matter for fit are method, fast_mle, tau_mode and nthreads (Python: the keyword arguments method, fast_mle, tau_mode, num_threads; R: par_method and cores).

ctl%method / ctl%fast_mle Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe Student other families FV_MLE (default) MLE MLE of \((\rho, \nu)\) MLE FV_MLE + fast_mle = .true. \(\tau\)-inversion, no optimisation MLE MLE FV_ITAU \(\tau\)-inversion \(\rho = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\), \(\nu\) by MLE not supported (see warning)

FV_ITAU with families that have no tau inversion

In select, FV_ITAU silently restricts the candidates to families 0 to 6. A direct fit of another family with ctl%method = FV_ITAU does not fall back to MLE: it evaluates the likelihood at a zero parameter vector, which is not a valid estimate. Use FV_MLE for those families.

The independence copula has nothing to fit: fit sets par = 0 and loglik = 0.

docs.title: Selecting the family
docs.text:
select tries every family of ctl%family_set(1:ctl%nfam) in every admissible rotation, fits each candidate and keeps the one with the best criterion ctl%selcrit:

FortranPythonR 
call cop%select(u1, u2)                 ! default controls: BIC over families 0..22
print *, fv_fam_name(cop%family), cop%rotation, cop%par

cop = fv.Bicop().select(u)              # default: BIC over families 0..22
print(cop.family, cop.rotation, cop.parameters)

cop <- bicop(u)                         # default: BIC over families 0..22 ("all")
cop
  • With the default allow_rotations = .true. a rotatable family is tried at 0 and 180 degrees when \(\hat\tau > 0\) and at 90 and 270 degrees when \(\hat\tau < 0\); rotationless families once.
  • With preselect = .true. (default) candidates whose tail behaviour contradicts the data are dropped before fitting, see Fitting.
  • Candidates are fitted in parallel, and slow candidates that cannot win are abandoned early (racing, see Fitting).

The criteria are log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, mBIC (with prior ctl%psi0) and mBICv; for a single pair copula FV_MBICV behaves like FV_MBIC. The formulas are in Fitting. Independence is among the default candidates, so a weakly dependent pair can legitimately come back as FV_INDEP.

What `select` compares, on the sample of the Python example ($n = 3000$ draws of the 180-degree Gumbel with $\theta = 1.8$): every family of the default set (codes 0 to 22) was fitted with `fit` at rotations 0 and 180 (rotationless families once), and the sixteen candidates with the smallest BIC are shown with their BIC and AIC distance to the best one (symmetric log scale, $k$ = number of parameters). BIC keeps the true one-parameter family, Galambos is a close second; AIC, with its smaller penalty, prefers the two-parameter BB1, as in the output of the example. The choices marked on the left are those of `select` itself.

docs.title: Number of parameters
docs.text: npars() returns 0 for independence, 1 for the one-parameter families, 2 for Student, the BB families, BB2 to BB10 and t-EV, 3 for Tawn, and gen_npar(family) (1 to 3) for the generic families. For TLL and Bernstein it returns the rounded effective degrees of freedom. npars_eff() returns the same count as a real number, with the unrounded effective degrees of freedom of a nonparametric fit (aux(2); 0 before a fit).

docs.title: Parameter bounds
docs.text:
fv_par_bounds(fam, lb, ub) returns the box in which the MLE is searched. The box of the hand-coded families:

code family lower upper 1 gaussian \(\rho \ge -1\) \(\rho \le 1\) 2 student \(\rho \ge -1\), \(\nu \ge 2\) \(\rho \le 1\), \(\nu \le 30\) 3 clayton \(\theta \ge 10^{-10}\) 28 4 gumbel 1 50 5 frank \(-35\) 35 6 joe 1 30 7 bb1 \((0, 1)\) \((7, 7)\) 8 bb6 \((1, 1)\) \((6, 8)\) 9 bb7 \((1, 0.01)\) \((6, 25)\) 10 bb8 \((1, 10^{-4})\) \((8, 1)\) 11 tawn \((0, 0, 1)\) \((1, 1, 60)\) 12 plackett \(10^{-3}\) \(10^{3}\) 13 fgm \(-1\) 1 14 amh \(-1\) 0.9999 15, 16 galambos, husler_reiss 0.01 30 17 bb2 \((0.01, 0.01)\) \((30, 30)\) 18, 19, 20 bb3, bb5, bb9 \((1, 0.01)\) \((10, 30)\) 21 bb10 \((0.01, 0)\) \((30, 1)\) 22 bb4 \((0.01, 0.01)\) \((15, 15)\) 23 tev \((-0.95, 1)\) \((0.99, 30)\)

Independence, TLL and Bernstein return lb = ub = 0. The boxes of the generic families follow from their generator and Pickands parts, see The generic engine.

These boxes bound the search; evaluation accepts parameters outside them (for example a Gumbel with \(\theta = 80\) evaluates fine), but fit will not return such values.

docs.title: Weights
docs.text: fit and select accept weights(n), one non-negative weight per observation. The log-likelihood becomes \(\sum_i w_i \log c(u_{i1}, u_{i2})\), Kendall's \(\tau\) used for starts and preselection becomes the weighted \(\tau_b\), and loglik reports the weighted sum. Weights are not normalised: doubling all of them doubles loglik. The BIC-type penalties still use the number of observations \(n\), not \(\sum_i w_i\).

docs.title: A complete example
docs.text:
FortranPythonR bicop_demo.f90
program bicop_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 3000
  type(fv_bicop) :: cop, fit, best
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u1(n), u2(n), w(n), h(n), back(n), c(3), wt(n)
  real(dp) :: a(3) = [0.2_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.8_dp], b(3) = [0.3_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp]
  integer :: i

  ! a 180-degree rotated Gumbel (lower-tail dependence), theta = 1.8
  cop%family = FV_GUMBEL; cop%rotation = 180; cop%par(1) = 1.8_dp
  call cop%pdf(a, b, c);   print '(a,3f9.4)', 'pdf    ', c
  call cop%cdf(a, b, c);   print '(a,3f9.4)', 'cdf    ', c
  call cop%hfunc1(a, b, c); print '(a,3f9.4)', 'hfunc1 ', c

  ! simulation: u2 = hinv1(u1, w) turns independent uniforms into a sample of the copula
  call random_seed(put=[(3 * i + 1, i = 1, 33)])
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w)
  call cop%hinv1(u1, w, u2)
  call cop%hfunc1(u1, u2, h); print '(a,es9.2)', 'max |hfunc1(u1, hinv1(u1, w)) - w| =', maxval(abs(h - w))
  call cop%hfunc2(u1, u2, h); call cop%hinv2(h, u2, back)
  print '(a,es9.2)', 'max |hinv2(hfunc2(u1, u2), u2) - u1| =', maxval(abs(back - u1))

  ! fit a fixed family and rotation
  fit%family = FV_GUMBEL; fit%rotation = 180
  call fit%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,f8.4,a,f10.2)', 'fit: theta =', fit%par(1), '  loglik =', fit%loglik

  ! choose family and rotation by BIC (default controls), then by AIC
  call best%select(u1, u2)
  print '(3a,i0,a,2f8.4)', 'BIC choice: ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), ' rot ', best%rotation, ' par', best%par(1:2)
  ctl%selcrit = FV_AIC
  call best%select(u1, u2, ctl)
  print '(3a,i0,a,i0)', 'AIC choice: ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), ' rot ', best%rotation, '  npars ', best%npars()

  ! observation weights: here the second half of the sample counts twice
  wt = 1.0_dp; wt(n / 2 + 1:) = 2.0_dp
  call fit%fit(u1, u2, weights=wt)
  print '(a,f8.4,a,f10.2)', 'weighted fit: theta =', fit%par(1), '  weighted loglik =', fit%loglik
end program bicop_demo
bicop_demo.py
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n = 3000
a = np.array([[0.2, 0.3], [0.5, 0.5], [0.8, 0.9]])

# a 180-degree rotated Gumbel (lower-tail dependence), theta = 1.8
cop = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 180, [1.8])
print("pdf    " + "".join(f"{x:9.4f}" for x in cop.pdf(a)))
print("cdf    " + "".join(f"{x:9.4f}" for x in cop.cdf(a)))
print("hfunc1 " + "".join(f"{x:9.4f}" for x in cop.hfunc1(a)))

# simulation: u2 = hinv1(u1, w) turns independent uniforms into a sample of the copula
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
u1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
u2 = cop.hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))
u = np.column_stack([u1, u2])
h = cop.hfunc1(u)
print(f"max |hfunc1(u1, hinv1(u1, w)) - w| ={np.max(np.abs(h - w)):9.2E}")
back = cop.hinv2(np.column_stack([cop.hfunc2(u), u2]))
print(f"max |hinv2(hfunc2(u1, u2), u2) - u1| ={np.max(np.abs(back - u1)):9.2E}")

# fit a fixed family and rotation
fit = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 180).fit(u)
print(f"fit: theta ={fit.parameters[0]:8.4f}  loglik ={fit.loglik():10.2f}")

# choose family and rotation by BIC (the default), then by AIC
best = fv.Bicop().select(u)
print(f"BIC choice: {best.family} rot {best.rotation} par" + "".join(f"{p:8.4f}" for p in best.parameters))
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, criterion="aic")
print(f"AIC choice: {best.family} rot {best.rotation}  npars {best.npars}")

# observation weights: here the second half of the sample counts twice
wt = np.ones(n); wt[n // 2:] = 2.0
fit = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 180).fit(u, weights=wt)
print(f"weighted fit: theta ={fit.parameters[0]:8.4f}  weighted loglik ={fit.loglik():10.2f}")
bicop_demo.R
library(fortvine)
n <- 3000
a <- rbind(c(0.2, 0.3), c(0.5, 0.5), c(0.8, 0.9))

# a 180-degree rotated Gumbel (lower-tail dependence), theta = 1.8
cop <- bicop_dist("gumbel", 180, 1.8)
cat("pdf    ", sprintf("%9.4f", dbicop(a, cop)), "\n", sep = "")
cat("cdf    ", sprintf("%9.4f", pbicop(a, cop)), "\n", sep = "")
cat("hfunc1 ", sprintf("%9.4f", hbicop(a, 1, cop)), "\n", sep = "")

# simulation: u2 = hinv1(u1, w) turns independent uniforms into a sample of the copula
set.seed(3)
u1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
u2 <- hbicop(cbind(u1, w), 1, cop, inverse = TRUE)
u <- cbind(u1, u2)
h <- hbicop(u, 1, cop)
cat(sprintf("max |hfunc1(u1, hinv1(u1, w)) - w| =%9.2E\n", max(abs(h - w))))
back <- hbicop(cbind(hbicop(u, 2, cop), u2), 2, cop, inverse = TRUE)
cat(sprintf("max |hinv2(hfunc2(u1, u2), u2) - u1| =%9.2E\n", max(abs(back - u1))))

# fit a fixed family and rotation
fit <- bicop(u, family_set = "gumbel", rotation = 180)
cat(sprintf("fit: theta =%8.4f  loglik =%10.2f\n", fit$parameters, fit$loglik))

# choose family and rotation by BIC (the default), then by AIC
best <- bicop(u)
cat("BIC choice: ", best$family, " rot ", best$rotation, " par", sprintf("%8.4f", best$parameters),
    "\n", sep = "")
best <- bicop(u, selcrit = "aic")
cat("AIC choice: ", best$family, " rot ", best$rotation, "  npars ", best$npars, "\n", sep = "")

# observation weights: here the second half of the sample counts twice
wt <- rep(c(1, 2), each = n / 2)
fit <- bicop(u, family_set = "gumbel", rotation = 180, weights = wt)
cat(sprintf("weighted fit: theta =%8.4f  weighted loglik =%10.2f\n", fit$parameters, fit$loglik))

Output:

The density, CDF and h-function lines are the same in every language; the rest depends on the sample, and the three languages draw different uniforms. On the Fortran sample the selected family is Galambos rather than the true Gumbel (the Python and R samples give Gumbel itself; their AIC choices are two-parameter BB families). Galambos and Gumbel are both one-parameter extreme-value copulas with upper-tail dependence (here rotated to the lower tail) and their densities are very close; with 3000 observations the likelihood slightly prefers Galambos. That is expected behaviour, not a fitting failure.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: fit and select use ctl%nthreads (see Performance). The evaluation methods take no thread argument: they use fv_threads() (the FORTVINE_THREADS variable or half the logical CPUs) and only go parallel for more than 4096 points. cdf runs on the OpenMP default team (OMP_NUM_THREADS).

docs.title: C interface
docs.text:
The kernel module fortvine exports 13 routines with bind(C) names, so the library can be called from C, C++, Python (ctypes, cffi), Julia (ccall) or R (.C / .Call) without a Fortran compiler on the caller's side. They cover pair-copula evaluation, fitting and selection, vine selection, vine density and Rosenblatt transforms, and the rank utilities.

The C interface is lower-level than the typed Fortran API: no derived types and no optional arguments. A second module, fortvine_capi (src/fortvine_capi.f90), adds C routines over the typed API for everything the 13 kernel routines leave out: observation weights, discrete margins, TLL and Bernstein, every control, non-simplified vines, pdf_grid, the fit cache and the abort flag (see The extended interface). The Python and R packages are built on both.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Linking. bash build.sh produces build/libfortvine.a and a shared library (libfortvine.so, .dylib or .dll). With the static archive, link the Fortran and OpenMP runtimes as well, e.g. gcc prog.c build/libfortvine.a -lgfortran -lquadmath -fopenmp. On Windows the DLL depends on the MinGW runtime DLLs (libgomp-1.dll, libquadmath-0.dll, libwinpthread-1.dll), which must be on the DLL search path.

Arguments. Scalars marked value are passed by value; everything else (arrays and scalar outputs) by pointer. Integers are C int, reals C double.

Array layout: observations are the last Fortran dimension. Fortran arrays are column-major, so an array declared u(2, n) in Fortran is, in C or NumPy (row-major), a contiguous n x 2 array in which the two values of one observation are adjacent. In general:

Fortran declaration C / NumPy row-major view meaning u(2, n) double u[n][2], NumPy (n, 2) pair data, one row per observation u(d, n) double u[n][d], NumPy (n, d) data matrix, one row per observation u(d, bins, nsamp) NumPy (nsamp, bins, d) grid for fv_vine_pdf st(d, d), fam(d, d), rot(d, d) = (edge, tree) NumPy (d, d) indexed [tree, edge] vine edge arrays par(3, d, d) = (k, edge, tree) NumPy (d, d, 3) indexed [tree, edge, k] vine parameters x0(3, njob) NumPy (njob, 3) per-job parameter vectors

So the usual NumPy/PyTorch data matrix of shape (n, d) can be passed as is. Column-major callers (Julia, R) pass the transpose: a d x n matrix. Indices stored in the arrays (order, st) are 1-based variable labels in natural order, exactly as in fv_vinecop; tgt of fv_vine_pdf and the dataset index ds of fv_fit_jobs are 0-based.

Control vectors. Options that the Fortran API keeps in fv_controls are passed as small integer and real arrays:

entry ci(6) (pair routines) and ci(1:6) of vine selection ci(1) selection criterion: 0 loglik, 1 AIC, 2 BIC, 3 mBIC, 4 mBICv ci(2) method: 0 MLE, 1 tau inversion ci(3) preselect: 0 / 1 ci(4) allow rotations: 0 / 1 ci(5) fast MLE: 0 / 1 ci(6) tau mode: 0 auto, 1 exact, 2 approximate entry additional entries of ci(10) for fv_vine_select ci(7) tree criterion: 0 tau, 1 rho, 2 joe, 3 Hoeffding, 4 xi, 5 MI, 6 Ferreira ci(8) tree algorithm: 0 Prim, 1 Kruskal ci(9) truncation level, \(-1\) for \(d - 1\) ci(10) 1 if a fixed structure is given in order_io / struct_in, else 0

cr(2) of fv_vine_select holds [threshold, psi0]. The defaults of fv_controls correspond to ci = [2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, -1, 0], cr = [0.0, 0.9].

docs.title: fv_version
docs.text:
int fv_version(void);

Returns the interface version, currently 1.

docs.title: fv_bicop_eval
docs.text:
void fv_bicop_eval(int fam, int rot, const double par[3], int n, const double *u,
                   int what, double *out, int nthreads);
argument description fam, rot value family code and rotation par[3] in parameters n value number of points u in, u(2, n) points what value 0 logpdf, 1 pdf, 2 hfunc1, 3 hfunc2, 4 hinv1, 5 hinv2 out out, out(n) result nthreads value threads (used for \(n > 4096\))

hinv1 returns \(v\) with \(h_1(u_1, v) = u_2\), hinv2 returns \(v\) with \(h_2(v, u_2) = u_1\), as in fv_bicop. Not usable for TLL/Bernstein (no aux argument).

docs.title: fv_bicop_pdf_hfuncs
docs.text:
void fv_bicop_pdf_hfuncs(int fam, int rot, const double par[3], int n, const double *u,
                         double *pdf, double *h1, double *h2, int nthreads);

Density and both h-functions in one pass, pdf(n), h1(n), h2(n) (cheaper than three fv_bicop_eval calls). Parametric families only.

docs.title: fv_bicop_fit
docs.text:
void fv_bicop_fit(int n, const double *u, int fam, int rot, const int ci[6],
                  double par[3], double *ll, int nthreads);

Fits family fam with rotation rot to u(2, n) as fv_bicop%fit does; returns par and the log-likelihood ll. Of ci only the method, fast-MLE and tau-mode entries matter.

docs.title: fv_bicop_select
docs.text:
void fv_bicop_select(int n, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset, const int ci[6],
                     double psi0, int *fam, int *rot, double par[3], double *ll, int nthreads);

Selects among the nf family codes in famset (all rotations allowed by ci), as fv_bicop%select. psi0 (value) is the mBIC prior. Outputs: fam, rot, par, ll.

docs.title: fv_fit_jobs
docs.text:
void fv_fit_jobs(int njob, int n, int nds, const double *u, const int *ds, const int *fam,
                 const int *rot, const int *method, const double *x0, const double *lb,
                 const double *ub, int usew, const double *w, double *par, double *ll,
                 int nthreads);

Runs njob independent fits in parallel, each on one of nds datasets of equal length n.

argument description njob, n, nds value number of jobs, observations per dataset, number of datasets u in, u(2, n, nds) the datasets (NumPy (nds, n, 2)) ds(njob) in 0-based dataset index of each job fam(njob), rot(njob) in family and rotation of each job method(njob) in 0 evaluate the log-likelihood at x0; 1 MLE within [lb, ub] starting at x0; 2 Student with \(\rho\) fixed at x0(1), \(\nu\) by MLE x0, lb, ub in, (3, njob) start (or evaluation point) and box of each job usew value 1 if w holds observation weights (shared by all datasets) w(n) in weights (ignored if usew = 0, but must be a valid pointer) par, ll out, (3, njob), (njob) estimates and log-likelihoods

This is the routine to use when you want to drive the search yourself (custom starts, boxes, profile likelihoods). Parametric families only.

docs.title: fv_vine_select
docs.text:
void fv_vine_select(int n, int d, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset,
                    const int ci[10], const double cr[2], int *order_io,
                    const int *struct_in, int *struct_out, int *fam_out, int *rot_out,
                    double *par_out, double *ll_out, int nthreads, int *info);
argument description n, d value observations, dimension u in, u(d, n) pseudo-observations (NumPy (n, d)) nf, famset(nf) value, in candidate families ci(10), cr(2) in controls, see above order_io(d) in/out with ci(10) = 1: the fixed order; on return the order of the selected vine struct_in(d, d) in with ci(10) = 1: the fixed natural-order structure array; otherwise ignored (still pass a d x d array) struct_out, fam_out, rot_out out, (d, d) structure, families, rotations, (edge, tree) par_out out, (3, d, d) parameters ll_out out, (d, d) edge log-likelihoods nthreads value threads info out 0 on success; 2, 3, 4 indicate an internal failure

The number of trees fitted is ci(9) (or \(d - 1\) for \(-1\)); pass the same value as trunc to the evaluation routines below. Rows of struct_out beyond that level are 0.

docs.title: fv_vine_pdf
docs.text:
void fv_vine_pdf(int nsamp, int bins, int d, int tgt, const double *u, const int *order,
                 int trunc, const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot, const double *par,
                 double *out, int nthreads);

Vine density on u(d, bins, nsamp) in original variable order; out(bins, nsamp). Variable tgt (0-based; \(-1\) for none) is the only one that may vary across the bins of a sample, which lets the routine evaluate the other edges once per sample (as pdf_grid). For a plain density call use bins = 1, tgt = -1.

docs.title: fv_vine_rosenblatt, fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt
docs.text:
void fv_vine_rosenblatt(int n, int d, const double *u, const int *order, int trunc,
                        const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot, const double *par,
                        double *out, int nthreads);
void fv_vine_inverse_rosenblatt(int n, int d, const double *u, const int *order, int trunc,
                                const int *st, const int *fam, const int *rot,
                                const double *par, double *out, int nthreads);

Rosenblatt transform and its inverse, u(d, n) to out(d, n), see Vine copulas. To simulate, apply the inverse to independent uniforms.

docs.title: fv_pseudo_obs
docs.text:
void fv_pseudo_obs(int n, int d, const double *x, double *out, int nthreads);

Column-wise pseudo-observations of x(d, n): average ranks (ties share the mean rank) divided by \(n + 1\).

docs.title: fv_kendall_tau, fv_tau_matrix
docs.text:
double fv_kendall_tau(int n, const double *x, const double *y);
void   fv_tau_matrix(int n, int d, const double *x, double *tm, int nthreads);

Kendall's \(\tau_b\) (tie-corrected, \(O(n \log n)\)) of two vectors, and the symmetric d x d matrix of all pairwise values for x(d, n) (diagonal 1).

docs.title: The extended interface
docs.text:
fortvine_capi passes a pair copula or a vine as its arrays and rebuilds the fv_bicop / fv_vinecop object inside each call, so the caller owns all state (the Python and R objects are plain arrays and can be saved). Each routine only converts its arguments and calls the typed API.

Controls. One integer vector ci(12) and cr(2) = [threshold, psi0] carry every field of fv_controls, together with the family set famset(nf):

entry meaning ci(1:6) as above: criterion, method, preselect, allow rotations, fast MLE, tau mode ci(7:9) as above: tree criterion, tree algorithm, truncation level (\(-1\): \(d - 1\)) ci(10) threads (0: FORTVINE_THREADS or half the CPUs) ci(11) select_trunc: truncation level chosen by mBICv ci(12) select_threshold: threshold chosen by mBICv

A vine as arrays. d, trunc, order(d), st(d, d), fam(d, d), rot(d, d), par(3, d, d), aux(naux, d, d), disc(d) (1 for a discrete variable), and the relaxed edges nrel, erel(2, *), wa(d, *), wk(nk, *), pk(3, nk, *) (each sized \(\max(\mathrm{nrel}, 1)\)). naux is fvc_naux() when an edge is TLL or Bernstein, otherwise 1; nk = fvc_nk() is the number of anchors of a relaxed edge.

int  fvc_naux(void);                         /* length of a TLL / Bernstein estimate */
int  fvc_nk(void);                           /* anchors of a relaxed edge */
void fvc_fam_name(int fam, char buf[48]);    /* blank padded */
int  fvc_families(int nmax, int *codes, int *npars);   /* all 111; npars -1 for tll, bernstein */
void fvc_par_bounds(int fam, double lb[3], double ub[3]);
void fvc_gen_flip(int *fam, double par[3]);  /* generic family of C(u2, u1) */
void fvc_set_abort(int flag);                /* fv_abort: stop a running selection */
void fvc_fitcache(int op, int capacity, int64_t *hits, int64_t *misses, int *used);
                                             /* op 0 disable, 1 enable, 2 clear, 3 stats */

void fvc_bicop_eval(int fam, int rot, const double par[3], int naux, const double *aux,
                    int n, const double *u, int what, double *out);
                    /* what 0 logpdf, 1 pdf, 2 h1, 3 h2, 4 hinv1, 5 hinv2, 6 cdf */
void fvc_bicop_fit(int n, const double *u, int usew, const double *w, int sel, int nf,
                   const int *famset, const int ci[12], const double cr[2], int *fam, int *rot,
                   double par[3], double *ll, int naux, double *aux, double *npe);

void fvc_vine_select(int n, int d, const double *u, const double *um, const int *disc,
                     int usew, const double *w, int fixed, int nf, const int *famset,
                     const int ci[12], const double cr[2], int *trunc, int *order, int *st,
                     int *fam, int *rot, double *par, double *edge_ll, int naux, double *aux,
                     double *ll, double *npe, double *thr, int *info);
void fvc_vine_eval(int d, int trunc, const int *order, const int *st, const int *fam,
                   const int *rot, const double *par, int naux, const double *aux,
                   const int *disc, int nrel, const int *erel, const double *wa,
                   const double *wk, const double *pk, int what, int n, const double *u,
                   const double *um, int seed, int nthreads, double *out);
                   /* what 0 density (out(1, :)), 1 Rosenblatt, 2 inverse, 3 simulate */
void fvc_vine_pdf_grid(/* vine arrays as in fvc_vine_eval */ ..., int nb, int n,
                       const double *ug, const double *ugm, int tgt, int nthreads, double *out);
void fvc_vine_relax(int n, int d, const double *u, int usew, const double *w, int tgt, int mode,
                    int nf, const int *famset, const int ci[12], const double cr[2],
                    int trunc, const int *order, const int *st, int *fam, int *rot, double *par,
                    double *edge_ll, int naux, double *aux, const int *disc, int nmax, int *nrel,
                    int *erel, double *wa, double *wk, double *pk, double *ll, double *npe);
void fvc_vine_rel_params(int d, int nrel, const double *wa, const double *wk, const double *pk,
                         int n, const double *uc, double *prel);   /* prel(3, nrel, n) */
void fvc_vine_structure(int kind, int d, const int *order, int trunc, int *st, int *trunc_out);
void fvc_vine_matrix(int d, const int *order, int trunc, const int *st, int *m);

fvc_bicop_fit fits the given fam/rot (sel = 0) or selects among famset (sel = 1), with weights w(n) if usew = 1; npe is the number of parameters (effective degrees of freedom for TLL and Bernstein). fvc_vine_select takes u(d, n) and, for discrete variables, um(d, n) \(= F(x^-)\); with fixed = 1 the structure in order, st, trunc is kept; info is 0, or \(-2\) if naux is too small for the family set. In fvc_vine_eval the Rosenblatt transform of a vine with discrete variables is randomised with seed (0: the conditional distribution function itself), and simulation is reproducible for seed > 0. fvc_vine_relax updates the vine in place (later trees are refitted) and writes the relaxed edges (nrel = -1 if more than nmax). tgt, mode, nb and the grid layout are those of relax and pdf_grid.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text: None: every feature of the typed API can be reached from C through fortvine_capi. The 13 kernel routines above do not take weights, discrete margins or TLL/Bernstein estimates (do not include codes 24 or 25 in their family sets); use the fvc_* routines for those. The generic families (codes \(\ge 10000\)) work through every routine.

docs.title: Example in C
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

/* prototypes of the fortvine C interface (all arrays column-major, observations last) */
int    fv_version(void);
void   fv_bicop_eval(int fam, int rot, const double par[3], int n, const double *u,
                     int what, double *out, int nthreads);
void   fv_bicop_fit(int n, const double *u, int fam, int rot, const int ci[6],
                    double par[3], double *ll, int nthreads);
void   fv_bicop_select(int n, const double *u, int nf, const int *famset, const int ci[6],
                       double psi0, int *fam, int *rot, double par[3], double *ll, int nthreads);
double fv_kendall_tau(int n, const double *x, const double *y);

int main(void) {
  enum { N = 2000 };
  double par[3] = {2.0, 0.0, 0.0}, *u = malloc(2 * N * sizeof(double));
  double *w = malloc(N * sizeof(double)), *x = malloc(N * sizeof(double)), *y = malloc(N * sizeof(double));
  srand(1);
  for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {          /* u[2*i] = first variable, u[2*i+1] = level w */
    u[2 * i] = (rand() + 0.5) / (RAND_MAX + 1.0);
    u[2 * i + 1] = (rand() + 0.5) / (RAND_MAX + 1.0);
  }
  /* simulate a Clayton(2) pair: second column = hinv1(u1, w) */
  fv_bicop_eval(3, 0, par, N, u, 4, w, 1);
  for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) { u[2 * i + 1] = w[i]; x[i] = u[2 * i]; y[i] = w[i]; }
  printf("fortvine C API version %d, tau = %.3f\n", fv_version(), fv_kendall_tau(N, x, y));

  int ci[6] = {2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1};       /* BIC, MLE, preselect, rotations, no fast_mle, exact tau */
  double p[3], ll;
  fv_bicop_fit(N, u, 3, 0, ci, p, &ll, 4);
  printf("Clayton fit: theta = %.4f, loglik = %.2f\n", p[0], ll);

  int famset[6] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, fam, rot;
  fv_bicop_select(N, u, 6, famset, ci, 0.9, &fam, &rot, p, &ll, 4);
  printf("selected family %d, rotation %d, par %.4f %.4f\n", fam, rot, p[0], p[1]);
  free(u); free(w); free(x); free(y);
  return 0;
}

gcc -O2 capi.c build/libfortvine.a -lgfortran -lquadmath -fopenmp -o capi

Output (MinGW-w64 gcc 16.1, Windows; rand() sequences differ between C libraries, so other platforms give slightly different numbers):

fortvine C API version 1, tau = 0.522
Clayton fit: theta = 2.0579, loglik = 923.65
selected family 3, rotation 0, par 2.0579 0.0000

docs.title: Example in Python (ctypes)
docs.text:
A pair copula: simulate a Gumbel sample with hinv1, select a family, evaluate the density.

import os, ctypes as ct
import numpy as np

# Windows only: make the MinGW runtime DLLs (libgomp-1.dll, ...) findable
os.add_dll_directory("C:/path/to/mingw64/bin")
lib = ct.CDLL("path/to/fortvine/build/libfortvine.dll")       # .so / .dylib elsewhere

dptr = np.ctypeslib.ndpointer(dtype=np.float64, flags="C_CONTIGUOUS")
iptr = np.ctypeslib.ndpointer(dtype=np.int32, flags="C_CONTIGUOUS")
lib.fv_bicop_eval.argtypes = [ct.c_int, ct.c_int, dptr, ct.c_int, dptr, ct.c_int, dptr, ct.c_int]
lib.fv_bicop_eval.restype = None
lib.fv_bicop_select.argtypes = [ct.c_int, dptr, ct.c_int, iptr, iptr, ct.c_double,
                                ct.POINTER(ct.c_int), ct.POINTER(ct.c_int), dptr,
                                ct.POINTER(ct.c_double), ct.c_int]
lib.fv_bicop_select.restype = None

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 2000
u = rng.uniform(size=(n, 2))           # row-major (n, 2) == Fortran u(2, n)
par = np.array([2.0, 0.0, 0.0])
v = np.empty(n)
lib.fv_bicop_eval(4, 0, par, n, u, 4, v, 1)   # Gumbel(2): v = hinv1(u1, w)
u[:, 1] = v

ci = np.array([2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1], dtype=np.int32)       # BIC, MLE, preselect, rotations, -, exact tau
famset = np.arange(0, 12, dtype=np.int32)
fam, rot, ll = ct.c_int(), ct.c_int(), ct.c_double()
p = np.zeros(3)
lib.fv_bicop_select(n, u, famset.size, famset, ci, 0.9, ct.byref(fam), ct.byref(rot), p, ct.byref(ll), 4)
print("family", fam.value, "rotation", rot.value, "par", p.round(4), "loglik", round(ll.value, 2))

dens = np.empty(n)
lib.fv_bicop_eval(fam.value, rot.value, p, n, u, 1, dens, 1)
print("mean log density", np.log(dens).mean().round(4))

Output:

family 4 rotation 0 par [1.9756 0.     0.    ] loglik 728.44
mean log density 0.3642

A vine: select on a NumPy (n, d) matrix and check that the density routine reproduces the sum of the edge log-likelihoods.

I = ct.c_int
d64, i32 = dptr, iptr
lib.fv_vine_select.argtypes = [I, I, d64, I, i32, i32, d64, i32, i32, i32, i32, i32, d64, d64, I, ct.POINTER(I)]
lib.fv_vine_pdf.argtypes = [I, I, I, I, d64, i32, I, i32, i32, i32, d64, d64, I]
lib.fv_pseudo_obs.argtypes = [I, I, d64, d64, I]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d = 1500, 4
z = rng.standard_normal((n, d)); z[:, 1] += z[:, 0]; z[:, 2] += z[:, 1]; z[:, 3] += 0.5 * z[:, 0]
u = np.empty_like(z); lib.fv_pseudo_obs(n, d, z, u, 4)
famset = np.arange(0, 12, dtype=np.int32)
ci = np.array([2, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, -1, 0], dtype=np.int32)
cr = np.array([0.0, 0.9])
order = np.zeros(d, np.int32); st_in = np.zeros((d, d), np.int32)
st, fam, rot = (np.zeros((d, d), np.int32) for _ in range(3))
par = np.zeros((d, d, 3)); ll = np.zeros((d, d)); info = I()
lib.fv_vine_select(n, d, u, famset.size, famset, ci, cr, order, st_in, st, fam, rot, par, ll, 4, ct.byref(info))
print("info", info.value, "order", order)
print("fam[tree, edge]:\n", fam)
print("sum of edge logliks", ll.sum().round(3))
dens = np.empty((n, 1))
lib.fv_vine_pdf(n, 1, d, -1, u.reshape(n, 1, d).copy(), order, d - 1, st, fam, rot, par, dens, 4)
print("sum log pdf      ", np.log(dens).sum().round(3))

Output:

info 0 order [3 2 1 4]
fam[tree, edge]:

sum of edge logliks 1465.024

The data are a Gaussian Markov tree (1-2-3 and 1-4), so the first tree has three Gaussian edges (family 1) and the higher trees are independent; row t of fam lists the edges of tree t.

docs.title: Controls (fv_controls)
docs.text:
fv_controls gathers every option of fitting and selection in one record. All fields have defaults, are public and can be set independently:

FortranPythonR 
type(fv_controls) :: ctl          ! defaults
ctl%selcrit = FV_AIC              ! change only what you need
call vc%select(u, ctl)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, criterion="aic")     # the other options keep their defaults

vc <- vinecop(u, selcrit = "aic")                 # the other options keep their defaults

The same record is accepted by fv_bicop%fit, fv_bicop%select, fv_vinecop%select and fv_vinecop%relax; each routine reads the fields that concern it (see the last column). Passing no record is the same as passing fv_controls(). The Python and R functions take the options as keyword arguments with the same defaults; the names are listed on the Python and R pages, and options without a binding are noted in the tabs below.

docs.title: Field reference
docs.text: field type default meaning used by family_set(FV_NFAM) integer [FV_ALL, FV_NONPAR, 0, ...] candidate family codes; only the first nfam entries are read select nfam integer 23 number of entries of family_set in use select selcrit integer FV_BIC selection criterion select method integer FV_MLE FV_MLE or FV_ITAU (Kendall's tau inversion) fit, select tree_crit integer FV_TREE_TAU dependence measure that weights the spanning trees vine select tree_algo integer FV_PRIM spanning-tree algorithm, FV_PRIM or FV_KRUSKAL vine select tau_mode integer FV_TAU_EXACT how Kendall's tau is computed for starts and preselection fit, select trunc_lvl integer \(-1\) last tree to fit; \(-1\) means \(d-1\) vine select nthreads integer 0 OpenMP threads; 0 means FORTVINE_THREADS or half the logical CPUs all preselect logical .true. drop candidates whose tails contradict the data before fitting select allow_rotations logical .true. try 90/180/270-degree rotations select fast_mle logical .false. one-parameter families by tau inversion only fit, select threshold real(dp) 0 edges whose tree criterion is below it become independence vine select psi0 real(dp) 0.9 prior probability of a dependent edge for mBIC / mBICv select select_trunc logical .false. choose the truncation level by mBICv vine select select_threshold logical .false. choose threshold by mBICv vine select

docs.title: Families: family_set and nfam
docs.text:
family_set has room for FV_NFAM = 192 codes. By default it holds FV_ALL (codes 0 to 23, every hand-coded parametric family) followed by FV_NONPAR (24 TLL, 25 Bernstein), and nfam = 23 uses the first 23 entries: codes 0 to 22, every parametric family except t-EV, whose fit is the slowest. The two most common changes need only nfam:

FortranPythonR 
ctl%nfam = size(FV_ALL)         ! 24: add t-EV (code 23)
ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC          ! 26: also TLL and Bernstein

best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=list(range(24)))     # codes 0..23: add t-EV
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set="all")               # codes 0..25: also TLL and Bernstein

best <- bicop(u, family_set = 0:23)                         # codes 0..23: add t-EV
best <- bicop(u, family_set = 0:25)                         # codes 0..25: also TLL and Bernstein

Any other set is written explicitly:

FortranPythonR 
ctl%family_set(1:5) = [FV_INDEP, FV_GAUSSIAN, FV_CLAYTON, FV_GUMBEL, FV_FRANK]
ctl%nfam = 5

ctl%nfam = size(FV_PARAMETRIC)  ! vinecopulib's parametric set (codes 0..11)
ctl%family_set(1:ctl%nfam) = FV_PARAMETRIC

fs = ["indep", "gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank"]   # names or codes

fs = list(range(12))            # vinecopulib's parametric set (codes 0..11)
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=fs)

fs <- c("indep", "gaussian", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank")  # names or codes

fs <- "parametric"              # vinecopulib's parametric set (codes 0..11)
best <- bicop(u, family_set = fs)

Adding the generic families:

FortranPythonR 
integer, allocatable :: gen(:)
gen = fv_generic_families()                       ! 85 codes
ctl%family_set(1:24) = FV_ALL
ctl%family_set(25:24 + size(gen)) = gen
ctl%nfam = 24 + size(gen)                         ! 109 candidates

gen = [f.code for f in fv.families() if f.code >= 10000]     # 85 codes
fs = list(range(24)) + gen                                  # 109 candidates
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set=fs)

fs <- list(0:23, "generic")                       # "generic": the 85 generic codes; 109 candidates
best <- bicop(u, family_set = fs)

Leave out FV_INDEP (0) if an edge must never be independence. The independence copula costs nothing to "fit" and is the natural fallback for weak dependence, so keeping it is recommended.

docs.title: selcrit
docs.text:
constant value criterion FV_LOGLIK 0 log-likelihood (no penalty) FV_AIC 1 Akaike FV_BIC 2 Bayesian (Schwarz) FV_MBIC 3 modified BIC with prior psi0 on dependence FV_MBICV 4 mBIC with prior psi0**t in tree t (vines); for a single pair as FV_MBIC

The formulas are in Fitting. For nonparametric families the penalties use the effective degrees of freedom.

The five criteria on one sample ($n = 1000$) of a 10-dimensional D-vine whose Kendall's $\tau$ fades with the tree (0.5 in tree 1, 0.25, 0.12, 0.06, then 0.03; Clayton, Gumbel and Gaussian pairs, 45 parameters). (a) Non-independence edges kept per tree (the grey band is the number of edges in the tree; the markers are shifted sideways to stay visible). The log-likelihood criterion keeps almost every edge; AIC and mBIC drop part of the weak trees; BIC and mBICv keep the strong low trees and little else. (b) The price and gain: log-likelihood on the sample against the number of parameters of each selected vine, and of the true vine. BIC and mBICv select the same vine here.

docs.title: method and fast_mle
docs.text: FV_MLE (0) maximises the likelihood. FV_ITAU (1) sets parameters from Kendall's tau and is restricted to families 0 to 6 in selection. fast_mle = .true. with FV_MLE uses tau inversion for the one-parameter families Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Joe only. See Kendall's tau inversion.

docs.title: tree_crit
docs.text:
The tree criterion is the edge weight of the maximum spanning trees in vine selection. Each is returned in absolute value; with 10 or fewer observations every criterion is 0.

constant value measure weighted FV_TREE_TAU 0 Kendall's \(\tau_b\) yes FV_TREE_RHO 1 Spearman's \(\rho\) (Pearson correlation of the ranks) yes FV_TREE_JOE 2 \(-\tfrac12\log(1 - r^2)\), \(r\) the Pearson correlation of the normal scores (Gaussian mutual information) yes FV_TREE_HOEFFD 3 Hoeffding's \(D\) on the empirical copula binned to \(\min(128, \max(32, \sqrt n))\) cells per axis no FV_TREE_XI 4 Chatterjee's \(\xi\), symmetrised as the larger of the two directions (Chatterjee 2021) no FV_TREE_MI 5 mutual information, Kraskov-Stögbauer-Grassberger estimator with \(k = 3\) (Kraskov et al. 2004) no FV_TREE_FERREIRA 6 Ferreira's tail-dependence coefficient, largest of the four corners (Ferreira 2013) no

"Weighted" means that observation weights passed to select enter the criterion; the unweighted measures ignore them. Kendall's tau is the default because it is invariant, robust and matches the rank-based start values. The non-monotone measures (Hoeffding, \(\xi\), mutual information) also detect dependence that is not concordance, at the cost of a spanning tree that may place weak-\(\tau\) pairs early. The same measures are available directly through fv_dependence.

A five-dimensional sample ($n = 2000$) whose variables 1 and 2 are strongly but not monotonically dependent (an equal mixture of Clayton and 90-degree Clayton, so $\hat\tau \approx 0$), while a weak monotone link joins variables 4 and 5. (a) The pair (1, 2) in normal scores. (b) Log-likelihood of the vine selected with each `tree_crit`, relative to the best: on this sample only mutual information puts the edge (1, 2) into tree 1 (green), and its vine is about 220 log-likelihood units better; the concordance measures link the two groups through the weak monotone pair instead, and so do Hoeffding's $D$, $\xi$ and Ferreira's coefficient. (c) Selection time with 8 threads: the criterion itself costs little next to the pair fits.

docs.title: tree_algo
docs.text: FV_PRIM (0) and FV_KRUSKAL (1) both return a maximum spanning tree, so they give the same tree unless several candidate edges have exactly equal weights; both break such ties deterministically.

docs.title: tau_mode
docs.text:
constant value tau used for starts and preselection FV_TAU_AUTO 0 exact below 800 observations, normal-score approximation above FV_TAU_EXACT 1 exact \(\tau_b\), \(O(n \log n)\) FV_TAU_APPROX 2 \(\tfrac2\pi\arcsin(r)\) of the normal-score correlation \(r\)

It does not affect the tree criterion FV_TREE_TAU, which is always exact.

docs.title: trunc_lvl, select_trunc
docs.text: trunc_lvl = k (with \(1 \le k \le d-1\)) fits only the first k trees; 0 fits none (an independence copula). select_trunc = .true. stops earlier if a tree does not improve the mBICv, see Truncation. The level reached is stored in vc%trunc.

docs.title: threshold, select_threshold, psi0
docs.text:
threshold in \([0, 1]\) sets edges with a weak tree criterion to independence (sparse vines, Nagler et al. 2019). select_threshold = .true. searches the threshold by mBICv, see Thresholding. psi0 in \((0, 1)\) is the prior probability of a non-independence edge in mBIC; a smaller value favours sparser models.

The sample of the previous figure, selected with the default BIC and a fixed (a) `trunc_lvl` from 1 to 9 or (b) `threshold` from 0 to 0.3: log-likelihood $\ell$ (blue) and $-\text{BIC}/2$ (green), with the number of parameters at a few points (grey). The dashed lines are the values chosen by `select_trunc_lvl=True` and by `select_threshold=True` with `criterion="mbicv"` (Python names of `select_trunc` and `select_threshold`). Beyond tree 4 the trees add almost nothing. Raising the threshold removes edges in the order of their $|\hat\tau|$: the weak edges of the high trees cost nothing, those of tree 3 ($\tau = 0.12$) go between 0.08 and 0.16 and those of tree 2 ($\tau = 0.25$) between 0.22 and 0.28, each step with a visible loss.

docs.title: preselect, allow_rotations
docs.text:
preselect filters rotations by tail asymmetry before fitting, see Preselection. Turning it off tries every rotation compatible with the sign of \(\tau\) and slows selection down moderately.

allow_rotations = .false. uses only rotation 0. Rotatable families (Clayton, Gumbel, Joe, the BB families, the extreme-value families, generic families) then model positive dependence only, and are skipped entirely on pairs with \(\tau \le 0\); negatively dependent pairs can then only be captured by the rotationless families (Gaussian, Student, Frank, Plackett, FGM, AMH). See Rotations.

docs.title: nthreads
docs.text: nthreads > 0 uses that many OpenMP threads for the call. 0 defers to fv_threads(): the FORTVINE_THREADS environment variable if it is a positive integer, otherwise half the logical CPUs reported by OpenMP. See Performance.

docs.title: Recipes
docs.text:
Fast exploratory fitSparse high-dimensional vineLike vinecopulib's defaultsEverything FortranPythonR 
ctl%family_set(1:6) = [FV_INDEP, FV_GAUSSIAN, FV_STUDENT, FV_CLAYTON, FV_GUMBEL, FV_FRANK]
ctl%nfam = 6
ctl%trunc_lvl = 3            ! three trees are often enough to see the main structure

fs = ["indep", "gaussian", "student", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank"]
# three trees are often enough to see the main structure
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, family_set=fs, trunc_lvl=3)

fs <- c("indep", "gaussian", "student", "clayton", "gumbel", "frank")
# three trees are often enough to see the main structure
vc <- vinecop(u, family_set = fs, trunc_lvl = 3)
FortranPythonR 
ctl%selcrit = FV_MBICV
ctl%select_trunc = .true.
ctl%select_threshold = .true.

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, criterion="mbicv", select_trunc_lvl=True, select_threshold=True)

vc <- vinecop(u, selcrit = "mbicv", trunc_lvl = NA, threshold = NA)
FortranPythonR 
ctl%nfam = size(FV_PARAMETRIC)
ctl%family_set(1:ctl%nfam) = FV_PARAMETRIC
ctl%selcrit = FV_BIC

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, family_set=list(range(12)), criterion="bic")

vc <- vinecop(u, family_set = "parametric", selcrit = "bic")
FortranPythonR 
integer, allocatable :: gen(:)
gen = fv_generic_families()
ctl%family_set(1:FV_NCLASSIC) = [FV_ALL, FV_NONPAR]
ctl%family_set(FV_NCLASSIC + 1:FV_NCLASSIC + size(gen)) = gen
ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC + size(gen)            ! 111 candidate families

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, family_set=["all", "generic"])   # 111 candidate families

vc <- vinecop(u, family_set = list(0:25, "generic"))   # 111 candidate families

Tip

A fv_controls value can be reset with ctl = fv_controls(), which restores every default.

docs.title: Discrete and mixed data
docs.text: Counts, ordinal scores, rounded measurements and zero-inflated variables have marginal distributions with jumps. A copula still links such margins (Sklar's theorem holds), but the probability integral transform \(F(X)\) is no longer uniform, and the likelihood of an observation is a probability mass rather than a density. fortvine handles this with the convention of vinecopulib's var_types = "d" (Panagiotelis, Czado & Joe 2012; Panagiotelis, Czado, Joe & Stöber 2017): each discrete variable is described by two numbers per observation.

docs.title: Input: u and u_minus
docs.text:
For a discrete variable \(X_j\) with distribution function \(F_j\):

\[ u_{ij} = F_j(x_{ij}), \qquad u^-_{ij} = F_j(x_{ij}^-) = P(X_j < x_{ij}), \]

so that \(u_{ij} - u^-_{ij} = P(X_j = x_{ij})\). For integer data \(F_j(x^-) = F_j(x - 1)\). Pass

  • u(n, d): \(F(x)\) for every column (continuous columns as usual),
  • u_minus(n, d): \(F(x^-)\) for the discrete columns; entries of continuous columns are not read (copying u there is fine),
  • discrete(d): .true. for the discrete columns.

The Python and R packages follow vinecopulib instead: var_types gives "c" or "d" per variable, and with \(k\) discrete variables the data have \(d + k\) columns, \(F(x)\) of every variable followed by \(F(x^-)\) of the discrete ones, in their order.

FortranPythonR 
call vc%select(u, ctl, discrete=[.false., .false., .true.], u_minus=um)
ll = vc%loglik(u, u_minus=um)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, var_types=["c", "c", "d"])   # F(x) of every variable, then F(x-) of variable 3
ll = vc.loglik(u)

vc <- vinecop(u, var_types = c("c", "c", "d"))             # F(x) of every variable, then F(x-) of variable 3
ll <- sum(log(dvinecop(u, vc)))

\(F_j\) can be a fitted parametric margin or the empirical distribution function; with the latter, using the denominator \(n + 1\) (as fv_pseudo_obs_nd does for continuous columns) keeps \(u < 1\).

The discreteness flags are stored in vc%disc. Every evaluation of a vine with any discrete variable then requires u_minus (pdf, loglik, rosenblatt) or ugm (pdf_grid). fv_bicop methods have no u_minus argument; to fit or select a single pair with discrete margins, use a two-dimensional fv_vinecop.

docs.title: The likelihood of a pair
docs.text:
Let \(a, b\) be the two (conditional) margins of an edge, with \(a^-, b^-\) their left limits. The pair-copula likelihood used by fortvine is the joint probability divided by the product of the marginal masses, so that it is a density with respect to the product of the margins and directly comparable between candidates:

margins of the observation contribution both continuous \(c(a, b)\) \(a\) discrete, \(b\) continuous \(\dfrac{h_2(a, b) - h_2(a^-, b)}{a - a^-}\) \(a\) continuous, \(b\) discrete \(\dfrac{h_1(a, b) - h_1(a, b^-)}{b - b^-}\) both discrete \(\dfrac{C(a,b) - C(a^-,b) - C(a,b^-) + C(a^-,b^-)}{(a - a^-)(b - b^-)}\)

A variable declared discrete whose observation has \(a - a^- \le 10^{-12}\) is treated as continuous for that observation, so mixed (partly continuous, partly atomic) margins such as zero-inflated data are handled row by row.

docs.title: Conditional margins in higher trees
docs.text:
The next tree needs \(F(b \mid a)\) and its left limit. If the conditioning variable \(a\) is discrete, the conditional distribution averages over its jump:

\[ F(b \mid a) = \frac{C(a, b) - C(a^-, b)}{a - a^-} = \frac{1}{a - a^-}\int_{a^-}^{a} h_1(s, b)\, ds . \]

fortvine computes this from the closed-form CDF when the jump is at least \(10^{-3}\) and the family has one, and by Gauss-Legendre quadrature of the h-function otherwise (the Student copula always uses quadrature). Both \(F(b \mid a)\) and \(F(b^- \mid a)\) are propagated, and a conditional margin is discrete exactly when the variable it describes is.

docs.title: Fitting with discrete margins
docs.text:
• Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe: the exact discrete likelihood with its score and curvature in closed form, maximised by Newton's method (as on continuous data).
  • Other one-parameter families: Brent's method on the exact discrete likelihood.
  • Multi-parameter families: the start grid followed by Nelder-Mead in logit coordinates on the exact discrete likelihood (value only: no dual-number scores on this path). The two-stage subsample scheme applies for \(n > 1800\).
  • TLL, Bernstein: the estimate is computed from the mid-points \(\big(F(x) + F(x^-)\big)/2\) of the discrete margins, and its log-likelihood is then evaluated with the discrete formulas above.

Discrete fits are slower than continuous ones, mainly because the multi-parameter families lose the exact scores and because every observation needs two to four copula evaluations. The generic-family pre-screen is skipped on discrete edges, and relax is not available for vines with discrete variables.

docs.title: Rosenblatt transform
docs.text:
For a discrete variable the conditional distribution function \(F(x_k \mid \cdot)\) evaluated at the data is not uniform. rosenblatt therefore returns, by default, Brockwell's (2007) randomised transform for the discrete columns,

\[ w_{ik} = W_{ik}\, F(x_{ik} \mid \dots) + (1 - W_{ik})\, F(x_{ik}^- \mid \dots), \]

with independent uniforms \(W_{ik}\); under the model the \(w_{ik}\) are iid uniform, so the usual goodness-of-fit diagnostics apply. Continuous columns are transformed as usual.

FortranPythonR 
call vc%rosenblatt(u, w, u_minus=um)                          ! randomised, seed 1
call vc%rosenblatt(u, w, u_minus=um, seed=7)                  ! another randomisation
call vc%rosenblatt(u, w, u_minus=um, randomize=.false., out_minus=wm)   ! F(x|.), F(x-|.)

w = vc.rosenblatt(u)                                        # randomised, seed 1
w = vc.rosenblatt(u, seed=7)                                # another randomisation
w = vc.rosenblatt(u, randomize_discrete=False)              # F(x|.)

w <- rosenblatt(u, vc)                                      # randomised; the seed follows set.seed()
w <- rosenblatt(u, vc, randomize_discrete = FALSE)          # F(x|.)

The uniforms come from a counter-based hash of (seed, row, column), so the result is reproducible and independent of the number of threads and of the Fortran random generator. randomize = .false. returns \(F(x_k \mid \dots)\) itself, and out_minus(n, d) (optional) receives \(F(x_k^- \mid \dots)\).

The Rosenblatt transform of the [example](#example) below (a latent Gaussian D-vine whose third variable is a count with four levels), computed with the Python package (`rosenblatt(u, seed=3)`). (a) The discrete column: randomised (blue) it is uniform; without randomisation (`randomize_discrete=False`, gold) it keeps the four atoms of the count. Variable 3 is `order(d)` here, so its non-randomised value is $F(x_3)$ itself. (b) Empirical distribution functions of the three randomised columns, on the diagonal of the uniform distribution, with their means and variances ($1/2$ and $1/12 \approx 0.0833$ expected). (c) Columns 1 and 3 in normal scores: no dependence is left.

Simulation

inverse_rosenblatt and simulate do not use the discreteness flags: they return a sample \(U\) of the copula on the continuous scale. Discrete observations are obtained by applying the marginal quantile functions, \(x_j = F_j^{-1}(u_j)\), which is the standard latent-variable construction.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
A latent Gaussian D-vine whose third variable is observed only as a count with four levels:

FortranPythonR discrete_demo.f90
program discrete_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 2000, d = 3
  type(fv_vinecop) :: gen, vc
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: v(n, d), u(n, d), um(n, d), r(n, d)
  integer :: k(n), j, i

  ! latent Gaussian-copula sample; variable 3 is then made a count with 4 levels
  call gen%set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
  gen%fam(1:2, 1) = FV_GAUSSIAN; gen%par(1, 1:2, 1) = 0.7_dp
  call gen%simulate(n, v, seed=2)
  k = min(int(4.0_dp * v(:, 3)**1.5_dp), 3)            ! counts 0..3

  ! continuous columns: u_minus = u (not used); discrete column: empirical F(x) and F(x-)
  u = v; um = v
  do i = 1, n
    u(i, 3) = count(k <= k(i)) / (n + 1.0_dp)
    um(i, 3) = count(k < k(i)) / (n + 1.0_dp)
  end do

  ctl%nthreads = 4
  call vc%select(u, ctl, discrete=[.false., .false., .true.], u_minus=um)
  call vc%print()
  print '(a,f10.2)', 'discrete log-likelihood:', vc%loglik(u, u_minus=um)

  ! randomised (Brockwell) Rosenblatt transform: iid uniform under the model
  call vc%rosenblatt(u, r, u_minus=um, seed=3)
  do j = 1, d
    print '(a,i0,a,f7.4,a,f7.4)', 'column ', j, ': mean', sum(r(:, j)) / n, &
      '  variance', sum((r(:, j) - 0.5_dp)**2) / n
  end do
  print '(a,f8.4)', 'tau(r1, r3):', fv_kendall_tau(r(:, 1), r(:, 3))
end program discrete_demo
discrete_demo.py
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n, d = 2000, 3

# latent Gaussian-copula sample; variable 3 is then made a count with 4 levels
gen = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3])
for e in range(2):
    gen.set_pair_copula(0, e, fv.Bicop("gaussian", 0, [0.7]))
v = gen.simulate(n, seed=2)
k = np.minimum((4.0 * v[:, 2] ** 1.5).astype(int), 3)       # counts 0..3

# F(x) of every variable (empirical for the count), then F(x-) of the discrete one: d + 1 columns
ks = np.sort(k)
fx = np.searchsorted(ks, k, side="right") / (n + 1.0)
fxm = np.searchsorted(ks, k, side="left") / (n + 1.0)
u = np.column_stack([v[:, 0], v[:, 1], fx, fxm])

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, var_types=["c", "c", "d"], num_threads=4)
print(vc)
print(f"discrete log-likelihood:{vc.loglik(u):10.2f}")

# randomised (Brockwell) Rosenblatt transform: iid uniform under the model
r = vc.rosenblatt(u, seed=3)
for j in range(d):
    print(f"column {j + 1}: mean{r[:, j].mean():7.4f}  variance{np.mean((r[:, j] - 0.5) ** 2):7.4f}")
print(f"tau(r1, r3):{fv.kendall_tau(r[:, 0], r[:, 2]):8.4f}")
discrete_demo.R
library(fortvine)
n <- 2000; d <- 3

# latent Gaussian-copula sample; variable 3 is then made a count with 4 levels
gen <- vinecop_dist(list(rep(list(bicop_dist("gaussian", 0, 0.7)), 2), list(bicop_dist("indep"))),
                    dvine_structure(1:3))
set.seed(2)
v <- rvinecop(n, gen)
k <- pmin(floor(4 * v[, 3]^1.5), 3)                    # counts 0..3

# F(x) of every variable (empirical for the count), then F(x-) of the discrete one: d + 1 columns
Fk <- ecdf(k)
u <- cbind(v[, 1:2], Fk(k) * n / (n + 1), Fk(k - 1) * n / (n + 1))

vc <- vinecop(u, var_types = c("c", "c", "d"), cores = 4)
print(vc)
cat(sprintf("discrete log-likelihood:%10.2f\n", sum(log(dvinecop(u, vc)))))

# randomised (Brockwell) Rosenblatt transform: iid uniform under the model
set.seed(3)
r <- rosenblatt(u, vc)
for (j in 1:d)
  cat(sprintf("column %d: mean%7.4f  variance%7.4f\n", j, mean(r[, j]), mean((r[, j] - 0.5)^2)))
cat(sprintf("tau(r1, r3):%8.4f\n", cor(r[, 1], r[, 3], method = "kendall")))
