Treating the count as continuous instead (its mid-ranks \((u + u^-)/2\) passed as ordinary pseudo-observations) gives 0.679 for the second parameter on the same (Fortran) data: the ties attenuate the dependence estimate, and the effect grows as the number of distinct values shrinks.

(a) What a discrete column contributes: each observation of a count with four equiprobable levels is the interval $[u^-, u] = [F(x^-), F(x)]$ (blue), not a point; the mid-rank (gold) is the naive point summary. (b) A Gaussian copula with $\rho = 0.7$ whose second variable is cut into $K$ equiprobable levels, $n = 1000$, 30 samples per $K$ (mean and 10-90 % band): the discrete likelihood (a two-dimensional vine with `var_types=["c", "d"]`) is unbiased for every $K$, the mid-ranks fitted as continuous data underestimate $\rho$ (0.62 at two levels, 0.68 at four) until the count has about ten distinct values.

docs.title: Fitting and selection
docs.text: This page describes what happens when fortvine fits a pair copula, how it chooses among candidate families, and which shortcuts keep vine selection fast without changing its result. The knobs are fields of fv_controls; the code lives in src/fortvine.f90 (fit_one_raw, newton_fit, edge_cands, vine_select_x).

docs.title: The life of one candidate
docs.text:
Every candidate (family, rotation) for a pair goes through the same steps:

  1. Rotate the data so that the unrotated family can be used, and compute Kendall's \(\tau\) of the rotated pair.
  2. Specify the fit: method (MLE, evaluation at the \(\tau\)-inversion, nonparametric estimate), start value and parameter box.
  3. Optimise the log-likelihood in the box.
  4. Score the result with the selection criterion.

Steps 3 and 4 dominate the cost; most of this page is about doing them with as few passes over the data as possible.

docs.title: Start values and search boxes
docs.text:
family start box Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe \(\tau\)-inversion of the winsorised \(\tau\) (\(0.01 \le \lvert\tau\rvert \le 0.9\)) parameters of \(\tau \pm 0.1\), intersected with the full box Student \(\rho = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\) \(\rho\) from \(\tau \pm 0.1\); \(\nu \in [2.01, 30]\) BB1, BB6, BB7, BB8 lower bounds + 0.1, then a \(3^k\) grid full box Tawn \((0.5, 0.5, 1 + 6\lvert\tau\rvert)\) \([0.3, 1] \times [0.3, 1] \times [1.5, 7]\) Plackett ... t-EV (12-23) centre of the box, then a family-specific grid full box generic (\(\ge 10000\)) grid ranked by Blomqvist's \(\beta\) full box

The narrowed boxes of the one-parameter families, the Student and Tawn reproduce vinecopulib's adjust_parameters_bounds; they make the optimisation cheap and are almost never binding because the MLE of these families is close to the \(\tau\)-inversion. The full boxes are listed in Pair copulas.

The likelihood the optimiser climbs. (a) $\ell(\theta) - \ell(\hat\theta)$ of a Gumbel copula on 500 draws with $\theta = 1.6$ (each point a `loglik` call), the narrowed box of the parameters with Kendall's $\tau$ in $\hat\tau \pm 0.1$ (shaded), the MLE of `fit` and the $\tau$-inversion of `fit(method="itau")`, which is a fraction of a log-likelihood unit lower. (b) $\ell(\theta, \delta) - \ell_{\max}$ of BB1 on 1000 draws with $(\theta, \delta) = (0.6, 1.4)$: a tilted ridge, along which the BHHH curvature and the BFGS polish find the maximum returned by `fit` (gold).

docs.title: One-parameter families in closed form
docs.text:
For the Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Joe families on continuous margins fortvine writes the log-density, its first two derivatives in the parameter, both h-functions and the CDF in closed form. One pass over the data then gives log-likelihood, score and curvature.

  • Gaussian. The score equation is a cubic in \(\rho\), \(W\rho^3 - B\rho^2 + (A - W)\rho - B = 0\) with \(W = \sum w_i\), \(A = \sum w_i (x_i^2 + y_i^2)\), \(B = \sum w_i x_i y_i\) of the normal scores; its real roots in the box (and the box ends) are compared, so the MLE is exact.
  • Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe. Newton's method from the \(\tau\)-inversion. Because that start is already \(\sqrt{n}\)-consistent, the first step is Le Cam's one-step estimator and the iteration usually stops after two passes, when the quadratic model predicts a remaining gain below \(10^{-6}\) log-likelihood units. Steps that lower the likelihood are halved.

The same closed forms are used for pairs with discrete margins (see Discrete data).

docs.title: Multi-parameter families: Fisher scoring with exact scores
docs.text:
All other parametric families are fitted by a projected Newton-type method on the log-likelihood \(\ell( heta) = \sum_i w_i \log c(u_{i1}, u_{i2}; heta)\):

  • Exact scores. \(\partial \log c / \partial heta\) is obtained by evaluating the log-density in forward-mode dual numbers (src/fortvine_ad.f90): the family formulas are compiled once for real numbers and once for duals with 1, 2 or 3 derivative slots, so the scores are exact to rounding, with no finite differences. See Exact parameter scores.
  • Curvature. The BHHH approximation \(-\sum_i w_i\, s_i s_i^ op\) (outer product of the per-observation scores \(s_i\)) replaces the Hessian. It is positive definite near the optimum and costs nothing beyond the scores.
  • Steps. A Levenberg-Marquardt damping factor is raised when a trial step lowers the likelihood (by interpolating the step length at which the quadratic model peaks) and lowered after each accepted step. Parameters at an active bound with the score pointing outwards are frozen for that step.
  • Ridges. Where BHHH alone would zig-zag (t-EV's \(( ho, \log u)\) ridge, and the final polish of every family), the curvature model is updated by BFGS from the exact score changes. A step sequence that shrinks geometrically in one direction is extrapolated to its limit (Aitken), kept only if it improves the likelihood.
  • Scale. For BB8, Husler-Reiss, BB2, BB9 and BB10, a positive parameter whose box spans at least two decades is optimised as \(\log heta\).
  • Stopping. The iteration ends when the predicted gain \( frac12 g^ op s\) and the actual change are both below a relative tolerance (\(10^{-8}\) for the final fit), or when the step no longer moves the parameters.

The Student copula is handled separately: for fixed \( u\) the score in \( ho\) is analytic and solved by Newton's method, and \( u\) is found by Brent's one-dimensional minimisation of the profile likelihood. t-EV starts with a Brent profile in \(\log u\) and finishes with a joint Newton fit in \(( ho, \log u)\) using the exact \( u\)-score of the \(t\) distribution function.

If Newton's method cannot start at all (a non-finite likelihood at every start), a Nelder-Mead search in logit-transformed box coordinates is used as a fallback.

docs.title: Two-stage fitting for large samples
docs.text:
For \(n > 1800\) every multi-parameter fit runs in two stages:

  1. Search on a subsample. A deterministic stride subsample of about 600 observations (every \(\lfloor n/600 \rfloor\)-th row) is used for the start grid and for Newton iterations with a loose tolerance (\(10^{-4}\)).
  2. Polish on all data. Starting from the subsample optimum, the full-data Newton iteration with the normal stopping rule takes typically one to three passes.

The stopping rule of stage 2 is the full-data one, so the result is still the full-data MLE; the subsample only provides a good start.

(a) Accuracy: root mean square error of $\hat\theta$ over 200 samples per $n$ (true $\theta = 2$) for the MLE and the $\tau$-inversion (`method="itau"`). Both decrease like $n^{-1/2}$; the MLE is the more efficient estimator, by a factor of about 1.5 in RMSE for Clayton. (b) Cost: wall-clock time of one `fit` (one thread, best of five) on the first $n$ rows of a BB1 sample. The closed-form one-parameter fits and the inversion are linear in $n$; the multi-parameter fits of BB1 and Tawn become *cheaper* when $n$ crosses 1800, where the two-stage scheme starts (shaded): the start grid and most Newton steps then run on the 600-row subsample.

docs.title: Multi-start grids
docs.text:
Some likelihoods are multimodal or have long ridges (BB5 can drift towards its Gumbel limit, BB9 has a ridge in \(\delta\)). For BB5, BB9 and all generic families, Newton's method is started from the three best points of the start grid; distinct optima (relative distance above 5 %) are kept, and every optimum within 2 log-likelihood units of the best one on the subsample is polished on all data. Other families use a single start, which reproduces vinecopulib's optima.

The grids are value-only likelihood evaluations:

  • BB1, BB6, BB7, BB8: \(3^k\) points at logistic positions \(-2, 0, 2\) of the box;
  • Plackett ... t-EV: a short hand-chosen list per parameter (log-spaced for scale parameters);
  • generic families: four values per parameter (\(4^k\) points), log-spaced in wide positive boxes and linear in unit boxes. The points are ranked by the distance of their Blomqvist \(\beta = 4C(\tfrac12,\tfrac12) - 1\) to the empirical \(\beta\) (one closed-form \(C\) value per point, no likelihood pass), and only the three closest are scored by the likelihood.

docs.title: Preselection by tail asymmetry
docs.text:
With ctl%preselect = .true. (default), candidates are filtered before any fit, following vinecopulib's preselect_family. On the normal scores \(z_1, z_2\) of the pair two correlations are computed: \(c_1\) among the points in the upper-right quadrant and \(c_2\) among those in the lower-left quadrant (for \(\tau < 0\): upper-left and lower-right). Then:

  • Frank is dropped if \(\lvert c_1 - c_2\rvert > 0.3\) (strong tail asymmetry);
  • if \(c_1 - c_2 > 0.05\) (more dependence in the upper corner), a rotatable family is kept only in the rotations that put its tail dependence there;
  • if \(c_1 - c_2 < -0.05\), symmetrically for the lower corner;
  • otherwise every rotation matching the sign of \(\tau\) is kept.

The BB families and the generic families are always kept in the rotations matching the sign of \(\tau\). Which families count as "lower tail" or "upper tail" is fixed per hand-coded family; for the generic engine it is derived from the code (gen_lt, gen_ut).

docs.title: Racing: screen, then polish
docs.text:
Selecting among many candidates spends most of its time polishing candidates that will lose. fortvine therefore races them:

  1. Cheap first. In vine selection, the closed-form and one-parameter fits of every edge are scheduled first, so each edge has a best score within milliseconds; the remaining jobs are scheduled longest-first.
  2. Screen. A two-stage fit stops at its subsample optimum and computes the exact full-data log-likelihood \(\ell_s\) there, together with an upper bound for what the polish could still gain: \(\ell_s + \max(10 d,\; d + 0.08\lvert\ell_s\rvert + 5)\), where \(d\) is the Fisher-scoring predicted gain of one full step (for the Student \(\ell_s + 0.15\lvert\ell_s\rvert + 5\)).
  3. Polish or discard. The candidate is polished only if the criterion value of its bound can still beat the best score achieved so far on that edge. During the polish, the bound is re-evaluated each step, and the fit gives up as soon as it can no longer reach the target.

The bounds are empirical. The screen bound was calibrated on 23 true families \(\times\) 25 candidates \(\times\) both rotations at \(n = 5000\), where no polish gained within 11 log-likelihood units of it; the give-up bound of the polish on about 2300 traced polishes with \(n\) between 1500 and 30000. Since the best score only increases and never exceeds the final best, the selected candidate is always polished to the end; as long as the bound holds, the selection result is the same as without racing.

docs.title: Generic-family pre-screen in vine selection
docs.text: The 85 generic families make the family set several times larger. When the sample has more than 1800 rows and the family set contains generic codes, each generic candidate of an edge is first fitted on the ~600-row subsample only (Blomqvist start, one Newton fit, tolerance \(10^{-3}\)); its log-likelihood is scaled by \(n/600\) and scored with the selection criterion. Only the four best generic candidates per edge go on to the full-data racing. The hand-coded candidates are never pre-screened, and discrete edges skip this step.

docs.title: Fit cache
docs.text:
Repeated selections on the same data (tuning loops, bootstrap over options, thresholding passes) refit many identical pairs. The fit cache stores the result of each pair fit under a 64-bit key built from every bit of the pair data, the weights, the \(F(x^-)\) values of discrete margins, the family, rotation, method, start and box:

FortranPythonR 
call fv_fitcache_enable(20000)          ! room for 20000 fits
call vc%select(u, ctl)                  ! fills the cache
call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed=.false.)   ! identical pairs: cache hits
call fv_fitcache_stats(hits, misses, used)
call fv_fitcache_disable()              ! frees the table

fv.fitcache_enable(20000)               # room for 20000 fits
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)            # fills the cache
vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u)            # identical pairs: cache hits
hits, misses, used = fv.fitcache_stats()
fv.fitcache_disable()                   # frees the table

fitcache_enable(20000)                  # room for 20000 fits
vc <- vinecop(u)                        # fills the cache
vc <- vinecop(u)                        # identical pairs: cache hits
fitcache_stats()                        # hits, misses, used
fitcache_disable()                      # frees the table
  • A hit returns exactly the fit computed earlier for identical input, so results do not change.
  • The table is open-addressed (16 probes); when full, the colliding slot is overwritten.
  • Racing screens are cached under their own key, so a repeated selection reproduces them too.
  • The cache is shared by all threads (guarded by an OpenMP critical section) and by every fit and select call while it is enabled. fv_fitcache_clear() empties it, fv_fitcache_capacity() returns its size (0 when disabled).
  • One-parameter fits inside vine selection bypass the cache (they are cheaper than a lookup); fv_bicop%fit caches them.

vc%select with ctl%select_threshold enables a temporary cache for its passes if none is active.

docs.title: Selection criteria
docs.text:
For a fitted candidate with log-likelihood \(\ell\), \(k\) parameters (effective degrees of freedom for TLL and Bernstein) and \(n\) observations, fortvine maximises

ctl%selcrit score FV_LOGLIK \(\ell\) FV_AIC \(\ell - k\) (that is, \(-\text{AIC}/2\)) FV_BIC (default) \(\ell - \tfrac12 k \log n\) (\(-\text{BIC}/2\)) FV_MBIC \(\ell - \tfrac12 k\log n + \log\psi_0\) for a dependent candidate, \(\ell + \log(1-\psi_0)\) for independence FV_MBICV as FV_MBIC with \(\psi = \psi_0^{\,t}\) in tree \(t\) of a vine

\(\psi_0\) is ctl%psi0 (default 0.9). The modified BIC puts a prior probability \(\psi\) on an edge being dependent; in its vine version (mBICv, Nagler et al. 2019) that probability decreases geometrically with the tree level, which favours sparse vines in high dimensions. For a whole vine with \(q_t\) non-independence edges in tree \(t\),

\[ \text{mBICv} = -2\ell + k\log n - 2\sum_{t=1}^{d-1}\Big[q_t \log\psi_0^{\,t} + (d - t - q_t)\log\big(1-\psi_0^{\,t}\big)\Big], \]

which is the quantity minimised by select_trunc and select_threshold.

docs.title: Kendall's tau inversion
docs.text:
For the families with a known relation between Kendall's \(\tau\) and the parameter, the parameter can be set from the sample \(\tau\) instead of maximising the likelihood:

family inversion Gaussian, Student \(\rho = \sin(\pi\tau/2)\) (Student: \(\nu\) by MLE with \(\rho\) fixed) Clayton \(\theta = 2\lvert\tau\rvert / (1 - \lvert\tau\rvert)\) Gumbel \(\theta = 1 / (1 - \lvert\tau\rvert)\) Frank numerical inversion of \(\tau(\theta) = 1 - \tfrac{4}{\theta}\big(1 - D_1(\theta)\big)\), \(D_1\) the Debye function Joe numerical inversion of \(\tau(\theta) = 1 + 2\,\dfrac{\psi(2) - \psi(2/\theta + 1)}{2 - \theta}\), \(\psi\) the digamma function

The numerical inversions use Newton's method with the analytic \(d\tau/d\theta\) inside a bracket. Two controls use them:

  • ctl%method = FV_ITAU (method="itau" in Python, par_method = "itau" in R): every candidate is fitted by inversion; families without an inversion (codes above 6) are not considered in selection. The log-likelihood is evaluated at the inverted parameter so that criteria remain comparable.
  • ctl%fast_mle = .true. (with FV_MLE; fast_mle=True in Python, fast_mle = TRUE in R): only the five one-parameter families above use the inversion; everything else, including the Student, is fitted by MLE. Since the closed-form MLE of those families is already cheap, the saving is small in fortvine.

ctl%tau_mode decides how \(\tau\) itself is computed: FV_TAU_EXACT (default) is the tie-corrected \(\tau_b\) in \(O(n\log n)\) (Knight 1966); FV_TAU_APPROX uses \(\tfrac2\pi\arcsin\) of the Pearson correlation of the normal scores; FV_TAU_AUTO uses the exact value below 800 observations and the approximation above. With weights the weighted \(\tau_b\) is always used. In tree 1 of an unweighted vine selection with a free structure and the \(\tau\) tree criterion, the exact \(\tau\) matrix computed for the tree weights is reused.

docs.title: Example: what the options cost
docs.text:
FortranPythonR fitting_demo.f90
program fitting_demo
  use fortvine_api
  use iso_fortran_env, only: int64
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 5000, d = 5
  type(fv_vinecop) :: truth, vc
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u(n, d)
  integer(int64) :: hits, misses, t0, t1, rate
  integer :: e, used

  call truth%set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
  do e = 1, d - 1
    truth%fam(e, 1) = FV_BB1; truth%par(1:2, e, 1) = [0.6_dp, 1.4_dp]
  end do
  truth%fam(1:d - 2, 2) = FV_STUDENT; truth%par(1, 1:d - 2, 2) = 0.3_dp; truth%par(2, 1:d - 2, 2) = 5.0_dp
  call truth%simulate(n, u, seed=5)
  ctl%nthreads = 4

  call run('MLE, BIC (default)')
  ctl%fast_mle = .true.;  call run('fast_mle')
  ctl%fast_mle = .false.; ctl%method = FV_ITAU; call run('itau')
  ctl%method = FV_MLE;    ctl%selcrit = FV_MBICV; call run('MLE, mBICv')

  ! the fit cache: a repeated selection on identical data reuses every cached pair fit
  ctl%selcrit = FV_BIC
  call fv_fitcache_enable(20000)
  call run('cache, first pass')
  call run('cache, second pass')
  call fv_fitcache_stats(hits, misses, used)
  print '(a,i0,a,i0,a,i0)', 'cache hits ', hits, '  misses ', misses, '  slots used ', used
  call fv_fitcache_disable()
contains
  subroutine run(label)
    character(*), intent(in) :: label
    call system_clock(t0, rate)
    call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed=.false.)
    call system_clock(t1)
    print '(a20,a,f10.2,a,i3,a,f7.3,a)', label, '  loglik', vc%loglik(u), '  npars', vc%npars(), &
      '  time', real(t1 - t0, dp) / rate, ' s'
  end subroutine run
end program fitting_demo
fitting_demo.py
import time

import fortvine as fv

n, d = 5000, 5
truth = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
for e in range(d - 1):
    truth.set_pair_copula(0, e, fv.Bicop("bb1", 0, [0.6, 1.4]))
for e in range(d - 2):
    truth.set_pair_copula(1, e, fv.Bicop("student", 0, [0.3, 5.0]))
u = truth.simulate(n, seed=5)


def run(label, **options):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, num_threads=4, **options)
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"{label:>20s}  loglik{vc.loglik(u):10.2f}  npars{vc.npars:3d}  time{t1 - t0:7.3f} s")


run("MLE, BIC (default)")
run("fast_mle", fast_mle=True)
run("itau", method="itau")
run("MLE, mBICv", criterion="mbicv")

# the fit cache: a repeated selection on identical data reuses every cached pair fit
fv.fitcache_enable(20000)
run("cache, first pass")
run("cache, second pass")
s = fv.fitcache_stats()
print(f"cache hits {s.hits}  misses {s.misses}  slots used {s.used}")
fv.fitcache_disable()

  cache, second pass  loglik   7099.77  npars 14  time  0.060 s
cache hits 268  misses 391  slots used 355

The Python and R samples come from other random streams, so their log-likelihoods differ from the Fortran ones; the pattern is the same. The R package is compiled by R's own toolchain (on Windows Rtools43, gfortran 12.3), which makes the same code two to three times slower here; see Benchmarks.

FV_ITAU is fastest because it drops every family above code 6 (here the true BB1 is no longer available, which costs about 92 log-likelihood units). The second cached selection takes 6 % of the time of the first and returns the same vine. It needs fewer lookups (260 hits) than the first pass had misses (402), because a candidate that was screened and then polished in the first pass costs two fits there but is found at once under its final key.

The Python example re-run with the fit cache, which the Python package now exposes (`fitcache_enable`, `fitcache_stats`). (a) Selection time with 4 threads (best of three runs, one run for the cache passes). (b) Log-likelihood of the selected vine relative to the best: every option except `itau` selects the same vine (6820.9); `itau` loses 77 units because the true BB1 family is no longer a candidate. The second cached pass returns the same vine in under 10 % of the time of the first. Timings depend on the machine.

docs.title: Aborting a running fit
docs.text:
The kernel module exposes a volatile logical fv_abort (in module fortvine, not re-exported by fortvine_api). Setting it to .true. from another thread makes fits in flight stop at their next Newton step and new ones return immediately; the results are then meaningless and are not cached. Reset it to .false. before the next call.

In Python, fv.set_abort(True) / fv.set_abort(False) set and clear the flag (through fvc_set_abort), and Ctrl-C interrupts a running vine selection or relax (see the Python page). R has no abort function: R cannot run code while a computation is in progress.

docs.title: The generic engine
docs.text:
Besides the 26 hand-coded families, fortvine contains a generic pair-copula engine (src/families_gen.inc) that builds Archimedean, extreme-value and Archimax copulas, their compositions and their Khoudraji asymmetrisations from a small set of parts. One implementation evaluates all of them, in log space and with exact parameter derivatives. The engine has 114 valid codes: 85 new families (codes \(\ge 10000\)) and 29 that reproduce a hand-coded family or another generic code.

The family pages (Archimedean, extreme-value, Archimax, Khoudraji) describe the copulas; this page describes the code scheme, the parameters, the exclusions and how to extend the engine. The complete list is in the catalogue.

docs.title: One formula
docs.text:
Every generic family is of the form (Capéraà, Fougères & Genest 2000; Joe 2014, sections 3.5 and 3.18)

\[ C(u, v) = \Psi\big(\,\ell(\Phi(u), \Phi(v))\,\big), \qquad \Phi = \Psi^{-1}, \]

with two ingredients:

  • the outer generator \(\Psi\): either none (\(\Psi(s) = e^{-s}\)), a Laplace transform of a positive random variable with one or two parameters, or a composition \(\Psi(s) = \psi_{\text{po}}\big(-\log\zeta_{\text{pin}}(s)\big)\) of two one-parameter Laplace transforms (Joe 2014, appendix A.1.2);
  • the inner function \(\ell\) on the log scale: either \(\ell(s, t) = s + t\), which makes \(C\) Archimedean, or \(\ell(s, t) = (s + t)\, A\!\left(\frac{t}{s+t}\right)\) with a Pickands dependence function \(A\), which makes \(C\) Archimax (and extreme-value when \(\Psi = e^{-s}\)).

With \(S = \Phi(u)\), \(T = \Phi(v)\) and \(L = \ell(S, T)\) the h-functions and density are

\[ h_1 = \frac{\Psi'(L)\,\ell_s}{\Psi'(S)}, \qquad h_2 = \frac{\Psi'(L)\,\ell_t}{\Psi'(T)}, \qquad c = \frac{\Psi''(L)\,\ell_s\,\ell_t + \big(-\Psi'(L)\big)\big(-\ell_{st}\big)}{\Psi'(S)\,\Psi'(T)} . \]

Since \(\Psi' < 0 \le \Psi''\), \(\ell_s, \ell_t \ge 0\) and \(\ell_{st} \le 0\), both terms of the numerator are non-negative, so the density is a log-sum-exp of two finite logarithms and never suffers from cancellation.

docs.title: The Khoudraji wrapper
docs.text:
Any member can be made asymmetric with Khoudraji's (1995) device

\[ C_K(u, v) = u^{1-a}\, v^{1-b}\; C\big(u^{a}, v^{b}\big), \qquad a, b \in [0.01, 1], \]

whose density, with \(x = u^a\), \(y = v^b\), is \(u^{-a}v^{-b}\,C(x,y)\,\big[(1-a)(1-b) + (1-a)\,b\,y\,\tfrac{h_2}{C} + (1-b)\,a\,x\,\tfrac{h_1}{C} + ab\,xy\,\tfrac{c}{C}\big]\), again a sum of non-negative terms.

docs.title: The code scheme
docs.text:
\[ \texttt{fam} = 10000\,k + 100\,\text{og} + \text{ie} \] part values meaning \(k\) 1, 2 1 plain, 2 Khoudraji-wrapped (two extra parameters \(a, b\)) og 0 to 7, 11 to 26 outer generator \(\Psi\) ie 0 to 13 inner function: 0 Archimedean, 1 to 13 a Pickands function

gen_is(fam) is true for every code \(\ge 10000\). The parts are extracted as og = mod(fam, 10000) / 100 and ie = mod(fam, 100).

docs.title: Outer generators (og)
docs.text:
og name \(\Psi(s)\) parameters box 0 none \(e^{-s}\) none 1 positive stable (PS) \(\exp(-s^{1/\theta})\) \(\theta\) \([1, 20]\) 2 gamma \((1+s)^{-1/\theta}\) \(\theta\) \([10^{-3}, 20]\) 3 Sibuya \(1 - (1-e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\) \(\theta\) \([1, 20]\) 4 logarithmic series \(-\theta^{-1}\log\big(1 - (1-e^{-\theta})e^{-s}\big)\) \(\theta\) \([10^{-3}, 35]\) 5 exponentially tilted PS \(\exp\big(\delta^{-1} - (\delta^{-\theta} + s)^{1/\theta}\big)\) \(\theta, \delta\) \([1, 10] \times [0.01, 25]\) 6 generalised Sibuya \(\delta^{-1}\big[1 - (1 - \eta e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\big]\), \(\eta = 1-(1-\delta)^\theta\) \(\theta, \delta\) \([1, 8] \times [10^{-3}, 1]\) 7 negative binomial \(\big[(1-\pi)/(e^{s} - \pi)\big]^{1/\theta}\) \(\theta, \pi\) \([0.01, 30] \times [0, 0.99]\) 11 to 26 composition po.pin \(\psi_{\text{po}}\big(-\log\zeta_{\text{pin}}(s)\big)\) \(\theta_{\text{po}}, \theta_{\text{pin}}\) see below

With og = 0 to 7 alone (\(\ell = s + t\)) these are Gumbel, Clayton, Joe, Frank, BB9, BB8 and BB10, all available as hand-coded families; their value is as building blocks for Archimax copulas.

The compositions combine po, pin \(\in\) {1 PS, 2 gamma, 3 Sibuya, 4 log series} as og \(= 10 + 4(\text{po} - 1) + \text{pin}\). Inside a composition the boxes are PS \([1, 10]\), gamma \([10^{-3}, 15]\), Sibuya \([1, 10]\), log series \([10^{-3}, 30]\); the outer parameter comes first.

docs.title: Inner functions (ie)
docs.text:
\(w = t/(s+t)\) is the share of the second margin, the convention of fortvine's Tawn and Galambos families.

ie name \(A(w)\) parameters box 0 none (Archimedean) \(\ell = s + t\) none 1 logistic \(\big[(1-w)^\theta + w^\theta\big]^{1/\theta}\) \(\theta\) \([1, 20]\) 2 negative logistic \(1 - \big[(1-w)^{-\theta} + w^{-\theta}\big]^{-1/\theta}\) \(\theta\) \([0.01, 20]\) 3 Hüsler-Reiss \(w\,\Phi_N(z_1) + (1-w)\,\Phi_N(z_2)\), \(z_{1,2} = \lambda^{-1} \pm \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\log\tfrac{w}{1-w}\) \(\lambda\) \([0.01, 20]\) 4 symmetric mixed \(1 - \theta w(1-w)\) \(\theta\) \([0, 1]\) 5 asymmetric logistic \((1-\psi_1)(1-w) + (1-\psi_2)w + \big[(\psi_1(1-w))^\theta + (\psi_2 w)^\theta\big]^{1/\theta}\) \(\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta\) \([0.01,1]^2 \times [1, 20]\) 6 asymmetric logistic, type 1 ie 5 with \(\psi_2 = 1\) \(\theta, \psi_1\) \([1, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) 7 asymmetric logistic, type 2 ie 5 with \(\psi_1 = 1\) \(\theta, \psi_2\) \([1, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) 8 asymmetric negative logistic \(1 - \big[(\psi_1(1-w))^{-\theta} + (\psi_2 w)^{-\theta}\big]^{-1/\theta}\) \(\psi_1, \psi_2, \theta\) \([0.01,1]^2 \times [0.01, 20]\) 9 asym. negative logistic, type 1 ie 8 with \(\psi_2 = 1\) \(\theta, \psi_1\) \([0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) 10 asym. negative logistic, type 2 ie 8 with \(\psi_1 = 1\) \(\theta, \psi_2\) \([0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]\) 11 asymmetric mixed \(1 - (\theta+\phi)w + \theta w^2 + \phi w^3\), \(\phi = -\tfrac\theta3 + \kappa\big(\tfrac{1-\theta}{2} + \tfrac\theta3\big)\) \(\theta, \kappa\) \([0, 1]^2\) 12 Khoudraji-Hüsler-Reiss \((1-a)(1-w) + (1-b)w + v\,A_3(z)\), \(v = a(1-w) + bw\), \(z = bw/v\) \(\lambda, a, b\) \([0.01, 20] \times [0.01, 1]^2\) 13 Khoudraji-mixed as ie 12 with \(A_4\) \(\theta, a, b\) \([0, 1] \times [0.01, 1]^2\)

(\(\Phi_N\) is the standard normal distribution function.) The parametrisation \(\kappa \in [0, 1]\) of ie 11 maps the unit square onto the admissible region of Tawn's (1988) asymmetric mixed model, so the box constraints are enough to keep \(A\) a valid Pickands function. ie 12 and 13 are the Khoudraji asymmetrisations of ie 3 and 4 written as Pickands functions, so that they can be combined with an outer generator.

All thirteen inner functions, as the Pickands functions of the extreme-value codes $10000 + \text{ie}$ (og = 0), recovered from the library's distribution function as $A(w) = -\log C(e^{-(1-w)}, e^{-w})$; the shaded triangle between $\max(w, 1 - w)$ (comonotone) and 1 (independence) is the admissible region. (a) The symmetric ones, $A(w) = A(1 - w)$. (b) The asymmetric logistic family: types 1 and 2 (ie 6, 7 and 9, 10, dashed for type 2) with the same parameters are mirror images, $A_7(w) = A_6(1 - w)$, which is what `gen_flip` uses. (c) The asymmetric mixed model and the two Khoudraji-type inner functions.

docs.title: Examples of codes
docs.text:
code \(k\) og ie name (fv_fam_name) 10203 1 2 gamma 3 HR Archimax(gamma|HuslerReiss) 11700 1 17 gamma.Sibuya 0 Arch(gamma.Sibuya) 10013 1 0 13 Khoudraji-mixed 10006 1 0 6 Tawn-type1 20200 2 2 gamma 0 Khoudraji-Clayton 20300 2 3 Sibuya 0 Khoudraji-Joe

Because of the three-parameter limit, the Khoudraji wrapper can only be applied to the one-parameter Archimedean generators and to the one-parameter Pickands functions; the new Khoudraji codes are 20200 (Clayton), 20300 (Joe) and 20400 (Frank), and the extreme-value ones are already covered by ie 5, 8, 12 and 13.

docs.title: Parameters and bounds
docs.text: Parameters are stored in par(1:3) in the order outer, inner, Khoudraji: first the 0 to 2 parameters of og, then the 0 to 3 of ie, then \(a, b\) if \(k = 2\). A code is valid only if the total is between 1 and 3. gen_npar(fam) returns the count, fv_par_bounds(fam, lb, ub) the box assembled from the tables above.

docs.title: Valid codes and duplicates
docs.text:
gen_valid(fam) accepts a code only if it is well defined and identifiable. Excluded are:

  • og outside 0-7 and 11-26, ie above 13, or a total of more than three parameters;
  • og 0 with ie 0 (the independence copula) and og 1 with ie 1 (equal to the logistic extreme-value copula, Gumbel);
  • the compositions PS.PS and Sibuya.Sibuya (they collapse to one family), and the three with a logarithmic-series inner part under PS, Sibuya or logarithmic series (og 14, 22, 26), which cannot be evaluated accurately in double precision;
  • compositions with a gamma inner part (og 12, 16, 20, 24) combined with a Pickands function: they fail the engine's consistency tests;
  • Khoudraji wrapping (\(k = 2\)) of inner functions 5 to 13, which are already asymmetric.

gen_dup(fam) marks valid codes whose copula is available elsewhere: the Archimedean codes of og 0-7, 12, 15, 16, 19, 20 (Gumbel, Clayton, Joe, Frank, BB9, BB8, BB10, BB3, BB1, BB2, BB6, BB7), the extreme-value codes 10001, 10002, 10003, 10005 (Gumbel, Galambos, Hüsler-Reiss, Tawn), PS and gamma outer with the negative logistic inner (BB5, BB4), any one-parameter generator with the logistic inner (equal to its composition with PS), the compositions with a PS inner part (gamma.PS, Sibuya.PS, logseries.PS) with the logistic inner, Khoudraji-wrapped extreme-value codes (they equal ie 5, 8, 12, 13) and Khoudraji-Gumbel (equal to Tawn). Duplicates are kept because they are useful for testing: test/test_genfam.f90 checks that they reproduce the hand-coded families.

codes = fv_generic_families()                   ! 85 codes, duplicates left out (default)
codes = fv_generic_families(new_only=.false.)   ! all 114 valid codes

The code space, one cell per (og, ie): top the plain codes $10000 + 100\,\text{og} + \text{ie}$, bottom the Khoudraji-wrapped ones ($20000 + \dots$, ie 0 to 4; ie 5 to 13 are already asymmetric and excluded). Dark: the 85 new families listed by `fv.families()`; light: the 29 valid codes that duplicate another family; white: excluded codes (`fv_fam_name` returns `invalid`). The vertical line separates the single generators (og 0 to 7) from the compositions po.pin (og 11 to 26); most compositions combine with the Archimedean inner part (ie 0) or the symmetric Pickands functions (ie 1 to 4) only.

docs.title: Names
docs.text: fv_fam_name(fam) returns the literature name where one exists (Gumbel, BB4, Tawn-type1, Galambos, ...) and otherwise a name built from the parts: Arch(<generator>) for Archimedean codes, Archimax(<generator>|<inner>) for Archimax codes, the inner name alone for extreme-value codes, with the prefix Khoudraji- for \(k = 2\). Generator names are PS, gamma, Sibuya, logseries, tiltedPS, genSibuya, negbin and po.pin for compositions. Invalid codes return invalid.

docs.title: Tail dependence, symmetry and transposition
docs.text:
• gen_lt(fam): lower-tail dependence, present when a gamma part (polynomially decaying Laplace transform) is the outer generator or either part of a composition.
  • gen_ut(fam): upper-tail dependence, from a PS or Sibuya part or from any Pickands inner.
  • gen_exch(fam): exchangeable, true for \(k = 1\) and ie \(\le 4\).
  • gen_flip(fam, par): replaces the code and parameters by those of the transposed copula \(C(v, u)\); see Rotations and asymmetry.

The two tail flags drive the preselection of generic candidates.

The tail flags checked numerically for the six new Archimedean compositions: (a) $\lambda_L(q) = C(q, q)/q$ and (b) $\lambda_U(q) = \{2q - 1 + C(1-q, 1-q)\}/q$ from the library's `cdf`, down to $q = 10^{-5}$ ($\tau$ from 20 000 simulated pairs). The three codes with a gamma part (11700, 11800, 12400) level off at a positive $\lambda_L$, the others decay to 0; the four with a PS or Sibuya part (11300, 11700, 12300, 12500) level off at a positive $\lambda_U$, while gamma.logseries and logseries.gamma have none, as `gen_lt` and `gen_ut` state.

docs.title: Exactness
docs.text:
The engine is written once with abstract arithmetic and compiled four times: for real(dp) (evaluation) and for the three dual-number types of fortvine_ad with 1, 2 and 3 derivative slots (exact parameter scores). Every generator returns \(\log\Psi\), \(\log(-\Psi')\) and \(\log\Psi''\); every inner function returns \(\ell\), \(\log\ell_s\), \(\log\ell_t\) and \(\log(-\ell_{st})\). Each argument \(s\) travels together with \(\log s\), because \(\Phi(u)\) of a gamma-inner composition overflows long before its logarithm does. Stable building blocks are used throughout: \(\log(1 - e^{x})\) by Mächler's (2012) two-branch rule, \(\log\Phi_N(z)\) by an asymptotic series below \(z = -30\), series expansions where a Sibuya or logarithmic-series expression would cancel, and partial derivatives of \(A\) written per family so that \(A - wA'\) is never formed by subtraction. See Numerics.

In fitting, generic families start from a grid ranked by Blomqvist's \(\beta\), use three Newton starts, and in vine selection are pre-screened on a subsample (only the four best per edge are fitted on all data), see Fitting.

docs.title: Extending the engine
docs.text:
Adding a family part means adding cases to a few routines; everything else (density, h-functions, inverses by Newton, CDF, scores, fitting, rotations, selection) follows.

A new one- or two-parameter generator (for example as og = 8):

  1. families_gen.inc, subroutine prim(k, th, de, s, ls, l0, l1, l2): add case (8) returning l0 \(= \log\Psi(s)\), l1 \(= \log(-\Psi'(s))\), l2 \(= \log\Psi''(s)\), given s and ls \(= \log s\). Use only the generic operations of fortvine_ad (flog, fexp, flog1p, fexpm1, flse, fval, ...) so the code compiles for reals and duals.
  2. Same file, primphi: the inverse \(s = \Phi(x)\) and \(\log s\), given x, log x and log(1-x).
  3. Same file, gpsi and gphi: they dispatch case (1:7) to prim/primphi and treat everything else as a composition; widen the range to include the new code.
  4. fortvine.f90: gen_npo (parameter count), gen_bounds (box), gen_valid (the accepted og range), gen_name (name array GN), gen_lt / gen_ut (tail flags) and, if the new copula exists elsewhere, gen_dup.

To use a generator as the inner part of a composition, also add its Bernstein function \(g = -\log\zeta\) to bern (returning \(g\), \(\log g\), \(\log g'\), \(-g''\)) and its inverse to berninv, and extend the composition index arithmetic, which assumes four inner generators.

A new Pickands function (as ie = 14):

  1. families_gen.inc, subroutine pick(k, Rp, w, lw, l1w, aa, lsd, ltd, la2): add case (14) returning \(A(w)\), \(\log(A - wA')\), \(\log(A + (1-w)A')\) and \(\log A''\) from w, lw \(= \log w\), l1w \(= \log(1-w)\) and the parameters Rp(1:3).
  2. fortvine.f90: gen_npi, gen_bounds, gen_exch, gen_flip (how the parameters change under \(A(w) \mapsto A(1-w)\), if not exchangeable), gen_name (array IN), gen_valid (ie > 13 is rejected) and gen_codes (its loop runs to ie = 13 and its buffer is sized for it).

Then run bash build.sh test: test/test_genfam.f90 checks every valid code for self-consistency on a grid (\(\partial h_1/\partial v = c\), \(\partial h_2/\partial u = c\), \(\partial C/\partial u = h_1\)), and that maximum likelihood recovers simulated parameters. tools/catalogue.f90 regenerates the family catalogue.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
program generic_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0)
  integer, allocatable :: all(:), new(:)
  integer :: codes(6) = [10203, 11700, 10013, 20200, 10101, 10100], k, f
  real(dp) :: lb(3), ub(3)

  all = fv_generic_families(new_only=.false.)
  new = fv_generic_families()
  print '(a,i0,a,i0)', 'valid generic codes: ', size(all), '   without duplicates: ', size(new)
  print '(a)', '   code  name                                  valid  dup  npar  exch  lower upper'
  do k = 1, size(codes)
    f = codes(k)
    print '(i7,2x,a36,4x,l1,4x,l1,3x,i2,4x,l1,5x,l1,5x,l1)', f, fv_fam_name(f), gen_valid(f), gen_dup(f), &
      gen_npar(f), gen_exch(f), gen_lt(f), gen_ut(f)
  end do
  call fv_par_bounds(10203, lb, ub)
  print '(a,3f8.3,a,3f8.3)', 'bounds of 10203: lower', lb, '  upper', ub
end program generic_demo

  11700  Arch(gamma.Sibuya)                      T    F    2    T     T     T
  10013  Khoudraji-mixed                         T    F    3    F     F     T

Code 10101 (PS outer with logistic inner) is rejected because it is the Gumbel copula again; the flags of invalid codes are not meaningful. For fitting and selecting generic families see the example in example/ex03_generic_families.f90 and Generic families.

docs.title: Nonparametric pair copulas
docs.text: Two families are not described by a parameter vector but by an estimate of the copula density itself: the transformation local-likelihood estimator FV_TLL (code 24) and the empirical Bernstein copula FV_BERNSTEIN (code 25). They are useful when no parametric family fits a pair (multimodal dependence, mixtures, dependence that changes sign), and as a benchmark for the parametric choice. Their mathematical background is on the family page; this page covers how fortvine estimates, stores and uses them.

docs.title: Using them
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
cop%family = FV_TLL
call cop%fit(u1, u2)               ! cop%aux holds the estimate
call cop%pdf(x1, x2, dens)         ! evaluated from cop%aux
print *, cop%npars_eff()           ! effective degrees of freedom

cop = fv.Bicop("tll").fit(u)       # cop.aux holds the estimate
dens = cop.pdf(x)                  # evaluated from cop.aux
print(cop.npars)                   # effective degrees of freedom

cop <- bicop(u, family_set = "tll")    # cop$aux holds the estimate
dens <- dbicop(x, cop)                 # evaluated from cop$aux
cop$npars                              # effective degrees of freedom

In selection they are candidates like any other family, but they are not in the default family set: use ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC (codes 0 to 25) or list them in family_set (Python: the groups "nonparametric" or "all"; R: "nonparametric" or the codes 0:25). Their penalty in AIC/BIC/mBIC is the effective number of parameters.

Both families ignore rotation (an estimate already has whatever orientation the data have) and par (always 0).

docs.title: The aux vector
docs.text:
The estimate lives in aux, a vector of length NAUX = 933:

entries TLL Bernstein aux(1) 24 25 aux(2) effective degrees of freedom \((m-1)^2\) aux(3) grid size, 30 order \(m\) (\(1 \le m \le 15\)) aux(4:33) grid points \(g_1 = 0 < \dots < g_{30} = 1\) on the \(u\) scale cell weights \(W_{ij}\), aux(3 + i + (j-1)*m), \(m^2\) values aux(34:933) copula density at the \(30 \times 30\) grid nodes, aux(33 + i + (j-1)*30) = \(c(g_i, g_j)\) unused

fv_bicop%fit and select allocate aux with NAUX entries for these families (and with one entry otherwise). In a vine, vc%aux has first extent NAUX whenever the family set of the last select contained code 24 or 25, and vc%aux(:, e, t) is the estimate of edge \((e, t)\). Python (Bicop.aux; aux[t, e] of a Vinecop, indexed from 0) and R ($aux of a bicop_dist) hold the same vector.

docs.title: TLL: transformation local likelihood
docs.text:
The TLL estimator (Geenens, Charpentier & Paindaveine 2017) estimates the density of the normal scores and maps it back to the copula scale. fortvine implements the local-constant variant of vinecopulib on a \(30 \times 30\) grid:

  1. Normal scores. \(z_{ik} = \Phi^{-1}\big(R_{ik}/(n+1)\big)\) from the ranks \(R_{ik}\) of each margin.
  2. Bandwidth. A Gaussian kernel with bandwidth matrix \(B = n^{-1/3}\, s \begin{pmatrix} 1 & r \\ r & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), where \(r\) is the correlation of the normal scores (clipped to \(\pm 0.95\)) and \(s = (\lvert r\rvert / \lvert\rho_{\text{ACE}}\rvert)^{\rho_{\text{ACE}}/2}\) shrinks the bandwidth when the maximal correlation \(\rho_{\text{ACE}}\) from the ACE algorithm (Breiman & Friedman 1985) exceeds the linear one, that is, when the dependence is non-linear.
  3. Kernel density \(\hat f\) of \((z_1, z_2)\) on a \(30 \times 30\) grid of normal-score nodes equally spaced in \([-3.25, 3.25]\) (the outer nodes are mapped to \(u = 0\) and \(u = 1\)).
  4. Back-transform. \(\hat c(\Phi(z_1), \Phi(z_2)) = \hat f(z_1, z_2) / (\varphi(z_1)\varphi(z_2))\) at the nodes, followed by three rounds of rescaling rows and columns so that both margins of the interpolated density integrate to one.

Evaluation. The density is bilinear between the nodes. The h-functions integrate the interpolated density along the free variable (with a floor of \(10^{-4}\) and normalisation to total mass one); because the integrand is piecewise linear, the integral is piecewise quadratic and its inverse is solved in closed form in each cell. The CDF is the exact double integral of the interpolant.

Effective degrees of freedom. The influence of an observation on its own fitted value, \(K(0)\,\det(B)^{-1/2} / (n \hat f(z_i))\) with \(K\) the standard bivariate normal kernel, is interpolated from the grid and summed over the observations (weighted if weights are given). The result, at least 1, is aux(2).

docs.title: Bernstein copula
docs.text:
The empirical Bernstein copula (Sancetta & Satchell 2004) of order \(m\) has density

\[ c(u, v) = m^2 \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m} W_{ij}\, b_{i-1,m-1}(u)\, b_{j-1,m-1}(v), \qquad b_{k,m-1}(x) = \binom{m-1}{k} x^k (1-x)^{m-1-k}, \]

where \(W\) holds the fraction of observations in each of the \(m \times m\) cells of the unit square. To make \(c\) a proper copula density, every row and column of \(W\) must sum to \(1/m\); fortvine enforces that with 50 alternating row/column rescalings (Sinkhorn balancing), starting from the cell counts plus a tiny constant. The order is selected by AIC among \(m = 1, \dots, 15\), with \((m-1)^2\) parameters and the restriction \((m-1)^2 < n/4\); \(m = 1\) is the independence copula.

h-functions are sums of the same form with binomial tail probabilities and are exact; their inverses use a bracketed Newton iteration with the density as derivative.

docs.title: Weights and discrete margins
docs.text: Both estimators accept observation weights: weighted kernel sums and weighted ACE for TLL, weighted cell counts for Bernstein. With discrete margins (in a vine) the estimate is computed from the mid-points \((F(x) + F(x^-))/2\) of the discrete margins, and its log-likelihood is then evaluated with the exact discrete formulas, see Discrete data.

docs.title: Cost
docs.text:
Measured with one thread on Gaussian(0.5) samples (fit only, the time of BB1 for comparison):

\(n\) TLL fit TLL edf Bernstein fit Bernstein edf BB1 fit 1 000 0.004 s 58 0.001 s 25 0.003 s 10 000 0.041 s 136 0.014 s 81 0.008 s 100 000 0.40 s 344 0.18 s 196 0.086 s

TLL cost is linear in \(n\) (900 kernel sums with a cut-off at \(e^{-40}\) per term); Bernstein fits all orders up to the AIC optimum. Evaluating TLL costs one bilinear interpolation for the density and a 30-node integration for an h-function; Bernstein costs \(O(m^2)\) per point. In vine selection the nonparametric candidates are scheduled among the first of the slow jobs.

Degrees of freedom are large

The effective degrees of freedom grow with \(n\) (roughly like \(n^{1/3}\) for TLL), so BIC rarely selects a nonparametric family when a reasonable parametric one exists; AIC or the log-likelihood criterion do so more readily. That is the intended trade-off, but compare the numbers above before relying on BIC to choose between the two worlds.

The table above as curves, from the Python package on the first $n$ rows of one Gaussian sample ($\rho = 0.5$), one thread. (a) Effective degrees of freedom (`npars`): TLL grows slightly faster than $n^{1/3}$ (dotted); Bernstein follows the order $m$ chosen by AIC and stops at $(m - 1)^2 = 196$, the largest order $m = 15$. (b) Time of one `fit`: both estimators are linear in $n$ and within a small factor of the BB1 maximum-likelihood fit.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
An equal mixture of a Clayton copula and a 90-degree rotated Gumbel copula, a shape no single parametric family can represent:

FortranPythonR np_demo.f90
program np_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 3000
  type(fv_bicop) :: a, b, tll, bern, best
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u1(n), u2(n), w(n), v(n), pick(n), d3(3)
  integer :: i

  ! an equal mixture of a Clayton and a 90-degree Gumbel: no parametric family fits it
  a%family = FV_CLAYTON; a%par(1) = 4.0_dp
  b%family = FV_GUMBEL; b%rotation = 90; b%par(1) = 3.0_dp
  call random_seed(put=[(5 * i, i = 1, 33)])
  call random_number(u1); call random_number(w); call random_number(pick)
  call a%hinv1(u1, w, u2); call b%hinv1(u1, w, v)
  where (pick > 0.5_dp) u2 = v

  tll%family = FV_TLL; call tll%fit(u1, u2)
  bern%family = FV_BERNSTEIN; call bern%fit(u1, u2)
  print '(a,f9.2,a,f7.2,a,i0)', 'tll:       loglik', tll%loglik, '  edf ', tll%npars_eff(), '  aux size ', size(tll%aux)
  print '(a,f9.2,a,f7.2,a,i0)', 'bernstein: loglik', bern%loglik, '  edf ', bern%npars_eff(), '  order m = ', nint(bern%aux(3))
  call tll%pdf([0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp], [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.1_dp], d3)
  print '(a,3f8.3)', 'tll density at (0.1,0.1), (0.5,0.5), (0.9,0.1):', d3

  call best%select(u1, u2)                                    ! parametric families only (default)
  print '(3a,f9.2)', 'best parametric: ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), '  loglik', best%loglik
  ctl%nfam = FV_NCLASSIC                                      ! + tev, tll, bernstein
  call best%select(u1, u2, ctl)
  print '(3a,f9.2)', 'BIC, with nonparametric: ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), '  loglik', best%loglik
  ctl%selcrit = FV_AIC
  call best%select(u1, u2, ctl)
  print '(3a,f9.2)', 'AIC, with nonparametric: ', trim(fv_fam_name(best%family)), '  loglik', best%loglik
end program np_demo
np_demo.py
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n = 3000

# an equal mixture of a Clayton and a 90-degree Gumbel: no parametric family fits it
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
u1, w, pick = rng.random(n), rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
a = fv.Bicop("clayton", 0, [4.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))
b = fv.Bicop("gumbel", 90, [3.0]).hinv1(np.column_stack([u1, w]))
u = np.column_stack([u1, np.where(pick > 0.5, b, a)])

tll = fv.Bicop("tll").fit(u)
bern = fv.Bicop("bernstein").fit(u)
print(f"tll:       loglik{tll.loglik():9.2f}  edf {tll.npars:7.2f}  aux size {tll.aux.size}")
print(f"bernstein: loglik{bern.loglik():9.2f}  edf {bern.npars:7.2f}  order m = {round(bern.aux[2])}")
d3 = tll.pdf(np.array([[0.1, 0.1], [0.5, 0.5], [0.9, 0.1]]))
print("tll density at (0.1,0.1), (0.5,0.5), (0.9,0.1):" + "".join(f"{x:8.3f}" for x in d3))

best = fv.Bicop().select(u)                                       # parametric families only (default)
print(f"best parametric: {best.family}  loglik{best.loglik():9.2f}")
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set="all")                     # + tev, tll, bernstein
print(f"BIC, with nonparametric: {best.family}  loglik{best.loglik():9.2f}")
best = fv.Bicop().select(u, family_set="all", criterion="aic")
print(f"AIC, with nonparametric: {best.family}  loglik{best.loglik():9.2f}")

docs.title: Performance and threads
docs.text: fortvine is parallelised with OpenMP and written so that results do not depend on the number of threads. This page explains how the thread count is chosen, what runs in parallel, how to build for speed, and which modelling options cost the most.

docs.title: How many threads
docs.text:
Every routine that can run in parallel resolves its thread count with fv_threads(req):

  1. req > 0 (from ctl%nthreads or an nthreads argument): exactly that many threads;
  2. otherwise the environment variable FORTVINE_THREADS, if it holds a positive integer;
  3. otherwise half the number of logical processors reported by OpenMP (max(1, omp_get_num_procs() / 2)), and 1 if the library was built without OpenMP.

Half the logical CPUs is a deliberate default: on machines with simultaneous multithreading it usually equals the number of physical cores, which is where the likelihood loops stop scaling, and it leaves the rest of the machine responsive.

export FORTVINE_THREADS=8       # default for every call that does not set nthreads
routine thread count taken from fv_bicop%fit, %select, fv_vinecop%select, %relax ctl%nthreads fv_vinecop%pdf, %pdf_grid, %rosenblatt, %inverse_rosenblatt, %simulate optional nthreads argument fv_tau_mat, fv_pseudo_obs_nd optional nthreads argument fv_bicop%pdf, %logpdf, %hfunc1, %hfunc2, %hinv1, %hinv2 fv_threads() (environment or default); parallel only above 4096 points fv_bicop%cdf the OpenMP default team (OMP_NUM_THREADS), not fv_threads C interface the nthreads argument of each routine

docs.title: What runs in parallel
docs.text:
operation parallel over pair-copula evaluation (pdf, h-functions, inverses) observations (above 4096) vine pdf, pdf_grid, Rosenblatt, inverse Rosenblatt observations one likelihood pass of a fit 128 fixed blocks of observations fv_bicop%select candidates (family, rotation) vine selection, per tree tree criteria of candidate edges, then all (edge, candidate) fits as one job list, then the h-functions of the selected edges Kendall's \(\tau\) matrix variable pairs pseudo-observations columns

In selection the parallelism is nested. The outer team runs the (edge, candidate) jobs; a job whose likelihood passes are large enough can borrow idle threads from a shared pool (at most one per 2000 observations, a fair share of what is idle, reserved atomically so the budget in nthreads is never exceeded). Short jobs run single-threaded; this keeps all threads busy both at the start of a tree, when there are many jobs, and at its end, when a few slow fits remain. Jobs are ordered cheapest-first and then longest-first, see Racing.

docs.title: Results do not depend on the thread count
docs.text: Every likelihood pass sums the contributions of 128 fixed blocks of observations in a fixed order, whatever the number of threads, so log-likelihoods, scores and therefore the fitted parameters and the selected model are bit-identical for any thread count (see the example below). The randomisation of the discrete Rosenblatt transform uses a counter-based hash, so it is reproducible as well. simulate uses the Fortran intrinsic random generator once, before the parallel part, and is reproducible for a given seed.

docs.title: Building for speed
docs.text:
build.sh compiles with

FFLAGS="-O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fno-math-errno -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp"

plus -cpp (the family formulas are included through the preprocessor) and -fPIC. Notes:

  • -march=native tunes for the build machine; the library may not run on older CPUs. For a library you distribute, override it: FFLAGS="-O3 -funroll-loops -fno-math-errno -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp" bash build.sh.
  • Without -fopenmp the library builds serially (all OpenMP code sits behind !$ sentinels) and fv_threads() returns 1.
  • Do not add -ffast-math or -ffinite-math-only: the code tests for NaN and infinity to reject failed evaluations (for example x /= x), and those tests are removed under finite-math assumptions.
  • The fpm.toml manifest builds the same sources with fpm build; pass the flags with --flag.

Setting the environment variable FORTVINE_PROFILE (to any value) makes vine selection print the time spent per tree on criteria, candidates, fits and h-functions, and the mBICv of every threshold pass. It is meant for diagnosing slow selections.

docs.title: What costs time
docs.text:
Selection time is roughly (number of edges) \(\times\) (candidates per edge) \(\times\) (cost per candidate). Each factor has a knob.

Edges: truncate. A vine has \(d(d-1)/2\) edges, but trees beyond the first few are often close to independence. ctl%trunc_lvl = k fits only \(\sum_{t \le k} (d - t)\) edges; ctl%select_trunc = .true. stops automatically when a tree no longer pays for itself; ctl%threshold (or select_threshold) turns weak edges into independence without fitting them. For \(d = 50\), truncating after 5 trees keeps 235 of the 1225 edges.

Candidates: keep the family set focused. The default set has 23 families; adding all 85 generic families multiplies the candidate count by almost five. The pre-screen of generic candidates (four per edge reach the full data) recovers most of that cost for \(n > 1800\), but not all. Keep preselect = .true.: whenever the tails of a pair are clearly asymmetric it drops the rotations of a family that put its tail dependence in the wrong corner, before any fit.

Cost per candidate.

  • The five closed-form one-parameter families (Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe) take a couple of passes over the data and are essentially free.
  • Two-parameter BB-type families need a start grid and a few Newton passes; with \(n > 1800\) most of the work is done on a 600-row subsample.
  • The Student copula (profile in \(\nu\)) and t-EV are the most expensive parametric fits; t-EV is not in the default set for that reason.
  • TLL and Bernstein cost about as much as a slow parametric family, see Nonparametric.
  • Discrete margins make every multi-parameter fit derivative-free and every observation two to four copula evaluations, see Discrete data.

Repeated work: cache it. If you select several times on the same data (comparing criteria, thresholds, family sets), enable the fit cache; identical pair fits are then looked up instead of recomputed.

Prediction. For predictive densities on a grid of one variable, use pdf_grid instead of calling pdf on an expanded array; edges that do not involve the varying variable are evaluated once per sample.

Two of the knobs, measured with the Python package and 8 threads (one run each; timings depend on the machine). (a) Candidates: selection time of a five-dimensional vine (the BB1 / Student D-vine of the [fitting example](fitting.md#example-what-the-options-cost)) for four family sets. Each larger set costs a roughly constant factor; the 109-family set with the generic codes is 7 times ($n = 20\,000$) to 80 times ($n = 1000$) slower than the default set, and *faster* above $n = 1800$ than below, where the generic pre-screen on a 600-row subsample starts (shaded). (b) Edges: selection time of a 20-dimensional vine ($n = 2000$, Kendall's $\tau$ fading from 0.5 in tree 1 to 0.03 from tree 5 on) against `trunc_lvl`, with the number of fitted edges in grey; the time grows with the number of fitted edges. The dashed line is the level chosen by `select_trunc_lvl` (mBICv), which here keeps 17 of the 19 trees because even $\tau = 0.03$ is detectable at $n = 2000$.

docs.title: Example: thread scaling
docs.text:
program perf_demo
  use fortvine_api
  use iso_fortran_env, only: int64
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 10000, d = 8
  type(fv_vinecop) :: truth, vc
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u(n, d)
  integer(int64) :: t0, t1, rate
  integer :: e, k, nt(4) = [1, 2, 4, 8]

  call truth%set_dvine([(e, e = 1, d)])
  truth%fam(1:d - 1, 1) = FV_GUMBEL; truth%par(1, 1:d - 1, 1) = 1.8_dp
  truth%fam(1:d - 2, 2) = FV_CLAYTON; truth%par(1, 1:d - 2, 2) = 0.8_dp
  call truth%simulate(n, u, seed=9)
  do k = 1, size(nt)
    ctl%nthreads = nt(k)
    call system_clock(t0, rate)
    call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed=.false.)
    call system_clock(t1)
    print '(a,i2,a,f7.2,a,f14.6)', 'nthreads', nt(k), ':', real(t1 - t0, dp) / rate, ' s   loglik', vc%loglik(u)
  end do
end program perf_demo

Output (an 8-dimensional vine, 10 000 observations, default family set; timings from one test machine, compiled with -O3 -march=native):

nthreads 1:  10.17 s   loglik  27197.910281
nthreads 2:   5.13 s   loglik  27197.910281
nthreads 4:   2.61 s   loglik  27197.910281
nthreads 8:   1.40 s   loglik  27197.910281

The selected vine, and with it the log-likelihood to the last printed digit, is the same for every thread count.

The same program in Python, with 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads (`num_threads`) on a 32-thread machine (8 performance cores with two threads each, 16 efficiency cores); the sample comes from NumPy, so the numbers differ from the Fortran output above. (a) Wall-clock time of the vine selection ($n = 10\,000$, one run) and of `pdf`, `rosenblatt` and `inverse_rosenblatt` of the selected vine on 200 000 points (best of three). (b) Speed-up over one thread, with the ideal line. Scaling is close to ideal up to 8 threads; at 16 threads, which share cores or run on efficiency cores, selection reaches about 9 and the evaluations 9 to 10. The selected vine and its log-likelihood (27899.336747) are identical for every thread count.

docs.title: Rotations and asymmetry
docs.text: Many copula families can only express positive dependence, and many have tail dependence in one corner only. Rotating the unit square extends each such family to the other three corners; transposing it (swapping the two arguments) matters for families that are not symmetric in their arguments. This page defines both operations exactly as fortvine implements them.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A rotation by \(r \in \{0, 90, 180, 270\}\) degrees turns the data counter-clockwise, following vinecopulib. With \(c\) the density of the unrotated family, the rotated densities are

\[ c_{90}(u_1, u_2) = c(u_2,\, 1-u_1), \qquad c_{180}(u_1, u_2) = c(1-u_1,\, 1-u_2), \qquad c_{270}(u_1, u_2) = c(1-u_2,\, u_1), \]

and the distribution functions

\[ C_{90}(u_1,u_2) = u_2 - C(u_2, 1-u_1),\quad C_{180}(u_1,u_2) = u_1 + u_2 - 1 + C(1-u_1, 1-u_2),\quad C_{270}(u_1,u_2) = u_1 - C(1-u_2, u_1). \]

The h-functions follow by differentiation. Writing \((a, b)\) for the rotated point that is passed to the unrotated family and \(g_1, g_2\) for its h-functions there:

rotation \((a, b)\) \(h_1(u_1, u_2)\) \(h_2(u_1, u_2)\) 0 \((u_1, u_2)\) \(g_1(a, b)\) \(g_2(a, b)\) 90 \((u_2, 1-u_1)\) \(g_2(a, b)\) \(1 - g_1(a, b)\) 180 \((1-u_1, 1-u_2)\) \(1 - g_1(a, b)\) \(1 - g_2(a, b)\) 270 \((1-u_2, u_1)\) \(1 - g_2(a, b)\) \(g_1(a, b)\)

The inverse h-functions are mapped in the same way, so every rotated copula has exact hinv1 / hinv2 and can be used in Rosenblatt transforms and simulation.

docs.title: Which families rotate
docs.text:
rotation is ignored by families that already cover both signs of dependence or are radially symmetric:

rotationless codes independence 0 Gaussian, Student 1, 2 Frank 5 Plackett, FGM, AMH 12, 13, 14 TLL, Bernstein (nonparametric; the estimate itself carries any orientation) 24, 25

Every other family, including all generic families, accepts the four rotations. The catalogue has a "rotations" column.

docs.title: Rotations, negative dependence and tails
docs.text:
A 90- or 270-degree rotation reverses the sign of concordance: if the unrotated family has Kendall's \(\tau > 0\), the rotated one has \(-\tau\). A 180-degree rotation keeps \(\tau\) and moves tail dependence to the opposite corner (the survival copula). For a family whose tail dependence sits at the lower-left corner (Clayton) or the upper-right corner (Gumbel, Joe), the corners after rotation are:

base tail 0 90 180 270 lower-left, \((0, 0)\) (Clayton type) \((0,0)\) \((1,0)\) \((1,1)\) \((0,1)\) upper-right, \((1, 1)\) (Gumbel type) \((1,1)\) \((0,1)\) \((0,0)\) \((1,0)\)

Here \((1, 0)\) means \(u_1 \to 1\) while \(u_2 \to 0\). Two-tailed families such as BB1 or BB7 carry both of their tails along.

The four rotations of Clayton ($\theta = 3$, top) and Gumbel ($\theta = 2.5$, bottom), densities in normal scores $z = \Phi^{-1}(u)$ with $u_1$ on the horizontal axis. The sharp tip of each density is its tail-dependent corner, at the positions of the table above: Clayton's moves from $(0, 0)$ at 0° to $(1, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ and $(0, 1)$, Gumbel's from $(1, 1)$ to $(0, 1)$, $(0, 0)$ and $(1, 0)$. $\hat\tau$ is Kendall's tau of 2000 pairs $(u_1, h_1^{-1}(u_1, w))$ from the same uniforms in every panel: 90 and 270 degrees flip its sign, 180 degrees keeps it.

In selection, the sign of the sample \(\tau\) decides which rotations are tried: 0 and 180 for \(\tau > 0\), 90 and 270 for \(\tau < 0\). Preselection may then remove one of the two, depending on where the data show stronger tail dependence (details). With ctl%allow_rotations = .false. only rotation 0 is used, so negatively dependent pairs can only get rotationless families.

docs.title: Asymmetric families and edge flips
docs.text:
A copula is exchangeable if \(C(u_1, u_2) = C(u_2, u_1)\). Most classical families are, but some are not:

  • Tawn (code 11) with \(\psi_1 \neq \psi_2\);
  • generic families with an asymmetric Pickands function (inner index ie = mod(fam, 100) from 5 to 13) and every Khoudraji wrapper (codes 20000 and above); gen_exch(fam) tells which;
  • TLL and Bernstein estimates, which need not be symmetric.

For these the order of the arguments matters. Inside a vine the first argument of the pair copula of edge \((e, t)\) is the variable order(e) (see Vine copulas). During selection fortvine builds the trees from unordered edges and orients them only at the end, when the trees are converted to the natural-order matrix. If that conversion needs an edge with its two variables swapped, the fitted pair copula is replaced by its exact transpose \(C^\top(u_1, u_2) = C(u_2, u_1)\), not refitted:

family transpose Tawn swap \(\psi_1 \leftrightarrow \psi_2\) (parameters 1 and 2) TLL, Bernstein transpose the density grid / cell-weight matrix generic, asymmetric logistic / negative logistic (05, 08) swap \(\psi_1 \leftrightarrow \psi_2\) generic, their types 1 and 2 (06 \(\leftrightarrow\) 07, 09 \(\leftrightarrow\) 10) change the code, keep \((\theta, \psi)\) generic, asymmetric mixed (11) \((\theta, \phi) \mapsto (\theta + 3\phi, -\phi)\), then back to \((\theta, \kappa)\) generic, Khoudraji-Husler-Reiss / Khoudraji-mixed (12, 13) swap \(a \leftrightarrow b\) any Khoudraji wrapper (\(k = 2\)) swap \(a \leftrightarrow b\) exchangeable families nothing

The rotation is transposed too: since \((C_{90})^\top = (C^\top)_{270}\) and vice versa, a flipped edge with rotation 90 becomes 270 and the other way round; 0 and 180 stay. The routine for the generic families is the public gen_flip(fam, par), which may change both the code and the parameters in place (Python: fv.gen_flip(family, parameters) returns the new code and parameters; R: gen_flip(model) returns the transposed bicop_dist, with 90 and 270 swapped).

Why the transpose is exact

For the outer generator nothing changes (it is symmetric in \(s\) and \(t\)). For the Pickands part, transposition maps \(A(w)\) to \(A(1-w)\); the asymmetric logistic models swap their asymmetry weights, and the asymmetric mixed model \(A(w) = 1 - (\theta+\phi)w + \theta w^2 + \phi w^3\) becomes the same polynomial with \(\theta' = \theta + 3\phi\), \(\phi' = -\phi\). For the Khoudraji construction \(C_K(u,v) = u^{1-a}v^{1-b}C(u^a, v^b)\) with exchangeable \(C\), swapping the arguments is the same as swapping \(a\) and \(b\).

Top: three asymmetric copulas, Tawn type 1 (10006), the asymmetric mixed model (10011) rotated by 90 degrees and the hand-coded Tawn (11), densities in normal scores with the diagonal $u_1 = u_2$ dotted. Bottom: their transposes, from `gen_flip` for the generic codes (type 1 becomes type 2 with the same parameters; 10011 gets new $(\theta, \kappa)$ and rotation 270) and by swapping $\psi_1, \psi_2$ for Tawn. Each bottom density is the top one mirrored across the diagonal; the largest difference of $c(u, v)$ and $c^\top(v, u)$ over 1000 random points is printed below each column.

If you build a vine by hand with asymmetric pair copulas, you are responsible for the orientation: the copula you assign to edge \((e, t)\) is applied with order(e) as its first argument.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
FortranPythonR rot_demo.f90
program rot_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 2000
  type(fv_bicop) :: c, t
  real(dp) :: u(4) = [0.1_dp, 0.3_dp, 0.6_dp, 0.95_dp], v(4) = [0.7_dp, 0.2_dp, 0.9_dp, 0.4_dp]
  real(dp) :: p1(4), p2(4), x1(n), x2(n), w(n)
  integer :: r, k, i, fams(3) = [FV_TAWN, 10011, 10006]
  real(dp) :: pars(3, 3)

  ! Kendall's tau of a Clayton(3) sample under each rotation
  c%family = FV_CLAYTON; c%par(1) = 3.0_dp
  call random_seed(put=[(i, i = 1, 33)])
  call random_number(x1); call random_number(w)
  do r = 0, 270, 90
    c%rotation = r
    call c%hinv1(x1, w, x2)
    print '(a,i4,a,f7.3)', 'rotation', r, ':  tau =', fv_kendall_tau(x1, x2)
  end do

  ! exact transpose of asymmetric families: c_T(u, v) = c(v, u), also under rotation 90 <-> 270
  pars(:, 1) = [0.4_dp, 0.9_dp, 3.0_dp]; pars(:, 2) = [0.6_dp, 0.3_dp, 0.0_dp]; pars(:, 3) = [2.5_dp, 0.4_dp, 0.0_dp]
  do k = 1, 3
    c%family = fams(k); c%par = pars(:, k); c%rotation = 90
    t = c
    if (t%family == FV_TAWN) then
      t%par(1:2) = c%par([2, 1])                      ! Tawn: swap psi1 and psi2
    else
      call gen_flip(t%family, t%par)                  ! generic families
    end if
    t%rotation = 270
    call c%pdf(u, v, p1); call t%pdf(v, u, p2)
    print '(5a,es9.2)', 'transpose of ', trim(fv_fam_name(c%family)), ' is ', trim(fv_fam_name(t%family)), &
      ': max |c(u,v) - c_T(v,u)| =', maxval(abs(p1 - p2))
  end do
end program rot_demo
rot_demo.py
import numpy as np
import fortvine as fv

n = 2000
uv = np.array([[0.1, 0.7], [0.3, 0.2], [0.6, 0.9], [0.95, 0.4]])

# Kendall's tau of a Clayton(3) sample under each rotation
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x1, w = rng.random(n), rng.random(n)
for r in (0, 90, 180, 270):
    c = fv.Bicop("clayton", r, [3.0])
    x2 = c.hinv1(np.column_stack([x1, w]))
    print(f"rotation{r:4d}:  tau ={fv.kendall_tau(x1, x2):7.3f}")

# exact transpose of asymmetric families: c_T(u, v) = c(v, u), also under rotation 90 <-> 270
for fam, par in [("tawn", [0.4, 0.9, 3.0]), (10011, [0.6, 0.3]), (10006, [2.5, 0.4])]:
    c = fv.Bicop(fam, 90, par)
    if c.family == "tawn":
        tfam, tpar = c.family_code, c.parameters[[1, 0, 2]]     # Tawn: swap psi1 and psi2
    else:
        tfam, tpar = fv.gen_flip(c.family_code, c.parameters)   # generic families
    t = fv.Bicop(tfam, 270, tpar)
    err = np.max(np.abs(c.pdf(uv) - t.pdf(uv[:, ::-1])))
    print(f"transpose of {c.family} is {t.family}: max |c(u,v) - c_T(v,u)| ={err:9.2E}")
rot_demo.R
library(fortvine)
n <- 2000
uv <- rbind(c(0.1, 0.7), c(0.3, 0.2), c(0.6, 0.9), c(0.95, 0.4))

# Kendall's tau of a Clayton(3) sample under each rotation
set.seed(1)
x1 <- runif(n); w <- runif(n)
for (r in c(0, 90, 180, 270)) {
  x2 <- hbicop(cbind(x1, w), 1, bicop_dist("clayton", r, 3), inverse = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("rotation%4d:  tau =%7.3f\n", r, cor(x1, x2, method = "kendall")))
}

# exact transpose of asymmetric families: c_T(u, v) = c(v, u), also under rotation 90 <-> 270
models <- list(bicop_dist("tawn", 90, c(0.4, 0.9, 3)), bicop_dist(10011, 90, c(0.6, 0.3)),
               bicop_dist(10006, 90, c(2.5, 0.4)))
for (cop in models) {
  tr <- if (cop$family == "tawn") {
    bicop_dist("tawn", 270, cop$parameters[c(2, 1, 3)])   # Tawn: swap psi1 and psi2
  } else {
    gen_flip(cop)                                         # generic families (rotation 90 -> 270)
  }
  err <- max(abs(dbicop(uv, cop) - dbicop(uv[, 2:1], tr)))
  cat(sprintf("transpose of %s is %s: max |c(u,v) - c_T(v,u)| =%9.2E\n", cop$family, tr$family, err))
}
