The theoretical \(\tau\) of Clayton(3) is \(3/5 = 0.6\); the four samples differ only by sampling noise and sign (and between the languages, which draw different uniforms). The last three lines confirm that the transposed, 270-degree copula evaluated at swapped arguments equals the original 90-degree copula to rounding.

docs.title: Vine copulas (fv_vinecop)
docs.text: A regular vine (R-vine) copula builds a \(d\)-dimensional copula from \(d(d-1)/2\) bivariate pair copulas arranged on a nested sequence of trees \(T_1, \dots, T_{d-1}\) (Bedford & Cooke 2002; Aas et al. 2009). Edge \(e\) of tree \(t\) links two variables conditionally on \(t-1\) others, and its pair copula is applied to conditional distribution functions computed from the trees below. fv_vinecop stores such a model and provides selection, density, Rosenblatt transforms and simulation.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
field type meaning d integer dimension trunc integer number of trees actually stored; edges of trees > trunc are independence order(d) integer, allocatable structure order (variable labels, 1-based) st(d, d) integer, allocatable natural-order structure array, st(edge, tree) fam(d, d), rot(d, d) integer, allocatable family code and rotation of edge (e, t) par(3, d, d) real(dp), allocatable parameters of edge (e, t) in par(:, e, t) edge_ll(d, d) real(dp), allocatable log-likelihood of each edge at selection time aux(:, d, d) real(dp), allocatable nonparametric estimates; first extent NAUX if the family set contained TLL/Bernstein, else 1 disc(d) logical, allocatable discrete variables (original labels), set by select threshold real(dp) threshold used by the last select nrel, erel, wa, wk, pk non-simplified edges added by relax

Only edges with t <= trunc and e <= d - t are meaningful.

docs.title: How the structure is stored
docs.text:
The vine is described by two arrays, in the natural-order convention of vinecopulib:

  • order(1:d) is a permutation of the variable labels.
  • For tree t and edge e (1 <= e <= d - t) the edge joins the variables order(e) and order(st(e, t)), conditionally on order(st(e, 1)), ..., order(st(e, t-1)).

The pair copula of edge (e, t) is evaluated as \(c\big(u_{\,\text{order}(e) \mid D},\; u_{\,\text{order}(\text{st}(e,t)) \mid D}\big)\): the variable order(e) is its first argument. For exchangeable families this does not matter; for asymmetric ones (Tawn, the Khoudraji and asymmetric extreme-value members of the generic engine) it does, see Rotations and asymmetry.

vc%matrix() converts this into the R-vine matrix of vinecopulib in original labels: row t of column e holds order(st(e, t)), and the anti-diagonal holds order (m(d - j + 1, j) = order(j)).

docs.title: Creating a vine
docs.text:
method what it does init(d) allocates every array for dimension d, sets order = [1, ..., d], every edge to independence and trunc = 0 (an empty structure) set_dvine(order [, trunc]) a D-vine (path) in the given order: tree 1 links order(1)-order(2), order(2)-order(3), ... set_cvine(order [, trunc]) a C-vine (star in every tree). The root of tree t is order(d - t + 1): the last element of order is the first root

Both set_* routines call init first, so they discard any families set before. trunc (default d - 1) limits the number of trees.

C-vine root order

set_cvine([1, 2, 3, 4]) makes variable 4 the root of tree 1, 3 the root of tree 2 and so on. To make variable 1 the first root, pass the order reversed: set_cvine([4, 3, 2, 1]).

docs.title: Setting families and parameters by hand
docs.text:
After set_dvine / set_cvine (or init plus your own order, st and trunc), assign the pair copulas directly:

FortranPythonR 
call vc%set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4])
vc%fam(1:3, 1) = FV_GUMBEL; vc%par(1, 1:3, 1) = 2.0_dp          ! tree 1: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4)
vc%fam(1:2, 2) = FV_FRANK;  vc%par(1, 1:2, 2) = 3.0_dp          ! tree 2: (1,3|2), (2,4|3)
vc%fam(1, 3) = FV_CLAYTON; vc%rot(1, 3) = 90; vc%par(1, 1, 3) = 1.5_dp

vc = fv.Vinecop().set_dvine([1, 2, 3, 4])                   # arrays are indexed [tree, edge] from 0
for e in range(3):
    vc.set_pair_copula(0, e, fv.Bicop("gumbel", 0, [2.0]))  # tree 1: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4)
for e in range(2):
    vc.set_pair_copula(1, e, fv.Bicop("frank", 0, [3.0]))   # tree 2: (1,3|2), (2,4|3)
vc.set_pair_copula(2, 0, fv.Bicop("clayton", 90, [1.5]))    # tree 3: (1,4|2,3)

pcs <- list(rep(list(bicop_dist("gumbel", 0, 2)), 3),       # tree 1: (1,2), (2,3), (3,4)
            rep(list(bicop_dist("frank", 0, 3)), 2),        # tree 2: (1,3|2), (2,4|3)
            list(bicop_dist("clayton", 90, 1.5)))           # tree 3: (1,4|2,3)
vc <- vinecop_dist(pcs, dvine_structure(1:4))

Such a model can be evaluated, transformed and simulated straight away. Python also has set_cvine; R builds D- and C-vine structures (dvine_structure(), cvine_structure()), or takes the structure of a selected vine (fit$structure). For a nonparametric edge, allocate vc%aux(NAUX, d, d) yourself (init only allocates a first extent of 1) and copy the aux vector of a fitted fv_bicop into vc%aux(:, e, t).

docs.title: Selection
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call vc%select(u, ctl, fixed, info, weights, discrete, u_minus)

vc = fv.Vinecop.from_data(u, family_set=None, criterion="bic", trunc_lvl=None, threshold=0.0,
                          tree_criterion="tau", tree_algorithm="prim", num_threads=1,
                          weights=None, var_types=None)
vc.select(u, fixed=True)            # on a Vinecop that holds a structure

vc <- vinecop(u, family_set = "all", structure = NA, selcrit = "bic", trunc_lvl = Inf,
              threshold = 0, tree_crit = "tau", tree_algorithm = "mst_prim", cores = 1,
              weights = numeric(), var_types = NULL)

u(n, d) are pseudo-observations; every other argument is optional (the controls are keyword arguments in Python and R). select chooses the structure (unless it is fixed), then the family, rotation and parameters of every edge.

docs.title: The Dissmann algorithm
docs.text:
With a free structure, selection proceeds tree by tree (Dissmann et al. 2013):

  1. Candidate edges. In tree 1 every pair of variables is a candidate. In tree \(t \ge 2\) the vertices are the edges of tree \(t-1\), and two of them may be joined only if they share a vertex in tree \(t-1\) (the proximity condition), which guarantees a valid R-vine.
  2. Edge weights. Each candidate gets the absolute value of the tree criterion ctl%tree_crit (Kendall's \(\tau\) by default) of its two pseudo-observation columns.
  3. Spanning tree. The tree with the largest total weight is found with Prim's (default) or Kruskal's algorithm (ctl%tree_algo).
  4. Pair copulas. For every kept edge the family, rotation and parameters are selected as in fv_bicop%select, with all (edge, candidate) fits of the tree running in parallel.
  5. Next tree's data. The h-functions of the fitted pair copulas give the conditional pseudo-observations on which tree \(t+1\) is built.

Selecting the tree by dependence strength first places the strongest dependencies in the low trees, where estimation error propagates least. The tree criteria available are listed in Controls.

Left: the C-vine of the [example](#example) (Clayton $\theta = 2$ in tree 1, Frank $\theta = -3$ in tree 2, Gumbel 90° in tree 3), drawn tree by tree; the nodes of tree $t \ge 2$ are the edges of tree $t - 1$ (conditioned pair | conditioning set). Right: `select` with a free structure on 2000 draws from it (Python `Vinecop.from_data`). The Dissmann algorithm recovers the star around variable 1 and the second tree; the last edge is the same copula with its arguments in the other order, hence Gumbel 270° instead of 90°. Edge labels give the family and Kendall's $\tau$ of each pair copula; $\ell$ is the log-likelihood on the sample.

docs.title: Fixed structure
docs.text:
Pass fixed = .true. to keep the stored structure and select only the pair copulas. When fixed is absent it defaults to .true. whenever the object already holds a structure (trunc > 0), for example after set_dvine, set_cvine or a previous select.

Re-selecting with the same object

Calling vc%select(u, ctl) a second time on an already selected vine keeps the first structure and its truncation level. To search the structure again, either use a fresh fv_vinecop, call vc%init(d) first, or pass fixed = .false..

docs.title: Truncation
docs.text:
A truncated vine sets every pair copula above tree \(k\) to independence, which removes \(\binom{d-k}{2}\) edges and can make high-dimensional models much cheaper.

  • ctl%trunc_lvl = k stops after tree k (-1, the default, means d - 1).
  • ctl%select_trunc = .true. lets the data decide: after each tree, the mBICv of that tree is compared with the mBICv of an all-independence tree \(t\), and selection stops at the first tree that does not improve on it (as vinecopulib's select_trunc_lvl).

The level reached is stored in vc%trunc.

docs.title: Thresholding
docs.text:
ctl%threshold = c (default 0) declares every edge whose tree criterion is below c an independence edge without fitting it; such edges also get the weight of an independent pair in the spanning-tree step. ctl%select_threshold = .true. chooses c by mBICv: starting from \(c = 1\) (every edge independent), each pass lowers \(c\) to the \(\lceil 5\% \rceil\)-th largest criterion among the edges still below it, reselects the vine and accumulates its mBICv over the trees; the search stops when the mBICv no longer decreases or \(c < 0.01\), and the best vine is kept (vinecopulib's select_threshold, Nagler et al. 2019). All passes share pair fits through the fit cache, which is switched on for the search if you have not enabled it. With weights, the mBICv uses the effective sample size \((\sum w_i)^2 / \sum w_i^2\). The chosen value is returned in vc%threshold.

Combining select_threshold with select_trunc applies vinecopulib's truncation rule inside each pass.

docs.title: Other options
docs.text:
• weights(n): observation weights for every pair fit and for the weighted tree criteria (tau, rho, joe; the other criteria ignore weights). Python and R: weights.
  • discrete(d), u_minus(n, d): discrete or mixed margins, see Discrete and mixed data. u_minus is required when any variable is discrete. Python and R: var_types ("c" or "d" per variable), with the \(F(x^-)\) columns of the discrete variables appended to the data.
  • info: 0 on success. Non-zero values (2, 3, 4) mean that the internal spanning-tree or tree-to-matrix step failed; they are not expected for valid input and indicate a bug.

select removes any non-simplified edges (it calls unrelax).

docs.title: Density and log-likelihood
docs.text:
FortranPythonR 
call vc%pdf(u, dens)                ! dens(n)
ll = vc%loglik(u)                   ! sum(log(dens))
call vc%pdf_grid(ug, tgt, out)      ! ug(d, bins, n), out(bins, n)

dens = vc.pdf(u)                    # dens[n]
ll = vc.loglik(u)                   # sum(log(dens))
out = vc.pdf_grid(ug, tgt)          # ug[n, bins, d], out[n, bins]

dens <- dvinecop(u, vc)             # dens[n]
ll <- sum(log(dens))
out <- dvinecop_grid(u, vc, tgt, grid)   # variable tgt of each row set to grid[b]; out[n, bins]

pdf evaluates the joint copula density at every row of u(n, d); loglik is the sum of its logarithms. With discrete variables both need u_minus.

pdf_grid is designed for predictive densities: ug(d, bins, n) holds, for each of n samples, bins points that differ only in variable tgt (1-based label). Edges whose inputs do not involve tgt are evaluated once per sample rather than once per bin, which saves most of the work when only one variable varies. The result is out(bins, n). With discrete variables pass the matching ugm(d, bins, n) of \(F(x^-)\) values.

(a) Predictive densities from `pdf_grid` with target 2 on 200 bins, for the vine selected on the fixed C-vine structure of the example and three of its samples (other variables held at their observed values). As a function of $u_2$ the joint density is proportional to the conditional density $c(u_2 \mid u_1, u_3, u_4)$, so each curve is divided by its integral; the dotted lines are the observed $u_2$. (b) Time of `pdf` on the expanded $(n \cdot \text{bins}, d)$ array divided by the time of `pdf_grid` on the same points, for a 10-dimensional D-vine (500 samples, 4 threads). For the end variable of the path (10) only 9 of the 45 edges depend on it and `pdf_grid` is up to 6.5 times faster; for a variable in the middle (5) more edges involve it and the gain is about 2.

docs.title: Rosenblatt transform and simulation
docs.text:
The Rosenblatt transform maps a sample of the copula to independent uniforms (Rosenblatt 1952); its inverse maps independent uniforms to a sample of the copula.

FortranPythonR 
call vc%rosenblatt(u, w)            ! u(n, d) -> w(n, d)
call vc%inverse_rosenblatt(w, u)    ! w(n, d) -> u(n, d)
call vc%simulate(n, u, seed=42)     ! u(n, d) drawn from the vine

w = vc.rosenblatt(u)                # u(n, d) -> w(n, d)
u = vc.inverse_rosenblatt(w)        # w(n, d) -> u(n, d)
u = vc.simulate(n, seed=42)         # u(n, d) drawn from the vine

w <- rosenblatt(u, vc)              # u (n x d) -> w (n x d)
u <- inverse_rosenblatt(w, vc)      # w (n x d) -> u (n x d)
set.seed(42)
u <- rvinecop(n, vc)                # u (n x d) drawn from the vine

The conditioning order follows the structure. The variable order(d) is returned unchanged, and the others are replaced by conditional distribution functions given variables that come after them in order; for a D-vine with order \((1, \dots, d)\) the output is \(w_d = u_d\), \(w_{d-1} = F(u_{d-1} \mid u_d)\), ..., \(w_1 = F(u_1 \mid u_2, \dots, u_d)\). The columns of w keep the original variable labels.

The Rosenblatt transform as a goodness-of-fit check, on the 2000 draws of the example's C-vine. (a) Variables 2 and 3 of the sample, in normal scores. (b) The same columns after `rosenblatt` under the vine selected on the C-vine structure: no dependence is left. (c) Kendall's $\tau$ of every pair of transformed columns, under that vine (blue) and under a vine truncated after tree 1 (gold). Under a correct model the $w_j$ are independent and the $\hat\tau$ stay inside the band of $\pm 2$ standard deviations of $\hat\tau$ for independent data; the truncated vine ignores the Frank and Gumbel edges of trees 2 and 3, and the dependence they carry remains in $w$.

simulate(n, out, seed, nthreads) draws w with the Fortran intrinsic random_number and applies inverse_rosenblatt. If seed is given, it reseeds the intrinsic generator (which changes the generator state of the calling program too); without seed the current state is used. Python's simulate(n, seed) draws its uniforms with NumPy and R's rvinecop() with runif() (so set.seed() applies), which gives other samples than the Fortran generator.

With discrete variables rosenblatt returns Brockwell's randomised transform by default, see Discrete and mixed data.

docs.title: Counting parameters
docs.text: npars_eff() sums the parameters of all edges up to trunc, using the effective degrees of freedom for nonparametric edges and (NK - 1) extra parameter sets per non-simplified edge; npars() is its rounded value.

docs.title: Inspecting a vine
docs.text:
vc%print([unit]) writes the dimension, truncation level, order and one line per edge (family name, rotation, parameters) to unit (default 6). Generic family names are cut to 12 characters in this listing; use fv_fam_name(vc%fam(e, t)) for the full name.

vc%matrix() returns the d x d R-vine matrix described above (Python: vc.matrix; R: as_rvine_matrix(vc)).

docs.title: Non-simplified edges (relax)
docs.text:
Most vine models assume that the pair copulas of trees \(t \ge 2\) do not depend on the values of their conditioning variables (the simplifying assumption, Haff et al. 2010; Spanhel & Kurz 2019). relax lifts that assumption edge by edge, in the spirit of local likelihood estimation of conditional copulas (Acar, Craiu & Yao 2011):

FortranPythonR 
call vc%relax(u, tgt, mode, ctl [, weights, nrel_out])

vc.relax(u, target=0, mode="test", weights=None)   # mode="all": every eligible edge
vc.nrel, vc.relaxed_edges                          # count; (tree, edge), 0-based
p = vc.rel_params(u)                               # (n, nrel, 3) parameters at each sample
vc.unrelax()

rel <- vinecop_relax(vc, u, tgt = 0, mode = 1)     # mode = 2: every eligible edge
rel$relaxed$erel                                   # edge (row 1) and tree (row 2)
p <- vinecop_rel_params(rel, u)                    # n x nrel x 3 parameters at each sample
un <- vinecop_unrelax(rel, u)                      # delete the relaxed edges

For every parametric edge of tree \(t \ge 2\) whose conditioned pair contains variable tgt (tgt = 0: any edge) and whose conditioning set \(D\) does not:

  1. \(w\) is the first principal component of the normal scores \(\Phi^{-1}(u_j)\), \(j \in D\) (loadings stored in wa).
  2. The edge's family is fitted with Gaussian kernel weights in the rank of \(w\) (bandwidth 0.15 in rank units) at five anchors, the 10, 30, 50, 70 and 90 % quantiles of \(w\) (values in wk, parameters in pk). Between anchors the parameters are interpolated linearly in \(w\), beyond them held constant.
  3. mode = 2 relaxes every eligible edge. mode = 1 relaxes only those for which a test of constant conditional correlation rejects at the 5 % level: the Fisher-\(z\) heterogeneity of the normal-score correlation across the quartiles of \(w\), with a null distribution from 99 circular shifts of \(w\) (which preserves serial dependence; after Kurz & Spanhel 2022).
  4. An independence edge that is relaxed becomes Gaussian. Edges of later trees are refitted (same families) on the conditional data that the relaxed edges now produce.

nrel_out returns the number of relaxed edges. relax does nothing if trunc < 2 or any variable is discrete. vc%rel_params(uc) returns the per-sample parameters prel(3, nrel, n) of the relaxed edges for samples uc(d, n).

The non-simplified example of the [Python page](../python.md#non-simplified-vines): three variables whose copula of $(U_1, U_3)$ given $U_2$ is Gaussian with correlation $-0.6 + 1.4\,u_2$, selected as a D-vine and then relaxed with `mode = 1` (the test relaxes the single tree-2 edge). (a) The Frank parameter of edge (1, 3 | 2) at the five anchors `wk` (dots) with the linear interpolation between them and the constant beyond, the single parameter of the simplified vine (dashed) and, for reference, the Frank copula fitted to 20 000 draws of the true conditional Gaussian copula at each $u_2$ (diamonds). The log-likelihood rises by 179. (b) Predictive density of $u_3$ at $u_1 = 0.5$ for three values of $u_2$ (`pdf_grid`, target 3): in the non-simplified vine (solid) the dependence between $u_1$ and $u_3$ changes sign with $u_2$; the simplified vine (dashed) applies the same edge copula for every $u_2$, so its curves differ only through the tree-1 edges.

Which methods honour relaxed edges:

method uses the \(w\)-dependent parameters pdf, loglik, pdf_grid yes rosenblatt, inverse_rosenblatt, simulate no: they use par, which relax sets to the parameters at the middle anchor npars, npars_eff, print yes (counted / listed)

unrelax does not restore the original fit

vc%unrelax() only deletes the relaxed-edge records. The parameters relax wrote (the middle-anchor values of relaxed edges, Gaussian instead of independence, refitted later trees) stay in fam and par. Keep a copy of the vine (saved = vc) if you want to go back to the simplified model.

pdf_grid after relax

pdf_grid takes the conditioning values of the relaxed edges from the first bin of each sample. That is exact when tgt of pdf_grid was also the tgt passed to relax (then no relaxed edge conditions on it); with relax(..., tgt = 0, ...) it is an approximation.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
FortranPythonR vine_demo.f90
program vine_demo
  use fortvine_api
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0), n = 2000, d = 4
  type(fv_vinecop) :: cv, fitd, free
  type(fv_controls) :: ctl
  real(dp) :: u(n, d), r(n, d), back(n, d), ug(d, 3, 2), dens(3, 2)
  integer :: m(d, d), i, k

  ! a C-vine written by hand; set_cvine roots tree t at order(d - t + 1)
  call cv%set_cvine([4, 3, 2, 1])                 ! roots: variable 1, then 2, then 3
  cv%fam(1:3, 1) = FV_CLAYTON; cv%par(1, 1:3, 1) = 2.0_dp
  cv%fam(1:2, 2) = FV_FRANK;   cv%par(1, 1:2, 2) = -3.0_dp
  cv%fam(1, 3) = FV_GUMBEL; cv%rot(1, 3) = 90; cv%par(1, 1, 3) = 1.4_dp
  m = cv%matrix()
  print '(a)', 'R-vine matrix (original labels):'
  do i = 1, d
    print '(4i3)', m(i, :)
  end do
  call cv%simulate(n, u, seed=11)

  ! Rosenblatt transform and its inverse
  call cv%rosenblatt(u, r); call cv%inverse_rosenblatt(r, back)
  print '(a,es9.2)', 'max round-trip error:', maxval(abs(back - u))

  ! keep the C-vine structure, let select choose families and parameters
  ctl%nthreads = 4
  call fitd%set_cvine([4, 3, 2, 1])
  call fitd%select(u, ctl)                          ! fixed = .true. by default here
  do k = 1, d - 1
    print '(a,i0,a,*(1x,a))', 'tree ', k, ':', (trim(fv_fam_name(fitd%fam(i, k))), i = 1, d - k)
  end do

  ! a free structure search, truncated after the first tree
  ctl%trunc_lvl = 1
  call free%select(u, ctl)
  print '(a,i0,a,f10.2,a,f10.2,a)', 'trunc = ', free%trunc, '   loglik', free%loglik(u), &
    '   (full C-vine:', fitd%loglik(u), ')'

  ! conditional density of variable 2 on a 3-point grid, other variables fixed per sample
  ug(:, :, 1) = 0.3_dp; ug(:, :, 2) = 0.7_dp
  ug(2, :, 1) = [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp]; ug(2, :, 2) = [0.1_dp, 0.5_dp, 0.9_dp]
  call fitd%pdf_grid(ug, 2, dens)
  print '(a,3f9.4)', 'pdf_grid sample 1:', dens(:, 1)
  print '(a,3f9.4)', 'pdf_grid sample 2:', dens(:, 2)
end program vine_demo

docs.title: Numerics and stability
docs.text: Copula densities are products and quotients of quantities that span hundreds of orders of magnitude. A strongly dependent Gumbel or BB7 copula, for example, has a density of order \(10^{6}\) on the diagonal near a corner and of order \(10^{-30}\) a short distance away, and the formulas that produce those numbers subtract nearly equal terms. Done naively in double precision, such computations lose digits (cancellation), overflow, or underflow to zero, and a likelihood maximiser that meets a NaN or a spurious zero goes astray. This page describes what fortvine does to stay accurate across the whole parameter box of every family, as implemented in src/fortvine.f90, src/families_*.inc and src/fortvine_ad.f90.

docs.title: Inputs: clamping to the open unit square
docs.text:
Every routine first clamps its copula data,

\[ u \;\mapsto\; \min\bigl(\max(u, \varepsilon), 1 - \varepsilon\bigr), \qquad \varepsilon = 10^{-10} \]

(clampu, constant EPSU). Many densities are infinite or undefined at the boundary of \([0, 1]^2\) (Clayton at the origin, Gumbel along the axes, every family at a point where \(\log u\) or \(\Phi^{-1}(u)\) diverges), and data sometimes contain exact 0s or 1s. Clamping makes every evaluation finite while changing nothing for data that are honestly inside the square: pseudo-observations \(R/(n+1)\) are at least \(1/(n+1)\) away from the boundary. One consequence is visible in the tests: an h-function cannot be inverted more precisely than this clamp, so hinv round-trips are checked to \(2 \times 10^{-10}\).

Outputs are guarded on the other side: densities are returned as \(\max(e^{\log c}, \text{tiny})\), so a density is never exactly 0 and its logarithm is always finite; h-functions and inverse h-functions are clipped to \([0, 1]\). Inside the likelihood, a non-finite log-density term is replaced by \(\log(\text{tiny}) \approx -708.4\) with a zero score, so that an invalid region of the parameter space can never look attractive to the optimiser.

docs.title: Working in log space
docs.text:
Every family returns \(\log c\), never \(c\), and every product is a sum of logarithms:

  • Pair copulas. The kernels produce \(\log c(u_1, u_2)\) directly from logarithms of the generator, its derivatives and the Pickands function; pdf exponentiates only at the very end.
  • Vines. The vine density is the product of \(d(d-1)/2\) pair densities. fortvine accumulates \(\sum \log c_e\) along the trees and exponentiates once per observation. A ten-dimensional density can be \(10^{\pm 100}\) without any intermediate overflow.
  • Prediction grids. pdf_grid evaluates the vine at many values of one target variable per sample. Edges that do not depend on the target are evaluated once per sample, the others once per grid point; the two parts are kept as separate log sums and combined bin by bin, \(c_k = \exp(\ell_{\text{common}} + \ell_k)\). Every grid density therefore has the same relative accuracy as a direct pdf call, whatever its magnitude: the test suite checks pdf_grid = pdf to a relative error of \(10^{-12}\).
  • Likelihoods are sums of log-densities, accumulated in 128 fixed blocks in a fixed order, so the value does not depend on the number of OpenMP threads.

Why fortvine works in log space. (a) $\log_{10} c$ of a Gumbel copula with $\theta = 5$ ($\tau = 0.8$) over normal scores in $[-5, 5]^2$: more than 50 orders of magnitude between the diagonal near the corners and the off-diagonal corners. (b) The same density along the diagonal and the anti-diagonal up to the input clamp ($z = \pm 6.3$), and the anti-diagonal of a weaker Gumbel copula ($\theta = 2$). Every value is `logpdf`; the density itself is formed only at the end, so none of these magnitudes is ever computed as an intermediate product.

docs.title: Elementary functions without cancellation
docs.text:
Three helpers appear throughout, in real and in dual-number form:

Function Purpose How \(\operatorname{log1p}(x) = \log(1 + x)\) small \(x\) \(\log(u) \cdot x / (u - 1)\) with \(u = 1 + x\) (exact cancellation of the rounding error in \(u\)); \(x\) itself if \(u = 1\) \(\operatorname{expm1}(x) = e^x - 1\) small \(\lvert x\rvert\) \((u - 1) \cdot x / \log u\) with \(u = e^x\) for \(\lvert x \rvert \le 1/2\) \(\operatorname{log1mexp}(x) = \log(1 - e^{x})\), \(x < 0\) both ends \(\log(-\operatorname{expm1}(x))\) for \(x > -\log 2\), \(\operatorname{log1p}(-e^x)\) otherwise (Mächler 2012) \(\operatorname{lse}(p, q) = \log(e^p + e^q)\) sums of exponentials \(\max(p, q) + \operatorname{log1p}(e^{-\lvert p - q\rvert})\)

The first two are the classical correction tricks for log1p and expm1 built from log and exp alone; they are written out because the dual-number versions need them, and so that the real and dual paths agree exactly. The switch at \(-\log 2\) in log1mexp is the point where both formulas have the same relative accuracy.

docs.title: Examples from the hand-coded families
docs.text:
• Clayton. \(\log(a^{-\theta} + b^{-\theta} - 1)\) is computed as \(m + \log(e^{t_1 - m} + e^{t_2 - m} - e^{-m})\) with \(t_j = -\theta \log u_j\) and \(m = \max(t_1, t_2)\), so neither power overflows for small \(u\) and large \(\theta\). Its inverse h-function is written as \(\exp\bigl(-\operatorname{log1p}(a^{-\theta}\operatorname{expm1}(-\tfrac{\theta}{\theta+1}\log w))/\theta\bigr)\), avoiding the difference \((w a^{\theta+1})^{-\theta/(\theta+1)} - a^{-\theta}\) of two large, nearly equal numbers.
  • Frank. The three factors \(e^{-\theta u_1} - 1\), \(e^{-\theta u_2} - 1\) and \(e^{-\theta} - 1\) are expm1 values, so the density stays accurate for \(\theta\) near 0 (where all three are tiny) and the denominator never cancels.
  • Joe, BB6, BB7. The parameter-free transforms \(\log(1 - u)\) are computed once per observation (with log1p for BB6/BB7), and powers \((1 - u)^\theta\) are formed as \(\exp(\theta \log(1 - u))\); the Joe inverse h-function works with \(\operatorname{log1mexp}(\theta \operatorname{log1p}(-u)) = \log(1 - (1 - u)^\theta)\).
  • Gumbel / Joe inverse h-functions are not solved for \(v\) directly. With \(x = -\log u\), the condition \(h_1 = w\) becomes \(G(d) = L\) for an increasing, concave function \(G\) of a transformed unknown \(d\); Newton's method from a lower bound then converges monotonically and cannot overshoot (hinv_gumbel, hinv_joe).
  • Student t. The distribution function uses the continued fraction of the regularised incomplete beta function, with its convergents rescaled whenever they leave \([10^{-150}, 10^{150}]\); quantiles start from Hill's (1970) Algorithm 396 approximation and are polished by Halley's method inside a maintained bracket. The normal quantile is Wichura's (1988) AS 241 with about \(10^{-16}\) relative accuracy.

docs.title: The generic engine: log-space by construction
docs.text:
The generic families (codes 10000 and up, src/families_gen.inc) are all of the form

\[ C(u, v) = \Psi\bigl(\ell(S, T)\bigr), \qquad S = \Phi(u),\; T = \Phi(v),\; \Phi = \Psi^{-1}, \]

with \(\Psi\) a Laplace transform and \(\ell\) either \(s + t\) (Archimedean) or \((s + t) A\bigl(t/(s+t)\bigr)\) with a Pickands function \(A\). Writing \(L = \ell(S, T)\) and \(\ell_s, \ell_t, \ell_{st}\) for its partial derivatives,

\[ h_1 = \frac{\Psi'(L)\, \ell_s}{\Psi'(S)}, \qquad c = \frac{\Psi''(L)\, \ell_s \ell_t + \bigl(-\Psi'(L)\bigr)\bigl(-\ell_{st}\bigr)}{\Psi'(S)\, \Psi'(T)} . \]

Since \(\Psi' < 0 \le \Psi''\), \(\ell_s, \ell_t \ge 0\) and \(\ell_{st} \le 0\), both terms of the density numerator are non-negative. The engine never forms them: every generator returns \(\log \Psi\), \(\log(-\Psi')\) and \(\log \Psi''\), every inner function returns \(\log \ell_s\), \(\log \ell_t\) and \(\log(-\ell_{st})\), and the numerator is \(\operatorname{lse}(\log \Psi'' + \log \ell_s + \log \ell_t,\ \log(-\Psi') + \log(-\ell_{st}))\). A sum of two non-negative terms computed this way has no cancellation at all.

docs.title: Carrying \(\log S\) next to \(S\)
docs.text:
The arguments \(S = \Phi(u)\) can be astronomically large. For a gamma-inner composition (the construction behind BB2 and BB3), \(\Phi(u)\) contains \(e^{\delta x}\) with \(x\) itself large near the boundary, and overflows double precision long before \(\log \Phi(u)\) does. The engine therefore passes every argument as the pair \((s, \log s)\) and evaluates formulas from whichever is safe:

  • \(\log(1 + s)\) is taken as \(\log s + \operatorname{log1p}(e^{-\log s})\) when \(\log s > 0\) (lop), so it is correct even when \(s\) itself is Inf;
  • \(s = \operatorname{expm1}(t)\) comes with \(\log s = t + \operatorname{log1mexp}(-t)\) for \(t > 30\) (em1);
  • the inner Pickands argument \(w = T/(S+T)\) is formed as \(\log w = \log T - \operatorname{lse}(\log S, \log T)\) and \(\log(1 - w) = \log S - \operatorname{lse}(\log S, \log T)\), which stay exact when \(w\) underflows because \(S\) and \(T\) differ by hundreds of orders of magnitude.

docs.title: Cancellation-free Pickands derivatives
docs.text:
The partial derivatives of \(\ell(s, t) = (s + t)A(w)\) are

\[ \ell_s = A(w) - w A'(w), \qquad \ell_t = A(w) + (1 - w) A'(w), \qquad -\ell_{st} = \frac{w (1 - w) A''(w)}{s + t}, \]

and \(A - wA'\) tends to 0 under strong dependence, so evaluating it as written subtracts two numbers close to 1. The engine instead uses a closed form per Pickands family in which the cancellation has been carried out analytically:

  • Logistic / asymmetric logistic (Tawn 1988), with \(M = [(p_1 (1 - w))^\theta + (p_2 w)^\theta]^{1/\theta}\) and the two shares \(s_p + s_q = 1\) of the bracket: \(\ell_s = (1 - p_1) + M s_p / (1 - w)\), \(\ell_t = (1 - p_2) + M s_q / w\), and \(A'' = (\theta - 1) M s_p s_q \bigl(p_1 p_2 / (p q)\bigr)^2\); every term is positive.
  • Negative logistic / asymmetric negative logistic (Galambos 1975; Joe 1990): with \(R = (p/q)^\theta\), \(\ell_s = 1 - p_1 (1 + R)^{-1 - 1/\theta}\), evaluated as \((1 - p_1) - p_1\operatorname{expm1}(\cdot)\) from \(\operatorname{lse}(0, \log R)\).
  • Hüsler-Reiss (Hüsler & Reiss 1989): \(\ell_s = \Phi(z_2)\), \(\ell_t = \Phi(z_1)\) with \(z_{1,2} = 1/\lambda \pm \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\log\frac{w}{1-w}\), and \(\log \Phi\) is computed from an asymptotic (Mills ratio) series below \(z = -30\), where \(\Phi\) itself underflows near \(z \approx -38\).
  • Tawn's mixed model and its asymmetric version use polynomial forms in \(w\) that are positive term by term.
  • Khoudraji-transformed Pickands functions reuse the base family's derivatives: \(\ell_{K,s} = (1 - a) + a\, \ell_{0,s}\) and \(A_K'' = a^2 b^2 A_0''(z) / v^3\).

docs.title: Asymptotic branches
docs.text:
Some Laplace transforms have closed forms that are exact in real arithmetic but useless in floating point at the edges of their domain. The engine switches to series expansions there:

  • Sibuya generator \(\Psi(s) = 1 - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\): for \(e^{-s} < 10^{-8}\), \(\log \Psi = -s - \log\theta + \operatorname{log1p}\bigl((1 - 1/\theta)\, e^{-s}/2\bigr)\), where the direct form would compute \(\log(1 - 1) = -\infty\). As an inner function of a composition, its second derivative contains a factor \(1 - e^{-s}/\theta - (1 - e^{-s})^{1/\theta}\) whose \(O(e^{-s})\) terms cancel exactly; below \(e^{-s} = 10^{-3}\) that factor is summed as a series with the leading terms removed analytically (relative error below \(10^{-10}\) at the switch), and below \(10^{-8}\) the leading term \((1 - 1/\theta)e^{-s}/2\) is used.
  • Logarithmic series generator: with \(z = (1 - e^{-\theta}) e^{-s}\), the quantity \(1 - z\) is formed as \((1 - e^{-s}) + e^{-(\theta + s)}\), free of cancellation as \(z \to 1\); for tiny \(z\), \(\log(-\log(1 - z)) = \log z + \operatorname{log1p}(z/2)\); and as an inner function, \(L - z = \sum_{j \ge 2} z^j / j\) is summed directly when \(z < 10^{-3}\). Near \(s = 0\) the composition \(-\log\bigl(L/\theta\bigr)\) is rewritten as \(-\operatorname{log1p}\bigl(-\operatorname{log1p}(\tau)/\theta\bigr)\) to avoid the difference \(\log\theta - \log L\).
  • Inverses \(\Phi\) of the Sibuya and logarithmic-series transforms have matching asymptotic forms (e.g. \(x - \log\theta + (\theta - 1)e^{-x}/2\) for the Sibuya inverse when \(e^{-x} < 10^{-8}\)).

docs.title: Combinations left out
docs.text: Two kinds of composition are deliberately not offered: a logarithmic-series inner transform under a positive stable, Sibuya or logarithmic-series outer one (Joe 2014, appendix A.1.2 notes the numerical difficulty; in double precision it could not be made accurate), and a gamma-inner composition combined with a Pickands inner function, which failed the consistency tests described in Validation. gen_valid rejects these codes.

docs.title: Inverse h-functions
docs.text:
Wherever no closed form exists, \(h(v) = w\) is solved by Newton's method with the exact density as the derivative (\(\partial h_1(u, v)/\partial v = c(u, v)\)), started at the independence solution \(v = w\). A bracket \([lo, hi]\) is updated from the sign of \(h(v) - w\) at every step, and any Newton step that leaves the bracket is replaced by bisection, so the iteration always converges. It stops when \(|h(v) - w| \le 10^{-15}\), the bracket is narrower than \(10^{-15}\), or the step is below \(10^{-15}\) relative; three to six evaluations are typical, against about 52 for plain bisection to the same accuracy.

The residual \(|h(h^{-1}(w)) - w|\), not the forward error \(|h^{-1}(w) - v|\), is the right accuracy measure: where the density is nearly zero (deep in a tail of a strongly dependent copula), \(h\) is flat and any \(v\) in a wide interval maps to the same \(w\) to machine precision.

The residual $|h_1(h_1^{-1}(w \mid u) \mid u) - w|$ on a $181 \times 181$ grid of normal scores $\Phi^{-1}(u), \Phi^{-1}(w) \in [-4.5, 4.5]$ for the specialised monotone Newton iteration of Gumbel and the generic safeguarded Newton iteration of BB7 and a three-parameter Archimax copula. Most of the square is at rounding level ($10^{-16}$ and below); the largest residuals, $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-10}$, sit in bands of extreme conditioning values $u$, where $h_1(\cdot \mid u)$ is steepest; that is the scale of the $10^{-10}$ input clamp, to which the test suite checks the round trip.

Time per point of `pdf`, `hfunc1` and `hinv1` on 200 000 random points, one thread (best of three, one Windows laptop; absolute numbers depend on the machine). The number next to each group is the cost of the inverse relative to the h-function: below 1 for the closed-form inverses (Gaussian, Student, Clayton, Frank), about 2 (Gumbel) and 5 (Joe) for the monotone Newton iterations, and 6 to 7 for the safeguarded Newton iteration of every other family, in line with the three to six evaluations quoted above.

docs.title: How accurate is it?
docs.text:
The generic engine re-implements 18 hand-coded families from a completely different formula (see Validation). Against a 40-50 digit mpmath reference (the log-density obtained by differentiating the closed-form \(C\) in multiple precision) on the \(9 \times 9\) grid \(u, v \in \{0.003, 0.05, \dots, 0.997\}\) used by the test suite:

Family parameters generic engine, max abs. error of \(\log c\) hand-coded, max abs. error Hüsler-Reiss \(\lambda = 1.8\) \(4.8 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.5 \times 10^{-7}\) at \((0.997, 0.003)\) BB5 \(\theta = 1.4\), \(\delta = 1.2\) \(6.4 \times 10^{-15}\) \(3.4 \times 10^{-10}\) at \((0.997, 0.003)\) BB4 \(\theta = 1.1\), \(\delta = 1.3\) \(6.9 \times 10^{-15}\) \(2.6 \times 10^{-10}\) at \((0.003, 0.997)\) Galambos \(\theta = 1.3\) \(3.2 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.2 \times 10^{-11}\) at \((0.003, 0.997)\)

The errors of the hand-coded forms sit in the off-diagonal corners, where their formulas subtract nearly equal Pickands terms; the log-space engine stays at rounding level everywhere. Both are far more accurate than anything a likelihood fit can resolve, but the comparison shows that the design choices above are not cosmetic.

Known limit: near-comonotone parameters

When a copula is within a hair of comonotonicity (Blomqvist's \(\beta = 4C(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) - 1 > 0.9\); for the Gaussian copula \(\beta = \tau\)), the density is concentrated within rounding distance of the diagonal and double precision itself runs out, for the generic and the hand-coded BB families alike. The parameter boxes keep fits away from that regime; the consistency tests skip it explicitly.

docs.title: Exact parameter scores
docs.text:
Maximum likelihood needs the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the copula parameters, the score

\[ g(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\, s_i(\theta), \qquad s_i(\theta) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} \log c(u_{i1}, u_{i2}; \theta) \in \mathbb R^k, \]

for every candidate family and every edge of a vine, many thousands of times during one selection. Writing out \(\partial \log c / \partial\theta\) by hand for 111 families, some with three parameters and nested generators, is error-prone and was done only for a few families in the literature (Schepsmeier & Stöber 2014 derive them for the classic bivariate families). Finite differences are the usual fallback, with their well-known costs. fortvine takes a third route: each family's log-density is written once, in generic code, and compiled both for ordinary reals and for dual numbers that carry exact derivatives alongside every value.

docs.title: Dual numbers
docs.text:
A dual number is a value together with its gradient with respect to the parameters,

\[ \tilde x = \bigl(x,\ \nabla_\theta x\bigr), \qquad \nabla_\theta x \in \mathbb R^k . \]

Arithmetic on dual numbers applies the chain rule to every operation:

\[ \widetilde{x y} = \bigl(x y,\ x \nabla y + y \nabla x\bigr), \qquad \widetilde{f(x)} = \bigl(f(x),\ f'(x)\, \nabla x\bigr). \]

Starting from the parameters themselves, \(\tilde\theta_j = (\theta_j, e_j)\), and the data as constants, \(\tilde u = (u, 0)\), any formula evaluated in dual arithmetic delivers \(\log c\) and its exact gradient in one pass. This is forward-mode automatic differentiation; the result is exact up to floating-point rounding, like the value itself.

src/fortvine_ad.f90 defines the types and their operator overloads:

type, public :: hd
  real(dp) :: v = 0.0_dp          ! value
  real(dp) :: g(3) = 0.0_dp       ! gradient with respect to up to 3 parameters
end type hd
  • hvar(x, i) creates the \(i\)-th independent variable, hconst(x) a constant;
  • + - * / ** are overloaded for every combination of hd and real(dp);
  • hexp, hlog, hlog1p, hexpm1, hsqrt, habs and the normal hpnorm, hdnorm propagate gradients through the elementary functions (each through one helper, hunary(x, f, f')), and hlse is a log-sum-exp.

hd always has three gradient slots, the most any family needs. Most families have one or two parameters, so src/fortvine_adk.inc is a template of the same type with a fixed width AD_N; the end of fortvine_ad.f90 instantiates it twice through the preprocessor,

#define AD_MOD fortvine_ad1
#define AD_T hd1
#define AD_N 1
...
#include "fortvine_adk.inc"

giving modules fortvine_ad1 (type hd1, one slot) and fortvine_ad2 (type hd2, two slots). Their scores are 1.1 to 2 times cheaper than through hd because no work is spent on unused slots.

docs.title: One generic interface for reals and duals
docs.text: The modules also define generic names that resolve to the real or the dual version, depending on the argument type: fval (the value), flog, fexp, flog1p, fexpm1, fsqrt, fabs, fpnorm, fdnorm, flse. A family written with these names and with the type left open compiles for every type.

docs.title: Writing each family once
docs.text:
The family code lives in three include files that never declare a concrete type for the quantities depending on the parameters. They use preprocessor macros instead:

Macro Meaning VT the value type: real(dp), type(hd), type(hd1) or type(hd2) VCONST(x) lift a real constant into VT (hconst, h1const, h2const; empty in real mode) LPDF_NAME name of the compiled log-density of the core families (families_core.inc) EXT_NAME name of the compiled extended families (families_ext.inc: Plackett, FGM, AMH, Galambos, Hüsler-Reiss, BB2-BB5, BB9, BB10) GEN_NAME name of the compiled generic engine (families_gen.inc, codes 10000+) REALMODE defined only for the real-valued build, which additionally computes the h-functions

src/fortvine.f90 includes the files once per type:

#define VT type(hd)
#define VCONST hconst
#define LPDF_NAME lpdf_hd
#define EXT_NAME ext_lpdf_hd
#define GEN_NAME gen_ext_lpdf_hd
#include "families_core.inc"
#include "families_ext.inc"
#include "families_gen.inc"
#undef VT
...                                     ! the same for type(hd1) -> lpdf_h1, ... and type(hd2) -> lpdf_h2, ...
#define VT real(dp)
#define REALMODE
#define EXT_NAME ext_eval_r              ! evaluation: log-density and both h-functions
#include "families_ext.inc"
...
#define GEN_NAME gen_eval_rv
#include "families_gen.inc"

so one source line of, say, the Tawn Pickands function becomes four compiled routines: a plain evaluator used by pdf, hfunc1, vine densities and simulation, and three score evaluators of widths 3, 1 and 2 used by the optimiser. A correction to a formula reaches all of them at once, and the value computed in dual arithmetic is, operation for operation, the value computed in real arithmetic, so the numerical safeguards described in Numerics (log-space evaluation, log1p/expm1 forms, asymptotic branches) protect the scores as well as the values.

Branches on the value of a dual quantity are written with fval(x), e.g. if (fval(z) > -30.0_dp) selects between the direct and the asymptotic form of \(\log\Phi(z)\). The derivative of the branch taken is exact; at a switch point the two branches agree to the accuracy of the expansion.

docs.title: Families with their own derivative code
docs.text:
A few families bypass the dual numbers because something faster or better is available:

  • The one-parameter Gaussian, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank and Joe copulas have hand-derived first and second parameter derivatives of the log-density (and of the h-functions and \(C\), for discrete margins). One pass over the data then yields \(\ell\), \(\ell'\) and \(\ell''\), and Newton's method started at the Kendall's-tau inversion converges in about two passes (a Le Cam one-step estimator followed by a check); the Gaussian likelihood equation is solved exactly as a cubic.
  • The Student copula's \( u\) and the t-EV copula's \( u\) enter through the \(t\) distribution function, whose derivative in the degrees of freedom has no closed form; fortvine profiles \( u\) by Brent's method while \( ho\) is solved by Newton's method on its exact score, and for the t-EV copula finishes with a joint Fisher-scoring step that uses a differentiated continued fraction for the \( u\)-score.
  • Pair copulas with discrete margins are fitted on the exact discrete likelihood with value-only methods (Brent for one parameter, Nelder-Mead from a grid otherwise).

Every other family, hand-coded or generic, gets its scores from dual numbers.

docs.title: From scores to a maximiser: Fisher scoring
docs.text:
The score alone does not give a step length. Newton's method would also need the Hessian, \(\sum_i \partial^2 \log c_i / \partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top\), which forward-mode duals do not provide without carrying \(k^2\) more numbers through every operation. fortvine instead uses the outer-product approximation of Berndt, Hall, Hall & Hausman (1974), BHHH:

\[ H(\theta) \;\approx\; -\sum_i w_i\, s_i(\theta)\, s_i(\theta)^\top . \]

At the true parameter, the expected outer product of the score equals the Fisher information (the information matrix identity), so the step

\[ \delta = \bigl(B + \lambda \operatorname{diag}(B)\bigr)^{-1} g, \qquad B = \sum_i w_i s_i s_i^\top, \]

is a Fisher-scoring step, with a Levenberg-Marquardt damping \(\lambda\) that is increased when a step fails to improve the likelihood and decreased tenfold after each success. The implementation (newton_fit in src/fortvine.f90) adds:

  • Box constraints by projection: a parameter at a bound whose score points outward is held fixed for the step (an active set), the others are solved by Cholesky factorisation of the free block, and the new point is clipped into the box.
  • Backtracking by interpolation: a rejected step is shortened to the maximiser of the quadratic through the old value, the step's directional derivative and the trial value, limited to between 10 % and 50 % of its length.
  • Log scale for positive parameters whose box spans two or more decades in families where that was measured to help (BB8, Hüsler-Reiss, BB2, BB9, BB10): the optimiser works in \(z = \log\theta\) with score \(\theta\, \partial\ell/\partial\theta\).
  • Aitken extrapolation when successive steps shrink geometrically in one direction (a slow crawl along a ridge or towards a bound).
  • A BFGS update of the curvature model from the exact score changes for ridge-shaped likelihoods (used for the subsample stage and for t-EV), where BHHH alone zig-zags.
  • Convergence when the Newton decrement \(\tfrac12 g^\top\delta\), the predicted remaining gain, falls below \(10^{-8}(1 + |\ell|)\), or the step becomes negligible.
  • Two stages. A fit first runs on a deterministic stride subsample of about 600 observations from a few starting points (grid, Blomqvist-beta or tau-based starts), and only the best result is polished on all \(n\) observations, which typically takes 1-3 full-data iterations. The final stopping rule is the full-data one, so the result is the full-data MLE.
  • Racing during selection: the predicted gain also bounds how much a candidate can still improve; a candidate whose bound falls below the best criterion already achieved is abandoned.

Because the BHHH matrix is a sum of outer products it is positive semi-definite by construction, so every undamped step is an ascent direction, unlike Newton steps with an indefinite Hessian far from the optimum.

docs.title: Why not finite differences?
docs.text:
A central finite-difference gradient of a \(k\)-parameter log-likelihood needs \(2k\) extra likelihood evaluations, each a full pass over the data, and has an error of order \(h^2 \lVert \partial^3\ell \rVert + \varepsilon\lvert\ell\rvert/h\), minimised near \(h \approx \varepsilon^{1/3}\) at a relative accuracy of roughly \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-6}\). Forward differences (\(k\) extra passes) do worse, about \(\sqrt\varepsilon \approx 10^{-8}\) at best. Several properties of copula likelihoods make this worse in practice:

  • Bounds. Many optima lie on or next to the parameter box (\(\delta \to 1\) in BB families, \(\psi \to 1\) in Tawn models, \(\nu\) at its upper bound). A difference stencil must be one-sided there, losing an order of accuracy.
  • Scale. Parameters range over several decades (a Hüsler-Reiss \(\lambda\) of 0.05 and of 20 are both legitimate), so no single step \(h\) is right everywhere.
  • Branches. The numerically safe evaluation switches formulas at thresholds (asymptotic expansions, log1mexp's switch, clamping). A stencil that straddles a switch differentiates the switching error, not the function.
  • Per-observation scores. BHHH needs the score of every observation, not only of the sum; with finite differences that is \(n \times 2k\) density evaluations stored or recomputed, with each per-observation difference noisier than the total.

Relative error of forward and central finite differences of fortvine's log-likelihood ($n = 2000$ points from the family itself, derivative taken at 0.85 times the true parameter) against the relative step $h/\theta$. The reference is Ridders' extrapolation of the same function; the dotted line is its error estimate. The V shape is the trade-off described above: truncation error to the right, rounding error to the left. Even with the step chosen after the fact from the reference, forward differences stop at $10^{-8}$ to $10^{-7}$; central differences reach $10^{-11}$ to $10^{-10}$ here, but at a step that moves with the family and the parameter and costs two extra likelihood passes per parameter. Exact dual-number scores need neither.

Dual numbers avoid all four: the gradient costs one pass whose arithmetic is roughly \((1 + k)\) times that of the value, it is exact wherever the value is accurate, it needs no step size, and it is available per observation for free. In fortvine the one pass that evaluates the log-likelihood also returns the gradient and the BHHH matrix, which is what makes fitting all 112 parametric candidates of a vine edge affordable (see the benchmarks).

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: fortvine is tested by two self-contained property suites that need no reference library: every check compares the library against a mathematical identity (an h-function is the integral of the density, an inverse undoes its forward map, a maximum-likelihood estimate is at least as likely as the truth, ...) or against an independent computation inside the suite (brute-force numerical integrals, \(O(n^2)\) definitions, duplicated data). Identities hold for every family and rotation, so they scale to 111 families where a table of reference values would not.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
bash build.sh test

compiles and runs test/test_fortvine.f90 and test/test_genfam.f90 against the freshly built static library. With fpm, fpm test runs the same programs (see Installation). The suites print a line per failed check (FAIL: ...), a few informative values, and finish with

  fixed-structure loglik selected / truth, npars:     7585.37     7573.05   18   18
== non-simplified edges
  held-out loglik relaxed / simplified      646.55        0.00
  constant correlation: relaxed in 1 of 20 samples
ALL TESTS PASSED
ok    generic Gumbel reproduces the hand-coded family
...
      126 near-(counter)monotone parameter draws skipped (|beta| > 0.9)
ok    every generic family x 4 rotations: dh/du = c and dC/du = h on a 9 x 9 grid
...
ALL GENERIC FAMILY TESTS PASSED

Either program stops with a non-zero exit code if any check fails, which makes the suites usable in CI; the repository's GitHub workflow runs bash build.sh test examples on Ubuntu with -O2 -ffree-line-length-none -fopenmp and two threads. Both suites together take about 6 seconds on 8 threads.

Randomised checks

Most checks draw fresh random data on every run (call random_seed()); the tolerances are set so that sampling noise does not cause failures. The number of skipped near-comonotone draws (126 above) therefore varies between runs.

docs.title: test_fortvine: the hand-coded families, vines and features
1. h-functions, inverses and densities (every family × rotation)
docs.text:
For the 23 parametric families 1-23, in every rotation that applies:

  • Inversion. On 400 random points, \(\lvert h_1(h_1^{-1}(h_1(v \mid u) \mid u) \mid u) - h_1(v \mid u)\rvert < 2 \times 10^{-10}\), and the same for \(h_2\). The residual, not the forward error, is tested: where the density is nearly zero the forward problem is ill-conditioned for any method (Numerics). The tolerance reflects the \(10^{-10}\) input clamp.
  • \(h_1\) is the integral of the density: \(h_1(0.8 \mid 0.37) - h_1(0^+ \mid 0.37)\) equals a 4000-point midpoint integral of \(c(0.37, t)\) over \(t \in (0, 0.8)\) to \(2 \times 10^{-4}\).
  • \(h_2\) differentiates to the density: a central difference of \(h_2\) in \(u\) matches \(c(0.37, 0.61)\) to \(10^{-5}\) relative.
  • Limits: \(h_1(v \mid u) \to 1\) as \(v \to 1\) and \(\to 0\) as \(v \to 0\).

docs.title: 2. Maximum-likelihood recovery
docs.text: For each of the 23 families, 20 000 observations are simulated and refitted. The fitted log-likelihood must be at least the log-likelihood of the true parameters (up to \(10^{-6}\) relative; 0.05 units for t-EV), which is the defining property of a maximiser. Parameters must be within 30 % of the truth (relative to \(\max(1, |\theta|)\)), except for BB5, BB9 and t-EV, whose likelihoods have near-flat ridges on which the parameters are weakly identified.

docs.title: 3. Vines
docs.text:
On a six-dimensional D-vine mixing Tawn (rotated 90°), Student, Clayton and Gumbel pairs (3000 observations):

  • inverse_rosenblatt(rosenblatt(u)) = u to \(10^{-7}\);
  • selecting families and parameters on the true structure reaches the true log-likelihood up to 2 units per parameter (printed: 7585.37 selected vs 7573.05 true, 18 parameters each);
  • pdf_grid equals pdf on the flattened grid to \(10^{-12}\) relative;
  • the density of a fully selected vine is positive everywhere.

docs.title: 4. Kendall's tau
docs.text: On 700 heavily tied observations (values rounded to 11 levels), the \(O(n \log n)\) tau-b equals the \(O(n^2)\) definition by enumeration of all pairs to \(10^{-12}\).

docs.title: 5. Nonparametric families (TLL, Bernstein)
docs.text: The fitted estimators capture at least 75 % of the true log-likelihood with more than one effective parameter; hinv inverts hfunc to \(10^{-8}\); the h-function is the integral of the density (\(10^{-6}\) for Bernstein, \(2 \times 10^{-2}\) for TLL, whose interpolant is clamped and renormalised as in vinecopulib); and BIC selection prefers the true Gumbel family over TLL and Bernstein.

docs.title: 6. Weights
docs.text:
• The weighted Kendall tau with weights 1 and 2 equals the tau of the data with the weight-2 rows duplicated, to \(10^{-12}\).
  • Weighted MLE equals the MLE on duplicated rows for a one-parameter (Clayton) and a two-parameter (BB1) family: parameters to \(10^{-3}\), log-likelihoods to \(10^{-6}\) relative.
  • A vine selected with unit weights is identical (families, structure, log-likelihood to \(10^{-6}\)) to the unweighted selection.

docs.title: 7. Discrete margins
docs.text:
• For every family × rotation (and a fitted Bernstein copula), the pair "density" of a (discrete, continuous), (continuous, discrete) and (discrete, discrete) observation, i.e. the closed-form differences of h-functions or of \(C\), matches a brute-force midpoint integral of the continuous density over the cell to \(2 \times 10^{-5}\).
  • Vine selection with a five-category variable reaches the true log-likelihood up to one unit per parameter.

docs.title: 8. Truncation and tree criteria
docs.text:
• With dependence only in tree 1, mBICv truncation selects level 1; with dependence in every tree it selects no truncation (\(d - 1\)).
  • Every alternative tree criterion (Spearman, Joe, Hoeffding, Chatterjee's xi, mutual information, Ferreira) gives a valid vine whose log-likelihood is at least 95 % of the tau-based one.
  • The Kraskov-Stögbauer-Grassberger mutual information of a Gaussian pair is within 0.04 of \(-\tfrac12\log(1 - \rho^2)\), and Chatterjee's xi detects dependence.

docs.title: 9. Distribution functions, discrete Rosenblatt, caches
docs.text:
• cdf of the Gaussian, TLL and Bernstein copulas equals a \(1000 \times 1000\) midpoint integral of the density to \(2 \times 10^{-6}\); the bivariate normal \(C(\tfrac12, \tfrac12) = \tfrac14 + \arcsin(\rho)/(2\pi)\) to \(10^{-14}\).
  • The TLL (discrete, discrete) mass is the exact integral of its interpolant (\(10^{-6}\)).
  • Discrete Rosenblatt: \(F(x^-\mid\cdot) \le F(x\mid\cdot)\), equality for continuous columns, the randomised PIT lies between them, and it is i.i.d. uniform (maximum Kolmogorov distance below \(1.63/\sqrt n\), all pairwise correlations below \(4/\sqrt n\)). In the exact two-variable case the transformed columns equal \(h_1\) at \(F(x)\) and at \(F(x^-)\) to \(10^{-9}\).
  • A trivariate Gaussian vine with two discrete variables reproduces exact rectangle probabilities to \(10^{-8}\).
  • TLL and Bernstein are selected on discrete pairs with sensible likelihoods; select_threshold refitted at the chosen threshold gives the same vine (\(10^{-9}\)); a repeated selection is served entirely from the fit cache and is bit-identical; the joint t-EV fit is a local maximum.

docs.title: 10. Non-simplified vines
docs.text: When the conditional correlation really varies with the conditioning variable, the constant-conditional-correlation test rejects and relaxes exactly one edge, the relaxed vine predicts held-out data better by more than 50 log-likelihood units, and its parameter count includes the anchor parameters. Under a simplified truth the test relaxes an edge in at most 4 of 20 samples (printed: 1 of 20), i.e. it holds its 5 % level.

docs.title: Reproduction of the hand-coded families
docs.text:
Eighteen generic codes describe copulas that also exist as hand-coded families, built from completely different formulas: the Archimedean ones from a Laplace transform with \(\ell = s + t\), the extreme-value ones from a Pickands function with \(\Psi = e^{-s}\), BB4 and BB5 as Archimax copulas, Tawn as a Khoudraji-Gumbel copula. On the \(9 \times 9\) grid \(\{0.003, 0.05, 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.66, 0.83, 0.95, 0.997\}^2\) the suite requires agreement of the log-density to \(10^{-6}\) and of both h-functions to \(10^{-9}\). The measured differences are far smaller:

generic code hand-coded family max \(\lvert\Delta \log c\rvert\) max \(\lvert\Delta h\rvert\) 10100 Gumbel \(2.7 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.6 \times 10^{-15}\) 10200 Clayton \(3.6 \times 10^{-15}\) \(4.8 \times 10^{-15}\) 10300 Joe \(2.7 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.2 \times 10^{-15}\) 10400 Frank \(2.2 \times 10^{-14}\) \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\) 10500 BB9 \(3.6 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\) 10600 BB8 \(2.4 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\) 10700 BB10 \(2.8 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.7 \times 10^{-15}\) 11500 BB1 \(5.3 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\) 11600 BB2 \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\) \(7.1 \times 10^{-15}\) 11200 BB3 \(5.3 \times 10^{-15}\) \(3.6 \times 10^{-15}\) 11900 BB6 \(3.6 \times 10^{-15}\) \(8.9 \times 10^{-16}\) 12000 BB7 \(1.1 \times 10^{-14}\) \(3.3 \times 10^{-15}\) 10002 Galambos \(1.2 \times 10^{-11}\) \(1.6 \times 10^{-15}\) 10005 Tawn \(4.4 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.2 \times 10^{-15}\) 10202 BB4 \(2.6 \times 10^{-10}\) \(4.3 \times 10^{-15}\) 10102 BB5 \(3.4 \times 10^{-10}\) \(1.9 \times 10^{-15}\) 20001 Tawn (as Khoudraji-Gumbel) \(3.1 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.1 \times 10^{-15}\) 20003 Khoudraji-Hüsler-Reiss (inner code 10012) \(2.7 \times 10^{-15}\) \(1.8 \times 10^{-15}\)

Two independent implementations agreeing to \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-14}\) is strong evidence that both are right. For the four larger log-density differences, a multiple-precision reference shows that it is the hand-coded formula that loses digits in the off-diagonal corners, while the generic engine stays at \(10^{-15}\) (Numerics). The generic Hüsler-Reiss code 10003 is not in the suite's list: its hand-coded counterpart differs from it by up to \(1.5 \times 10^{-7}\) at \((0.997, 0.003)\), again the hand-coded side's error.

$|\log c_{\text{hand}} - \log c_{\text{generic}}|$ for four families with both implementations, on a $161 \times 161$ grid of normal scores covering $u, v \in [0.001, 0.999]$ (a wider range than the suite's grid): Gumbel ($\theta = 3$), Galambos ($\theta = 1.3$), BB5 $(1.4, 1.2)$ and BB4 $(1.1, 1.3)$. Gumbel agrees to rounding everywhere; for the other three the difference grows towards the off-diagonal corners, where the hand-coded Pickands expressions cancel (the [Numerics](numerics.md#how-accurate-is-it) comparison with a multiple-precision reference attributes it to the hand-coded side).

docs.title: Derivative consistency in four rotations
docs.text:
For every valid generic code (including the duplicates, fv_generic_families(.false.)), in all four rotations, at two random interior parameter points each, on the \(9 \times 9\) grid:

\[ \frac{\partial h_1(v \mid u)}{\partial v} = c(u, v), \qquad \frac{\partial h_2(u \mid v)}{\partial u} = c(u, v), \qquad \frac{\partial C(u, v)}{\partial u} = h_1(v \mid u), \]

with central differences of relative step \(10^{-6}\,u(1 - u)\) and a tolerance of \(10^{-3}\) relative to \(1 + c\). These three identities tie the density, both h-functions and the distribution function together, so an error in any one of them (or in a rotation's bookkeeping) is caught. Non-finite values at the extreme corners of strongly dependent members are tolerated as long as most of the grid is finite; finite wrong values are not. Parameter draws with Blomqvist \(\lvert\beta\rvert > 0.9\) are skipped as outside the precision of double arithmetic (see the known limit).

docs.title: Flip-transpose identity
docs.text:
In a vine, an edge's pair copula is sometimes needed with its arguments exchanged. For every asymmetric generic family in every rotation, the flipped family produced by gen_flip (Khoudraji \(a \leftrightarrow b\), asymmetric logistic \(\psi_1 \leftrightarrow \psi_2\), type-1 ↔ type-2 codes, the reparametrised asymmetric mixed model), with rotation 90 ↔ 270, must satisfy

\[ \log c_{\text{flip}}(u, v) = \log c(v, u) \]

on the grid to \(10^{-10}\).

docs.title: MLE recovery
docs.text:
For four generic families of different kinds (Khoudraji-Hüsler-Reiss, the Archimax gamma|Hüsler-Reiss, the two-parameter Archimedean gamma.Sibuya, Khoudraji-Frank), 3000 simulated observations are refitted and the fitted log-likelihood must reach that of the true parameters (\(10^{-6} n\)).

Finally, the list fv_generic_families() must contain more than 80 codes, all valid.

docs.title: What is not tested here
docs.text:
• Agreement with other libraries. The benchmarks compare fortvine's selections and likelihoods with pyvinecopulib (vinecopulib) and torchvine, which is a different kind of check (same answers as an established implementation), run separately via bench/run_bench.py.
  • Near-comonotone parameters (\(|\beta| > 0.9\)), see above.
  • The C interface beyond what the examples exercise (interop example).

The figure below is such a cross-library check, run outside the test suites by tools/page_figures.py validation with pyvinecopulib 1.0.1: the 11 parametric families both libraries share, 20 random parameter sets and rotations each.

fortvine against pyvinecopulib. (a) Largest log-density difference on 500 random points per parameter set, (b) the same for both h-functions: rounding level for most families, up to $10^{-9}$ for some Frank and BB6 parameter sets. (c) Maximised log-likelihoods of the two libraries on 1000 points simulated from the family (10 per family; symmetric log scale, linear within $\pm 10^{-6}$). They agree to within $1.1 \times 10^{-5}$ with one exception, a Student fit whose $\nu$ runs into fortvine's upper bound of 30 (pyvinecopulib allows 50): there the parameter boxes differ, not the maximisers.
